case_title: C. Muniappan & Ors. v. State of Tamil Nadu
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC ss.302, 302 r/w 114, 307, 307 r/w 114, 147, 148, 149, 188, 341; Tamil Nadu (Prevention of Damage and Loss) / TNP (POL) Act ss.3 and 4 r/w s.149 IPC (charge under s.188 later held not permissible)
weapon: Petrol (sprinkled inside the bus and set alight with a match stick)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured students, teachers, bus driver and cleaner); test identification parade and in-court identification; Judicial Magistrate's reports; arrest evidence; confessional statement of A-4; photographs/video by photographer (not relied on, hostile); investigation records
confession: Extra-judicial confessional statement of A-4 (C. Muniappan) was exhibited in full, which the Court held impermissible; the Court held no prejudice because other sufficient material established his involvement, so it was not relied upon as decisive.
aggravating_circumstances: Offence committed after previous planning with extreme brutality; murders of helpless, innocent, unarmed young girl students in a totally unprovoked situation; bus full of students set alight with students inside; pleas of teachers ignored; demonstrators damaged public transport
mitigating_circumstances: None noted for A-2 to A-4; for the other appellants, the long lapse of time since the incident (over ten and a half years) and time already served
trial_court_outcome: Convicted; A-2 and A-3 convicted under s.302 IPC (3 counts) and s.307 IPC (46 counts); A-4 under s.302 r/w s.114 (3 counts) and s.307 r/w s.114 (46 counts); A-2 to A-4 sentenced to death; other accused sentences ordered consecutive (about 7 years 3 months to 7 years 9 months)
high_court_outcome: Death sentences of A-2 to A-4 confirmed; sentences of other accused directed to run concurrently (maximum two years); conviction of A-24 altered from s.148 to s.147 IPC
offence_finally_established: A-2 and A-3: murder under s.302 IPC (3 counts) and attempt to murder under s.307 IPC (46 counts); A-4: s.302 r/w s.114 IPC (3 counts) and s.307 r/w s.114 IPC (46 counts); other appellants: ss.147/148, 149, 341 IPC and TNP (POL) Act ss.3-4 with sentences reduced to period undergone; s.188 IPC conviction not sustainable
neutral_facts: A political agitation in a town blocked a road in breach of a prohibitory order. Protesters damaged public buses, and one town bus had its seats set alight. Two buses carrying university students on an educational tour had been parked nearby. The bus carrying 47 female students was then approached by men who carried petrol in plastic cans. One man sprinkled petrol inside the bus through a window shutter while another sprinkled petrol through the second shutter, then a match was lit and thrown into the bus and it caught fire while students were still inside. The teachers on board pleaded with the men to stop. Students escaped through the front entrance, some stretched out through the shutters and were pulled out by male students, but three students could not escape and were burnt to death, and about twenty others received burn injuries. The driver and cleaner of the bus stated that two men on a motorcycle stopped beside the bus; one sprinkled petrol and both fled, the motorcycle engine having been kept running. Injured students and teachers identified the accused in a test identification parade held in jail and in court, with the identification process conducted by a Judicial Magistrate who prepared reports. Several initial investigators conducted the investigation in a charged atmosphere, after which the case was transferred to a specialised investigation unit. One accused was arrested later and gave a confessional statement. Post-mortem examinations were conducted on the three deceased students.
attempt_completion: Completed (deaths of three students); attempt (s.307 IPC counts for injured students)
physical_harm: Three students burnt to death; about twenty to twenty-eight students suffered burn injuries and several others serious injuries
number_of_offences: 22 charges framed (de novo trial); for A-2 to A-4, s.302 IPC (3 counts) and s.307 IPC (46 counts) finally upheld; s.188 IPC conviction not sustainable
financial_property_loss: Damage to three government buses (broken glass, seats set on fire) and the University bus burnt; value not stated
premeditation_planning: Court found the offence was committed after previous planning (aggravating circumstance) and with extreme brutality
motive: Court accepted: to cause greater damage so that people would learn a 'lesson' (protest turned violent when public transport vehicles were damaged)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness evidence of PW-1, PW-2, PW-4, PW-5, PW-8, PW-11, PW-12, PW-14, PW-97 and PW-99; test identification parade and in-court identification of A-2 to A-4; Judicial Magistrate PW-89 and reports Exh. P.137 and P.142; arrest of A-4 (not disbelieved); presence established by the clubbed incidents
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses found reliable; omissions and discrepancies held trivial and not going to the heart of the case; evidence of hostile witnesses (PW-86, PW-51) used only in part; PWs 4 and 5 deposition held trustworthy under cross-examination
post_offence_conduct: A-2 and A-3 fled on a motorcycle which A-4 kept running to escape; indicates intent to flee and avoid the clutches of law
custody_duration: A-4 was taken into custody on 3.2.2000 and released on bail on 9.2.2000 (in another crime); most appellants had served more than 14 months of sentence
bail_history: Appellants other than A-2 to A-4 were on bail; A-4 released on bail on 9.2.2000; bail bonds discharged by the Supreme Court
trial_duration: offence: 2.2.2000; trial judgment: 16.2.2007; High Court: 6.12.2007; Supreme Court: 30.08.2010
legal_representation: Appellants: Sushil Kumar, P.N. Prakash, P.H. Manoj Pandian and others (with Udai U. Lalit noted as senior counsel at trial); State of Tamil Nadu: Altaf Ahmed, R. Shunmugasundaram and others
investigation_status: Two FIRs registered; investigation initially by several inspectors then transferred to CBCID; charge sheet filed 28.4.2000 against 31 accused; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: No s.195 CrPC written complaint for s.188 IPC charge (trial and conviction under s.188 void); irregularities in initial investigation; full exhibition of A-4's confessional statement; ten of eleven witnesses turned hostile at first trial; trial transferred to another court
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions, Salem): convicted, death for A-2 to A-4; High Court: death confirmed, other sentences concurrent; Supreme Court: appeals dismissed, death confirmed for A-2 to A-4, other sentences reduced to period undergone
prosecution_argument: Contradictions trivial; s.188 charge defect not fatal to the prosecution case; clubbing caused no prejudice as both crimes were parts of one incident; change of investigating officer inevitable; test identification parade properly conducted; hostile witness evidence cannot be discarded in toto
defence_argument: No trial warranted; prosecution inherently improbable; material contradictions among eyewitnesses; s.188 IPC charge invalid without written complaint; cases wrongly clubbed; arrest of A-4 a jugglery; identification based on media photographs; forensic report did not support petrol; hostile witnesses unreliable
legal_principle_applied: Defect in investigation not by itself a ground for acquittal, court must examine evidence de hors lapses; s.195 CrPC mandatory; omissions and discrepancies not going to heart of case disregarded; test identification as corroboration only; hostile witness evidence usable in part; death sentence only in rarest of rare cases
precedent_relied_upon: M.S. Ahlawat v. State of Haryana (AIR 2000 SC 168); Sachida Nand Singh v. State of Bihar (1998) 2 SCC 493; Daulat Ram v. State of Punjab (AIR 1962 SC 1206); Aloke Nath Dutta (2007) 12 SCC 230; Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1980 SC 898); Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1983 SC 957); Devender Pal Singh v. State of NCT of Delhi (AIR 2002 SC 1661); State of H.P. v. Lekh Raj (AIR 1999 SC 3916); T.T. Antony v. State of Kerala (2001) 6 SCC 181
sentencing_rationale: Brutal, diabolical and cruel manner of murder of helpless, unprovoked young students; aggravating circumstances outweighed absence of mitigation; shocks collective conscience of society; death confirmed for A-2 to A-4. Other appellants' sentences reduced to period undergone due to time served and lapse of ten and a half years
judicial_mitigating_factors: For other appellants: lapse of over ten and a half years since the incident, long time served and on bail. None noted for A-2 to A-4
judicial_aggravating_factors: Previous planning; extreme brutality; exceptional depravity; helpless, innocent, unarmed young victims; totally unprovoked; pleas of teachers ignored; students trapped in bus
other_sentence_order: Sentences of other appellants reduced to period undergone; bail bonds discharged; appeals dismissed and death sentence of A-2 to A-4 confirmed for execution in accordance with law

case_title: Main Pal v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour (house about 15-16 houses away per witnesses); alleged prior dispute over a water course with the complainant's son, per defence witness DW-1. Court made no finding on the dispute.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.452; IPC s.354
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony of the complainant and her daughter-in-law; FIR statement; investigating officer's evidence (PW-3)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.452 and 354 IPC; six months rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.1,000 (default one month simple imprisonment)
high_court_outcome: Criminal revision dismissed; conviction upheld; sentence reduced to four months rigorous imprisonment
neutral_facts: On a night in March 1996, the complainant and her daughter-in-law were sleeping in the complainant's house at about 11.30 PM. No adult male was in the house apart from children. The accused jumped over the front wall, broke the outside bulbs and ran away. Around 12.30 AM the accused returned by scaling the door and caught the daughter-in-law's hand. She raised an alarm and the complainant woke up, after which the accused ran away. The complainant's FIR statement and testimony described the incident this way. The daughter-in-law identified the accused and gave evidence of both visits. In cross-examination, the complainant and the daughter-in-law agreed the accused had not touched, teased or abused the complainant and had not gone towards or spoken to her. Both said the accused lived 15-16 houses away and the families were not on visiting terms. A defence witness, the former village sarpanch, said a quarrel over a water course with the complainant's son had turned into the complaint. The police investigated the complaint and submitted a report under Section 173 of the Code.
physical_harm: No injury mentioned; alleged catching of daughter-in-law's hand and breaking of outside bulbs
financial_property_loss: Not applicable (only breaking of outside bulbs alleged; no value stated)
premeditation_planning: Not stated (charge alleged preparation for hurt or assault; court made no finding)
motive: alleged: a water-course quarrel with the complainant's son, per defence witness DW-1; the court did not decide motive
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW-1 and PW-2 as elicited in cross-examination, that the accused caught the daughter-in-law's hand and ran away when she raised an alarm; the court relied on the record of what the evidence showed rather than making a fresh finding of guilt
witness_credibility: Not assessed by the court on credibility; the court noted the complainant's admission that the accused did not touch, tease or abuse her
post_offence_conduct: Ran away after the alarm was raised, as described in the evidence; no other post-offence conduct stated
trial_duration: offence: 22/23.3.1996 (night of incident; FIR registered 23.3.1996); trial judgment: 2.2.2001; High Court: 16.3.2010; Supreme Court: 07.09.2010
legal_representation: Appellant: Vikas Sharma, K.M. Gupta, Praveen Swarup. State counsel: Not stated
investigation_status: FIR registered 23.3.1996; police investigation completed and report submitted under s.173 CrPC; trial held
procedural_irregularity: Charge named the mother-in-law (PW-1) as the victim, while the evidence concerned the daughter-in-law; the court held this a material error causing prejudice
appeal_history: Trial court (Magistrate, 2.2.2001): convicted under ss.452 and 354 IPC, six months RI. Sessions appeal (Addl. Sessions Judge, 20.2.2002): dismissed. High Court (revision, 16.3.2010): conviction upheld, sentence reduced to four months RI. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction set aside, new trial directed
prosecution_argument: Not stated in the Supreme Court judgment; the lower courts held that an accused cannot take advantage of a technical defect in the charge
defence_argument: The charge named the complainant but the evidence concerned the daughter-in-law; the accused was not required to defend that charge, so he should be acquitted
legal_principle_applied: Ss.211, 212, 215 and 464 CrPC: an accused must know the exact charge; an error in the charge is fatal only where it misled the accused and caused failure of justice; courts apply a broad vision looking to substance and fair trial
precedent_relied_upon: Willie (William) Slaney v. State of Madhya Pradesh AIR 1956 SC 116; Gurbachan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1957 SC 623; Shamsaheb M. Multtani v. State of Karnataka (2001) 2 SCC 577; State of West Bengal v. Laisal Haque AIR 1989 SC 129; State of A.P. v. Thakkidiram Reddy (1998) 6 SCC 554; Dalbir Singh v. State of UP (2004) 5 SCC 334; Dumpala Chandra Reddy v. Nimakayala Bali Reddy (2008) 8 SCC 339; Sanichar Sahni v. State of Bihar (2009) 7 SCC 198. State of Himachal Pradesh v. Geeta Ram (2000) 7 SCC 452 distinguished
other_sentence_order: New trial directed after framing a charge substituting 'her daughter-in-law Sheela Devi' for 'abovenamed Prakashi Devi' in the second part of the charge

case_title: V.P. Shrivastava v. Indian Explosives Ltd. & Ors.
accused_occupation: Senior employees of Fertilizer Corporation of India Limited (FCIL), a government company; both availed the Voluntary Suppression Scheme and were discharged
accused_victim_relationship: Business counterparty: the accused were senior employees of supplier FCIL, which had a tripartite supply arrangement with the complainant company Indian Explosives Ltd. (IEL)
offence_category: Cheating/Fraud (as alleged by IEL; the Court held no offence of cheating was made out)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.420 (cheating), s.406 (criminal breach of trust), s.120B (criminal conspiracy); complaint also invoked Companies Act 1956 ss.540 and 542
evidence_type: No trial evidence; the Court examined only the complaint's allegations and averments in IEL's civil suit plaint
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Magistrate took cognizance of the private complaint and issued summons; no trial verdict (pre-trial stage)
high_court_outcome: Petition under s.482 CrPC dismissed (complaint not quashed)
neutral_facts: The complainant is a company that manufactures and sells industrial explosives and obtained ammonium nitrate, a major raw material, from a supplier company. Under a tripartite arrangement with the supplier and a coal company, the complainant was to pay an equivalent value to the coal company, which would supply coal to the supplier, and the supplier would supply ammonium nitrate to the complainant. The supplier supplied ammonium nitrate for some time, then stopped because of a breakdown of a gas compressor and financial difficulties. The supplier had earlier been declared a sick company, and its winding up was under consideration by the relevant authority. The complainant alleges that the accused, who were senior employees of the supplier, deliberately concealed this status and the supplier's large dues to other creditors. It alleges that this induced the complainant to pay about Rs. 4.20 crore to the coal company between September and November 2001, without receiving ammonium nitrate in return. The complaint also alleges collusion between the accused. The material relied on is the complaint and the averments in the complainant's civil suit plaint against the supplier.
physical_harm: Not stated
financial_property_loss: Rs. 4,20,41,622 (alleged payment to BCCL, as alleged by complainant)
premeditation_planning: Not found: the Court held no dishonest intention at the inception of the agreement could be inferred
motive: alleged: to induce IEL to enter into the tripartite agreement and part with money by suppressing the supplier's sick status
key_evidence_accepted: None as trial evidence; the Court relied on the complaint's own averments and the plaint in the civil suit
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: not given (agreement entered 'some time in the year 2001'); trial judgment: not given (complaint filed 22 May 2003; cognizance order 30 October 2003); High Court: 28 February 2007; Supreme Court: 24 September 2010
legal_representation: Accused: Mr. Jaideep Gupta, senior counsel (with others listed). Respondent IEL: Mr. Sanjoy Ghosh. State counsel: Not stated
investigation_status: Private complaint filed; no police investigation referred to; magistrate took cognizance and issued summons
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court (Magistrate): cognizance taken and summons issued. High Court: s.482 petition dismissed. Supreme Court: appeals allowed, High Court order set aside, complaint quashed
prosecution_argument: Complainant (IEL) argued the accused suppressed FCIL's sick status to induce the agreement, amounting to cheating and criminal breach of trust (ss.415, 405 IPC); trial should decide truth of allegations
defence_argument: Complaint lacks ingredients of cheating and criminal breach of trust; no averment of dishonest intention or entrustment; complainant knew FCIL's financial health; dispute is civil and the complaint is mala fide
legal_principle_applied: Cheating requires fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of the inducement; later failure to perform is not enough. Criminal breach of trust requires entrustment. s.482 CrPC may quash a complaint that does not disclose the offence on its face
precedent_relied_upon: Ram Jas v. State of UP (1970) 2 SCC 740; Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar (2000) 4 SCC 168; S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar (2002) 1 SCC 241; Kuriachan Chacko v. case_title: Raja Gounder & Anr. v. State of Tamil Nadu
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (brother); prior dispute over land
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW.1, the victim's wife); medical (post-mortem)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; sentence not stated in judgment
high_court_outcome: Conviction affirmed (Crl. A. No. 573 of 2001, judgment dated 09.07.2004, found against the appellants)
neutral_facts: The victim was killed in a fatal assault during the night. The accused were the victim's brothers, and relations between the parties had been strained by a dispute over land. The incident occurred at about 10.00 p.m. at a short distance from the victim's house. The victim's wife had seen the attack on her husband. She first sent word to her parents in their village and then went to the police station, and the first information report was lodged about 13 hours after the incident. The victim's sister and the accused's mother were cited as prosecution witnesses. No independent witness was examined, and the case rested on the account of the victim's wife. The first information report referred to two injuries on the victim, whereas the post-mortem examination detected eight injuries. The medical evidence was examined against the eyewitness account, and the attack took place in the dark of night.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; eight injuries detected at post-mortem
motive: Land dispute between the brothers (accepted by courts below as the motive)
key_evidence_accepted: Ocular testimony of PW.1 (victim's wife); post-mortem and medical evidence found consistent with it
witness_credibility: PW.1 found credible; delay and absence of independent witness explained; later resiling by parents viewed as common in fratricides
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 09.07.2004; Supreme Court: 28.09.2010
legal_representation: Appellants: K. Sarada Devi; Respondent (State): S. Thananjayan
investigation_status: FIR lodged about 13 hours after incident; charge sheet and later stages not stated
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302; High Court (Crl. A. No. 573 of 2001, 09.07.2004): conviction upheld; Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Delay of 13 hours in FIR unexplained and used to fabricate story; sister and mother cited but not produced; FIR named two injuries though eight found at post-mortem
legal_principle_applied: Delay in FIR explained by conduct of a young widow; absence of independent witness acceptable in family dispute; minor variance with ocular and medical evidence not fatal; interference declined
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Ranjeet Singh @ Dara v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (step-son of the victim); the appellant was a regular visitor to the house
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence; oral evidence of witnesses; medical evidence (post-mortem report); documentary evidence; recovery of the sword and blood-stained items
confession: Oral statement made when the door was opened that the accused had killed the victim; recounted in the evidence and treated by the Court as part of the oral evidence connecting the accused, not separately analysed as a confession
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 5000, in default one year rigorous imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 469 of 2000) dismissed; conviction under s.302 IPC confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim, a woman, lived on the first floor of a family house with her adult son; a relative of the accused lived on the ground floor with his wife. The accused, who lived in another city, was a regular visitor to the house. On the day of the incident the accused arrived by car at about 11.30 a.m. The ground-floor occupant's wife offered the accused a meal, and the accused said the accused would eat with the ground-floor occupant. Shortly afterwards the household maid heard screams from the victim's room. At about 2.30 p.m. the victim's son came to collect money and found the room locked from inside. He heard the accused talking on a telephone and asked the accused to open the door, which the accused refused. The ground-floor occupant also asked for the door to be opened, and the accused replied that the door would be opened only when police arrived. When police arrived, the accused opened the door and stated that the accused had killed the victim. The accused was holding a blood-stained sword, and the accused's clothing and hands were blood-stained. The victim was lying on a bed, her body smeared with blood. The sword, its sheath, blood-stained bedsheets and a gold bala were seized, and the accused's clothing and hand washings were taken. The post-mortem examination recorded seventeen injuries, all but three of them incised wounds that could be caused by a sharp-edged weapon such as a sword. The accused gave no explanation for being in the locked room or for holding the blood-stained sword. An injury report on the accused recorded an examination time of 11.30 a.m., which the accused relied on to suggest being in police custody at that time; its author was not examined as a witness.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; seventeen injuries, mostly incised wounds from a sharp-edged weapon such as a sword, to the abdomen, head, limbs and buttock
motive: alleged: apprehension that the father would favour the illegitimate son (PW-11) over the legitimate sons; the Court did not decide the motive
key_evidence_accepted: Oral evidence of PW-1, PW-9, PW-11, PW-12 and PW-13 (the accused's presence in the locked room, the statement at the door, the blood-stained sword); post-mortem report Ex. P-11; seizure of the sword and blood-stained items; the failure to explain presence and the sword
witness_credibility: PW-11 was cross-examined at length without anything useful elicited and his account was consistent with PW-13; PW-10's naming of another family member was held to be possibly confusion, and the discrepancies noticed by the courts below did not justify discarding the prosecution evidence
post_offence_conduct: Refused to open the locked door to the son and the ground-floor occupant and said he would open it only when police arrived; then opened the door and stated he had killed the victim
trial_duration: offence: 6.9.1997; trial judgment: 7.3.2000; High Court: 13.3.2006; Supreme Court: 20.9.2010
legal_representation: Appellant: K.T.S. Tulsi, Senior Advocate (with Ram Nivas, Raj Kamal, A.P. Dhamija, Sanjeev Malhotra); State: C.D. Singh (with Sunny Choudhary, Shashank Parihar, Sakshi Kakkar)
investigation_status: FIR registered as Case No. 165/97 under s.302 IPC; accused arrested; charge sheet and trial completed (conviction at trial)
procedural_irregularity: Defence argued FIR registration was delayed and a copy was not sent to the Magistrate for five days; the courts below found no prejudice and sufficient explanation, and the Court did not find a fatal irregularity
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment and fine Rs. 5000; High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction confirmed; Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Delay in sending FIR copy caused no prejudice and the delay was explained by PW-13; the delay alone cannot discard the prosecution evidence; the appellant had a motive; the appellant was caught red-handed with blood-stained hands and sword; Ex. D5 is falsified by Ex. P22
defence_argument: False implication; the real culprit was shielded; the FIR was deliberately delayed; investigation incomplete; the appellant was in police custody at 11.45 hrs for medical examination; injuries to his hands made wielding a sword impossible; discrepancies in the evidence of PW-10, PW-11 and PW-13
legal_principle_applied: In a case based primarily on circumstantial evidence, the chain must be complete and consistent only with guilt (Hanumant); under Article 136 the Court interferes with concurrent findings of fact only in very exceptional circumstances; no such circumstances were shown
precedent_relied_upon: Hanumant Govind Nargundkar v. State of M.P. 1952 SCR 1091 (relied on); Ganga Kumar Srivastava v. State of Bihar (2005) 6 SCC 211 (principles on Article 136 interference; held not to apply to the appellant's case); also referred to: Rangaiah (2008) 16 SCC 737; Ghurey Lal (2008) 10 SCC 450; Abdulwahab Abdulmajid Baloch (2009) 11 SCC 625; Budh Singh (2006) 9 SCC 731; Rajeevan (2003) 3 SCC 355; Dharamver (2010) 4 SCC 469; Rabindra Mahto (2006) 10 SCC 432; Aqeel Ahmed (2008) 16 SCC 372
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Satya Narayana Tiwari and Anr v. State of U.P.
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband of the victim); Relative (mother-in-law of the victim)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B; IPC s.498-A; Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 s.4
weapon: Half-burnt cloth with a knot (ligature) used for strangulation; kerosene used for burning
evidence_type: Circumstantial; medical (post mortem report); recovery memos (blood and bindi, broken bangles, burnt phone); testimony of the victim's father and a relative on dowry demand; false police report as conduct evidence
aggravating_circumstances: Death by strangulation followed by burning; persistent dowry demand for a Maruti car; deliberate false report to police claiming suicide to mislead the investigation; pre-planning by the accused
trial_court_outcome: Both accused acquitted
high_court_outcome: Convictions under IPC s.304-B, s.498-A and DPA s.4 upheld as sentenced: life for s.304-B, 3 years RI for s.498-A, 6 months RI for s.4 DPA, concurrent
offence_finally_established: Dowry death under IPC s.304-B; cruelty under IPC s.498-A; Dowry Prohibition Act s.4
neutral_facts: A married woman aged about 24 was found dead in the bedroom of her matrimonial home about three years after her marriage. Her death was caused by strangulation and burning. The victim's father alleged that after about six months of marriage the accused, her husband and mother-in-law, repeatedly demanded a Maruti car as dowry. He stated that the victim told him of being tortured and maltreated for non-fulfilment of the demand, both over the telephone and on visits to her parental home. About three months before the death, the father and a relative went to the matrimonial home to try to resolve the matter. They were humiliated and told not to return without meeting the demand. The post mortem by a panel of three doctors recorded a ligature mark about 31 by 7 centimetres around the neck, a half-burnt cloth with a knot tied around the neck, superficial to deep burns over the body, and a smell of kerosene. The cause of death was recorded as suffocation with shock from strangulation with simultaneous ante-mortem burns. Investigators recovered blood and a bloodstained bindi from a balcony outside the room, broken bangles inside the room, and a burnt cordless phone and burnt wire stuck with the body. The body was found in a corner of the bedroom. The accused claimed the death was suicide. The mother-in-law lodged a police report stating that the victim had committed suicide. Both accused were absconding for some days before the husband surrendered and then the mother-in-law did.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by strangulation and burning; ligature mark around the neck 31 x 7 cm; superficial to deep burns over the whole body; sooty particles in the air passages
number_of_offences: 3 charged (IPC s.304-B, s.498-A, DPA s.4; inferred from the convictions, as the charge list is not set out); 3 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Yes. The court found the crime was committed with pre-planning, and the telephone call to the father and the false police report were part of a scheme to project suicide.
motive: Dowry: persistent demand for a Maruti car, not satisfied by the victim's father
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of the victim's father and a relative on the dowry demand and harassment; post mortem report and the evidence of the doctor; recovery memos (blood and bindi, bangles, burnt phone); the inquest and recovery witnesses; the investigating officer's evidence on absconding and surrender
witness_credibility: The father's and the relative's testimony was found credible and corroborative; the father was not found to act out of malice, since the other family members were not implicated. The defence sister's testimony was interested and not believed. The recoveries were not challenged in cross-examination. The court rejected the defence theory of suicide.
post_offence_conduct: Both accused absconded; the husband surrendered in court on 7.11.2000 and the mother-in-law on 13.11.2000. The mother-in-law lodged a false police report that the victim had committed suicide. The court held that absconding was not normal conduct of innocent persons.
bail_history: Bail granted by the Supreme Court on 27.10.2005; bail bonds cancelled on dismissal of the appeal
trial_duration: offence: 03.11.2000; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 12.07.2005; Supreme Court: 28.10.2010
legal_representation: Accused: Indu Malhotra, Rajesh and Vivek Jain. State: K.T.S. Tulsi, Shail Kr. Dwivedi (AAG), R.K. Gupta, Pradeep Misra, Suraj Singh, Vandana Mishra, Anurag Dubey, Meenesh Dube, Ravinder Singh and S.R. Setia
investigation_status: FIR registered on 03.11.2000; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: The trial judge treated non-production of the knot as a ground against the prosecution, though the knot had been removed during the post mortem. The court also noted that no charge under s.302 IPC was framed although the case was a murder.
appeal_history: Trial court: both accused acquitted. High Court: convicted under IPC s.304-B, s.498-A and DPA s.4, with concurrent sentences. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld.
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: The demand came about six months after marriage and there was no evidence of any demand in the three months before death, so the 'soon before' proximity test was not met (relying on Balwant). The defence also relied on the suicide theory, the alibi, an alleged manipulated post mortem report, and the claim that the victim's father received the telephone call from the accused.
legal_principle_applied: Ingredients of s.304-B IPC (Kunhiabdulla); 'soon before' as a relative term applying the proximity test; presumption under s.113-B Evidence Act; cruelty may be mental as well as physical; bride burning as rarest of rare
precedent_relied_upon: Kunhiabdulla v. State of Kerala, 2004 (4) SCC 13 (relied on; distinguished on facts in part); Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1980 SC 898 (referred to); Balwant v. State of Punjab, AIR 2005 SC 1504 (cited by defence and distinguished)
sentencing_rationale: The court held the case would have warranted death under s.302 IPC, but since no s.302 charge was framed it could not impose death. The High Court's sentence was therefore upheld, with the court noting such cases are the rarest of rare.
judicial_aggravating_factors: Bride burning is barbaric and brutal; crimes against women are social crimes calling for harsh punishment; victim was killed by strangulation then burning; deliberate false report to mislead the police
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds cancelled; accused to be taken into custody to serve the remaining sentence. The court also made general observations that dowry killings must be stamped out 'with an iron hand' (not a formal direction).

case_title: Sudhakaran v. State of Kerala
accused_occupation: Irregular casual jobs for sustenance (no specific occupation stated)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (murder); defence of insanity under IPC s.84 raised by accused
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW1, PW5 and neighbours), medical (post-mortem, PW9), recovery (chopper and clothing seized), forensic (blood group report), circumstantial
confession: Oral extra-judicial confession to neighbours, as alleged by PW5; the Supreme Court did not expressly rely on it
aggravating_circumstances: Brutal, callous killing with chopper on victim's neck; nine injuries; wounds on victim's palm and fingers indicating she was defending herself and attacked while awake
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction under s.302 IPC affirmed
neutral_facts: The victim was found dead in a bedroom of the accused's house on the evening of 3 November 2000, with a neck wound inflicted by a chopper. The prosecution case was that at about 7.30 p.m. the accused struck the victim on the neck with a chopper while she was in the bedroom. The accused then left the house and approached two neighbours sitting in front of their house, carrying the couple's eight-month-old child in one arm and a chopper in the other hand. One neighbour stepped towards the accused to take the child and saw the chopper. The neighbour and his son went inside and closed the door. Through the window, the son shone a torch and saw the accused's shirt stained with blood and a blood-stained chopper in hand. The accused asked another neighbour to look after the child, said he was going to the police station, and later put the chopper on the verandah floor when asked. He entrusted the child to a third neighbour and went away. Neighbours entered the house and found the victim lying on a cot, covered in blood, with no movement. The accused had told neighbours he had killed the victim. The post-mortem certificate recorded nine incised wounds on the victim's head, neck, ear, shoulders, back, and hand, including wounds on the palm and fingers. The doctor said the injuries could have been caused by the seized chopper. Blood-stained items were sent for forensic examination and found to contain human blood of group A. The chopper and clothing were seized and an FIR was registered on the basis of a neighbour's statement.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from nine incised wounds, including a deep incised wound on the back of the neck severing the vertebral column
number_of_offences: 1 charged (IPC s.302 is the only offence of conviction; charge sheet not quoted); 1 finally upheld
motive: alleged: accused's suspicion that the wife had been unfaithful, per the accused's remark recounted by PW2; not decided by the court
key_evidence_accepted: Ocular evidence of PW1 and PW5 (accused approaching with blood-stained chopper and child; torchlight sighting); PW3's account of blood on body; PW9 post-mortem evidence that injuries could be caused by the seized chopper
witness_credibility: High Court found PW1 to PW5 unimpeachable; Supreme Court accepted that ocular evidence was corroborated by medical evidence and gave no reason to disturb this
post_offence_conduct: Carried the blood-stained chopper, confessed to neighbours, left the child in a neighbour's care and went away; court found he arranged proper care for the child after the murder
trial_duration: offence: 3.11.2000; trial judgment: 30.11.2002; High Court: 21.10.2005; Supreme Court: 26.10.2010 (judgment date; hearing date not given)
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: T.V. George, Manjula Gupta; State/respondent: Shishir Pinaki, P.V. Dinesh
investigation_status: FIR registered on PW1's statement; accused arrested by Circle Inspector; inquest, seizure and forensic examination conducted; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment (30.11.2002); High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction affirmed (21.10.2005); Supreme Court: appeal dismissed (26.10.2010)
prosecution_argument: Not stated (the judgment records only the accused's submissions; the Supreme Court accepted the courts below's findings on the evidence)
defence_argument: Story unbelievable given the densely populated locality; defence wrongly discarded; accused suffered paranoid schizophrenia, shown by records treated 11 days after the incident and by medical witnesses; schizophrenia causes rapid emotional change so the accused could not be said to be in his senses at the time
legal_principle_applied: Under IPC s.84 the accused must show that, at the time of the offence, unsoundness of mind rendered him incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law; burden on accused under Evidence Act s.105 is no higher than in civil proceedings; prosecution must prove mens rea beyond reasonable doubt
precedent_relied_upon: Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v. State of Gujarat AIR 1964 SC 1563; Ratan Lal v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1970) 3 SCC 533; R. v. Daniel McNaughten (1843) 8 ER 718 (HL)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Brutal and callous commission of the murder of the wife
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Ram Chandra Bhagat v. State of Jharkhand
accused_victim_relationship: Cohabiting partner (not lawfully married); accused had promised marriage
statutory_provisions: IPC s.493
evidence_type: Documentary (agreement, Special Marriage application, voter lists) and oral testimony of five witnesses
confession: Written agreement (Ex.2) in which accused admitted living as married with victim; relied on by Misra J. Katju J noted the accused disputed the agreement.
aggravating_circumstances: Nine years of deception-based cohabitation; two children; accused later drove victim out
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.493 IPC; sentence not stated in judgment
high_court_outcome: Conviction under s.493 IPC upheld in Criminal Revision No. 788 of 2005 (order dated 08.09.2005)
neutral_facts: The victim worked in a government agriculture office in the early 1980s when she began an intimate relationship with the accused. The two lived together as a couple for about nine years and had two children. The victim alleged that the accused had assured her of marriage and had signed a written agreement to that effect dated 4 June 1990; the accused disputed that agreement. Evidence presented included an application made by the accused to a Special Marriage Officer, dated 13 April 1982, seeking information about marriage under the Special Marriage Act. A further document dated 4 June 1982, written on stamp paper, recorded that the accused was living a normal family life as a married couple with the victim and that the victim was the accused's wife. Voter lists for 1984, 1988 and 1993 for the village where the couple lived showed the victim as the accused's wife. Five witnesses testified that the two lived together as husband and wife at several places of the accused's official posting, including a block in Hazaribagh district, and that a son was born during the cohabitation. The accused was also said to have celebrated the birth of the couple's daughter and son with friends. A witness described a local social custom under which a woman who lives in a man's house for a long period is deemed to be his wife. No marriage ceremony had been performed between them. The accused later refused to accept the victim as wife and drove her out of the house.
offence_severity: Imprisonment up to ten years, and fine; no minimum stated
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: 1 charged; 0 finally decided (split bench, referred to Chief Justice of India)
motive: alleged: inducing cohabitation through a promise of marriage
key_evidence_accepted: Special Marriage application (Ex.3); marriage agreement (Ex.2); voter lists 1984, 1988, 1993 (Ex.6, 6/1, 6/2); oral testimony of PW-1, PW-3, PW-4, PW-5, PW-6 (Misra J)
witness_credibility: Witnesses supported the relationship as husband and wife; assessed as credible by Misra J. Katju J did not address witness credibility.
post_offence_conduct: Refused to accept victim as wife and drove her out of the house
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 08.09.2005; Supreme Court: 24.11.2010
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: Deba Prasad Mukherjee; State/respondent: Ratan Kumar Chaudhari
investigation_status: Not stated; case proceeded to trial and conviction by trial court
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.493 IPC; first appellate court: convicted; High Court: conviction upheld (08.09.2005); Supreme Court: split verdict, referred to Chief Justice of India
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Not stated in judgment; accused disputed the marriage agreement
legal_principle_applied: Katju J: strict construction; no assurance of future marriage means no belief of existing marriage, so s.493 not met. Misra J: three ingredients (deceit, inducement of belief of lawful marriage, cohabitation as result); no ritual or statutory ceremony required.
precedent_relied_upon: Moideenkutty Haji v. Kunhikoya, AIR 1987 Kerala 184; Dr. A.N. Mukerji v. State, AIR 1969 Allahabad 489 (both cited by Katju J)
other_sentence_order: Referral of the matter to the Chief Justice of India for placement before another Bench due to split opinion

case_title: Uttam Chakraborty v. State of Assam
accused_occupation: Mission Suklabaidhya (first accused): retired Army personnel. Uttam Chakraborty (second accused): Not stated
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (first accused was the victim's husband). Second accused was a friend of the husband, with no relationship to the victim described (Acquaintance).
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (murder)
weapon: Kerosene oil (fire/burns), as stated in the FIR; no other weapon described
evidence_type: Eyewitness (child witness PW-6); retracted section 164 CrPC statement of PW-1; medical (post-mortem and inquest); motive evidence from victim's mother; circumstantial (presence at scene)
aggravating_circumstances: Crime described as truly horrendous; murder committed in the matrimonial house; victim was about eight months pregnant and the foetus had been removed
trial_court_outcome: Both convicted under s.302 IPC; first accused sentenced to death; second accused sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Death reference confirmed; accused's appeal dismissed, convictions and sentences upheld
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302) against the first accused (Mission Suklabaidhya). The second accused's conviction was set aside.
neutral_facts: On a night in April 2004, the victim, who was about eight months pregnant, was found dead from burn injuries in the matrimonial home. The victim's household included the accused, a young child of about four or five years, and a domestic helper of about sixteen years. The victim had reportedly discovered an illicit relationship between the first accused and the domestic helper, and the couple had frequent quarrels. Around 2 a.m., a local resident and several others came to the victim's mother's house, told her the victim was ill, and took her to the police station. There she found the first accused and the domestic helper, who told her the victim had died of burn injuries. The mother lodged a first information report around 2.30 a.m., stating that she had learnt the victim died in a fire caused by kerosene oil, and alleging the victim had been killed by her husband. A shop-owner stated that around 10 to 10.30 p.m. he saw two men in an animated discussion, and that a girl came out shouting that the wife had died of burn injuries. The child witness identified the accused in court. The domestic helper had named both accused in a statement before a magistrate, but did not support that statement at trial. The victim's mother deposed to the illicit relationship. The executive magistrate who held the inquest noted a large cut injury on the body. The doctor who conducted the post-mortem found very severe cut injuries to the stomach indicating that the foetus had been removed.
physical_harm: Death from burn injuries; very severe cut injuries to the abdomen indicating removal of an eight-month foetus
number_of_offences: 1 charged (IPC s.302); 1 finally upheld (first accused only; second accused's conviction set aside)
motive: Accepted by the courts below as corroborated: the first accused's illicit relationship with the domestic helper, which the victim objected to, causing frequent quarrels
key_evidence_accepted: Child witness PW-6's testimony (credibility not doubted, but not a safe basis for a death sentence); PW-5's corroboration of motive; post-mortem findings of PW-7; murder in matrimonial house
witness_credibility: PW-6 credibility not doubted. PW-1 resiled from her section 164 statement at trial. PW-4's evidence cannot connect the second accused. PW-6 apparently mistook the second accused for PW-4.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 13/14 April 2004; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 26.04.2006; Supreme Court: April 6, 2010
legal_representation: Appellants: S.B. Sanyal, Azim H. Laskar, Sachiri Das (printed as 'Oas'), Rana Mukherjee, Abhijit Sengupta. State (respondent): J.R. Luwang, Navneert (for Corporate Law Group).
investigation_status: FIR lodged around 2.30 a.m.; section 164 CrPC statement of PW-1 recorded; investigation completed; charged with murder; tried
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: both convicted under s.302; first accused death, second life. High Court: death reference confirmed, appeal dismissed. Supreme Court: first accused's appeal (871/2006) dismissed as to conviction, sentence commuted to life; second accused's appeal (869/2006) allowed, conviction and sentence set aside.
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Not stated
legal_principle_applied: A section 164 CrPC statement is not substantive evidence; the court must examine other evidence given in court. Child witness evidence is not a safe basis for a capital sentence. A conviction requires evidence connecting the accused with the offence.
precedent_relied_upon: Suresh v. State of U.P. (1981) 2 SCC 569; Raja Ram Yadav & Ors. v. State of Bihar (1996) 9 SCC 287
sentencing_rationale: Although the child witness's credibility was not doubted, a capital sentence would be imprudent when based on a child witness's statement, so the death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment
judicial_aggravating_factors: Crime described by the Court as truly horrendous
other_sentence_order: Second accused directed to be set free forthwith, if not wanted in any other case

case_title: Sachidanand Thakur v. Union of India & Ors.
accused_occupation: Indian Army personnel (Guard Commander on security duty at time of offence)
accused_victim_relationship: Co-worker (fellow Army colleague)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; Army Act 1950 (other penalties; specific sections not stated)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (Army personnel); medical (post-mortem); recovery of fired cartridge cases matched to weapon; accused's remark on apprehension
confession: Oral remark 'MAINE JO KARNA THA KAR DIYA' made on apprehension; relied on by the Court to remove any doubt about culpability
aggravating_circumstances: Three shots fired at close range (8 to 10 ft) despite a warning that the person was a Quick Reaction Team member
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302 (Court Martial); sentenced to life imprisonment plus other penalties under Army Act 1950
high_court_outcome: Writ petition under Art. 226 dismissed; Court Martial findings confirmed; recall application dismissed
neutral_facts: On the night of 6 January 2000, the accused was on security duty as guard commander at a technical battery area of an army unit, armed with a 7.62 mm self-loading rifle and 20 cartridges. Following a report that stones had been thrown at the guard hut, the security junior commissioned officer ordered a Quick Reaction Team to be summoned. The team reached the guard hut at about 10.30 p.m., where the vehicle was challenged by the sentry on duty. Team members got out and moved to the right and left to locate the person who had thrown the stones. The accused ran toward one team member, the victim, while another team member followed and warned that the person being run toward was a member of the Quick Reaction Team and should not be fired upon. Despite this warning, the accused fired three shots from a distance of 8 to 10 feet, killing the victim at the spot. The accused was quickly apprehended by a sentry and the security junior commissioned officer. When questioned about what had been done, the accused replied 'MAINE JO KARNA THA KAR DIYA'. Evidence presented included the testimony of several army personnel who witnessed the shooting, post-mortem observations regarding the firing distance, and empty cartridge cases lifted from the site that matched the issued weapon.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from gunshot fire (three shots fired at 8 to 10 ft)
premeditation_planning: Not stated as premeditation; Court Martial found the shooting deliberate, and this finding was upheld
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness evidence of Army personnel including PW.14's warning; post-mortem observations (PW.16) on firing distance; fired cartridge cases matching the issued weapon; accused's remark on apprehension
witness_credibility: Court did not separately assess witness credibility; it accepted the Court Martial's findings of fact as free of error
post_offence_conduct: Quickly apprehended at the scene; made the remark 'MAINE JO KARNA THA KAR DIYA' when questioned
trial_duration: offence: 6 January 2000; trial judgment: not given (Court Martial date not stated); High Court: 23 December 2005 (recall application dismissed 23 November 2005); Supreme Court: 19 October 2010
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: D.K. Thakur, D. Jha, Debasis Misra. Respondents (Union of India and others): P.P. Tripathi, ASG, with N.S. Sweety Manchanda, Anil Katiyar, Anuj Bhandari, D.S. Mahra
investigation_status: Accused apprehended on the spot; tried by Court Martial. Police FIR and charge sheet not stated
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial (Court Martial): guilty under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: writ petition dismissed, findings confirmed, recall application dismissed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Court Martial findings of fact were categoric and based on correct appreciation of evidence; interference by courts in such matters should be minimal
defence_argument: Killing was an accident arising from suspicion of a terrorist attack; offence under s.302 not made out
legal_principle_applied: Supreme Court declines to disturb concurrent findings of fact of Court Martial upheld by High Court, finding no error in them
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
judicial_aggravating_factors: Three shots fired despite warning that the person was a Quick Reaction Team member; remark on apprehension removed doubt about culpability
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Om Pal Singh v. State of U.P.
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute; rivals competing for a liquor shop licence, with earlier assaults, theft complaint and an attempted killing
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (FIR initially registered under s.307 IPC, later altered to s.302)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (two witnesses), medical evidence, dying declaration, recovery of motorcycle and articles from the spot
aggravating_circumstances: Earlier attempt to kill the victim a couple of months before the incident; shooting of the victim as he moved away
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life
high_court_outcome: Criminal Appeal No. 604 of 1980 dismissed on 26.08.2002; conviction and life sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim had a long-running rivalry with the accused, arising from competition for a liquor shop licence near a railway station and later incidents, including an assault, a theft complaint and an earlier attempt on the victim's life a few months before the shooting. On the day in question, the victim was returning on a cycle from a government food-grain depot with two companions, who were about 15 to 20 paces behind him. The accused arrived on a motorcycle carrying a double-barrelled gun. On seeing the accused, the victim left his cycle and ran toward a neighbouring plot. A single shot was fired, and the victim fell with gunshot injuries. The accused fled, leaving the motorcycle at the scene. The two companions stated that they did not chase the accused. The victim was taken by bullock cart to a hospital, and a complaint was lodged at the police station. A magistrate recorded the victim's statement at the hospital, noting the victim was in a serious condition. A doctor examined the victim and found multiple gunshot wounds on the chest, abdomen, arms, hand and thigh, and a further wound on the neck. The victim died later that night. A post-mortem examination found multiple gunshot wounds of entry, consistent with the medical examination. Investigators collected the motorcycle, a basket of goods, blood-stained and unstained earth, wads from the spot, and blood-stained clothing of the victim.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple gunshot wounds to the chest, abdomen, arms, hand and thigh, with a further wound on the neck; death followed a few hours after the shooting
premeditation_planning: Not expressly found as premeditation; the court noted an earlier attempt, a couple of months before, made with the intention of killing the victim
motive: Accepted: prior enmity between the accused and the victim, arising from competition for a liquor shop licence and a series of hostile incidents, including an earlier attempt to kill the victim
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW2 and PW3; FIR content narrating the animosity; medical evidence (PW-5 and PW-10) consistent with ocular evidence; dying declaration recorded by the magistrate
witness_credibility: Both eyewitnesses found consistent and credible; their account matched the medical evidence and the dying declaration; the court found no reason to interfere
post_offence_conduct: Fled the scene leaving the motorcycle behind; no other post-offence conduct noted
trial_duration: offence: 11.6.1978; trial judgment: 21.3.1980; High Court: 26.8.2002; Supreme Court: 09.11.2010 (judgment date)
legal_representation: Appellant: Nagendra Rai (Senior Advocate) with Anurag Dubey, D.P. Pandey, Meenesh Dubey, S.R. Setia; State: S.R. Singh with Anuvrat Sharma, Alka Sinha, Ashutosh Kr. Sharma
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge sheet filed 18.07.1978; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Dying declaration recorded without a doctor's certificate of fitness (no doctor was present), not in question-and-answer form, and the victim was in a serious condition; the court held these did not render it unreliable
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, life imprisonment (21.03.1980). High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed (26.08.2002). Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Rivalry between the parties was clearly proved; with eyewitness evidence, motive was not necessary to prove; PW-2 and PW-3 are from the same village so had no reason to falsely implicate; the dying declaration was clear, cogent and properly recorded
defence_argument: Incident fabricated; medical evidence of multiple wounds, including on chest and back, inconsistent with a single shot; motive a made-up story and eyewitnesses gave hearsay; two empty cartridges unexplained; dying declaration unreliable and recorded without a doctor's fitness certificate
legal_principle_applied: A dying declaration may be acted upon if the recording magistrate is satisfied the declarant was fit and the statement is voluntary and truthful; doctor's certificate is a rule of caution, not mandatory; consistency of eyewitness testimony with medical evidence
precedent_relied_upon: Laxman v. State of Maharashtra (2002) 6 SCC 710 (relied on); Kanti Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2009) 12 SCC 498 (referred to); Modi's Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology (19th Ed.) (referred to)
other_sentence_order: None

accused_victim_relationship: Not stated

neutral_facts: During the intervening night of 20th/21st November 1991, shortly after midnight, the victim heard footsteps in a shared two-floor residential building and came out to investigate. He found one accused standing on the first-floor balcony. A scuffle followed, and shouts drew other occupants, who saw the victim and that accused grappling. The victim pinned the accused to the ground. The accused then drew a knife and stabbed the victim in the left side of the abdomen. A second accused, who had come from the balcony side, stabbed the victim on both thighs. When a relative tried to help, the first accused stabbed him in the right arm. The second accused held a knife at the throat of another relative and stabbed a further relative in the left shoulder. Other occupants and neighbours arrived, overpowered the accused, and tied them up on the ground floor. Police were informed. The victim was taken to a railway hospital but died on the way. Other injured persons received first aid, and their injuries were found to be simple. The evidence consisted of eyewitness testimony from several family members and a neighbour, supported by medical evidence.

post_offence_conduct: Both accused were overpowered and tied up by occupants; police informed; no other post-offence conduct noted

accused_occupation: Teacher (as stated in counsel's submission for one accused)
accused_victim_relationship: Land rival / prior dispute: dispute between the victim and an accused over sale of land
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.149; IPC s.323 r/w s.149; IPC s.148
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured wife and son), medical (post-mortem), circumstantial (site plans), recovery of articles
