neutral_facts: On the morning of 29 September 1991, the victim went to his field to harvest a bajra crop with his wife and son. A group of persons arrived armed with an axe, sickles, sticks and a jailli. They raised a challenge that they would teach the victim a lesson for interfering in a land purchase. One attacker struck the victim's knee with an axe, others felled him and beat him with sticks and sickles, and the attackers also struck the victim's wife and son when they tried to intervene. A bystander who intervened was struck on the knee. Attracted by an alarm, other villagers arrived. The attackers then lifted the injured victim and carried him to a tubewell belonging to one of the group, where he was left bleeding, and the attackers ran away. The victim's son informed the village, and the injured were taken to a Primary Health Centre. The victim was referred to a civil hospital, where he died the same afternoon. The victim's wife and son were discharged after medical examination. The wife's statement was recorded in the evening and a first information report was registered that night. The post-mortem report recorded 26 injuries, including fractures of both forearm bones, both leg bones and a foot, fractures of the ninth and tenth right ribs that lacerated the liver, and the doctor opined that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Investigating officers visited the field and the tubewell, collected chappals, a broken rapri, a rope, a blood-stained matchbox and blood-stained earth, and prepared site plans which matched the revenue official's plan. A kulhari was recovered on the interrogation of one of the accused. The defence stated that a defence witness had been injured in the same incident, but the X-ray film of that witness was not traceable and the injuries were not shown to be connected with the incident.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; 26 injuries including fractures of both forearm bones, both leg bones and a foot, and fractures of the 9th and 10th right ribs lacerating the liver; injuries to the victim's wife and son
premeditation_planning: Not identified: the court did not find premeditation or planning; it found the intention to cause death was evident from the injuries
motive: alleged: the victim had interfered in the purchase of agricultural land (dispute over land sale)
key_evidence_accepted: Ocular testimony of the injured wife and son (PW-1, PW-6), admitted to be present by the defence; post-mortem report and doctor's opinion; site plans and recoveries
witness_credibility: Injured eyewitnesses' presence admitted by the defence; delay in recording the wife's statement held explicable and not held against the prosecution; defence alibi witnesses found unreliable
post_offence_conduct: Left the injured victim at the tubewell and fled the spot
bail_history: On bail at the High Court stage; High Court directed custody to undergo the remaining sentence
trial_duration: offence: 29.9.1991; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 01.10.2008; Supreme Court: 16.12.2010
legal_representation: Accused: R.S. Cheema (Crl.A. 1071/2009) and K.B. Sinha (Crl.A. 1294/2009); counsel for the State and the complainant not individually named
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge-sheet filed against the main accused and others; further accused summoned under s.319 CrPC; investigation completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted as a lapse by the court; FIR delay held insignificant; delay in the defence witness's X-ray examination noted, with the film not traceable
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302/149 (life imprisonment). High Court: s.302/149 conviction set aside, convicted under s.304 Part II/149 with 5 years RI. Supreme Court: High Court judgment set aside and trial court judgment restored
prosecution_argument: Incident occurred in the victim's field and he was carried to the tubewell (site plans and recoveries support this); no delay in FIR; no obligation to explain the defence witness's injuries; alibi not cogent; High Court wrongly applied s.304 Part II instead of murder
defence_argument: FIR delayed and used to fabricate the story and shift the site of incident; injuries on the defence witness suppressed; no close relationship between the families; alibi established; reliance on Babu Ram, Binay Kumar Singh and Jayantibhai
legal_principle_applied: Intention to cause death inferred from the number, nature and location of injuries and medical opinion on sufficiency in ordinary course of nature; delay in FIR and non-explanation of unconnected injuries not fatal to prosecution; alibi must create a real doubt
precedent_relied_upon: Binay Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (1996) 8 Suppl. SCR 225 = (1997) 1 SCC 283 (held inapplicable); Jayantibhai Bhenkarbhai v. State of Gujarat (2002) 2 Suppl. SCR 255 = (2002) 8 SCC 165 (held inapplicable); Babu Ram & Ors. v. State of Punjab (2008) 3 SCC 709 (held inapplicable)
sentencing_rationale: Injuries and medical opinion showed intention to cause death, so the offence was not reduced to s.304 Part II; trial court's life imprisonment restored
judicial_aggravating_factors: Large number of injuries including fractures and injuries on vital parts; rib fractures damaging abdominal and thoracic organs; multiple armed attackers
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Raju & Anr. v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Prior dispute: the deceased allegedly misbehaved with women at a marriage ceremony, leading to the later assault
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; medical evidence (post-mortem and injuries)
aggravating_circumstances: Victim was chased, surrounded and held before being fatally stabbed with knives
mitigating_circumstances: Provocation from the deceased's misbehaviour toward women at a marriage ceremony; appellants were unarmed
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; sentenced to life imprisonment and fine of Rs.5,000 each (default three years RI)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC confirmed
offence_finally_established: IPC s.304 Part I r/w s.34
neutral_facts: The victim was reportedly intoxicated at a marriage ceremony where he misbehaved towards women who were singing and participating in festivities. Later that evening, around 10.30 p.m., as the victim was returning home after watching a film, a group of four men attacked him with fists near the gate of a government livestock farm. The victim ran toward his home but was chased and surrounded near another house. A witness, the victim's brother, stated he was nearby and saw the incident. Two of the men carried knives, while the other two were empty-handed. The brother's account was that two of the men held the victim while the other two stabbed him, one blow to the left chest and another to the waist. On an alarm being raised, the group fled. The victim was taken toward hospital but died on the way. A post-mortem examination found multiple ante-mortem injuries sufficient to cause death, with the cause given as shock and haemorrhage. The first information report was lodged by the brother, who identified the men who held and stabbed the victim. An eyewitness other than the brother also gave evidence of the incident, and the injuries on the victim's body were consistent with that account.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock and haemorrhage due to multiple ante-mortem injuries, including knife wounds to the chest and waist
number_of_offences: 1 charged (IPC s.302 r/w s.34); 0 finally upheld as charged (altered to s.304 Part I r/w s.34)
premeditation_planning: Not found; no common intention to murder established, and the assault was an immediate response to the earlier incident
motive: Response to the deceased's misbehaviour toward women at a marriage ceremony, with intention to preserve their honour and dignity
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness evidence of PW.5 (complainant) and PW.7, corroborated by injuries on the victim's body; post-mortem evidence of PW.8
witness_credibility: Eyewitness evidence of PW.5 and PW.7 was corroborated by the injuries, but the court held this did not by itself establish common intention as to the appellants
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 31 March 1994; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 30 October 2007; Supreme Court: 10 February 2010
legal_representation: Accused: Rishi Malhotra (Advocate). State of Haryana: Manjit Singh and Kamal Mohan Gupta (Advocates)
investigation_status: FIR lodged by the complainant; post-mortem conducted on 1 April 1994; trial completed before the trial court
procedural_irregularity: Appellant No.1 was found to be a juvenile at the time of the offence, so his case was referred to the Juvenile Justice Board rather than decided as an adult
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal allowed in part, conviction altered to s.304 Part I r/w s.34 IPC
prosecution_argument: Appellant No.2 was part of the group that chased the victim and held him while the co-accused stabbed him, showing common motive and common intention; conviction under s.302 r/w s.34 should be upheld
defence_argument: No prior meeting of minds or common intention to kill; appellants did not know the co-accused carried knives and only intended to teach the victim a lesson; s.302 r/w s.34 wrongly applied; juvenility of Appellant No.1 to be considered under the Juvenile Justice Act
legal_principle_applied: Liability under s.34 requires common intention; absent that, the role attributed attracts s.304 Part I rather than s.302 r/w s.34
precedent_relied_upon: V. Sreedharan vs. State of Kerala, 1992 Supp (3) SCC 21 (relied on); Hari Ram vs. State of Rajasthan and Anr., 2009 (6) SCALE 695 (referred to)
judicial_mitigating_factors: Provocation from the deceased's intoxicated misbehaviour toward women at a marriage ceremony; role limited to chasing and holding the victim, with no common intention to kill
other_sentence_order: Appellant No.1's records to be transmitted to the Juvenile Justice Board; Appellant No.2 entitled to set-off of detention under s.428 Cr.P.C.; fine default of 15 days RI for Appellant No.2

case_title: Javed Masood and Anr. v. State of Rajasthan
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute between the accused and PW-5 (the victim's brother, the FIR lodger), as admitted by PW-5 and noted by the Court; no accused-victim relationship described
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged with ss.147, 323, 324; trial convictions also under ss.148 and 201)
weapon: Gupties, swords, knives and gandasas (as alleged by the prosecution)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-5, PW-13, PW-14, rejected by the Court), police and independent witness testimony, medical (post-mortem)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of ss.148, 201 and 302 IPC; sentence amount not stated
high_court_outcome: Conviction under s.302 IPC upheld; convictions under ss.148 and 201 set aside
neutral_facts: On the afternoon of 25 May 1999, around 12.30 p.m., the victim was at a tyre shop. The prosecution case was that about ten to twelve armed persons, carrying gupties, swords, knives and gandasas, surrounded the victim and attacked him, inflicting multiple incised and penetrating wounds to the head, face, neck, chest, abdomen, back and arms. The assailants then fled. A police vehicle reached the spot within minutes and took the victim to hospital, where he was declared dead. The report lodged by the victim's brother was registered as an FIR and investigated. A charge-sheet was filed against two named persons, and investigation against others was kept pending. The shop owner testified that the victim came alone on a motorcycle to repay a debt and talked with him for about 15 minutes. He then went to the basement, and on returning found the victim gone. He later found the victim dead in a pool of blood in the street. Police removed the body within five to ten minutes. He said the victim's brother arrived about ten minutes after the removal, and that he had given no names because he had not seen the attack. Three police witnesses, including the constable and driver who lifted the body, stated that the victim's brother and two other alleged eyewitnesses were not present. The post-mortem report recorded excessive haemorrhage from injuries to the right lung and liver as the cause of death. Three named eyewitnesses testified that they saw the attack.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple incised and penetrating wounds; death attributed to haemorrhage from injuries to the right lung and liver
motive: alleged: incident arose out of acute enmity (defence contention); the Court did not decide the motive for the attack
key_evidence_accepted: Evidence of PW-6 (shop owner) that PW-5, PW-13 and PW-14 were not at the scene; corroborating police evidence of PW-18, PW-29 and PW-30; the post-mortem report. The Court rejected the eyewitness evidence of PW-5, PW-13 and PW-14.
witness_credibility: PW-5 (victim's brother) was a highly interested and partisan witness whose evidence was disbelieved; PW-13 and PW-14 were discarded; PW-6 and police witnesses PW-18, PW-29 and PW-30 were independent and reliable
post_offence_conduct: Alleged by the prosecution that the assailants fled the scene; the Court made no finding on this
trial_duration: offence: 25 May 1999; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 4.3.2008; Supreme Court: 09 March 2010
legal_representation: Appellants: A. Sharan, A.K. Singh, Samir Ali Khan. State: R. Gopalakrishnan
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge-sheet filed against the appellants; investigation kept pending under s.173(8) Cr.P.C. against others; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: The public prosecutor did not seek leave to declare PW-6 hostile; the prosecution never declared PWs 6, 18, 29 and 30 hostile
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.148, 201, 302. High Court: s.302 conviction upheld; ss.148 and 201 set aside. Supreme Court: appeal allowed; convictions and sentences set aside
prosecution_argument: Supported the judgment under appeal (convictions under s.302 IPC)
defence_argument: Presence of the eyewitnesses was highly doubtful; reliance placed on PW-6, PW-29, PW-18 and PW-30; the incident arose from acute enmity
legal_principle_applied: Concurrent findings are not usually disturbed under Article 136 unless vital evidence was ignored or the conclusion rests on evidence that cannot be accepted; the defence may rely on evidence of witnesses not declared hostile
precedent_relied_upon: Mukhtiar Ahmed Ansari v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2005) 5 SCC 258, which relied on Raja Ram v. State of Rajasthan, (2005) 5 SCC 272
other_sentence_order: Appellants directed to be released forthwith

case_title: Munnawar and Ors. v. State of U.P. Etc.
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.149 (conviction); s.307 (originally charged and convicted at trial)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; dying declarations (by police officer and executive magistrate); medical evidence (treating doctor and post-mortem); recovery of pistols; ballistic expert (defence witness)
aggravating_circumstances: Close-range firing (tattooing present); multiple wounds, several grievous and fatal, on sensitive parts of the body
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.307, sentenced to 4 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.5,000 each; acquitted under s.302
high_court_outcome: Accused's appeal dismissed; State appeal allowed; convicted under s.302/149 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The victim and two companions were travelling to a court hearing by bus, got off at about 11:15 a.m. at a bus stand, and walked towards the courts. Near the office of a bus union, several men armed with country-made pistols fired at the victim, who was seriously injured. The two companions ran to a nearby bus stand and the assailants fled. One companion took the victim to a hospital, where a doctor examined him at 11:35 a.m. and found him irritable but mentally conscious. A first information report was lodged about noon at a police station about two furlongs from the scene. A police sub-inspector recorded a statement from the victim at the hospital. The next day, an executive magistrate recorded a second dying declaration in the hospital in the presence of a doctor, who certified that the victim was fully conscious and lucid. The declaration named the assailants and the weapons used and described the site of the injuries. The victim died five days after the incident from septicemia following the gunshot injury. A post-mortem examination was conducted. Two country-made pistols were recovered at the instance of two of the accused. Medical evidence recorded seven wounds on the chest, neck, face, arm and back, with tattooing indicating close-range firing. Some wounds were grievous and fatal to life, and the victim had been given three units of blood on admission. A defence ballistic expert testified that a retained bullet could cause septicemia.
physical_harm: Death of the victim five days after the incident from septicemia following gunshot injuries; seven lacerated gunshot wounds (chest, neck, face, left hand, left forearm, right and left scapular regions), some grievous and fatal to life
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.302 and s.307; s.149 applied by High Court); 1 finally upheld (s.302/149)
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Second dying declaration recorded by the Executive Magistrate and endorsed by the attending doctor; presence of the two eyewitnesses; prompt FIR; medical evidence of the treating doctor on injuries and cause of death
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses found present at the scene; Magistrate and doctor found credible with no reason to disbelieve them; police officer's first dying declaration not relied on as the sole basis; treating doctor's evidence found independent and supportive
post_offence_conduct: Assailants fled the scene; one accused (Yaqoob) absconded during the investigation
trial_duration: offence: 20 May 2000; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 08 August 2007; Supreme Court: 5 May 2010
legal_representation: Accused: Sushil Kumar, Manoj Prasad, Aditya Kumar. State: T.N. Singh, Rajiv Dubey, Kamlendra Mishra
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial completed; accused convicted at trial and in High Court
procedural_irregularity: Delay in delivery of special report to Magistrate (held not of consequence); first statement recorded by police officer in case diary not recorded in manner prescribed by Police Regulations for dying declarations (held not decisive given second declaration)
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted s.307, acquitted s.302. High Court: accused's appeal dismissed; State appeal allowed, convicted s.302/149 and life imprisonment. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed, conviction upheld
prosecution_argument: Promptness of FIR belies claim that eyewitnesses were brought to scene later; second dying declaration reliable though first was not; medical evidence shows injuries were the proximate cause of death despite time lag
defence_argument: First dying declaration lacked victim's signature and doctor's fitness endorsement; second declaration not properly endorsed and unreliable under Balak Ram; victim admitted by police officer, so eyewitnesses were not present; death from negligent treatment, so at most s.307 applies
legal_principle_applied: A dying declaration recorded by a Magistrate and endorsed by a doctor should not be discarded save for very good reasons; reliability depends on the facts of each case, with no hard and fast rule
precedent_relied_upon: Balak Ram v. State of U.P. (1975) 3 SCC 219; K. Ramachandra Reddy & Anr. v. Public Prosecutor (1976) 3 SCC 618
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Arun Raj v. Union of India and Ors.
accused_occupation: Army personnel: Ex-Signalman (Lance Nayak) in 787 (Independent) Air Defence Brigade Signal Company
accused_victim_relationship: Co-worker (fellow army personnel); prior dispute, as the accused alleged the deceased and another soldier had abused him the previous day
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; Army Act s.69 (read with s.302 IPC)
evidence_type: Eyewitness; dying declaration; medical evidence; knife recovered as evidence (ME-1)
aggravating_circumstances: Single stab to chest of a sleeping victim with a sharp kitchen knife; knife concealed and brought in deliberately; time to deliberate (40-45 minutes); assault a day after the abuse
trial_court_outcome: General Court Martial found guilty under s.69 Army Act r/w s.302 IPC; initially 7 years RI and dismissal from service; on revision, sentenced to life imprisonment and dismissal from service
high_court_outcome: Writ petition dismissed; conviction under s.302 upheld
offence_finally_established: Murder under s.302 IPC (with s.69 Army Act)
neutral_facts: On 22 March 1998, the accused reported to a section in-charge that the victim and another soldier had abused him with a derogatory word. The section in-charge questioned them and they denied it. The accused also reported a heated exchange with the victim the previous night. Later that day the victim returned to the barrack after lunch and lay on his cot near the door. Another soldier, who had also just returned to the barrack, saw the accused approach the door wearing a half T-shirt and a lungi. The accused took a knife hidden in the lungi and stabbed the sleeping victim once on the right side of the chest. The eyewitness shouted at the accused and others gathered; the accused was separated from the victim, who was taken to hospital and later died. The regimental medical officer testified that the only external injury was the knife wound. The knife, made of iron with a sharp edge, was among the evidence collected. The victim had also given a dying declaration to another soldier, who testified. The eyewitness could not link the stabbing to the earlier abuse or argument. Timing evidence showed about 40 to 45 minutes between the accused's return from the higher officer's office and the stabbing, during which the accused and the victim were in the same barrack without any conversation.
offence_severity: Death or life imprisonment (as stated by the Confirming Authority); no minimum stated
physical_harm: Single stab wound to the right side of the chest; death of the victim
premeditation_planning: Yes. Court found due deliberation and planning: a 40-45 minute gap, concealment of the knife, and an attack a day after the abuse
motive: Revenge for the humiliation of the alleged abuse ('Gandu') the previous day, as accepted by the Court
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness account of PW-1 (as to the stabbing and timing); medical evidence of PW-9 (single stab wound); knife evidence (ME-1); dying declaration to PW-3
witness_credibility: High Court found PW-1 and PW-3 reliable. Supreme Court relied on PW-1's account and the cross-examination of PW-9 without separately assessing credibility
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 22.3.1998; trial judgment: not given (General Court Martial revised sentence order dated 15.1.1999); High Court: 25.8.2005; Supreme Court: 13.05.2010
legal_representation: Accused: K.K. Mani, Ankit Swarup, K. Lakshminarayan. Union of India: Brijender Chahar, R. Balasubramaniyam, Naresh Kaushik, Anil Katiyar, D.S. Mahra
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge-sheet prepared and forwarded to the Judicial Magistrate; court martial proceedings initiated
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial (General Court Martial): convicted, 7 years RI and dismissal, revised to life and dismissal on revision; Confirming Authority confirmed; petition to Chief of Army Staff rejected. High Court: writ petition dismissed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Findings and punishment should stand; the evidence proves an offence under s.302 IPC; judicial review is limited and cannot re-appreciate the Court Martial evidence
defence_argument: Grave and sudden provocation brings the case under Exception I to s.300 IPC; alternatively s.304 Part II applies as there was no intention to cause death, given a single blow
legal_principle_applied: Exception I to s.300 (grave and sudden provocation, judged by a reasonable person's reaction and time to cool); s.304 Part II ingredients; Virsa Singh 'thirdly' test (intention to cause a bodily injury sufficient to cause death); a single blow is not decisive
precedent_relied_upon: Relied on: State of Rajasthan v. Dhool Singh (2004) 12 SCC 546; Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1958 SC 465; Anil v. State of Haryana (2007) 10 SCC 274. Also cited: Mancini v DPP (1942) AC 200; Rex v Lesbini (1914) 3 KB 1116. Distinguished: Bhera; Kunhayippu; Masumsha Hasansha; Guljar Hussain; K. Ramakrishnan Unnithan; Pappu; Muthu
sentencing_rationale: Not stated (the Court addressed only conviction and dismissed the appeal; no sentencing reasoning given)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Due deliberation and planning; assault a day after the alleged abuse; vital body part (chest); deadly weapon; victim asleep
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Northern Mineral Ltd. v. Union of India and Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: Insecticides Act, 1968 s.29; s.24(3) and s.24(4) (evidentiary provisions)
evidence_type: Documentary: Insecticide Analyst (laboratory) report; sample and shelf-life details
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Discharge application under s.245 CrPC dismissed; no verdict recorded
high_court_outcome: Criminal revision dismissed
neutral_facts: An insecticide inspector drew a sample of a monocrotophos insecticide from the shop of the accused's dealer on 10 September 1993. The accused had manufactured this batch in September 1992. The sample was sent to a regional pesticides testing laboratory, whose report dated 13 October 1993 stated that the sample was misbranded because it did not conform to the relevant ISI specifications. A show cause notice dated 1 November 1993 was issued to the accused, which it received on 3 November 1993. The accused replied on 17 November 1993, expressing its intention to adduce evidence in controversion of the laboratory report and contending that the report was of no consequence. The accused did not specifically request re-analysis by the Central Insecticides Laboratory. The Joint Director, Agriculture, gave consent for prosecution on 23 February 1994, and the Insecticide Inspector filed a complaint on 16 March 1994 under section 29 of the Insecticides Act against the accused and the dealer. The insecticide's shelf life had expired in February 1994.
physical_harm: Not stated
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: The Court accepted that the accused had notified its intention to adduce evidence in controversion of the Insecticide Analyst report within 28 days, and that the insecticide's shelf life expired before the complaint was filed. The Court did not decide the merits of the analyst's finding.
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Replied to the show cause notice on 17 November 1993 expressing intention to adduce evidence in controversion of the report; no other conduct noted
trial_duration: offence: 10 September 1993 (sample drawn); trial judgment: 13 November 1999; High Court: 5 November 2001; Supreme Court: 7 July 2010
legal_representation: Appellant: Arun Nehra, Shobha, Mohinder Thakur. Respondents: P.K. Dey, Rashmi Malhotra, Rohitash S. Nagar, R.S. Nagar, D.S. Mehra, B.V. Balaram Das
investigation_status: Sample analysed by regional laboratory; show cause notice issued; complaint filed 16 March 1994 under s.29; discharge sought and refused
procedural_irregularity: No step taken by the Insecticide Inspector after the accused's intimation; complaint filed about a month after consent; sample not sent to the Central Insecticides Laboratory before shelf life expired
appeal_history: Trial court (CJM Patiala): discharge refused 13 Nov 1999. High Court: revision dismissed 5 Nov 2001. Supreme Court: appeal allowed; accused discharged
prosecution_argument: Respondents contended that, apart from intimating intention to adduce evidence, no specific request was made for analysis by the Central Insecticides Laboratory, so its non-performance did not defeat the accused's right
defence_argument: Accused argued that notifying intention to adduce evidence implies demand for Central Insecticides Laboratory analysis, that shelf life affects analysis, and that the accused's right was defeated by inaction
legal_principle_applied: Notifying intention to adduce evidence under s.24(3) confers the right to Central Insecticides Laboratory analysis without a specific demand; where this right is defeated by inaction and shelf-life expiry, continuing prosecution is futile and an abuse of process
precedent_relied_upon: State of Haryana v. Unique Farmaid (P) Ltd. (1999) 8 SCC 190; State of Punjab v. National Organic Chemical Industries Ltd. (1997) SCC (Crl.) 312; Gupta Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan JT 2002 (Suppl.1) SC 516
other_sentence_order: Advisory observation to authorities under the Act to act promptly and adhere to the statutory time-schedule; no formal direction

case_title: Sikandar Singh & Ors. v. State of Bihar
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/land dispute: a title suit over a plot of land was pending between the deceased's side and the accused, who were described as closely related parties
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.149; IPC s.307 r/w s.149; IPC s.147; IPC s.148; Arms Act s.27 (against one appellant)
weapon: Gun (fired by one accused at the deceased and his brother); spears, farsa and lathis carried by the other accused
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-4, PW-5 and villagers PWs 1-3); FIR; medical (post-mortem and injury reports)
aggravating_circumstances: Group of armed men with guns, spears, farsa and lathis confronted the deceased; firing at the deceased and at his brother who was trying to save him
trial_court_outcome: Convicted. Life imprisonment under s.302/149 for four appellants; 5 years under s.307/149 for them; 2 years under s.148 for one; 6 months under s.147 for three; 3 years under Arms Act s.27 for one; sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; convictions and sentences upheld
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302 r/w s.149); attempt to murder (IPC s.307 r/w s.149); rioting-type offences under IPC s.147 and s.148 as applicable; Arms Act s.27 for one appellant
neutral_facts: The victim was clearing a plot of land in front of a cattle shed where cattle grazed, while a title suit over the plot was pending between the victim's side and the accused. One accused arrived, protested that the land belonged to him, and heated arguments followed. Another person present urged that accused to eliminate the victim. That accused went to a house and returned with a gun, accompanied by other accused carrying spears, farsa and lathis. Abusive language was exchanged with the victim. The armed accused fired at the victim, who sustained multiple pellet wounds to the chest, abdomen, arm and forearm and died at the spot. The victim's brother, who came to intervene, was also shot and sustained small pellet wounds to the face, scalp and forehead. Several villagers rushed to the spot and witnessed the incident. The victim's uncle went to the police station and a first information report was recorded the same afternoon. The post-mortem recorded 41 pellet injuries on the chest, with penetration of the lungs and heart. The brother's injuries were described as simple, and no pellets were found in his wounds. An injury to one accused's arm and shoulder was also documented in a medical examination.
physical_harm: Deceased died from pellet wounds to chest, lungs and heart (41 pellet injuries on chest); brother (PW-4) suffered three pin-head size pellet holes on face, scalp and forehead, described as simple
number_of_offences: 5 charged (IPC ss.302, 307, 147, 148 with s.149 where applicable; Arms Act s.27); 5 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Not found as premeditation in terms; the Court found the armed group came out of the house with a common object to teach the complainant party a lesson
motive: Dispute over the plot of land with a pending title suit; the Court accepted that the accused were determined to teach the complainant party a lesson for asserting its right to the plot
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW-4 and PW-5; FIR lodged by PW-5 recording arms carried; post-mortem evidence of PW-7; injury evidence of PW-4
witness_credibility: Evidence of the eyewitnesses (PW-4 and PW-5) found cogent and creditworthy; Court declined a further review of the evidence

case_title: Ohan Singh v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Prior dispute: property dispute within the victim's family; the co-accused included the victim's brother. The appellant's own relationship to the victim is not otherwise stated.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.148, s.149, s.323, s.506, s.452, s.302 (charged); conviction finally under IPC s.304 Part II
evidence_type: Dying declaration; medical evidence (doctor's endorsement, medico-legal report); eyewitness testimony of injured persons; recovery of weapons
aggravating_circumstances: Very strong blow to the victim's head with an iron rod, which proved fatal; accused went to the house equipped with lathis and an iron rod; injuries to the victim's wife and daughter
mitigating_circumstances: Single blow; no intention to kill; family property dispute
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.148, 149, 323, 506, 452 and 302; sentenced to life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 2000 under s.302, with other sentences for the remaining offences
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
offence_finally_established: IPC s.304 Part II (culpable homicide not amounting to murder)
neutral_facts: The victim had a dispute with his brother over a residential house. On the day of the incident, the victim, his wife and his daughters were at home. A group of accused persons, including the victim's brother and other family members, entered the house and attacked the victim and his family. One accused was holding an iron rod and struck the victim a blow on the head and left ear. Other accused beat the victim with lathis on his back, hips and other parts of the body, and the victim's wife and daughter were also injured with lathi blows. The accused then ran away, threatening to kill the family on the next opportunity. The injured were taken to a government hospital. The attending doctor was asked whether the victim was fit to make a statement and certified that he was. A police head constable then recorded the victim's statement, which the doctor endorsed after confirming its accuracy and which the victim's children also signed. The statement described the role of each accused and formed the basis of the first information report. The medico-legal examination recorded multiple lacerated wounds, contusions and abrasions, including a lacerated wound on the right side of the head. The victim's condition later worsened and he was transferred to another hospital, where he died about a week after the incident. The post-mortem was conducted by a doctor. Investigators recovered lathis and dandas following disclosure statements by accused persons. At trial, the victim's wife and daughter did not support the prosecution account, and the victim's son and daughter were not examined as witnesses.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a head injury; multiple lacerations, contusions and abrasions to the victim; injuries to the victim's wife and daughter
premeditation_planning: Not found. The court held there was no evidence the accused went to the house intending to kill.
motive: Property dispute between the victim and his brother (accepted by the court as a family property dispute)
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration recorded by the police head constable after the doctor's fitness endorsement; the doctor's testimony and medico-legal report; injured witnesses' accounts
witness_credibility: The doctor (PW-1) and the dying declaration were found credible and corroborated. The hostility of the wife (PW-3) and daughter (PW-4) did not defeat the prosecution case.
post_offence_conduct: Declared a proclaimed offender; taken into custody on 18.12.1997
custody_duration: Taken into custody on 18.12.1997; total duration not stated
trial_duration: offence: 15.07.1997; trial judgment: 17.05.1999; High Court: 30.04.2008; Supreme Court: 22.07.2010
legal_representation: Appellant: Biswajit Swain (for Rajesh Prasad Singh); State: B.S. Mor (for T.V. George)
investigation_status: FIR registered under ss.148, 452, 323, 506 r/w s.149 IPC; case converted to s.302 after death; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Dying declaration recorded by a Head Constable rather than a Magistrate or doctor; the FIR sections could not be investigated by a Head Constable (undisputed). The court found no legal infirmity in admissibility.
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced (life imprisonment under s.302). High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; s.302 altered to s.304 Part II with 10 years RI and fine of Rs. 20,000.
prosecution_argument: Not separately recorded in the judgment. The State supported the conviction, relying on the admissibility and reliability of the dying declaration and the medical evidence.
defence_argument: Dying declaration recorded by Head Constable was unreliable and should have been recorded by a Magistrate; sons and daughter not examined and findings perverse; alternatively conviction should be under s.304 Part II
legal_principle_applied: Admissibility of dying declaration under s.32(1) Evidence Act, not dependent on who records it; hostile witnesses do not by themselves defeat the prosecution; conviction for murder altered to culpable homicide where intention/knowledge to cause death is not established
precedent_relied_upon: Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab (1979) 4 SCC 332 (relied on); Cherlopalli Cheliminabi Sahed v. State of A.P. (2003) 2 SCC 571 and Kanti Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2004) 10 SCC 113 (distinguished); State (Delhi Administration) v. Laxman Kumar (1985) 4 SCC 476 (referred); Jagriti Devi v. State of H.P. (2009) 14 SCC 771 and Gurmukh Singh v. State of Haryana (2009) 15 SCC 635 (referred)
sentencing_rationale: Court found no intention to kill or knowledge that the blow was likely to cause death, so the offence was altered to s.304 Part II
judicial_mitigating_factors: Single blow; no intention to kill; family property dispute
judicial_aggravating_factors: Accused went to the house equipped with lathis and an iron rod; a very strong blow to the head with the iron rod proved fatal
other_sentence_order: Default sentence of six months rigorous imprisonment for non-payment of fine

case_title: Ravindra Tukaram Hiwale v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.306; IPC s.498-A
evidence_type: Dying declaration
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Incident spontaneous, arising from a family quarrel that morning; no misbehaviour by the accused over a period of time (trial court finding)

offence_finally_established: IPC s.306 (abetment of suicide); IPC s.498-A (cruelty)
neutral_facts: The victim, a married woman, suffered serious burn injuries in the kitchen of the marital house at about 7.00 a.m. on 6 February 1990 and later died of those injuries. The prosecution case is that the victim had quarrelled with the accused, her husband, that morning over household chores and the feeding of the children. She then poured kerosene on herself and set herself alight. About three days after the burn injuries were sustained, at about 8.30 a.m. on 9 February 1990, the victim made a statement to a police head constable (PW.10), described as a dying declaration. In that statement she recounted the quarrel over household chores and the feeding of the children, and said that she had thereafter poured kerosene on herself and burnt herself. The prosecution relies on this declaration as the central evidence of how the burning occurred and of the events that morning. The accused and the victim had been married after the death of the accused's first wife.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from serious burn injuries
premeditation_planning: No premeditation or planning found; incident treated as spontaneous (trial court finding accepted by the Supreme Court)
motive: Family quarrel on the morning of the incident over household chores and feeding of the children
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration recorded by PW.10 (police head constable) on 9 February 1990, and the trial court's finding that the incident was spontaneous
witness_credibility: Not stated; the court did not separately assess witnesses and relied on the dying declaration
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: About four years of sentence undergone, as reported by the learned amicus curiae; accused in custody
bail_history: Not stated; Supreme Court directed release forthwith if not required in any other case
trial_duration: offence: 6 February 1990 (burn injuries) / 9 February 1990 (dying declaration); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 02.08.2006; Supreme Court: 2 August 2010
legal_representation: Accused: B. Sridhar (appellant's counsel), with the learned amicus curiae referred to by the court; State of Maharashtra: Shankar Chillargee, Asha G. Nair, Ravindra Keshavrao Adsure
investigation_status: Dying declaration recorded by a police head constable (PW.10); trial completed with a trial court judgment; other investigation steps not stated
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.498-A (one year) and s.306 (four years). High Court: accused's appeal dismissed; State's appeal allowed, s.306 sentence enhanced to six years. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, High Court's enhanced sentence quashed, trial court judgment confirmed
prosecution_argument: Not stated; the order records only the appellant's submission
defence_argument: The High Court wrongly enhanced the sentence based on a quarrelsome nature shown by two letters written about a year before the incident
legal_principle_applied: Appellate interference with quantum of sentence should be rare and only in exceptional cases; sentencing discretion within the statutory range rests with the trial court; older letters carry little weight against a dying declaration
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: Trial court's sentence restored: incident was spontaneous and arose from a morning family quarrel, with no misbehaviour over time; the High Court's reliance on older letters had little value; the incident occurred in February 1990 and the accused had served about four years
judicial_mitigating_factors: Spontaneous incident arising from a morning family quarrel; no misbehaviour over a period of time; about four years of sentence already undergone
other_sentence_order: Accused to be released forthwith if not required in connection with any other case

case_title: Virendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Prior dispute: the accused's family demanded that the victim reap their crop and became annoyed when he refused; no kinship stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34
weapon: Firearm (pistol/rifle) fired by a co-accused; the appellant was armed with a lathi
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (injured eyewitness and other witnesses), including the injured son, another son and a daughter of the victim
aggravating_circumstances: Accused went armed to teach the victim a lesson; prearranged plan; victim was shot after intervening to protect his son
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 read with s.34 IPC; sentence not stated
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 262 of 1986) dismissed; conviction under s.302 read with s.34 upheld
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 read with s.34
neutral_facts: The victim was asked by the accused and two family members to reap the accused's family's crop the next day. The victim replied that he was busy with his own harvest and with family ceremonies planned in the coming days, but the accused persons pressed him to reap the crop. The victim refused, and the accused's family became annoyed. The next morning at about 7 a.m., the accused and two others went to the victim's house. The accused and one companion were armed with lathis and the third was armed with a rifle. They asked the victim why he had not gone to reap the crop. After the victim repeated his refusal, the accused and a companion began abusing and beating the victim's son with lathis. Other family members, including the victim's mother, sister, another son and a relative, rushed to protect the son and were also struck with lathis and injured. The victim then intervened. One of the companions was told to shoot the victim, and fired a shot that struck the victim in the stomach, causing death. The same person also fired at the victim's son but the pellets missed him. Pellets injured another son and the daughter. After the shooting, the group ran away towards a canal. The incident was witnessed by two persons. An injured eyewitness, another son and the daughter gave detailed accounts describing the role of the accused in beating the family members and the shooting.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a gunshot wound to the stomach; the victim's son, another son, daughter and mother injured by lathi blows, a fracture of the mother's hand and pellet injuries
premeditation_planning: Court found a prearranged plan and prior meeting of minds: the three went armed to the victim's house to teach him a lesson
motive: Court accepted: to teach the victim a lesson for refusing to reap the accused's crop (revenge for disobeying their orders)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness accounts of the injured eyewitness, another son and the daughter about the beating, the exhortation and the shooting; the Court relied on the conduct of the group arriving armed
witness_credibility: Courts below found the prosecution witnesses consistent and not shaken in cross-examination; the Supreme Court recorded this without separate criticism
post_offence_conduct: Fled towards the canal after the shooting
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 17.5.2002; Supreme Court: 09.08.2010
legal_representation: Appellant: D.B. Vohra, T. Hashmi, S.K. Sabharwal. State (Respondent): Siddharth Dave, Vibha Datta Makhija
investigation_status: Not stated (investigation details not described; trial completed with conviction)
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 read with s.34 IPC. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: The appellant is vicariously liable under s.302 read with s.34 IPC for the shooting by a co-accused, given the prearranged plan and that all three were armed
defence_argument: Section 34 IPC could not be invoked against the appellant, since the fatal shot was fired by a co-accused and the appellant's own acts did not amount to the murder
legal_principle_applied: Section 34 requires common intention (prearranged plan or meeting of minds, anterior to the crime) and actual participation in the crime; distinguished from s.149
precedent_relied_upon: Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King Emperor AIR 1925 PC 1; Mehbub Shah v. King-Emperor AIR 1945 PC 148; Pandurang v. State of Hyderabad (1955) 1 SCR 1083; Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1963 SC 174; Ramaswami Ayyangar (1976) 3 SCC 779; Surendra Chauhan (2000) 4 SCC 110; Amrik Singh 1972 CrLJ 465 (SC); and others

case_title: Arumugam v. State represented by its Inspector of Police
accused_occupation: Agriculturist (as described for the family members named in the judgment, including the appellant's family)
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (step-son and step-mother); prior friction over the victim's conduct, which the accused disapproved of and had often asked her to change
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302
evidence_type: Extra-judicial confession (oral to a witness and written statement to the Village Administrative Officer); medical evidence; recovery of rope; witness testimony of step-sister
confession: Extra-judicial confession made to the step-sister and then to the Village Administrative Officer (written as Ex.P1); relied on by the Court
aggravating_circumstances: Planning (rope hidden in field earlier); annoyance over victim's conduct as motive
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal against conviction dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: A woman, the second wife of the accused's father, was killed in a field adjoining a village. The accused had been unhappy with the victim's conduct and had repeatedly asked her to behave in a dignified way, but she had replied that her life was her own affair. On the day of the incident, the victim and her step-daughter went to the field to do agricultural work. Later, the accused called the victim to help lift a bundle of firewood, and both walked into a sugarcane field. Shortly afterwards the accused returned alone and told the step-daughter that the victim had been strangled and killed. Around 4 p.m. the accused also told the Village Administrative Officer that the accused had murdered the victim. The officer recorded this in writing and took the accused to the police station, where a case was registered. The investigating officer recovered a rope on the accused's statement. The post-mortem, performed the next day, found a ligature mark about 3 cm wide encircling the neck. The doctor found death by asphyxia due to strangulation, occurring 27 to 30 hours before the autopsy. The step-daughter's husband and the accused's father did not support the prosecution. A charge sheet was filed after the investigation.
physical_harm: Death by asphyxia due to strangulation; 3 cm ligature mark around neck; no other injuries showing a struggle
premeditation_planning: Yes: Court found the accused prepared for the day and hid the rope in the field earlier
motive: Annoyance at the victim's conduct, the accused suspecting her of low character and finding her an embarrassment
key_evidence_accepted: Extra-judicial confession to step-sister and Village Administrative Officer; PW5's admission about accused's annoyance; medical evidence of strangulation and time of death; rope recovery
witness_credibility: Step-sister's evidence accepted, including her admission about the accused's annoyance; hostile father and brother-in-law's evidence held not to undermine the case; medical evidence held to support the ocular account
post_offence_conduct: Disclosed the killing to step-sister and then to the Village Administrative Officer; did not try to run away; handed over to police
trial_duration: offence: 19 March 2000; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 01.09.2005; Supreme Court: July 28, 2010
legal_representation: Accused: Venkat Subramanyam, V. K. Sidharthan, Anup Kumar; State: S. Thananjayan
investigation_status: FIR registered on extra-judicial confession; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted (defence argued the 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. gap in FIR registration was unexplained; the Court did not treat it as a lapse)
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, life imprisonment under s.302; High Court: appeal dismissed; Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Conviction rests on sound appreciation of evidence; extra-judicial confession to PW1 should not be discarded; medical evidence supports the prosecution story
defence_argument: Conviction solely on extra-judicial confession unjustified as father, step-sister and brother-in-law turned hostile; 4 p.m./6 p.m. FIR delay unexplained; medical evidence contradicted by decomposed body; victim too strong to be strangled
legal_principle_applied: Extra-judicial confession is weak evidence but may be relied on where distinctive features (prompt disclosure, no flight, corroboration) exist; hostile witnesses did not undermine the case; medical evidence must be consistent with ocular evidence
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
judicial_aggravating_factors: Premeditation and planning, including concealing the rope in advance
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Elavarasan v. State rep. by Inspector of Police
accused_occupation: Government servant posted as a Watchman at a PWD bungalow
accused_socioeconomic_status: Government servant; wife stated he earned a monthly salary of Rs.4000 which he handed over for household expenses
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (father of the deceased child; husband of injured wife PW2). Prior dispute over family property with the accused's paternal uncle, not with the victims
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged; replaced by s.304 Part II); IPC s.307 (2 counts charged; one count upheld); IPC s.342
weapon: Sharp-edged cutting weapon (Aruval) used on wife and mother; child's fatal injuries possibly caused by a blunt weapon or a hard blow of the bare hand (court's view)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured wife PW2) with corroboration from PW1 and PW8; medical (post-mortem and injury reports of PW15, PW16, PW19); observation mahazar Ex.P3; arrest inside house with weapon
aggravating_circumstances: Killing of a child about 1.5 years old; sharp-edged weapon used on wife (who was pregnant) and mother; accused barred the doors and threatened anyone entering
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden quarrel, heat of passion, no premeditation; child was in another room and not connected to the initial fight; sharp weapon not used on child; no cruel or unusual manner
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 (life imprisonment for murder of child); s.342 (1 year RI); s.307 two counts (10 years RI each); sentences concurrent; plea of insanity rejected
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld under s.302, s.307 (one count, attempt on PW2) and s.342; s.307 conviction for attempt on PW3 set aside
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (IPC s.304 Part II) for death of child 'A'; attempt to murder PW2 (IPC s.307, reduced sentence); wrongful confinement (IPC s.342)
neutral_facts: On the night of 11-12 December 2000, the family had gone to bed after dinner around 9 pm. A quarrel broke out between the accused and his wife around midnight, which escalated into an assault around 1 am. The quarrel reportedly arose from the accused's frustration over the sale of family property and his accusations against his wife. During the assault the accused used a sharp-edged cutting weapon on his wife, who was pregnant, causing numerous incised wounds. The accused's mother intervened to save the wife and was also cut with the weapon. The noise and cries woke the couple's young daughter, who was sleeping in an adjacent room and began to cry. The accused went into that room and struck the child, who sustained two injuries, including a fracture, and died. The wife testified as an injured eyewitness to the sequence of events and stated that she did not see the accused strike the child. A post-mortem found the cause of death to be coma resulting from head injuries sustained 24 to 36 hours earlier, consistent with the blunt side of a weapon. Medical reports recorded fifteen injuries on the wife, who was hospitalised for about one and a half months, and six injuries on the mother, two of whose fingers were later amputated. After the incident the accused bolted the doors from inside, refused to open them to police, and threatened to kill anyone who entered. Police, assisted by villagers, forced the door open and found the accused inside the house armed with an Aruval, with the injured women and the child in the house. An observation mahazar recorded writings on the inner walls of the house. Prosecution witnesses, including the mother, gave evidence about the accused's treatment for mental health concerns.
physical_harm: Child 'A' died from head injuries (coma) after two injuries with a fracture; wife suffered 15 injuries and was hospitalised about 1.5 months; mother suffered 6 injuries and loss of two fingers
number_of_offences: 3 sections charged (ss.302, 307 with 2 counts, 342); 3 convictions finally upheld (s.304 Part II replacing s.302, s.307 for PW2, s.342)
premeditation_planning: No premeditation found; the quarrel was sudden and the killing occurred in a sudden fight in the heat of passion
motive: alleged: quarrel over the accused's inability to sell property owned by his mother; the court accepted that the quarrel was sudden
key_evidence_accepted: Deposition of injured wife PW2; corroboration by PW1 and PW8; post-mortem evidence of PW19; injury reports of PW15 and PW16 (Ex.P19, Ex.P20)
witness_credibility: PW2 found completely reliable and unchallenged; PW3 (mother) turned hostile and her evidence about mental disorder was vague and not accepted at face value
post_offence_conduct: Bolted doors from inside, refused to open to police, threatened to kill anyone entering, and was found inside armed with an Aruval; court held that not fleeing did not show insanity
trial_duration: offence: 11-12 December 2000; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 22.3.2006; Supreme Court: 5 July 2011
legal_representation: Appellant: K.K. Mani, Abhishek Krishna, Mayur R. Shah. State/respondent: R. Venkataramani, V.G. Pragasam, Aljo K. Joseph, S. Aristotle, Prabu Ramasubramanian
investigation_status: Charge-sheet filed; committed to sessions; trial completed with 21 prosecution witnesses and court-ordered medical examination
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted (life for s.302; 10 years s.307 x2; 1 year s.342). High Court: appeal dismissed, s.307 conviction for PW3 set aside, others upheld. Supreme Court: partly allowed; s.302 altered to s.304 Part II with 10 years RI; s.307 reduced to 7 years; s.342 upheld
prosecution_argument: Trial and High Court correctly held insanity not proved; no credible evidence of legal insanity at time of offence; not fleeing or attacking without reason does not show unsoundness of mind; relied on Dr. Chandrashekaran's evidence
defence_argument: Material sufficiently proved unsoundness of mind: psychiatric evidence of Dr. Srinivasan, treatment by a psychiatrist, observation mahazar writings, unprovoked assault on family, and post-event conduct
legal_principle_applied: Insanity defence under IPC s.84 must be proved by the accused under Evidence Act s.105 on a preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt; insanity assessed at the time of the offence; intention inferred from weapon and injuries; sudden fight and heat of passion
precedent_relied_upon: Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v. State of Gujarat (1964) 7 SCR 361; State of U.P. v. Ram Swarup and Anr. (1974) 4 SCC 764; Bhikari v. State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1966 SC 1
sentencing_rationale: No intention to cause death, though knowledge that the injuries were likely to cause death; culpable homicide committed without premeditation in a sudden fight and heat of passion; conviction altered to s.304 Part II with 10 years RI
judicial_mitigating_factors: No premeditation; sudden quarrel in heat of passion; sharp weapon not used on child; did not act in a cruel or unusual manner or take undue advantage
other_sentence_order: Benefit of s.428 CrPC granted; sentences under s.307 and s.342 run concurrently with s.304 Part II sentence; default-of-fine sentence affirmed

case_title: Union of India & Ors. v. Bodupalli Gopalaswami
accused_occupation: Army officer (Commandant of a Company ASC (Supply) supply depot)
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: Army Act, 1950 s.52(f) (charge 1); s.63 (charges 2 to 5); s.71 (punishment); Pension Regulation 16(a)
evidence_type: Witness testimony (13 prosecution witnesses), documentary evidence, material objects, and the inspection team's report
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Limited overall-controlling role; charges technical in nature; subordinates held responsible for the lapses; matter over 20 years old and accused superannuated
trial_court_outcome: General Court Martial: guilty of charge 1, charge 4 and charge 5(c); not guilty of charges 2 and 3; sentenced to dismissal from service; pension forfeited later by President's order of 22.12.1995
high_court_outcome: Writ petition partly allowed: GCM proceedings, findings and dismissal upheld; order forfeiting pension quashed and reconsideration directed
offence_finally_established: Army Act s.52(f) (charge 1, intent to defraud, as a finding upheld); s.63 (charges 4 and 5(c), omissions prejudicial to good order and military discipline)
neutral_facts: The accused was the commanding officer of a military supply depot whose butchery supplied dressed meat, obtained from a private contractor, to indenting army units. The butchery was run by a supervisory officer, a veterinary officer, junior commissioned and non-commissioned officers, and the accused had overall charge of the depot. After complaints about irregularities, a team of three officers from a central investigating agency and two army officers carried out a surprise inspection of the butchery on 14 February 1990. The inspection team checked eleven vehicles returning from the butchery with meat. Of 1411.2 kg of dressed meat issued to various units, 14.5 kg was found to be heart, which was not an acceptable part of the carcass under the contract's special conditions. During discussions with the inspecting officers, the accused remarked that, to the best of the accused's knowledge, heart was an edible offal that could be issued on demand of units. The accused repeated this in a confidential report dated 15 February 1990. The prosecution case was that this remark amounted to accepting heart as part of the dressed meat with intent to defraud the government. There was no evidence that the accused had instructed heart to be accepted or that heart was regularly accepted. The supervisory and veterinary officers were separately charge-sheeted and punished. The prosecution also alleged that reserve stocks of animals were not maintained in the butchery between 11 and 22 March 1990, and that passed animals were not segregated from the contractor's other animals, contrary to the butchery's standard operating procedure.
offence_severity: Section 52(f): maximum ten years' imprisonment; Section 63: maximum seven years' imprisonment (minimum not stated)
physical_harm: None
number_of_offences: 5 charges (sections 52(f) and 63, i.e. 2 sections); 3 findings finally upheld (charges 1, 4 and 5(c))
motive: alleged: intent to defraud the government (charge 1); the Supreme Court found at best a wrong interpretation of clause 86
key_evidence_accepted: Inspection finding of 14.5 kg heart in 1411.2 kg of dressed meat; the accused's remark on heart as edible offal (as recorded); evidence that reserve shortfall and segregation lapses were largely the subordinates' or contractor's; Court did not disturb findings of guilt on charges 1, 4 and 5(c)
witness_credibility: Not assessed by the Supreme Court; it held that inadequacy and unreliability of evidence were not grounds for interference in judicial review
post_offence_conduct: Repeated the remark about heart in a confidential report dated 15.2.1990
trial_duration: offence: 14.2.1990 (inspection); trial judgment: 30.7.1993 (GCM sentence; trial commenced 22.1.1993); High Court: 25.8.2000; Supreme Court: 12.9.2011
legal_representation: Accused (respondent): Y. Rajagopala Rao, R. Balasubramanyam, Y. Ramesh, Sureshta Bagga. Union of India (appellants): P.P. Malhotra, ASG, with Rajiv Nanda, Rahul Kaushik, B.K. Prasad (for B.V. Balaram Das)
investigation_status: Surprise inspection (raid) conducted 14.2.1990; subordinate officials charge-sheeted and punished; charge-sheet against accused dated 30.12.1992; GCM convened and trial held
