appeal_history: Trial court (GCM): dismissal from service on 30.7.1993. High Court: writ partly allowed; pension forfeiture order quashed, proceedings and dismissal upheld. Supreme Court: Crl.A. 876/2003 (Union) allowed; Crl.A. 877/2003 (accused) allowed in part, dismissal substituted with forfeiture of eight years' service for pension and severe reprimand
prosecution_argument: Union of India contended that the High Court erred in quashing the order forfeiting pension, which was valid under Regulation 16(a) after dismissal
defence_argument: Presiding Officer was disqualified under Rule 39(2)(c) as he had summarily tried witnesses in the same incident and was biased, vitiating the GCM; the accused also contended that the punishment was disproportionate
legal_principle_applied: Judicial review of court martial is limited to lack of jurisdiction, excess of jurisdiction, or perverse or arbitrary action; punishment may be reviewed for proportionality only where shockingly disproportionate or perverse; Regulation 16(a) pension forfeiture is independent of s.71 punishment and falls if the dismissal is set aside
precedent_relied_upon: Union of India v. P.D. Yadav (2002) 1 SCC 405 (relied on); Union of India v. Major A. Hussain (1998) 1 SCC 537 (relied on); Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India (1987) 4 SCC 611 (relied on); Union of India v. R.K. Sharma (2001) 9 SCC 492 (referred to); Brig. A.K. Malhotra v. Union of India (1997) (4) SLR 51 (reversed in P.D. Yadav)
sentencing_rationale: Dismissal was shockingly disproportionate given the technical nature of the charges against the accused, the subordinates' responsibility and the contractor's breach; remand for a lesser punishment was not pursued because the matter was over 20 years old and the accused had superannuated; substituted punishment imposed
judicial_mitigating_factors: Technical and limited role of the accused; lapses attributable to subordinates and contractor; matter more than 20 years old; accused had superannuated
other_sentence_order: Pension order of 22.12.1995 set aside; pension claim to be processed and settled within six months; no back wages from dismissal to superannuation

case_title: Sham @ Kishor Bhaskarrao Matkari v. State of Maharashtra
previous_criminal_record: No. Court found unblemished antecedents; no prior criminal activity shown by prosecution
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (brother of the deceased Manohar; sister-in-law and nephews/niece also family members); prior dispute over land/property
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.307; IPC s.201 (acquitted under s.201 at trial)
weapon: None mentioned as a dangerous weapon; a large stone and a gas cylinder with tube were found near the body, but the court said no dangerous weapon was used
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured daughter PW-7; neighbour PW-1; landlord PW-3); medical (post-mortem PW-6 and PW-11); recovery (stone inside house); confession before Executive Magistrate
confession: Statement to Executive Magistrate (PW-16) recorded in hospital, treated as statement under s.164 CrPC; not a dying declaration; relied on by the Supreme Court
aggravating_circumstances: Killings of three persons and injuries to two children of one family; victims asleep and defenceless; brutality; High Court's list of aggravating circumstances (not adopted by the Supreme Court as grounds for death)
mitigating_circumstances: No pre-plan or pre-meditation; quarrel arose from land/property dispute; no dangerous weapon used; unblemished antecedents; accused was 28 and jobless; long custody (over 10 years, over 5 in death cell); no reason to think he cannot be reformed
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC: life imprisonment and fine Rs.25,000 (default 2 years RI); convicted under s.307 IPC: 7 years RI and fine Rs.1,000; acquitted under s.201 IPC
high_court_outcome: Accused's appeal dismissed (conviction upheld); State's appeal allowed; life imprisonment enhanced to death
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 (three deaths) and attempt to murder under IPC s.307 (conviction upheld; Supreme Court agreed with conviction under ss.302 and 307)
neutral_facts: The accused lived in a rented house with the victim (the accused's brother), the victim's wife and their three children. A neighbour living in an adjoining tenancy in the same building reported a quarrel between the accused and the victim at about 9.00 to 9.15 p.m., during which the accused said he would deal with the victim later. Around 3.00 to 3.30 a.m., the neighbour heard shouting, the cries of the victim's wife, the noise of beating and the groans of a small child from the house, and smelled gas leakage and something burning. The neighbour and the landlord went to the house and met the accused coming out, with blood on the hands and clothes, who said three thieves had entered and assaulted the family. Smoke was seen coming from the house, and the police were called. Officers found the victim and his wife dead, the wife partly burnt, and a large stone and a gas cylinder with tube near her body. Two children and a girl were injured, and one son later died in hospital. Doctors who conducted the post-mortems recorded injuries on the deceased. While in hospital, the accused made a statement to an Executive Magistrate admitting the killings and the injuries to the children. The injured daughter saw part of the occurrence. A stone was recovered from inside the house. The police registered a case, seized articles, and arrested the accused.
attempt_completion: Completed (three deaths); attempt also charged under s.307 for injuries to two children
physical_harm: Death of the victim (brother), the victim's wife and their son; injuries to two children; wife partly burnt
number_of_offences: 3 charged; 2 finally upheld (s.302 and s.307; s.201 was acquitted at trial)
premeditation_planning: Not found. The Supreme Court concluded there was no pre-plan or pre-meditation to eliminate the brother's family; the High Court had described the attack as pre-meditated
motive: Land/property dispute between the accused and the victim (accepted by the court)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of the injured daughter (PW-7); neighbour and landlord evidence (PWs 1 and 3); post-mortem medical opinion (PWs 6 and 11); recovery of stone; accused's confession before Executive Magistrate (PW-16)
witness_credibility: Found credible; court saw no reason to disbelieve PW-7, PW-1, PW-3 and the confessional statement
post_offence_conduct: Told neighbours and police that three thieves had attacked the household; found with blood on hands and clothes; the High Court found this story false (as noted in the judgment)
custody_duration: In jail since 30.06.2001 (over 10 years); in death cell since 03.05.2006 (over 5 years)
trial_duration: offence: 28/29.06.2001; trial judgment: 04/05.03.2003; High Court: 03.05.2006; Supreme Court: 30.09.2011
legal_representation: Accused: Tara Chand Sharma, Mahabir Singh Mangla, Uma Datta, Kishan Datta and Neelam Sharma. State: Sushil Karanjkar, Sachin Patil, Sanjay Kharde, Sankar A Chillarge and Asha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: FIR registered (Ex.P-22 treated as FIR); investigation completed; accused arrested; charge-sheet laid; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.302 and 307, life imprisonment for murder; High Court: accused's appeal dismissed, State's appeal allowed, death sentence imposed; Supreme Court: conviction upheld, death set aside, life imprisonment restored
prosecution_argument: Death sentence justified given three deaths and injuries to two children of one family; the State relied on Ajitsingh Hamamsingh Gujral
defence_argument: Several mitigating circumstances (including unblemished antecedents and absence of premeditation) mean death was not warranted; not a rarest of rare case
legal_principle_applied: Rarest of rare test; weighing of aggravating and mitigating circumstances per Bachan Singh and later decisions; death only where a rarest of rare case
precedent_relied_upon: Ajitsingh Hamamsingh Gujral v. State of Maharashtra, JT 2011 (10) SC 465 (distinguished); Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, (1980) 2 SCC 684 (referred); Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, (1983) 3 SCC 470 (referred); C. Muniappan v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2010) 9 SCC 567 (referred)
sentencing_rationale: Not a rarest of rare case; the High Court gave inadequate reasons for enhancement; no pre-plan, unblemished antecedents, no dangerous weapon, the accused cannot be shown to be a menace; trial court's life sentence restored
judicial_mitigating_factors: No pre-planning or pre-meditation; quarrel over land dispute; no dangerous weapon used; unblemished antecedents; no reason to think the accused cannot be reformed; not a menace to society; trial court's demeanour assessment favoured life sentence
judicial_aggravating_factors: Three deaths acknowledged; no other aggravating factor weighed by the Supreme Court
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Rafiq Ahmed @ Rafi v. State of U.P.
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.396 (dacoity with murder) and s.201 charged; convicted under IPC s.302 and s.201
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence; last-seen witnesses; recovery memo at accused's behest; investigating officer's evidence; medical (post-mortem) evidence; extra-judicial statement to police
confession: Statement by the accused to the investigating officer, in presence of two witnesses, that the body was concealed in a sugarcane field. Relied on as one circumstance in the chain (as reproduced from the High Court); the body recovery at his behest was also relied on.
aggravating_circumstances: Body concealed to screen from punishment; multiple incised wounds and severing of trachea by a sharp-edged weapon
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 and s.201 IPC; rigorous imprisonment for life (s.302) and 7 years RI (s.201), concurrent; co-accused acquitted under s.396
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence maintained
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302) and causing disappearance of evidence (IPC s.201)
neutral_facts: It was alleged that five persons, one of whom was the accused, committed a robbery of cash in a car owned by the accused during the night of 30 September to 1 October 1977, and that during that robbery the victim was murdered. The victim regularly collected money from customers on behalf of his uncle's business and, on the day in question, had collected more than Rs. 8,000 but did not return home that night. Two witnesses stated that at about 8.00 p.m. the victim boarded a taxi already occupied by other persons at a road junction, and that the accused was in the driver's seat. The accused was arrested along with the taxi. In the presence of two witnesses, the accused allegedly stated that the body had been placed in a sugarcane field. On his pointing out, the body was recovered in the presence of a witness, prepared as a recovery memo, and identified. The post-mortem examination found three incised wounds, three abrasions and severing of the trachea, caused by a sharp-edged weapon, and death was attributed to respiratory failure and haemorrhage. The investigating officer completed the investigation and a charge sheet was filed.
offence_severity: Death or imprisonment for life, and fine (IPC s.302)
physical_harm: Death of the victim from respiratory failure and haemorrhage following severing of trachea; three incised wounds and three abrasions
number_of_offences: 2 charged (s.396 and s.201); 2 finally upheld (s.302 and s.201)
financial_property_loss: Alleged: cash collected by the deceased (over Rs. 8,000) and other valuables looted; the Court did not separately quantify or decide this loss
motive: alleged: robbery (looting of cash and valuables from the deceased), as noted in the High Court circumstances reproduced by the Court
key_evidence_accepted: Last-seen evidence of PW2 and PW4; investigating officer (PW11) and PW3 evidence on recovery of body at appellant's behest by recovery memo; post-mortem findings; accused's presence in taxi with deceased
witness_credibility: Not separately assessed in detail; the Court treated the last-seen and recovery witnesses' statements as completing the chain of circumstances
post_offence_conduct: Concealed the body in a sugarcane field (as reproduced circumstance); did not explain his whereabouts; complete denial in s.313 statement
trial_duration: offence: night of 30 September 1977 and 1 October 1977; trial judgment: 17 August 1981; High Court: 29.?.2004 (day and month garbled in source); Supreme Court: 04 August 2011
legal_representation: Appellant: R. Anand Padmanabhan, Prithvi Raj B.N., G. Ramakrishna Prasad. State: T.N. Singh, Rajeev Dubey, Kamlendra Mishra, Jatinder Kumar Bhatia
investigation_status: FIR/case registered under s.364 IPC; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed under s.173 Cr.P.C.; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Conviction under s.302 without a s.302 charge being framed or altered; the Court held no prejudice was shown
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 and s.201 IPC. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence maintained. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Despite circumstantial evidence, the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt; the appellant suffered no prejudice from conviction under s.302
defence_argument: Conviction under s.302 without altering the s.396 charge deprived the appellant of fair defence and caused serious prejudice; s.302 is graver so the trial was vitiated; serious contradictions in witness statements; circumstantial chain not proved
legal_principle_applied: Cognate offences principle; prejudice must be shown as serious disability in protections (fair trial, presumption of innocence, proof beyond reasonable doubt); s.302 is incorporated in s.396 so conviction under s.302 without specific charge causes no prejudice
precedent_relied_upon: Shyam Behari v. State of U.P. AIR 1957 SC 320 (followed); Willie (William) Slaney v. State of M.P. AIR 1956 SC 116; Iman Ali v. State of Assam AIR 1968 SC 1464; Dalbir Singh v. State of U.P. (2004) 5 SCC 334; Shamsaheb M. Multani v. State of Karnataka (2001) 2 SCC 577; Anil @ Raju Namdev Patil (2006 Suppl (9) SCR 466); Sanagaraboina Sreenu (1997) 5 SCC 348; Lakhjit Singh (1994); R v. Coutts [2006] UKHL 39
judicial_aggravating_factors: Nature of sharp-edged injuries showed knowledge that they would cause death; body concealed to destroy evidence
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Gajraj v. State (NCT) of Delhi
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.380, s.452 and s.404 (charged); IPC s.302 and s.404 convictions upheld
weapon: Licensed revolver (recovered with live and spent cartridges)
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence, including mobile IMEI/SIM call records (scientific/documentary), recovery of revolver and handset, recovery memos, oral testimony of witnesses, and a bank deposit
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC (life imprisonment and Rs.50,000 fine) and s.404 IPC (3 years RI and Rs.5,000 fine); acquitted of s.380 and s.452 IPC; sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed on merits; conviction upheld; default imprisonment in lieu of fine under s.302 reduced from three years to six months
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302) and criminal misappropriation-type offence under IPC s.404
neutral_facts: The victim was found dead inside a house in Delhi, having suffered bullet injuries to the left side of the temporal region and the left side of the abdomen. Police received a telephone call about the body on the evening of 23 July 2005. The victim's wife, who had been in Chandigarh, stated that the victim had left Chandigarh for Delhi carrying a licensed revolver, a mobile phone SIM and a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs intended for negotiating a settlement. The sum was not fully recovered. Records showed that the victim's SIM became inactive on the date of the murder and that two incoming calls from a Chandigarh telephone had been received on that day. Investigators then found that a handset bearing a particular IMEI number, which had been used with the victim's SIM, was used with a SIM registered in the name of the accused, immediately after the murder and until 2 August 2005. Service provider records confirmed the registration of that SIM in the accused's name. Police recovered three mobile handsets from the accused, one bearing the IMEI number of the victim's handset, and a revolver with live and spent cartridges that had belonged to the victim. Recovery memos bore the signatures of the accused's brother and father, who later asserted that their signatures had been taken on blank papers. The accused was arrested on 6 August 2005. A deposit of Rs. 9,000 had been made into a bank account in the accused's name two days after the murder.
physical_harm: Death from bullet injuries to the left temporal region and left abdomen
number_of_offences: 4 charged (ss.302, 380, 452, 404 IPC); 2 finally upheld (ss.302 and 404 IPC)
financial_property_loss: Rs. 3 lakhs not recovered (per wife's statement); Rs. 9,000 deposit in the accused's bank account two days after the murder; the victim's mobile handset and licensed revolver also taken
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: IMEI/SIM call records showing the victim's handset used with the accused's SIM immediately after the murder; nodal officer evidence (PW22) on SIM registration; recovery of the revolver with cartridges and of the handset from the accused; recovery memos authenticated by signatures of the accused's brother and father; continued use of the SIM until arrest
witness_credibility: The Court accepted that the wife's (PW23) statement contained a discrepancy about the direction of calls but held it insignificant against scientific IMEI/SIM evidence. The brother (PW12) and father (PW13) denied signing the recovery memos, but neither disputed the authenticity of their signatures, so the Court held the signatures genuine.
post_offence_conduct: Immediately after the murder, the accused used the victim's handset with the accused's own registered SIM and continued using that SIM until arrest; the accused was in possession of the victim's handset and revolver
custody_duration: Arrested 6 August 2005; total custody duration not stated
trial_duration: offence: 23.7.2005; trial judgment: 21.4.2008; High Court: 18.3.2009; Supreme Court: 22.09.2011
legal_representation: Accused: Sanjay K. Agarwal. State: J.S. Attri, P.K. Dey and Sadhna Sandhu (for Anil Katiyar)
investigation_status: FIR registered (No. 297 of 2005, Police Station Krishna Nagar, on 7.1.2006); investigation led to arrest; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.302 and 404 IPC, acquitted under ss.380 and 452 IPC. High Court: appeal dismissed on merits; default sentence reduced to six months. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed; conviction upheld.
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: (1) The accused was implicated through a fabricated story, since the handset was traced via the victim's wife's disclosure and a discrepancy existed in her call timing evidence, so the handset recovery was a concoction; (2) the recovery witnesses (brother and father) said their signatures were obtained on blank papers; (3) the Rs. 9,000 deposit did not connect the accused to the crime
legal_principle_applied: Every mobile handset has a unique IMEI number recorded by service providers, so IMEI/SIM call records are conclusive scientific evidence that can outweigh discrepancies in oral evidence; recovery memo signatures not disputed by signatories are treated as authentic
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Ajitsingh Harnamsingh Gujral v. State of Maharashtra
accused_age: Not stated (High Court described him as around 50 to 52 years at the time; no single age given)
accused_socioeconomic_status: Businessman with several employees and a car; had suffered business losses earlier at Ludhiana
victim_age: Not stated (four victims; son about 20, daughters about 22 and 13, wife's age not given)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (wife); Relative: father of the son and two daughters who were killed
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302
weapon: Petrol poured with a red bucket (petrol can also found in the flat)
evidence_type: Circumstantial (no eyewitnesses); last-seen evidence; witness testimony on quarrels and dictatorial conduct; recovery under s.27 Evidence Act; chemical analyser report; panchanama of petrol can
confession: Section 27 disclosure statement by the accused pointing out the red bucket; relied on by the Court (not a confession to the killing)
aggravating_circumstances: Burning of four family members while asleep; gruesome, diabolical manner; pre-planned with large quantity of petrol brought into flat; victims were family members; accused absconded afterwards
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC for four murders; death sentence imposed
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; death sentence confirmed
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 (four counts: wife, son and two daughters)
neutral_facts: In the early hours of 10 April 2003, a fire broke out in the residential flat where the accused lived with his wife and three children. Witnesses testified that the accused and his wife were heard quarrelling loudly at about midnight on the previous night, and that the accused was seen returning to the flat around that time. The accused's family had a history of tension, and witnesses described the accused as a dictatorial and hot-tempered man who had beaten his wife with a leather belt and whose children resented his behaviour. Household servants sleeping in the veranda heard a loud noise at about 4.00 to 4.30 a.m. and found the flat on fire with a strong smell of petrol. After the fire was extinguished, the bodies of the wife, son and two daughters were found burnt in the children's bedroom. A witness had earlier seen a new ten-litre plastic can containing petrol in the flat. The accused's car was missing and he was not found at the scene. Police later recovered a red bucket from the flat's bathroom on the accused's own disclosure, and a chemical analysis of the bucket showed the presence of petrol. The electrician who inspected the premises found no short circuit. Post-mortem examinations showed that all four victims died from burning. The accused's own account of having left to visit a sick relative was not accepted by the investigators.
offence_severity: Death or imprisonment for life, and fine (no separate fine amount stated)
physical_harm: Death of four persons (wife, son and two daughters) by burning; son had incised injuries, explained by broken glass
number_of_offences: 1 charged (IPC s.302, four counts); 1 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Yes: Court found the murder pre-planned, not on spur of the moment, because a large quantity of petrol was brought into the flat
motive: Not identified (Court held motive could only be speculated; marital strain and quarrels were found but no motive was fixed)
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW3, PW4, PW5 and PW16 on midnight quarrel and last seen; testimony on dictatorial conduct and leather belt beatings; 10-litre petrol can found in flat; red bucket recovered on disclosure and tested positive for petrol; false alibi; accused's flight
witness_credibility: PW3 (brother-in-law), PW5 (mother-in-law), PW4 and PW16 found credible; no enmity or motive to lie shown against them
post_offence_conduct: Left the scene and was found with cash and safari dresses in Rajasthan; put forward an alibi of visiting a sick sister in Delhi, found false by the Court
trial_duration: offence: 10.4.2003; trial judgment: 19.3.2005; High Court: 26.6.2006; Supreme Court: 13.9.2011
legal_representation: Appellant: Jaspal Singh (senior counsel), Aman Vachher, Ashutosh Dubey, L.K. Sharma (for P.N. Puri). State of Maharashtra: Sushil Karanjkar (for Asha Gopalan Nair)
investigation_status: Report lodged by PSI; inquest, spot panchanama and post mortem done; accused arrested 14.4.2003; charge sheet filed; trial completed with 19 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: None noted (Court found 168 questions put under s.313 Cr.P.C., so the defence objection was rejected)
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, death sentence. High Court: appeal dismissed, death sentence upheld. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Case rested on a chain of circumstances: last seen with the wife, petrol brought into flat, bucket recovered, false alibi and flight; the Court's summary of the prosecution case is recorded, with no separate State submissions detailed
defence_argument: No motive proved and a happy married life of 25 years; the bucket was a police fabrication; alibi of visiting sick sister in Delhi; s.313 questions not put; injuries on son unexplained; petrol-splashing and bodies-on-ground inconsistencies
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence: complete chain of circumstances must point to accused; last-seen theory; s.114 Evidence Act natural conduct; rarest of rare test with Macchi Singh balance sheet
precedent_relied_upon: Wakkar v. State of UP (2011) 3 SCC 306; Krishnan (2008) 15 SCC 430; Sharad Birdhichand Sarda AIR 1984 SC 1622; Mohd. Mannan (2011) 5 SCC 317; Mohd. Azad (2008) 15 SCC 449; Mahender Singh Dahiya (2011) 3 SCC 109; S.K. Yusuf JT 2011 (6) SC 640; Santosh v. State of MP AIR 1975 SC 654; Bachan Singh AIR 1980 SC 898; Machhi Singh AIR 1983 SC 957; Common Cause (2008) 5 SCC 511
sentencing_rationale: Burning living persons is a horrible act causing excruciating pain; pre-planned; accused cannot be reformed or rehabilitated; balance sheet heavily against him; falls within rarest of rare cases
judicial_aggravating_factors: Pre-planned, cruel and barbaric killing of his own family; burning of living persons; no provocation; accused cannot be reformed
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Haresh Mohandas Rajput v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour (lived in close vicinity for a long time and was well acquainted with the victim and her family)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.376
weapon: Rope (alleged; the Trial Court disbelieved that it was the rope used, and the High Court's finding on it was given little weight)
evidence_type: Circumstantial; medical (post-mortem); recovery of body and blood-stained articles; chemical analysis; testimony of child witness; police and witness evidence of information given at police station
confession: Alleged extra-judicial confession to mother and son Khushal (PW.10). Not relied on: Khushal was declared hostile and the mother was not examined, so the Court held the confession was not proved.
aggravating_circumstances: Rape and strangulation of a 10-year-old girl; sexual assault injuries; body found concealed under the cot; blood on bed-sheet and floor
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302 and s.376; life imprisonment under s.302 and 10 years under s.376, sentences to run concurrently
high_court_outcome: Conviction confirmed; State's appeal for enhancement allowed and sentence altered from life imprisonment to death
neutral_facts: On a late afternoon in October 1999, the victim, a ten-year-old girl, was playing on a road near the accused's house with her brother and sister. When she was found missing, her brother searched for her without success. Her mother, who had been away at work, returned and also searched, but the victim could not be traced. The brother later said a friend had told him the victim was in the accused's house. He went to the rear of the house and said he saw the victim lying in a room, and when he asked the accused about her, the accused denied she was there. Another person entered from the back of the house but did not see her. On that day the accused's mother and son had gone out, leaving the accused alone in the house. The accused's son later went to the police and reported that the accused had killed the girl and that her body lay under a cot in the house. Police went to the house with the victim's father and recovered the body from under the cot, while the accused was sitting outside. Blood was found on a bed-sheet, on the cot and on the floor beneath it, and the clothing and cloth pieces were found to contain human blood. The post-mortem found injuries consistent with sexual assault, ligature marks on the neck and death by strangulation. The accused could not explain how the body came to be in his house and said he had gone to a liquor shop and left the house open.
physical_harm: Death by strangulation with ligature marks around the neck of a 10-year-old girl; genital injuries consistent with sexual assault, including torn hymen; multiple facial and limb contusions and abrasions, all ante-mortem
premeditation_planning: Not found. The Court did not find premeditation or planning; it noted only an attempt to conceal the body under the cot.
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Recovery of body from under cot in the accused's house; blood on bed-sheet and floor (spot panchnama); chemical report showing human blood on clothing and cloth pieces; post-mortem evidence of sexual assault and strangulation; police-station information given by the accused's son (PW.10); accused's admission in s.313 examination that he was sitting outside and that the body was recovered; the victim's disappearance from play and the accused's presence at the house.
witness_credibility: Mother (PW.1), father (PW.2), Deepak Jawahar Agarwal (PW.8) and Head Constable G.R. More (PW.4) were found credible and uncontradicted on cross-examination. Khushal (PW.10) was declared hostile and his evidence was assessed with caution. The child witness Nitesh (PW.3) was accepted on the disappearance and presence of the accused; his account of seeing the victim in the house was rejected by the Trial Court and the Supreme Court found no reason to interfere. The doctor's post-mortem evidence was not challenged.
post_offence_conduct: Found sitting outside his house when police arrived; gave an explanation of going to a liquor shop and leaving the house open, which the courts found false and unsubstantiated
trial_duration: offence: 24.10.1999; trial judgment: 19.9.2001; High Court: 11.01.2008; Supreme Court: 20.09.2011
legal_representation: Appellant: D.N. Goburdhan, Prabal Bagchi, Karitka Sharma, Balendu Shekhar. State: Arun R. Pednekar, Sanjay Kharde, Aisha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: FIR lodged; body recovered and panchnama prepared; accused arrested; chargesheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Police entered the house before the panchnama was prepared, which the Trial Court held weakened the rope recovery
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 and s.376 IPC, life imprisonment and 10 years concurrent. High Court: conviction upheld; death sentence substituted on State's appeal. Supreme Court: conviction affirmed; death sentence set aside and life imprisonment restored.
prosecution_argument: Dead body recovered from accused's house; medical evidence showed strangulation after sexual assault; any inconsistencies in witness statements were trivial; concurrent findings of the courts below should not be disturbed
defence_argument: No evidence connects the accused to the crime; circumstantial evidence did not exclude hypotheses of innocence; material inconsistencies in witness statements; no sufficient evidence for conviction; death sentence not justified on any ground
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence test: circumstances must be fully established, conclusive, consistent only with guilt, exclude every other hypothesis, and form a chain so complete that the accused's guilt is the only probable inference. Rarest of rare test for death sentence: aggravating circumstances must exist and mitigating circumstances must be absent, with reference to the Bachan Singh and Machhi Singh framework.
precedent_relied_upon: Krishnan v. State (2008) 15 SCC 430; Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra AIR 1984 SC 1622; Paramjeet Singh @ Pamma v. State of Uttarakhand AIR 2011 SC 200; Wakkar v. State of UP (2011) 3 SCC 306; Mohd. Mannan v. State of Bihar (2011) 5 SCC 317; Inspector of Police v. John David (2011) 5 SCC 509; SK Yusuf v. State of West Bengal AIR 2011 SC 2283; Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1980 SC 898 and Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1983 SC 957 (death sentence guidelines); C. Muniappan AIR 2010 SC 3718; Rabindra Kumar Pal (2011) 2 SCC 490; Surendra Koli (2011) 4 SCC 80; Sudam @ Rahul Kaniram Jadhav (2011) 7 SCC 125
sentencing_rationale: The case did not fall within the rarest of rare category, so the death sentence awarded by the High Court was set aside and life imprisonment restored
judicial_aggravating_factors: Court referred to the sexual assault and strangulation and the attempt to conceal the body; it nonetheless held the case did not fall within the rarest of rare category
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Rakesh & Another v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance (residents of the same village); alleged prior dispute over utensils that the victim refused to give, with alleged threats
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; Arms Act s.25 (cited in FIR)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW11); medical (post-mortem by PW8); recovery of weapons on disclosure statements; investigating officer testimony; arrest
confession: No confession noted; disclosure statements leading to recovery of weapons were relied on
aggravating_circumstances: Heinous crime (court's description); multiple sharp-edged wounds to neck, chest and abdomen
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; rigorous imprisonment for life and fine of Rs. 2,000 each (default one year)
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; conviction upheld (judgment dated 15.12.2006, after remand; earlier 10.2.2005 decision set aside by Supreme Court)
neutral_facts: On 5 March 1996, at about 11.30 a.m. on a market day, the victim was attacked in front of a house in a village by three men, including the accused, who were then caught on the spot by the victim's nephew, who had been following the victim and had raised an alarm. Several people gathered, but the assailants broke free and fled. The victim was taken to hospital, where a doctor declared him dead. A post-mortem examination was conducted the same afternoon by a doctor who found three incised wounds, on the neck, chest and abdomen, all caused by sharp-edged weapons. The doctor opined that death had occurred three to six hours before the examination; the doctor did not fix an exact time of death. The victim's nephew testified that he saw the accused, with another man, strike the victim with a knife, a gupti and a katarna, and that he had been at a short distance on a main road with an unobstructed view. He said that one of the accused had earlier wanted utensils from the victim, who refused, and had threatened him. Other persons present were questioned, and some did not support the prosecution. The nephew lodged a first information report at a police station about one kilometre away within about an hour, naming all three accused and describing the overt acts and the motive. The investigating officer was examined, the accused were arrested, and the weapons were recovered on the basis of the accused's disclosure statements. The accused and the victim were residents of the same village. The defence examined one witness who gave the time of the incident as 11.00 a.m.
physical_harm: Death; three incised wounds on the neck, chest and right abdomen caused by sharp-edged weapons
motive: alleged: accused wanted utensils from the deceased, who refused, and the accused threatened him
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of the eyewitness nephew (PW11); post-mortem evidence (PW8); investigating officer's testimony (PW21); PW9's statement; arrests; weapon recoveries on disclosure statements; prompt FIR
witness_credibility: Eyewitness nephew (PW11) found trustworthy and natural despite being a related witness, scrutinised carefully; PW21 found natural with no animus; PW6 and PW12 did not fully support prosecution, but PW11 was relied on
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: Rakesh served more than 14 years and was prematurely released; Rajesh served about 7½ years and remained in jail
trial_duration: offence: 5.3.1996; trial judgment: 21.2.1997; High Court: 15.12.2006 (after remand; earlier decision dated 10.2.2005 set aside); Supreme Court: 19.9.2011 (judgment date)
legal_representation: Appellants: Siddharth Aggarwal, Aditya Wadhwa, Stuti Gujral, Senthil Jagadeesan. State: Vibha Datta Makhija
investigation_status: FIR registered; arrests made; weapons recovered; chargesheet filed; trial completed in Sessions court
procedural_irregularity: High Court's 10.2.2005 decision was rendered in absence of the appellants' counsel; Supreme Court set it aside and remanded
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC (21.2.1997). High Court: first decision 10.2.2005 set aside by Supreme Court (20.7.2006) and remanded; High Court dismissed on 15.12.2006. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: No rule bars reliance on close relatives' evidence but it must be scrutinised; medical evidence on time of death is not conclusive; concurrent findings of fact should not be disturbed
defence_argument: Eyewitnesses PW10 and PW11 could not have been present; ocular evidence contradicts medical evidence on time of death; PW11 is closely related to the deceased and no independent witness supported his presence; mutually destructive evidence should be discarded
legal_principle_applied: Ocular evidence has primacy over medical evidence unless totally irreconcilable; related witness evidence is admissible if trustworthy but must be carefully scrutinised; exact time of death cannot be fixed; minor discrepancies do not discard evidence
precedent_relied_upon: State of U.P. v. Hari Chand (2009) 13 SCC 542; Abdul Sayeed v. State of MP (2010) 10 SCC 259; Bhajan Singh v. State of Haryana (2011) 7 SCC 421; Mangu Khan v. State of Rajasthan AIR 2005 SC 1912; Baso Prasad v. State of Bihar AIR 2007 SC 1019; Kartik Malhar v. State of Bihar (1996) 1 SCC 614; Himanshu @ Chintu v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2011) 2 SCC 36; Kishan Singh v. Gurpal Singh AIR 2010 SC 3624; Manju Ram Kalita v. State of Assam (2009) 13 SCC 330; Leela Ram v. State of Haryana (1999) 9 SCC 525
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: M. Nageshwar Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh
accused_occupation: Faculty member at a computer institute (also gave coaching to students at another computer centre)
accused_socioeconomic_status: Earned a salary of about Rs.20,000 per month (only income detail stated)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband and wife); the judgment also describes marital frictions alleged in the confessional statement
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (Penal Code s.302) only
weapon: Cyanide poison administered in a Limca cold drink bottle
evidence_type: Medical (post-mortem and forensic reports); oral evidence of witnesses (landlady, maid, shopkeeper); recovery of Limca bottle; disowned confessional statement (excluded)
confession: Detailed confessional statement attributed to the accused before police and panch witnesses; repudiated by accused, not supported by panch witness PW12; not relied on and excluded from consideration by the Supreme Court
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of s.302 IPC; prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt
high_court_outcome: State appeal allowed; acquittal reversed; convicted under s.302 IPC, rigorous imprisonment for life and fine of Rs.1,000 (default 3 months simple imprisonment)
neutral_facts: The victim, the accused's wife, was found unconscious in a chair in the rented first-floor flan the couple shared in a house owned by a landlady, and was taken to hospital by the landlady and her maid. The accused, who worked as a computer faculty member, arrived at the hospital later. The victim was declared dead the following day after repeated cardiac arrests. The post-mortem found cyanosis, froth in the mouth and nostrils, and a yellowish liquid in the stomach that smelled of bitter almonds. Forensic analysis of the stomach and organ samples found cyanide. The prosecution's case was that the accused bought a cold drink bottle from a general store, mixed cyanide into it at the house, and gave it to the victim, who had asked for a cold drink. The shopkeeper testified about the sale, but said he did not remember the buyer well and did not know where the buyer lived. A goldsmith said to have sold cyanide to the accused was examined, but he testified that police had coerced him into making his statement. A statement attributed to the accused before police, witnessed by two panch witnesses, was repudiated; one panch witness did not support it. An empty Limca bottle was later recovered from a shelf in the couple's bedroom and was found to contain cyanide, but the bottle reached the laboratory weeks after its recovery.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from cyanide poisoning
premeditation_planning: Not found by the court. Planning (buying cyanide, waiting for a chance) appears only in the disowned confessional statement, which the court excluded.
motive: alleged: marital frictions, the victim's refusal to cooperate and insistence on going to the U.S.A. with the accused (from the disowned confessional statement); not accepted by the court
key_evidence_accepted: Medical and forensic evidence that the victim died of cyanide poisoning; the testimony of the landlady and maid that the victim was found unconscious (not disputed). The court did not accept proof that the accused gave the cyanide.
witness_credibility: PW6 (shopkeeper) found unreliable; PW4 (goldsmith) retracted under police coercion, a major blow to the prosecution; PW12 (panch) hostile and denied recovery; PW18 (investigating officer) uncorroborated on the confession and bottle recovery; PW7 and PW3 gave accounts of finding the victim unconscious
post_offence_conduct: Alleged in the disowned confessional statement (feigned ignorance, discarded remaining liquid, concealed the bottle, tried to flee). Not accepted by the court.
custody_duration: Not stated (accused alleged custody from 4 September 2000 and formal arrest on 7 September 2000; the court did not decide this)
trial_duration: offence: September 2, 2000 (victim found unconscious; death September 3, 2000); trial judgment: not given; High Court: September 13, 2007; Supreme Court: January 5, 2011
legal_representation: Accused (appellant): Sushil Kumar, S. Udaya Kumar Sagar, Vinita Sasidharan, Aditya Kumar (Lawyer's Knit & Co.). State (respondent): D. Mahesh Babu, Ramesh Allan, D. Bharathi Reddy.
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge sheet filed; trial held and completed in the trial court
procedural_irregularity: Post-mortem samples reached the laboratory after 11 days without explanation; the Limca bottle reached the laboratory about 20 days after recovery without explanation; the seizure panch denied the recovery
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted under s.302. High Court: State appeal allowed, acquittal reversed, convicted under s.302 with life imprisonment. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction set aside, accused acquitted.
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Not stated
legal_principle_applied: Suspicion, however strong, cannot take the place of proof; a repudiated confessional statement not supported by other evidence is of no use and must be excluded from consideration
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
other_sentence_order: Accused to be released from jail forthwith unless required in another criminal case; High Court judgment set aside and trial court judgment restored

case_title: Alamelu & Anr. v. State represented by Inspector of Police
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance/neighbour: one accused was a local boy about one kilometre from the victim's house, not related to or on visiting terms with her family; court noted no prior relationship. Prosecution alleged he had proposed marriage and she refused.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.366 (kidnapping/abduction to compel marriage); IPC s.376 (rape); s.376 and s.366 read with s.109 for accused Nos. 2 to 8
evidence_type: Oral testimony of victim, father, and cousin; medical and radiological age evidence (PW8, PW13); documentary school transfer certificate; police recovery and mahazar evidence
confession: None relied on. The prosecution alleged an accused told police they were married; the court did not treat this as a confession relied upon.
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: All accused convicted under ss.366 and 376 (with s.109 for some); ten years rigorous imprisonment and Rs.500 fine each, default three months further RI
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; trial court conviction and sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim, a young woman, was allegedly approached on a village road in the afternoon of 31 July 1993 by one of the accused, who said he loved her and wanted to marry her. She refused. A car then reached her and she was allegedly pushed into it by that accused, while other accused were already inside. A relative of the victim's family reportedly received a call from the accused about the abduction, and another relative reported it to the victim's father about an hour later. The father sent relatives to search, who reported that the victim could not be located, and a complaint was lodged with police two days later. The prosecution alleged that the next morning the victim was taken to a temple at a hill location, where one accused tied a mangalsutra around her neck despite her resistance. She was then allegedly kept in a house and repeatedly raped over three days. Relatives were allegedly present at the temple. The victim was recovered on 10 August 1993 from premises where the accused had stayed with her. Police seized a mangalsutra and clothing under mahazars. The victim was medically examined on 12 August 1993, and a radiologist and the examining doctor gave age ranges. The evidence included testimony from the victim, her father, a cousin, and a school transfer certificate giving a date of birth.
physical_harm: Alleged repeated rape; the judgment records no injury findings
number_of_offences: 2 charged (ss.366 and 376 IPC, with s.109 for accused Nos. 2 to 8); 0 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Not found by the court; the court held the abduction story appeared concocted
motive: alleged: one accused wanted to marry the victim, who refused. The court did not accept this as an established motive.
key_evidence_accepted: Father's own admission at the panchayat that the daughter agreed to return after an hour; cousin's evidence that relatives were present at the temple; school transfer certificate and radiological age evidence were not accepted as proving minority
witness_credibility: Victim's testimony found unreliable and inconsistent, including on the abduction, the temple, and the house; father's testimony contradicted hers; relatives' evidence found unnatural. Expert age evidence did not rule out majority.
post_offence_conduct: Alleged: one accused took the victim to police and said they were married; she stayed with him until recovery on 10 August 1993. Court treated her conduct as inconsistent with coercion.
trial_duration: offence: 31 July 1993 (alleged); trial judgment: 28 April 2000; High Court: 6 February 2008; Supreme Court: 18 January 2011
legal_representation: Accused: R. Venkataramani, R. Ayyam Perumal, Aljo K. Joseph. State: S. Thananjayan
investigation_status: Complaint lodged 2 August 1993; FIR copy received 6 August 1993; accused arrested and victim recovered 10 August 1993; charge sheet filed 19 June 1996; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Transfer certificate marked only in 2000 after recall of victim; Headmaster who signed it not examined; no witness from the temple produced; High Court did not consider expert evidence on age variation
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted all accused. High Court: convictions affirmed. Supreme Court: appeals allowed, all accused acquitted.
prosecution_argument: Prosecution version was consistent; concurrent findings of the courts below on abduction and rape should not be disturbed under Article 136; father stated the victim was 15 years and 2 months old on 31 July 1993
defence_argument: Findings were perverse and ignored contradictions; there was no abduction, forcible marriage or rape; the story was false and the victim left home voluntarily; the complaint was lodged due to enmity
legal_principle_applied: Article 136 interference only where concurrent findings are manifestly perverse; benefit of doubt; date of birth in transfer certificate needs proof by a person who made the entry; victim's sole testimony may convict only if free from basic infirmities or improbabilities
precedent_relied_upon: Birad Mal Singhvi v. Anand Purohit, 1988 (Suppl.) SCC 604; Narbada Devi Gupta v. Birendra Kumar Jaiswal, (2003) 8 SCC 745; Jaya Mala v. Home Secretary, Government of J&K, (1982) 2 SCC 538; Ravinder Singh Gorkhi v. State of U.P., (2006) 5 SCC 584; Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan, (1952) SCR 377
other_sentence_order: Accused directed to be released forthwith

case_title: Jagga Singh and Anr. v. State of Punjab
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.307; IPC s.325 r/w s.34
evidence_type: Medical (post-mortem report); prosecution account of the incident and gunshot sounds; admitted gunshot injury
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.307 IPC; 7 years RI and fine for Jagga Singh; Jagtar Singh and Kaka Singh also sentenced to 7 years RI and fine

neutral_facts: The prosecution case is that at about 8.30 p.m. on 24 April 1992, three accused persons came to a house in a village. One of the accused fired a gun at the first victim, striking his right thigh, and the first victim fell down. The accused then took the second victim away towards a nearby village. About twenty minutes later, the sound of three or four gunshots was heard from that direction. The dead body of the second victim was found the next morning. The post-mortem examination of the second victim's body recorded only lacerated wounds, and no gunshot wound was found on it. The gunshot injury to the first victim's leg was admitted. The evidence therefore consisted of the account of the events at the house, the admitted firearm injury, the timing of the gunfire sounds, the discovery of the body and the post-mortem findings. The prosecution relied on these facts to establish the incident and the injuries caused during it.
physical_harm: First victim suffered a gunshot injury to the leg (leg/thigh wound, grievous hurt under s.325 finding); second victim found dead the next morning, with only lacerated wounds and no gunshot wound on post-mortem
number_of_offences: 2 charged (s.302 and s.307, each with s.34); 1 finally upheld (s.325 r/w s.34)
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Admitted gunshot injury to the first victim's leg; post-mortem report showing no gunshot wound on the second victim's body
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Sentence suspended pending appeal by order of 14.09.2007 on personal bonds of Rs. 20,000 each with two sureties of Rs. 10,000 each

legal_representation: Accused (appellants): Rajiv Garg, Ashish Garg and Annam D.N. Rao. State: Kuldip Singh

prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Not stated

case_title: Kilakkatha Parambath Sasi & Ors. v. State of Kerala
accused_victim_relationship: Political rival (alleged): accused described as members of one political party, victim and his brother as workers of a rival party. No other prior connection stated.
statutory_provisions: IPC ss.147, 148, 307, 324, 302 r/w s.149 (charged); four appellants convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34
weapon: Sword, axe and knife; the prosecution also suggested accused nos.5 to 7 were armed with a crow bar and sticks
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured brother and passengers/independent witnesses); medical (post-mortem and injury examination); FIR and promptness of recording; seizure of bus trip-sheet (documentary)
aggravating_circumstances: Deceased suffered 58 injuries, most incised and cutting, some of huge dimensions; attack by a group allegedly motivated by political animosity
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted all seven accused
high_court_outcome: Acquittal reversed for four accused (Sasi, Dasan, Ashokan, Babu): convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34 and sentenced to life imprisonment; acquittal of the other three maintained
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 r/w s.34
neutral_facts: Around mid-afternoon the victim and his brother boarded the same bus, having met by chance, with about ten to fifteen other passengers on board. Shortly after the bus reached a bus stand, the accused allegedly threatened to kill them and pushed both men off the bus onto the road. Other men ran from a nearby shop. Weapons were handed over, and the accused allegedly used a sword, an axe and a knife, while further men were said to have caused injuries with a crow bar and sticks. The brother received three incised wounds. The victim suffered 58 injuries, most of them incised and cutting wounds, some of large size, and died in hospital later that day. Police reached the scene about an hour after the incident and took the injured to hospital. The brother's statement was recorded at the hospital at about 5.30 p.m., and a formal report was registered at 7.15 p.m. and sent to the magistrate that night. The prosecution alleged that the assault arose from political rivalry between the groups involved. Evidence presented included the injured brother's account, statements from two passengers on the bus, an independent autorickshaw driver who said he witnessed the incident while getting his vehicle repaired, medical evidence from the post-mortem and from the examination of the brother, and the investigating officer's evidence that he had seized the bus trip-sheet. The bus crew were not examined as witnesses.
physical_harm: Victim (brother) died from 58 mostly incised and cutting wounds; injured witness PW-1 had three incised wounds
premeditation_planning: Not found by the Supreme Court. Prosecution alleged an unlawful assembly was formed and the attack occurred when the victims got off the bus; defence argued the accused were involved after deliberation.
motive: alleged: political animosity between the accused's party and the victim's party (Congress workers)
key_evidence_accepted: Injured eyewitness PW-1's account; PW-2 presence accepted though not named in FIR (named as present at hospital); PW-3 categoric eyewitness statement; PW-4 independent autorickshaw driver; promptly recorded FIR; medical evidence; seized trip-sheet
witness_credibility: PW-1 is an injured witness whose presence cannot be disputed and who was not an active political worker, so false implication appeared remote; PW-4 is truly independent with no reason to discard his evidence; PW-2's absence from the FIR does not mean he was not present; the Trial Court's doubts were held farfetched
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 24 March 1994; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 23.05.2003; Supreme Court: 4 February 2011
legal_representation: Accused/appellants: U.R. Lalit (senior counsel), E.M.S. Anam, Fazlin Anam. State of Kerala: Dinesh Dwivedi, G. Prakash, Beena Prakash, V. Senthil
investigation_status: FIR registered on the injured witness's statement; investigation completed; accused charged under IPC
procedural_irregularity: Bus crew not examined although the investigating officer seized the trip-sheet; the Supreme Court held this not fatal to the prosecution. The Trial Court's finding of FIR delay was held perverse.
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted all seven. High Court: acquittal reversed for four (convicted under s.302 r/w s.34, life imprisonment); acquittal of three upheld. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: High Court interference was justified because the trial judgment was perverse; there was no delay in lodging the FIR; PW-1, an injured witness, cannot be doubted, and not naming all seven at first was of no consequence since the three unnamed accused were acquitted
defence_argument: Unexplained FIR delay allowed the prosecution to fabricate a story against innocent persons; three accused were apparently not present; eyewitness accounts were discrepant and contradicted by medical evidence; PW-2 was not named in the FIR; bus crew not examined; the facts did not justify interference in an appeal against acquittal
legal_principle_applied: Appellate court should not interfere with acquittal save in exceptional cases, and only if the trial findings are not borne out by the evidence and are perverse; but the High Court may re-appraise evidence and must interfere if the trial findings were not possible on the evidence to avoid travesty of justice
precedent_relied_upon: Arulvelu and Anr. v. State represented by the Public Prosecutor and Anr., (2009) 10 SCC 206
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Sheo Shankar Singh v. State of Jharkhand & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Political/land rival and prior enmity: the deceased, a sitting MLA, opposed the accused's coal-theft activities and helped restore a petrol pump against the accused's family's interests (as the court accepted)
statutory_provisions: Charged: IPC s.302, s.34, s.120B, s.201; Arms Act s.27 (Umesh Singh). Convictions for appellants: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; Arms Act s.27 (Umesh Singh)
weapon: Pistol (9 mm bullets; empty cartridges recovered from scene)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (two eyewitnesses); identification (court and test identification parade); recovery/seizure (motorcycles, cartridges, blood-stained clothing); medical evidence; motive evidence; post-mortem
aggravating_circumstances: Killing of a sitting MLA by gunfire at close range; a further shot fired at the victim on the ground; body pushed down roadside slope
mitigating_circumstances: Accused not professional killers; no political angle to killing; nothing particularly brutal in manner of execution; difference of opinion on sentence between trial court and High Court
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life; Umesh Singh additionally convicted under Arms Act s.27 and sentenced to three years rigorous imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Convictions upheld; life sentence enhanced to death sentence; revision seeking enhancement allowed
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (both appellants); Arms Act s.27 (Umesh Singh)
neutral_facts: On an afternoon in April 2000, the victim, a sitting state legislator, was riding as a pillion passenger on a motorcycle driven by an informant on a road near a coal-handling site. The informant heard a gunshot from behind and saw a black motorcycle without a registration number running alongside on the left. It was driven by the accused, with a second man on the pillion holding a pistol. The pillion rider fired at close range; the victim was struck in the head, slumped onto the informant, and both men fell to the road. The driver stopped a short distance ahead. The second man walked back, threatened the informant to leave, fired another shot at the victim, pushed the body down the roadside slope, and both men rode away towards a nearby town. Two bystanders who arrived afterwards stated that they had earlier seen the accused riding the same unregistered motorcycle with a pillion passenger in the area. The informant's motorcycle was seized from the scene. A second black unregistered motorcycle was seized from premises linked to the accused; its registration certificate was in another person's name. Two 9 mm empty cartridges were recovered from the scene. The informant's blood-stained T-shirt and torn jeans were seized. A medical examination that evening recorded injuries consistent with a fall. The post-mortem recorded gunshot wounds to the head as the cause of death. The informant identified the pillion rider in court, and one bystander identified him in a test identification parade. Investigators did not send the clothing to a forensic laboratory or the cartridges to a ballistics expert, and the weapon was never recovered. Evidence of a dispute over a petrol pump and of the victim's action against coal theft was also given.
offence_severity: Death or imprisonment for life (as described in the judgment; life imprisonment is the normal rule and death an exception); no fine or minimum stated
physical_harm: Victim died of gunshot wounds to the head (multiple entry and exit wounds). The eyewitness suffered abrasions and injuries when he fell from the motorcycle.
number_of_offences: 5 charged (IPC ss.302, 34, 120B, 201; Arms Act s.27); 2 finally upheld for the appellants (IPC s.302 r/w s.34 for both; Arms Act s.27 for Umesh Singh)
motive: Accepted by the court: the accused were part of a coal mafia; the victim, an MLA, opposed coal theft and helped restore a petrol pump to a complainant, which annoyed the accused and their family. The victim was perceived as a hurdle to their activities.
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness accounts of PW16 and PW6; PW1 and PW2 sightings of accused on the motorcycle and PW1 test identification of Umesh Singh; seizure of motorcycles, cartridges, blood-stained clothing; medical evidence of PW16's injuries; prompt FIR; motive evidence from PW15, PW16 and PW19
witness_credibility: PW16 found consistent and reliable by both courts, with no enmity or bias shown; PW1 and PW2 corroborated his presence; PW6 accepted despite a month-and-a-half delay in recording his statement, as the investigating officer's explanation was accepted; PW1's identification accepted
post_offence_conduct: Fled the scene on the motorcycle after the shooting, per the accepted eyewitness account; no surrender or disclosure noted
trial_duration: offence: 14 April 2000; trial judgment: 18 November 2003 (guilt), 20 November 2003 (sentence order); High Court: 6 May 2005; Supreme Court: 15 February 2011
legal_representation: Accused: U.R. Lalit (senior counsel) with others; State/respondents: A.T.M. Rangaramanujam and Sunil Kumar (senior counsel)
investigation_status: FIR registered (Police Station Govindpur); investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: No reference made to forensic laboratory for blood-stained T-shirt or to ballistics expert for cartridges; PW16 not put through a test identification parade; month-and-a-half delay in recording PW6's statement
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, life imprisonment. High Court: convictions upheld, sentence enhanced to death. Supreme Court: convictions affirmed, death sentence commuted to life imprisonment
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Failure to hold a test identification parade for PW16 casts doubt on his identification of Umesh Singh; PW16 could not have looked back while driving; PW6 was not an eyewitness and his statement was delayed; no forensic or ballistic examination; motorcycle borrowing not corroborated; FIR lodging doubted; death sentence not warranted
legal_principle_applied: Motive recedes where eyewitness testimony is credible but supports the case if proved; TIP is corroboration only and its absence does not weaken in-court identification; mere delay in examining a witness is not fatal; investigative lapses do not justify total rejection; rarest of rare test for death penalty

neutral_facts: On the morning of 30 August 1984, the victim went out to relieve herself. While returning home she was intercepted by the accused, taken to a nearby field and raped. The accused threatened her with consequences if she disclosed the incident. She returned home and told her parents, who accompanied her to the police outpost at Pathriya, where no police official was present. The next day, around 12:15 p.m., she lodged a report at Sironj Police Station, about 22 km from the place of incident, although Unarasital police station was only 7 km away. At her insistence, and after declining examination at Sironj, she was medically examined at a hospital at Vasoda, about 55 km away. The examining doctor, who examined her about 24 hours after the incident, found no injury on the genitalia and deposed that the tear in the hymen was old, so there was no evidence of rape. The victim stated that her vagina had been stitched, but the doctor found no stitches. The investigation was conducted by Unarasital police, who seized the victim's petticoat and sent it for examination. The parents' account was based on what the victim had told them.

neutral_facts: On 29 December 1998, at about 5 p.m., the accused allegedly poured kerosene on the body of the victim, who was his wife, and set her on fire. Two persons immediately took the victim to a hospital, where a doctor treated her and informed the police station. A police sub-inspector went to the hospital and recorded a dying declaration. In it the victim stated that the accused often drank liquor, quarrelled with her and assaulted her when drunk. On the same day the accused had given her Rs. 200 for groceries and taken back Rs. 100 of it, so she bought groceries with the remaining Rs. 100. Later that day he returned, demanded the Rs. 100 back and asked her to return the groceries. When she refused, he became angry, tied her hands, poured kerosene on her body and set her ablaze. The victim died of the burn injuries on 19 January 1999. The treating doctor endorsed that the victim was in a fit mental condition to depose before the police. A Forensic Science Laboratory report found kerosene residue on the victim's brassiere, saree and petticoat. The two persons who took the victim to hospital turned hostile during their testimony. No second dying declaration was recorded before a Magistrate. The accused offered no explanation for the kerosene found on the victim's clothing, and no suggestion of suicide or accident was put forward.

neutral_facts: On 25 March 1996, a group of related men from one family, who lived close together in the same locality, gathered at a house and drank liquor to celebrate a family marriage proposal. Around 1 p.m. they came into the street and raised a challenge that they would teach a neighbouring family a lesson for having teased a daughter of one of the men. Some were armed with small knives and others with lathis. A member of the victim's family came out to persuade them not to abuse and to settle the dispute the next morning. Two other members of the victim's family then arrived. The men shouted that the victim's side should not be allowed to live. One man stabbed the victim on the right side of the abdomen. When a second family member came forward to help, another man stabbed him below the chest, and a third man stabbed him on the lower right flank. That injured man fell, and another man struck him on the right shoulder with a blunt weapon. Women from the families then threw bricks, and the attackers ran from the spot. The victim and the injured man were taken to a hospital in a truck, and the victim died on the way. A doctor who examined the injured man at the initial stage declared him unfit to make a statement. A doctor conducted the post-mortem and recorded a small red abrasion on the right shoulder region, which was attributed to one of the men said to be carrying a lathi. The fatal stomach wound was deep and caused death within a short time.

neutral_facts: The victim, a married woman, died within the matrimonial home. The prosecution case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence. Several witnesses who were relatives of the victim, including the victim's father, a cousin and a brother, deposed that the victim had been subjected to consistent ill-treatment at the matrimonial home. According to their evidence, the accused was having an illicit relationship with a sister-in-law, and when the victim complained about this, the victim was tortured. The victim had written letters to her father complaining of this ill-treatment; one such letter was placed on record as an exhibit. Witnesses also spoke of beating and visible injury marks on the victim. The post-mortem was conducted by a doctor, who recorded two incised injuries on the body: a deep incised wound on the front of the neck, at the level of the thyroid cartilage, which had completely cut the trachea and cut major neck veins, and a second incised wound on the upper right side of the abdomen through which the small intestine protruded. The doctor's evidence was that these injuries were sufficient to cause death. The body showed some petrification because of the time gap between death and the post-mortem examination. The victim's identity was confirmed by the father, a cousin and a brother, and the hospital released the body to the father, who had it cremated. The defence case was that the victim had been suffering from jaundice and died a natural death. The only witness called in support was not shown to be a medical practitioner and stated only that the victim had been referred for treatment to Patna on 02.09.1993; no record of jaundice treatment was produced.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from deep incised neck injury (trachea completely cut, neck veins cut) and incised abdominal injury; additional beating and injury marks
motive: alleged: Accused's illicit relationship with his brother's wife; the victim complained of it and was tortured for complaining

witness_credibility: Related witnesses PWs 5-8 found cogent and reliable after careful scrutiny; relatives not discarded merely for being related; defence witness PW-12 not shown to be a medical practitioner and did not depose to jaundice

neutral_facts: On the day in question, a community panchayat meeting that had been convened earlier was not held. Later that day, several members of the complainant party were walking away from the house of one of the accused when the accused confronted them with abuse. One accused stabbed the victim in the chest with a knife. The victim collapsed and died almost immediately. Other accused allegedly struck two members of the complainant party with swords and another with a cycle chain, while a further accused pelted stones at the injured persons. A report of the incident was lodged by one of the complainant party. Police prepared a spot map, arrested the accused, and recovered the weapons of offence at their instance. The wife raised shouts for help. Family members, including the victim's brother who later lodged the complaint, rushed to the spot and found the victim with severe facial injuries and bleeding heavily. The victim was taken by tractor to a hospital, where he was declared dead on arrival. The complaint lodged that night stated that an unidentified person had assaulted the victim with an axe and run away. Later, after the wife had become somewhat composed, she told the victim's two brothers that the accused had struck her husband on the face with an axe. The brothers said that, while entering the field earlier, they had also seen the accused going away with an axe in hand. Their statements were recorded by police soon after. neutral_facts: The victim, a seventeen-year-old woman, went with her younger sister to meet her aunt at the aunt's house. While they were talking, a group of persons including the accused arrived at the house, and the victim was forcibly lifted into a blue Maruti van despite raised alarm by the aunt, her husband and neighbours. The victim was taken to a vacant building near a bridge and placed in a separate room, where two men were said to have sexually assaulted her while others fondled her body; one was said to have inserted a finger into her anus and another bit her cheek. The victim was later taken in the same van to another house, where she was beaten, and she then escaped by bus to meet her mother and sister, to whom she narrated the incident. An FIR was recorded the following night. The FIR described one man as short-statured with a beard and did not name the accused. Medical examination found no injuries to the labia, an old healed hymen tear, and no significant injuries apart from a cheek bite. Statements were recorded under sections 164 and 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Male semen was found in the victim's undergarments but was not sent for forensic analysis. No spot map was prepared, the investigating officer did not visit the spot, and the victim could not identify the building when taken to the area. No identification parade was held, and the victim had seen the accused at the police station before identifying him in court. The aunt, her husband, their sons, neighbours, the victim's mother and sister were not examined.
