case_title: Dandu Jaggaraju v. State of A.P.
victim_caste: Kshatriya (victim); husband was a member of the Scheduled Castes
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (paternal uncle of the victim)
weapon: None mentioned (death by smothering with the victim's chunni pushed into her mouth)
evidence_type: Last-seen (circumstantial) evidence, medical (post-mortem) evidence, recovery of jewellery, identification by witnesses
aggravating_circumstances: None noted (alleged family-honour motive was not accepted by the Court)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.302, 201 and 379; sentence amount not specified in the judgment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim, a woman who had married a man against her family's wishes, lived with her husband and young child in a house owned by another family. About six years after the marriage, the accused, a paternal uncle of the victim, telephoned the victim on 14 August 2002, saying her grandmother was seriously ill and that he would come to pick her up. A household member was sent to a telephone booth to guide him. The accused arrived, was brought to the house, and was introduced by the victim as her uncle. The victim left with the accused on a white scooter, leaving her young son behind. Her husband returned that evening and was told she had gone with the accused. She did not return that night or the next day. The husband lodged a report on 16 August 2002 that she had gone to relatives and had not been seen since. Her body was recovered later that day. A second report then recorded the husband's suspicion, for the first time, that the accused had lured her away and killed her. A post-mortem found death by asphyxia due to smothering, with her scarf pushed into her mouth. The accused was arrested on 7 September 2002, and jewellery the victim was said to have been wearing when she disappeared was recovered from the accused's pockets. The prosecution relied on last-seen testimony from household members and a press reporter who saw the victim and the accused at a bus stand, on the jewellery recovery, and on the post-mortem findings. Witnesses who had seen the accused gave statements to a magistrate about four months later, and one witness identified the accused in court more than two years after the event.
physical_harm: Death by asphyxia due to smothering
financial_property_loss: Alleged loss of victim's jewellery (ornaments); the Court described them as 'disco jewellery' of trifling value
premeditation_planning: Not found by the Court; prosecution alleged the victim was lured away under a pretext
motive: alleged: family annoyance at the victim's marriage to a member of the Scheduled Castes, against family wishes (family honour); the Court found the motive clearly suspect and did not accept it
key_evidence_accepted: None accepted as connecting the accused. The Court found last-seen evidence uncertain and the jewellery recovery unbelievable; post-mortem cause of death was recorded but did not link the accused to the crime
witness_credibility: Last-seen witnesses (P.Ws. 2, 3, 6) found uncertain: late s.164 statements, no test identification parade, and P.W.6 knew the accused only by sight and first identified him in court two and a half years later
post_offence_conduct: Prosecution alleged the accused carried the victim's jewellery until arrest 24 days later; the Court found this completely unacceptable and not credible
custody_duration: In custody from arrest on 7 September 2002; still in custody at the time of the Supreme Court judgment
trial_duration: offence: 14 August 2002; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 20 February 2007; Supreme Court: 20 July 2011
legal_representation: Accused: Siddharth Dave (Amicus) with Jemtiben A.o.; State of Andhra Pradesh: D. Mahesh Babu, Ramesh Allanki, Savita Dhanda
investigation_status: Missing-person FIR 16 Aug 2002; second FIR after body recovery; investigation completed; accused arrested 7 Sept 2002 and tried
procedural_irregularity: No test identification parade held; s.164 statements recorded about four months after the incident
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.302, 201, 379 IPC. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: Last-seen evidence and jewellery recoveries together formed a complete chain; concurrent findings of guilt should not be disturbed
defence_argument: No evidence connected the accused to the crime; the first report was of a missing person with no suspicion expressed; apart from last-seen evidence, recoveries could not be believed; the chain was missing
legal_principle_applied: In circumstantial cases each link, including motive, must be proved; last-seen evidence, identification and recovery (including s.27 disclosure) must be reliable
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
other_sentence_order: Accused to be released forthwith if not wanted in any other case; Amicus fee fixed at Rs. 7,000

case_title: Shyamal Ghosh v. State of West Bengal
accused_victim_relationship: Prior dispute/extortion: accused demanded Rs.40,000 ('Tola Mastani Salami') over the victim's shop rooms and threatened him; no family or personal relationship stated.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.201, s.379, s.411 read with s.34
weapon: Sharp cutting weapon (chopper) for dismemberment; gumcha used for strangulation
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; circumstantial (last seen together); recovery of weapon, van and cycle; medical (post-mortem); documentary (FIR, post-mortem report, seizure memos)
confession: Admission by accused Bishu leading to recovery of the chopper; the Court relied on the recovery, not on the admission as a confession.
aggravating_circumstances: Brutal killing and dismemberment of the body; threats and extortion demand; absconding for days together
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of all charges (ss.302, 201, 379, 411 r/w s.34); death sentence under s.302; s.201 seven years RI and fine; s.379 three years and fine
high_court_outcome: Death reference answered in negative; s.379/34 acquittal; s.302/34 conviction maintained with life imprisonment and Rs.5,000 fine; s.201/34 sentence maintained
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 read with s.34 (murder); IPC s.201 read with s.34 (disappearance of evidence)
neutral_facts: The victim had constructed shop rooms on his own land for letting out. A group of men demanded Rs. 40,000 from him as a payment connected with the construction and threatened him with dire consequences if it was not paid. The threats were repeated over several weeks, including at the victim's house, and on 27 September the group said they would murder him if the money was not paid within a day. On the night of 29 September the victim left home on his bicycle to collect money from a business contact and set out for home around 11 p.m. Near a field on his route he was stopped by a group of men and an altercation followed. Eyewitnesses saw several of the accused strangle him with a gumcha. The body was then cut into pieces with a sharp cutting weapon and packed into gunny bags. On the following evening, witnesses saw several of the accused loading the gunny bags into a steel-coloured Maruti van at a rickshaw stand. Two gunny bags containing body parts were later found by a passer-by, who reported them to the police. The victim's wife and brother lodged a missing diary report and later identified the body. The van driver was arrested and the van was recovered on his statement. The victim's bicycle and a chopper were recovered on the statements of accused persons. Post-mortem found death due to ligature strangulation and that all body parts belonged to one person. Several accused absconded for a long period and were arrested later from other places. At identification, eyewitnesses identified all the accused in court, while the van driver did not identify one accused.
physical_harm: Death by strangulation by ligature; body severed into multiple pieces (head, limbs, torso)
number_of_offences: 4 charged; 2 finally upheld (s.302/34 and s.201/34); s.379 acquitted by High Court; s.411 not separately addressed by the Supreme Court
financial_property_loss: Victim's cash, four rings and HMT watch with him (reported by witness); extortion demand of Rs.40,000 (not paid)
premeditation_planning: Court found common intention to do away with the victim if the Rs.40,000 demand was not met; no express finding of premeditated planning beyond this
motive: Illegal demand of Rs.40,000 coupled with threats of dire consequences (accepted by the Court)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitnesses PW8, PW17, PW19 (altercation and strangulation); PW7, PW9, PW11 (loading of gunny bags into van); PW16 post-mortem; recoveries of chopper, van and cycle; last seen together evidence
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses found reliable and trustworthy; related witnesses (PW2, PW4, PW6) not rejected mechanically; hostile witnesses PW13 and PW23 relied on only to extent they support prosecution; minor timing variations not material
post_offence_conduct: Absconded immediately after the occurrence for days together, arrested later from Delhi and Sodhpur; one accused admitted absconding and surrendered after charges were framed
trial_duration: offence: 29th/30th September, 2003 (midnight); trial judgment: 13 September 2005; High Court: 5 February 2007; Supreme Court: 11 July 2012
legal_representation: Counsel listed collectively for the appearing parties; the judgment does not separate counsel for the accused and for the State
investigation_status: FIR registered (Case No. 332/03); investigation completed; charge sheet filed against six accused, two absconders later arrested and charged; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Investigation lapses: no FSL submission of gunny bags and weapons, no photographs or site plan; delay of 3 to 20 days in recording some witness statements; no test identification parade success for one accused
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, death sentence. High Court: s.379/34 acquitted, s.302/34 life imprisonment, death reference answered in negative. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Clear motive of demand of money; eyewitnesses reliable; absconding and s.313 statements support prosecution; hostile witnesses and investigation defects do not help accused; s.34 ingredients satisfied
defence_argument: Circumstantial chain incomplete; hostile witnesses PW13 and PW23; eyewitnesses PW8, PW17, PW19 did not name accused and were tutored or chance witnesses; delay in recording statements; no test identification parade identification; no common intention for s.34
legal_principle_applied: Last seen together theory and shifting of onus; s.34 IPC common intention and participation; contradiction and omission test; hostile witness principle; test identification parade as corroboration; defects in investigation not fatal
precedent_relied_upon: Govindaraju v. State (2012) 4 SCC 122; Brathi v. State of Punjab (1991) 1 SCC 519; Banti v. State of M.P. (2004) 1 SCC 414; State of U.P. v. Satish (2005) 3 SCC 114; S.K. case_title: Sri Bhagwan v. State of U.P.
accused_occupation: Small grocery shop owner (as argued on behalf of the appellant; not a court finding)
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (conviction); IPC s.326 (originally registered offence)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PWs 1 and 3); dying declaration (s.161 CrPC statement treated as s.32(1) declaration); medical evidence (injury report and post-mortem); recovery of gloves with chemical report
aggravating_circumstances: Acid attack causing extensive burns and death of the victim; accused reportedly attempted to flee on being seen
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and life sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: On the night of 26 May 1980, at about 10.45 p.m., two local residents who were guarding their colony nearby heard screams from a bus stand about 250 yards away and ran to the spot. They said they saw the accused pouring acid on the victim, who was suffering burn injuries. They said the accused was heard saying he would pay a sum of money that day. When the witnesses approached, the accused tried to run away but was caught by bystanders. The accused and the victim were taken to a police station by about 11.10 p.m., and a complaint by one of the witnesses led to an FIR under s.326 IPC. An officer recorded the victim's statement within about ten minutes so that he could be sent to hospital. In that statement the victim said the accused had thrown acid on him. A doctor examined the victim and recorded superficial burns on the face, neck, tongue, back, and other parts of the body. The victim died the next day from the burns, and a post-mortem was conducted. The investigating officer inspected the scene and collected an acid bottle, a bag, and gloves. A chemical report found acid on burnt rubber gloves. No acid marks were found on the accused's body. The defence pointed to the absence of a street light on the site plan, the victim's tongue injury, and the failure to seize the victim's clothes for chemical examination.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from extensive acid burns (superficial burns on face, neck, tongue, back and other body parts)
premeditation_planning: Not expressly found as premeditation; court noted the accused took precautions (wearing gloves) while throwing acid
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness accounts of PWs 1 and 3; victim's s.161 CrPC statement (Ex Ka-2) accepted as dying declaration; injury report Ka-17 and post-mortem report Ka-13 with PW-5 testimony; chemical report Ka-18 on burnt rubber gloves
witness_credibility: PWs 1 and 3 found convincing, natural and credible; not interested witnesses; not stock witnesses; no prior deposition in other cases shown; their statements were not diluted by their account of the victim's statement
post_offence_conduct: Attempted to flee the scene and was caught by bystanders; no other post-offence conduct noted
trial_duration: offence: 26.05.1980; trial judgment: 06.09.1982; High Court: 28.11.2008; Supreme Court: 06 December 2012
legal_representation: Accused: M.P. Shorawala, Jyoti Saxena, Ranbir Yadav, Anzu K. Varkey and Shashi Kiran. State: Ratnakar Dash, Alka Sinha and Anuvrat Sharma
investigation_status: FIR registered under s.326 IPC; case altered to s.302 IPC after death; site inspected and articles collected; charge-sheet filed; chemical examination completed; investigation taken over by S.H.O. on 28.05.1980; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Defence argued non-compliance with Police Regulation 115 (two witnesses, signatures for dying declaration); court held it did not apply to a s.161 statement. Clothes of the deceased not sent for chemical examination; court held this isolated and not fatal
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Eyewitnesses were strangers with no reason to implicate the accused; statement of the victim was a valid dying declaration under s.32(1) Evidence Act; FIR and bringing both persons to the police station showed the case was truly projected; the Police Regulation 115 point was not raised below and was irrelevant
defence_argument: Witnesses could not have seen the incident; victim with tongue burns could not make a statement; s.161 statement was not a valid dying declaration (no Police Regulation 115 attestation); no acid marks on accused; witnesses were stock witnesses; arrest suppressed; absence of street light on site plan; accused was grieving his father
legal_principle_applied: A s.161 CrPC statement by a victim who later dies may be treated as a dying declaration under s.32(1) Evidence Act and carry the same credence; conviction may rest on a true and voluntary dying declaration without corroboration; eyewitnesses assessed for interest and stock-witness status; police regulation does not override statutory provisions

case_title: Krishan v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.498A, s.109 read with s.34 (FIR originally under s.307, converted to s.302)
evidence_type: Dying declaration (primary); medical evidence (post-mortem); Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate and investigating officer testimony; partial support from hostile witnesses
aggravating_circumstances: Alleged in dying declaration: beatings under influence of liquor and demands for money for a car; court did not separately weigh these as aggravating
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted both accused (benefit of doubt; dying declaration held not safe to rely upon)
high_court_outcome: Conviction of Krishan upheld by reversing acquittal; acquittal of mother Shardi maintained
offence_finally_established: Murder (causing death of wife by burning); specific sections of conviction not separately stated in judgment
neutral_facts: The victim was admitted to a hospital with serious burn injuries after a fire at the matrimonial home. The investigating police officer obtained a doctor's endorsement that the victim was fit to make a statement. A Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate then recorded the victim's statement at the hospital in question-and-answer form, and the victim's thumb impression was taken on it and identified by the investigating officer. In the statement the victim said that the accused, the victim's husband, had often beaten the victim while under the influence of liquor and had demanded money from the victim's father to buy a car. The victim said that on the morning of the incident the accused poured kerosene oil on the victim's body and set it on fire, and that the victim's father-in-law and sister-in-law came and helped put out the fire. The accused's mother was said to have instigated the accused. The victim died a few days later. The post-mortem examination found superficial to deep burns covering about 75 per cent of the body, sparing the lower thighs, legs and feet, and concluded that the burns were ante-mortem and sufficient to cause death. The victim's father, mother and sister were examined at trial but did not fully support the prosecution. The father said the accused had demanded money for a vehicle and that he had refused. The mother said the victim was never harassed for dowry. The sister of the accused said the victim caught fire while preparing tea and that the accused was not at home. The investigating officer, the magistrate and other police witnesses gave evidence on the recording of the statement and the investigation.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from burns (about 75% of body surface, superficial to deep); burns ante-mortem and sufficient to cause death
number_of_offences: 3 charged (ss.302, 498A, 109 read with s.34); conviction upheld, sections of conviction not separately stated
motive: alleged: demands for money to buy a car from the victim's father, and beatings by the accused under influence of liquor (as stated in dying declaration; court did not separately decide motive)
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration (Ex. PR/2) recorded by SDJM after doctor's fitness endorsement; post-mortem findings of PW14; partial support from PW1, PW9, PW11, PW14, SDJM and other police witnesses
witness_credibility: Hostile witnesses PW1, PW3 and PW4 held not to undermine the dying declaration; their evidence relied on only to the extent it supports the prosecution (e.g. PW1 on car money demand); doctor's cross-examination answer on burnt thumb held to offer no advantage to defence
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: not given (FIR registered 30 March 1998; victim died 2 April 1998); trial judgment: 15 November 1999; High Court: 17 July 2007; Supreme Court: 13 December 2012
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: Ram Naresh Yadav and Dr. Kailash Chand; State/respondent: Kamal Mohan Gupta, Mohd. Zahid Hussain and Sanjeev Kumar
investigation_status: FIR registered 30 March 1998 on dying declaration, later amended to s.302 after death; site plan, inquest and post-mortem conducted; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted both accused. High Court: convicted Krishan, maintained acquittal of Shardi. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld
prosecution_argument: Dying declaration can be relied upon without corroboration if true; hostility of witnesses does not defeat it (State relied on Ram Sagar Yadav)
defence_argument: Dying declaration unsafe as sole basis without corroboration (Khushal Rao); doctor's answer that both hands were burnt including thumb meant thumb impression could not have been taken; hostile witnesses leave prosecution case unproved
legal_principle_applied: A dying declaration can be the sole basis of conviction if true, reliable and recorded per established practice; hostility of witnesses is relevant but not determinative

case_title: Govindaraju @ Govinda v. State by Sriramapuram P.S.
accused_victim_relationship: Prior dispute: an earlier police complaint of a fight between the accused and the deceased, as recounted by the victim's brother; the Court used this to doubt the accused's involvement
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34
evidence_type: Eyewitness (a police officer, PW-1, as sole eyewitness); recovery evidence (seizure and disclosure-based); medical evidence (post-mortem); forensic (FSL) report
confession: None. Recoveries linked to disclosure statements were found defective and not relied upon against the accused.
aggravating_circumstances: Ten stab injuries to the chest recorded in the post-mortem; the Court did not weigh these as aggravating for sentencing
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of IPC s.302 read with s.34
high_court_outcome: Leave to appeal granted against the accused; acquittal set aside; convicted under IPC s.302 and sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine of Rs.10,000
neutral_facts: On 7 December 1998, at about 10.45 p.m., a police sub-inspector returning from duty on his motorcycle reportedly saw three men chasing another man near a bar. The pursued man fell to the road, and the chasers stabbed him repeatedly on the chest with a knife. The officer, about 30 yards away, said one of the attackers told another to run because police were coming, and the group fled into a nearby conservancy area. The officer chased them but could not catch them. He returned, found the injured man, and with the help of a constable took him to hospital, where he was declared dead. An identity card in the victim's pockets identified him. The officer then lodged a written complaint at the police station, on which the first information report was registered. The investigating officer recorded witness statements and recovered knives and blood-soaked earth, and the items were sent to the forensic laboratory. The post-mortem recorded ten stab injuries to the chest, with death attributed to shock and haemorrhage. Several eyewitnesses later did not support the officer's account. The recovery memos lacked the accused's signatures on the disclosure statements, and the recovery witnesses did not support the recoveries. One knife recovered at another accused's instance was blood-stained, but it was not established whether the blood was human or of the victim's blood group. The head constable, the constable and the doctor were not examined, and no forensic expert testified.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock and haemorrhage due to ten stab injuries, chiefly to the chest
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Post-mortem report establishing knife injuries to the chest. The Court found the sole eyewitness's account unreliable and did not accept the recovery evidence against the accused.
witness_credibility: The sole eyewitness, a police officer (PW-1), was held not reliable: he was about 30 yards away on a motorcycle, did not name the accused in the FIR or to the investigating officer, and was not corroborated. Other eyewitnesses (PW-2, PW-7, PW-9, PW-10) turned hostile. The investigating officer (PW-11) was found to have left material witnesses unexamined.
post_offence_conduct: Alleged: after the attack the assailants fled into a conservancy area when police approached (prosecution version of PW-1; not established by the Court)
bail_history: Bail and surety bonds existed; the Supreme Court ordered the accused set at liberty and the bonds discharged. Earlier bail details not stated.
trial_duration: offence: 7 December 1998; trial judgment: 9 March 2000; High Court: 29 November 2006; Supreme Court: 15 March 2012
legal_representation: Accused (appellant): Rajesh Mahale, Krutin R. Joshi. State (respondents): Anitha Shenoy, Hetu Arora
investigation_status: FIR registered on the police officer's complaint; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial completed in the Sessions court
procedural_irregularity: Doctor, head constable, constable and FSL expert not examined; recovery memos lacked accused's signatures on disclosure statements; blood group of the stained knife not proved
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted (9 March 2000). High Court: leave granted against the accused, conviction under s.302 and life imprisonment (29 November 2006). Supreme Court: appeal allowed, accused acquitted.
prosecution_argument: The State contended the case was not one of false implication; PW-1 was the eyewitness; weapons were recovered from the appellant's house; panchas admitted their signatures; the collective documentary and ocular evidence proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_argument: All witnesses turned hostile; the sole police eyewitness was interested and the accused was falsely implicated; no independent witnesses; recovery not proved under s.27 Evidence Act; no seizure witness; ocular evidence not supported by medical or scientific evidence; the accused's role was lesser than that of the co-accused whose acquittal had become final.
legal_principle_applied: In an appeal against acquittal, presumption of innocence is reinforced; interference only where the trial judgment is perverse, with a clear distinction between perversity and merely another possible view. Police testimony must be reliable, trustworthy and corroborated; hostile witnesses' supportive parts may be used; adverse inference may be drawn for withholding material witnesses.

case_title: Rajesh Bhatnagar v. State of Uttarakhand
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband Mukesh Bhatnagar); Relative (brother-in-law Rajesh Bhatnagar and mother-in-law, co-accused)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B
evidence_type: Ocular (PW1 uncle, PW2 mother), medical (post-mortem and injury evidence), documentary (letters written by the deceased), recovery of articles from the scene, circumstantial
aggravating_circumstances: Death within seven years of marriage; persistent dowry demands; beatings and cruelty; brutal manner; false defence; absconding after the death
mitigating_circumstances: None noted (defence argued youth of accused and age of their mother; Court found no mitigating circumstances)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.304-B IPC; life imprisonment for all three accused
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and life sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim married the accused husband in May 1994 after an engagement during which the accused family demanded a refrigerator; the victim's family paid Rs.10,000 before the engagement ceremony was completed. After the marriage the accused demanded a television and a cooler, and the victim told her family she was beaten for not bringing them. She was sent back to her parental home and later returned to the matrimonial home after relatives gave an assurance; when leaving she said she feared her in-laws would kill her. In February 1996 a relative received a call that an accident had befallen the victim. The victim's mother and uncle went to the matrimonial home and learnt that she had been sprinkled with kerosene and set on fire for failing to bring the television and cooler. The victim's mother lodged a written complaint the same day. Police found the house open and the accused absent. At the scene police recovered a kerosene container, an empty container smelling of kerosene, burnt ash, a cloth rope, broken bangles and the victim's clothing. The post-mortem showed first and second degree burns over the whole body and death from ante-mortem injuries and shock. The accused husband had about twelve abrasions and contusions. The defence explanation was that he was hurt trying to break open a kitchen door during a stove fire; no burn injury was found on him and no cooking material was found in the kitchen. Letters written by the victim described beatings and cruelty.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by burning (first and second degree burns over the whole body) and ante-mortem injuries and shock; accused husband had about twelve abrasions and contusions
financial_property_loss: Rs.10,000 paid to accused for a refrigerator demanded at engagement
motive: Dowry demands for a refrigerator, television and cooler, which the victim's family could not meet
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent ocular testimony of PW1 (uncle) and PW2 (mother) and the complaint lodged on the day; the victim's letters read with that testimony; post-mortem evidence of burns; recovery of kerosene containers and burnt articles; injuries on accused without burns; trial court's reasons on the false stove-accident defence
witness_credibility: PW2 gave the same complete account in the police report and on oath; PW1 fully corroborated her; no contradiction or variation found
post_offence_conduct: Accused absconded and left the house open after the death; Court treated this as indicating guilt
trial_duration: offence: 17 February 1996 (complaint lodged that day; date of death not separately given); trial judgment: 2 December 1996; High Court: 14 October 2009; Supreme Court: 10 May 2012
legal_representation: Accused: Dinesh Kumar Garg, Meha Aggarwal, Ashutosh Garg. State: S.S. Shamshery, Rahul Verma, Abhishek Atrey, Jatinder Kumar Bhatia

procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.304-B and sentenced to life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Not separately recorded; the prosecution case was that the accused burnt the victim for failing to meet dowry demands, and the Court accepted that case
defence_argument: Ingredients of s.304-B not satisfied because the letters did not mention dowry; no proximity between the refrigerator demand and the death; injuries were sustained in trying to rescue the victim; accidental stove fire; youth of accused and age of mother warranted a lesser sentence
legal_principle_applied: Three ingredients of s.304-B (death within seven years of marriage otherwise than in normal circumstances; cruelty or harassment soon before death; connection with dowry demand); presumption of causation under s.113-B Evidence Act; proximity test for 'soon before'; adverse inference from false plea

case_title: Polamuri Chandra Sekhararao @ Chinna @ Babji v. State of A.P.
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (nephew: victim is son of accused's elder sister); prior friction, as the accused was not on good terms with the victim's mother and the victim pursued the accused's daughter
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302
evidence_type: Circumstantial (eyewitnesses PW-1 and PW-2 turned hostile); medical (post-mortem); recovery of knife; forensic (FSL blood on knife); police and technician witness evidence
confession: Oral statement at police station that he had killed the deceased with the knife, as alleged by the prosecution; the Court did not treat it separately as a confession and relied on the surrounding circumstances
aggravating_circumstances: Seventeen injuries, thirteen of them incised cut wounds; killing within the accused's compound; no explanation for the body's presence
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000 (default three months simple imprisonment)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: On an evening in April 2004, the victim rode a motorcycle to the accused's house, where the accused and two daughters were chatting outside. When the accused asked why the victim had come, the victim reportedly said he wished to marry both of the accused's daughters and challenged the accused to say to whom they would be given. Angered, the accused fetched a long knife from the bedroom and struck the victim several times. The victim collapsed and died there. The accused, accompanied by the two daughters, travelled to a police station on a two-wheeler and handed over the knife to the station writer, stating that the victim had been killed with it. A first information statement was registered on that basis. The victim's body, with multiple bleeding wounds, was found in the compound of the accused's house. The knife was seized in the presence of a steel plant technician. A forensic laboratory found human blood on the knife, though its blood group could not be traced. The post-mortem doctor recorded seventeen injuries, thirteen of them incised cut wounds, and opined death from shock and haemorrhage; the doctor said the wounds could have been caused by a knife like the one recovered. The two daughters had been examined as eyewitnesses but did not support the first information statement when examined in court. The accused had been living apart from the spouse, who lived with her parents together with the daughters, and the victim had been staying in the same house as them. The accused had strained relations with the victim's mother. The accused asserted an alibi of shopping with the daughters, which was not corroborated.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock and haemorrhage; seventeen injuries, thirteen of them incised cut wounds
premeditation_planning: Not found; the Court described the killing as provoked by the accused's anger at the victim's conduct
motive: Accepted by the Court: the accused was enraged by the victim's attempt to develop a close relationship with the accused's daughter, which was not to his liking, combined with the accused's poor relations with the victim's mother
key_evidence_accepted: Presence of the body in the accused's compound (admitted); the first information statement Ext P-1 and the accused's presence at the police station; the knife seizure (Ext P-5); the FSL report (Ext P-29); the doctor's evidence on the injuries; the accused's admitted facts
witness_credibility: Hostile daughters' presence at the police station was admitted and the correctness of Ext P-1 was not open to challenge; related witnesses PW-3, PW-4, PW-6 and PW-7 were not discredited merely because of their relationship; the alibi of the hostile witnesses was rejected for lack of support
post_offence_conduct: Went to the police station with the daughters and handed over the knife, stating he had killed the victim (prosecution case); did not explain how the body came to be in his compound
trial_duration: offence: 06.04.2004; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 28.03.2008; Supreme Court: 23.07.2012
legal_representation: Appellant: Chanchal Kumar Ganguli. State/Respondent: Amit K. Nain, D. Mahesh Babu, Mayur R. Shah, Savita Devi
investigation_status: Ext P-1 registered as a s.302 IPC case on 06.04.2004; knife seized under Ext P-5; FSL report obtained; 15 witnesses examined at trial; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: PW-1 supported Ext P-1 in examination-in-chief and was hostile in cross-examination; the trial court's conclusion rests on other circumstances; motive existed; the accused gave no explanation for the body and the alibi failed
defence_argument: With the hostile eyewitnesses discounted, Ext P-1 cannot be acted upon; PWs-3, 4, 6 and 7 are related to the deceased and their version cannot be relied on; no incriminating circumstance connects the accused
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial chain analysis; a hostile witness's earlier statement corroborated by admitted presence at the police station; related witnesses not disbelieved merely because of relationship; the accused had to explain the presence of the body in his premises
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
judicial_aggravating_factors: Brutal knife wounding causing instantaneous death; killing within the accused's compound; no explanation for the body's presence
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Munna Kumar Upadhyaya @ Munna Upadhyaya v. State of Andhra Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Employer: co-accused A-1 was the domestic servant of the victim father and lived in the servant quarters, with a persistent grudge against the victim's wife. The appellant (A-2) was A-1's nephew; no direct relationship with the victims is described.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; s.201; s.411; s.435 (for A-2). Charged alternatively under s.380 IPC.
weapon: Knives and a country-made pistol; petrol used to burn the car and bodies
evidence_type: Circumstantial (no eyewitness), supported by neighbour and servant testimony, forensic blood and DNA evidence, fingerprint evidence, ballistics, petrol pump witness, doctor's evidence, recoveries and a test identification parade
confession: Extra-judicial confessions to panchas and to a doctor were made. The High Court declined to rely on them. The Supreme Court held that the admissible portions, namely use of articles and recoveries under s.27, and the doctor's treatment history were relevant and could be relied on.
aggravating_circumstances: Brutal killing of four family members, including a child; planned killing; robbery of cash and jewellery; destruction of evidence by burning the car and bodies; false explanations to visitors
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC (life imprisonment) and s.201, s.435 and s.411 IPC (3 years RI each), sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction of A-2 affirmed. A-3 and A-4 acquitted. A-1's death sentence commuted to life imprisonment.
offence_finally_established: Murder r/w s.34 IPC (s.302/34); s.201 IPC; s.411 IPC; s.435 IPC
neutral_facts: The victim, a railway official, lived in an official bungalow with his wife, son and daughter. A domestic servant employed by him lived in the servant quarters and allegedly held a grudge against the victim's wife. He allegedly planned with relatives and an associate to kill the family and take cash and jewellery. According to the prosecution, on the day in question the servant admitted several people to the house while the victim was at work. Armed with knives and a pistol, the group killed the son, the wife and the daughter in turn, and one of the group was shot during a struggle. When the victim returned from work in the evening, he was also killed. The bedroom almirah was broken open and cash and jewellery were taken. The bodies and blood-stained clothing were placed in a car, which was driven to a railway track area, doused with petrol bought from a petrol pump, and set on fire. Visitors were turned away with conflicting explanations. Investigators found the walls and floor blood-stained and the floor washed with phenyl and acid. Chance fingerprints matching the accused were lifted from the bedroom almirah. Items including a pistol, cartridges, knives, a cell phone and gold ornaments were recovered after statements by the accused. A forensic expert found human blood and flammable traces. A ballistics expert linked the cartridges to the recovered pistol. A doctor treated an injured accused, who attributed the gunshot injury to a fall. No eyewitness saw the killings.
physical_harm: Death of four family members (the victim, his wife, son and daughter) by throat cutting and gunshot/knife injuries; the bodies were burned. Co-accused A-3 suffered gunshot injuries to the leg.
number_of_offences: 5 charged (ss.302/34, 201, 435, and alternatively 380 or 411); 4 finally upheld (ss.302/34, 201, 411, 435)
financial_property_loss: Cash of Rs.44,560 and gold ornaments taken from the almirah; the car was destroyed by fire
premeditation_planning: Yes. The Court found the accused planned the killings and carried them out one by one, with a pre-arranged plan on the day.
motive: alleged: a persistent grudge of the domestic servant (A-1) towards the victim's wife, with a plan to kill the family and take gold and cash
key_evidence_accepted: Blood-stained walls and floor washed with phenyl and acid; neighbour, watchman, maid and carpenter testimony about being turned away; petrol pump witness (PW-25) on the purchase of 10 litres of petrol; forensic blood and flammable-material reports; ballistics report; DNA report; doctor and clinic evidence of gunshot injuries; chance fingerprints of A-2 on the bedroom almirah; PW-12 identification of recovered ornaments; recoveries; A-2's false answers under s.313 CrPC
witness_credibility: Court found the witnesses reliable and corroborative: the watchman, maid, carpenter, neighbours, the surviving daughter (PW-12), petrol pump helper, forensic and fingerprint experts. The fingerprint expert was cross-examined without material favouring the accused.
post_offence_conduct: Gave neighbours and servants false explanations that the family had gone out; burned the car and bodies after buying petrol; took an injured co-accused to a clinic and hospital and then went missing; A-2 gave false and incorrect answers under s.313 CrPC and did not explain his injuries
trial_duration: offence: 17 March 2003 (incident spanning 17/18 March 2003); trial judgment: 24 January 2007 (page 22; page 16 refers to 22 January 2007); High Court: 28 March 2007; Supreme Court: 8 May 2012
legal_representation: Appellant (A-2): A.T.M. Ranga Ramanujam, Gouri Karuna Das Mohanti, Deepak Agnihotri, Prakhar Sharma, Anu Gupta. State: D. Mahesh Babu, Mayur R. Shah, Shishir Pinaki.
investigation_status: FIR registered under ss.302 and 201 IPC; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: The investigating officer did not state in examination-in-chief that he had taken and sent the accused's fingerprints; the Court held this not fatal. The Court also noted a delay in holding the identification parade, which it held not fatal.
appeal_history: Trial court: all five convicted. High Court: A-3 and A-4 acquitted; convictions of A-1, A-2 and A-5 upheld (A-1's death sentence commuted to life). Supreme Court: A-2's appeal dismissed; A-1's SLP withdrawn; A-5 did not appeal.
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: (a) Circumstantial case is weak and the chain of circumstances does not point only to guilt; (b) fingerprint evidence is invalid because collection and dispatch to the lab were not proved; (c) the test identification parade was not held lawfully, was delayed, and photographs had been published; (d) co-accused's acquittal shows the prosecution failed, so A-2 should also be acquitted
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain pointing only to guilt, with each circumstance proved; extra-judicial confession must be true, voluntary and credible; delay in an identification parade is not fatal per se; adverse inference may be drawn from false answers under s.313 CrPC
precedent_relied_upon: Relied on: Asraf Ali v. State of Assam (2008) 16 SCC 328; Manu Sao v. State of Bihar (2010) 12 SCC 310; B.A. Umesh v. Registrar General (2011) 3 SCC 85. Referred to: Sanatan Naskar (2010) 8 SCC 249; Balwinder Singh (1995); Pakkirisamy (1997) 8 SCC 158; Kavita (1998) 6 SCC 108; Raja Ram (2003) 8 SCC 180; Aloke Nath Dutta (2007) 12 SCC 230; Sansar Chand (2010) 10 SCC 604; Sk. Yusuf (2011) 11 SCC 754; Pancho (2011) 10 SCC 165; Sidhartha Vashisht (2010) 6 SCC 1. Distinguished: Chandran (1991); Rajesh Govind Jagesha (1999) 8 SCC 428
judicial_aggravating_factors: Brutal manner of the killings; the planned killing of a family including a child; the accused's false stories and destruction of evidence; A-2's false and incorrect answers under s.313 CrPC, which the Court said tilt the case in favour of the prosecution
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Ramesh Harijan v. State of U.P.
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour (the accused's house was adjacent to the house where the victim's grandmother lived); no other relationship stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.376
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW.7, PW.8 saw the rape; PW.1 last seen and alleged extra-judicial confession); medical (post-mortem and serology); recovery (bed sheet and cloth with blood and semen); circumstantial (last seen together)
confession: Alleged extra-judicial confession (PW.1 testified to it). Trial court disbelieved it as not made in the presence of PW.7 and PW.8; the Supreme Court did not rely on it
aggravating_circumstances: Victim a child aged 5-6 years; rape with vaginal injuries leading to death; victim had been left in the accused's neighbourhood
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of both charges (s.302 and s.376 IPC); no sentence
high_court_outcome: State appeal allowed; acquittal reversed; convicted under ss.302 and 376 IPC; life imprisonment on both counts, sentences concurrent
neutral_facts: A girl aged about five to six years was found dead on a cot in a village where she was staying with her blind, infirm maternal grandmother, who was too poor and unable to care for her. The girl's grandmother's thatched house had collapsed, so the grandmother and the girl used to sleep in a house very close by, which belonged to the accused. The victim's mother was first told the girl had died of paralysis, and the body was buried on a riverbank. Later, the mother received information from several villagers that the girl had been raped and killed by the accused, and she asked for the body to be exhumed. After an order of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, the body was dug out and examined on 3.2.1996 by two doctors. They found multiple contusions on the face, neck, shoulder and back, and vaginal injuries including lacerations, and stated that the death was caused by shock and haemorrhage from ante-mortem vaginal injuries. One witness deposed that he had been returning home at about 9.00 p.m. with a companion, heard whispering near the accused's house, and focused a torch and saw the accused raping the girl beneath a tree outside the house. The companion raised a cry, villagers gathered, and the accused ran away. Another witness deposed that the accused had confessed the crime to him in the presence of two others. A part of a bed sheet and white cloth were recovered during the investigation, and forensic examination found human blood and semen on them, as well as on a vaginal swab taken by the doctor. The accused was arrested at a road junction in the early hours of the following day while waiting for transport. Several other witnesses did not support the prosecution account.
physical_harm: Death of the child from shock and haemorrhage due to ante-mortem vaginal injuries; multiple contusions and abrasions on face, neck, shoulder and back; vaginal tears and lacerations
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Recovery of bed sheet and white cloth with blood and semen (serology report, vaginal swab); medical evidence of ante-mortem vaginal injuries; last seen evidence of PW.1, PW.7 and PW.8 accepted at least that the deceased was last seen with the accused; hostile witnesses' relevant parts usable
witness_credibility: Court accepted some exaggeration in PW.1, PW.7 and PW.8 but held minor discrepancies unimportant and the duty of the court is to unravel truth; hostile witnesses' evidence not discarded as a whole; PW.1's alleged enmity rejected as unproven on the time gap; trial court's reliance on discrepancies held erroneous
post_offence_conduct: Ran out when villagers gathered after the witness's cry (per PW.7); arrested at 3.35 a.m. at a road junction while waiting for transport
trial_duration: offence: 30.1.1996; trial judgment: 2.2.1999; High Court: 23.3.2007; Supreme Court: 21.05.2012
legal_representation: Accused: Rajender Pd. Saxena. State: Vikrant Yadav, Jyoti Sharma, Vinay Kumar Garg, Gunnam Venkateswara Rao (for the respondent)
investigation_status: FIR lodged 2.2.1996 at Haraiya Police Station; Case Crime No. 22 of 1996 registered; investigation completed; chargesheet filed; trial completed with 14 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: None noted (trial court's adverse inference for non-examination of the grandmother and failure to consider depositions were errors in appreciation, not procedural lapses)
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted of both charges. High Court: State appeal allowed, convicted on both counts. Supreme Court: accused's appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The High Court reversal was correct; the findings were based on correct appreciation of evidence and no interference was warranted
defence_argument: Witnesses PW.1, PW.7 and PW.8 were motivated and their improvements meant their evidence should be discarded; other witnesses turned hostile; no evidence the child slept at the accused's house; High Court findings perverse
legal_principle_applied: Appellate interference with acquittal only in exceptional cases where the acquittal is perverse; hostile witness evidence cannot be discarded as a whole; falsus in uno maxim not applicable in India; reasonable doubt must be fair, not fanciful

case_title: Pathan Hussain Basha v. State of A.P.
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband of the deceased); mother-in-law of the deceased (Relative: mother-in-law)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B read with s.498-A (Evidence Act s.113-B referred to in judgment)
weapon: None mentioned (death by hanging with a saree)
evidence_type: Eyewitness/oral testimony of relatives and neighbours (LW-1, LW-3, LW-7); medical (post-mortem by LW-13); recovery and seizure of saree; scene photographs
aggravating_circumstances: Persistent dowry demands; victim beaten and abused for dowry; victim refused return to parental home; death within a very short period after marriage
mitigating_circumstances: Age of the accused; substantial period already spent in jail; attendant circumstances
trial_court_outcome: All three accused convicted under ss.304-B and 498-A IPC; life imprisonment under s.304-B; 3 years RI under s.498-A (concurrent); fine Rs 1,000 each
high_court_outcome: Appeal partly allowed: father-in-law acquitted; conviction and sentence of husband and mother-in-law confirmed
offence_finally_established: Dowry death (IPC s.304-B) read with cruelty (IPC s.498-A)
neutral_facts: The victim was married in June 2002 in an arranged marriage. At the marriage, a dowry of Rs 25,000 was promised by the victim's side; Rs 15,000 was paid then and the balance of Rs 10,000 was promised within about four months. The victim's father could not pay the balance. The prosecution alleged that the accused, the victim's spouse and mother-in-law, pressed for the balance, harassed the victim for non-payment, refused to send the victim to the parental home, and that the victim had told relatives about the ill-treatment. A witness said that the couple was happy for the first months and that quarrels followed. On one visit to the parental home, the spouse demanded a fan, a ring and Rs 1,000 in cash, along with the balance dowry; when these were not met, the spouse left the victim there. On 15 February 2003, around 11 a.m., the accused left a witness in the house on an errand. When the witness returned, the victim was found hanging from a beam with a saree. The victim's parents came, cut the victim down and took the victim to hospital, where the victim was declared dead. Police registered the report, seized the saree used for hanging, photographed the scene and arranged a post-mortem. The doctor found an oblique ligature mark on the front and left sides of the neck and an abrasion on the chin, all antemortem, and recorded asphyxia from hanging as the cause of death. The victim's father's account was corroborated by two other witnesses. One witness stated that the dowry of Rs 15,000 was handed over at the marriage and that the balance was not paid. The witnesses described the persistent dowry demands and beating and abuse of the victim.
physical_harm: Death by asphyxia from hanging; antemortem oblique ligature mark on neck and abrasion on chin; victim reportedly beaten by accused
financial_property_loss: Rs 15,000 paid at marriage toward Rs 25,000 dowry; balance Rs 10,000 demanded and not paid; other items demanded (fan, ring, Rs 1,000 cash)
motive: Accepted by court: persistent dowry demands (balance of agreed dowry and other items such as fan, ring and Rs 1,000 cash)
key_evidence_accepted: Oral evidence of the victim's father (LW-1), LW-3 and LW-7 on dowry demands and cruelty; victim's reports of ill-treatment to parents; post-mortem findings (LW-13); seizure of saree
witness_credibility: Court found the prosecution evidence reliable and cogent; the witnesses' accounts were consistent and corroborated each other
post_offence_conduct: Did not explain how the death occurred and maintained silence; court held silence and denial do not discharge the onus
custody_duration: Arrested 16 February 2003; in jail for a considerable period (not quantified)
trial_duration: offence: 15 February 2003; trial judgment: 4 October 2004; High Court: 26 October 2006; Supreme Court: 16 August 2012
legal_representation: Appellants: Param Kumar Mishra (for Kumud Lata Das); State: D. Mahesh Babu
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation conducted and post-mortem done; accused arrested 16 February 2003; committed to Sessions Court; tried
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: all three convicted (ss.304-B, 498-A), life imprisonment; High Court: father-in-law acquitted, husband and mother-in-law convicted and sentence confirmed; Supreme Court: convictions upheld, sentence reduced to ten years RI
prosecution_argument: Not stated; the judgment records no State submissions beyond noting that the State did not challenge the father-in-law's acquittal
defence_argument: Sought lenient view on sentence given the age of the accused, the attendant circumstances, and the time already spent in jail
legal_principle_applied: Under s.304-B read with s.113-B Evidence Act, once basic ingredients are proved the accused must show the death was not caused by cruelty or dowry demand; denial or silence does not discharge the onus
precedent_relied_upon: Biswajit Halder v. State of W.B. (2008) 1 SCC 202 and Ashok Kumar v. State of Haryana (2010) 12 SCC 350 (relied on); also discussed: Tarsem Singh (2008) 16 SCC 155, Yashoda v. State of M.P. (2004) 3 SCC 98, Ran Singh (2008) 4 SCC 700, Satvir Singh (2001) 8 SCC 633, State of A.P. v. Raj Gopal Asawa (2004) 4 SCC 470
sentencing_rationale: Lenient view taken given the prosecution evidence, attendant circumstances, age of the accused and time already in jail; ends of justice met by reducing sentence to ten years RI
judicial_mitigating_factors: Age of the accused; substantial period already spent in jail; attendant circumstances
judicial_aggravating_factors: None expressly weighed; court noted as established the persistent dowry demands and beating and abuse of the victim
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Deepak @ Wireless v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured victim PW9); oral evidence of PW2 on stolen property; medical (PW1 postmortem doctor); recovery/seizure (PW4 panch witness, spot panchnama Ext. 28); test of identification in court
aggravating_circumstances: Murder of the victim's brother-in-law by group of five using knives and rods; grievous injuries to PW9, who was also assaulted after witnessing the attack
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.395, 396 and 397 IPC; RI 5 years and Rs.500 fine (s.395, default 3 years RI); life RI and Rs.500 fine (s.396); RI 3 years and Rs.500 fine (s.397, default 1 year RI)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
offence_finally_established: Dacoity with murder and grievous hurt (robbery) under IPC ss.395, 396 and 397
neutral_facts: In the early hours of 14 June 2004, at about 2 to 2.30 a.m., a group of men entered the house of the victims. The victim's brother-in-law was beaten with knives, an iron rod and a wooden club and died from his injuries. When the victim, the brother-in-law's sister-in-law, began shouting, the assailants turned on her and struck her on the eyes, head and back. She was left seriously injured and could not speak when brought to hospital. She told police that four to five men were involved, wearing pants and shirts, and that they fled on a motorcycle. At trial, in cross-examination, she stated that the number of persons was five. She identified the accused in court and described the clothing and physical features of the attackers. Police had earlier stopped a motorcycle carrying three fleeing men; two were apprehended, one of them the accused, and a third escaped. At the time of arrest, a knife, a motorcycle key and cash were seized from the accused, and the seizure was witnessed by a panch witness. The accused's clothes were examined and found to have blood stains. The victim's husband stated that cash of about Rs.4,000 to 5,000 and the ornaments worn by the victim were taken, and a spot panchnama recorded in his presence noted disturbed household articles and a forced window. A post-mortem doctor gave evidence on the head injuries and cause of death and on the injuries to the victim. The motorcycle used by the group had been stolen earlier and was recovered. Two of the men were juveniles and were dealt with separately, and two others remained absconding. Charge sheet was filed against the accused and the others.
physical_harm: Death of the victim's brother-in-law (cardio-respiratory arrest due to head injury, with asphyxia from blood aspiration; 11 injuries). Victim PW9 suffered incised wounds to forehead, eye and cheek, contusion, and fracture of mandible; hospitalised for 2-3 months with disabled movements.
financial_property_loss: Cash of approximately Rs.4,000 to 5,000 and ornaments worn by the victim
motive: Theft/robbery of cash and ornaments (court accepted an act of theft by the accused and others)
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW9 (injured eyewitness) on number of assailants (five) and her in-court identification of the appellant; PW2's evidence on stolen cash and ornaments, accepted with spot panchnama Ext. 28; PW1 postmortem and injury evidence; PW4 panch witness on seizure of clothes, knife, motorcycle key and cash
witness_credibility: PW9 found credible: first-hand witness who suffered injuries, definite answer in cross-examination on five assailants, unhesitant identification; slip in chief examination about stolen articles excused because of her serious injuries. PW2 evidence unshaken in cross-examination.
post_offence_conduct: Fled on a motorcycle at high speed, abandoned it and ran into an open field when chased; two men apprehended by police, the appellant among them
trial_duration: offence: 13/14.06.2004; trial judgment: 09.05.2005; High Court: 25.04.2007; Supreme Court: 04.09.2012
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: Rajiv Nanda. State/respondent: Aprajita Sinha and Asha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: Investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial completed with 10 prosecution witnesses

case_title: Rakhal Debnath v. State of West Bengal
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (the accused was the victim's husband)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.306 (abetment of suicide); IPC s.498A (cruelty); Evidence Act s.113A (presumption applied)
weapon: None mentioned (kerosene was used for self-immolation)
evidence_type: Medical (post-mortem report and doctor's evidence); recovery (kerosene cane, cloth, quilt, pillows, clothes); oral witness testimony; documentary (receipts Exhibits 3 and 3A); circumstantial
confession: Alleged statement by the accused to the doctor (PW19) that the burns came from a stove. Not relied on: the court held the stove explanation was ruled out by the accused's own version, and he denied making the statement when questioned under s.313 CrPC.
aggravating_circumstances: Death within 35 days of marriage; established cruelty; repeated demands for money from the victim's father; pledging of the victim's jewels; illicit relationship of the accused with the second accused
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of ss.306 and 498A IPC
high_court_outcome: State's appeal partly allowed; acquittal reversed. Convicted under s.306 (10 years RI, fine Rs.10,000, one year default) and s.498A (3 years RI, fine Rs.10,000, one year default), sentences consecutive. Second accused's acquittal confirmed.
offence_finally_established: Abetment of suicide under IPC s.306; cruelty under IPC s.498A
neutral_facts: The victim, a married woman, died from extensive burn injuries within 35 days of her marriage to the accused. Hospital records noted that, according to the accused, she was burned by a stove while preparing tea and bread in the kitchen. A post-mortem examination recorded first-degree burns extending from the top of the head to the tip of the leg, and the examining doctor gave evidence. Police recovered from the kitchen a 20-litre cane with about a litre of kerosene, a quilt, pillows, a piece of cloth soaked in kerosene, and the victim's clothes, which smelled of kerosene. The prosecution alleged that shortly after the marriage the accused demanded Rs.40,000 from the victim's father for business purposes. The father refused, and the accused remarked that he knew how to obtain money through his own daughter. The accused later pledged the victim's jewels with a third party for Rs.11,000. The victim was also alleged to be upset about the accused's illicit relationship with his niece, who lived in the same house. Several witnesses, including the victim's father, a neighbour, a cousin and a relative, testified that the victim had complained to them about the money demands, the relationship and her unhappiness in the marriage. The prosecution case was that the victim poured kerosene on herself and set herself on fire because of this pressure from the accused.
physical_harm: Death from extensive first-degree burns from head to leg, caused after kerosene was poured on the victim
financial_property_loss: Victim's jewels pledged for Rs.11,000 (father later paid Rs.11,000 to get them back, Exhibit 3); earlier demand of Rs.40,000 was refused
motive: Accepted by the court: the accused's demands for money from the victim's father, together with his illicit relationship with the second accused and his conduct towards the victim, instigated her suicide
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent testimony of PWs 3, 9 and 11 (and PWs 5, 10 and 12) on money demands and illicit relationship; pledge receipts Exhibits 3 and 3A and PW17's confirmation; jewels identified by PW3; post-mortem and PW15's evidence; kerosene-related recoveries from the kitchen
witness_credibility: Court found the witnesses credible: no inconsistency in PW3's evidence versus others who heard the victim's complaints, and nothing suggested any ulterior motive to depose falsely
post_offence_conduct: Accused told the doctor the burns came from a stove; the court held this explanation was ruled out by the accused's own version. No other post-offence conduct noted.
trial_duration: offence: 26.05.1987 (death); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 24.12.2008; Supreme Court: 04.09.2012
legal_representation: Accused: Ravi Kumar Tomar, Amitava Acharjee, H.B. Tiwari, Smriti. State: Chanchal Kumar Ganguly, Avijit Bhattacharjee.
investigation_status: Final report filed; charges under ss.306 and 498A framed; trial completed. Defence claimed the FIR was based on PW3's complaint, which PW3 did not write.
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted. High Court: acquittal reversed, convicted on both charges, sentenced. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: The death occurred within 35 days of marriage; PWs 3, 9 and 11 proved the money demand and illicit relationship; non-payment and pledging of the jewels showed dowry demand; kerosene recoveries and burn injuries showed suicide under the accused's instigation.
defence_argument: No definite medical opinion on manner of death; case rested on circumstantial evidence with no link to the accused; no evidence of abetment or cruelty; FIR not written by PW3; the trial acquittal was well considered.
legal_principle_applied: s.113A Evidence Act presumption applies only if suicide within seven years of marriage, and cruelty by the husband or relatives is shown, with regard to all other circumstances; cruelty means the s.498A meaning; the presumption is permissive and rebuttable.
precedent_relied_upon: Relied on: Ramesh Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2001) 9 SCC 618; Thanu Ram v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2010) 10 SCC 353. Cited: K. Prema S. Rao v. Yadla Srinivasa Rao (2003) 1 SCC 217; Devi Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2007) 14 SCC 176.
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable (the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and did not revisit the sentence)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Suicide within 35 days of marriage; established cruelty and demands for money; instigation by the accused
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: State of N.C.T. of Delhi v. Ajay Kumar Tyagi
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 s.7, s.13
evidence_type: Trap-based complaint by the complainant constable (as alleged by the prosecution); the Supreme Court did not assess evidence on merits

high_court_outcome: Criminal proceedings quashed under s.482 Cr.P.C. on the ground that the accused was exonerated in the departmental proceedings
neutral_facts: An application for a water connection in the name of a constable's wife was cleared at a lower level and the file was then sent to the accused, a junior engineer in a water board. The complainant, a police constable who was the applicant's husband, lodged a report with the anti-corruption branch alleging that the accused had demanded a bribe of Rs. 2000 to clear the file, with Rs. 1000 to be paid initially and the balance after clearance. A trap was laid. According to the prosecution, the accused demanded and accepted Rs. 1000 as the bribe. This led to registration of a first information report under Sections 7 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. After investigation, a charge-sheet was submitted in September 2002. In parallel, a departmental inquiry was initiated on the same allegation that the accused had demanded, accepted and obtained Rs. 1000 as illegal gratification in consideration of giving a report on the water connection. The inquiry officer recorded that the evidence on record did not substantiate the charge of demand and acceptance of bribe, and found the charge not proved due to lack of evidence on record.
attempt_completion: Completed (as alleged by the prosecution; not decided by the Supreme Court)
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: 2 charged (ss.7 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act); 0 finally upheld
financial_property_loss: Rs. 1000 alleged bribe amount (alleged by prosecution; not decided by the Court)
motive: alleged: monetary gratification (bribe) for clearing the water connection file
key_evidence_accepted: Not stated
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 25.8.2008; Supreme Court: 31 August 2012
legal_representation: Accused (respondent): Chelan Sharma, Bake Bihari Sharma (for Asha Gopalan Nair). State (appellant): J.S. Attry, Anjani Aiyagari, Gargi Khanna, B.V. Bairam Das
investigation_status: FIR registered under ss.7/13 PC Act; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed 19 September 2002; charges framed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: charges framed, outcome not stated. High Court: quashed criminal proceedings on 25.8.2008 under s.482 Cr.P.C. Supreme Court: High Court order set aside and appeal allowed; proceedings restored
prosecution_argument: The High Court's premise of exoneration was unfounded because the inquiry officer's report was not final and was yet to be considered by the disciplinary authority, which could disagree and punish the accused
defence_argument: At such a distance of time the disciplinary authority is precluded from passing any order, so the disciplinary proceeding should be deemed ended in exoneration; the criminal case should be quashed relying on P.S. Rajya

State of Bihar (1996) 9 SCC 1 distinguished; State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (1992 Supp (1) SCC 335) referred to
other_sentence_order: Accused to appear before the trial court within four weeks; trial judge directed to dispose of the criminal case expeditiously and avoid unnecessary adjournments; departmental proceeding to be reopened and kept in abeyance till conclusion of criminal case

case_title: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Surendra Kori
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC ss.420, 467, 468, 469, 471 r/w ss.34 and 120-B; Registration Act ss.34 and 81
evidence_type: Documentary (sale deeds, registration records), departmental and Deputy Collector enquiry reports, complainant's FIR and charge-sheet material
aggravating_circumstances: Alleged registration of more than 102 fictitious sale deeds for the same transaction to obtain Package benefits; alleged loss to the State; alleged failure to verify purchasers, sellers and land
trial_court_outcome: Not applicable; no trial verdict; charge-sheet pending
high_court_outcome: Under s.482 CrPC, FIRs, charge-sheets and criminal cases quashed (revision petitions allowed)
neutral_facts: A State Special Rehabilitation Package provided cash benefit in two instalments to persons displaced by a submerged dam project, to help them buy land. The second instalment was payable only after both seller and purchaser registered a sale deed and submitted proof of registration. Complaints alleged that various fake sale deeds were registered at the Registrar's office in Khargone to claim the benefit, and that beneficiaries were not affected by the project. A Collector's inquiry reported that some vendors were fictitious persons and that deeds were executed and registered fraudulently. Several FIRs were registered on a rehabilitation officer's complaint. The FIR for one registration recorded that a beneficiary received Rs.3,39,857 after a registration whose survey number was wrong and whose vendor could not be traced in the village. A departmental enquiry was then conducted, and it recorded procedural irregularities in registration, such as accepting photocopies of documents and not obtaining PAN details. The investigating officer alleged that the accused, a registering officer, had abetted the conspiracy and misused his position. The investigation was still continuing, and the charge-sheet stated that the accused's handwriting report and the district registrar's statement were awaited.

physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: 9 charged (IPC ss.34, 120-B, 420, 467, 468, 469, 471; Registration Act ss.34, 81); 0 finally upheld
financial_property_loss: Alleged loss to government of Rs.3,39,857 for one deed; alleged fraud on the Package in more than 102 deeds (prima facie)
premeditation_planning: Alleged conspiracy and planning; not decided by the Supreme Court, only prima facie indicated
motive: alleged: unlawful gain from fictitious sale deeds to obtain Special Rehabilitation Package benefits
key_evidence_accepted: None finally accepted; Court relied only on prima facie material in FIRs, charge-sheets and enquiry reports
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Suspended from service by Registration Department after enquiry
custody_duration: Not stated (charge-sheet says accused was arrested; duration not given)
