case_title: Laxman v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: accused from the rival group in the same village; dispute over the marriage settlement of the victim's granddaughter
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.149 (trial); IPC ss.147, 148 r/w s.149; IPC ss.337, 504 r/w s.149 (acquitted at trial); on appeal, IPC s.302 r/w s.34
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (three witnesses); medical evidence (post-mortem and injury examination by doctors); police complaint/FIR
aggravating_circumstances: Group assault by several accused, with axe and sticks; fatal head injury attributed to the accused armed with an axe
trial_court_outcome: Convicted six of eleven accused under s.302 r/w s.149 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 500 each; no separate sentence for ss.147/148 r/w s.149
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction of A-1, A-2 and A-7 under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC and life sentence confirmed; A-3, A-4 and A-10 acquitted by benefit of doubt
offence_finally_established: Murder: IPC s.302 read with s.34
neutral_facts: On a morning at about 7 a.m., the victim went to a nearby house to discuss the proposed marriage of his granddaughter to a son of the woman of that house. After the discussion, as the victim came out, a group of persons who had been sitting in another nearby house came out, approached him, scolded him about the marriage arrangement, and assaulted him with an axe, stones and sticks. Several relatives and villagers who came to rescue the victim were also assaulted and sustained injuries. The attack ended after police intervention. The victim was taken by bullock cart to a hospital and then referred to a civil hospital, where he died the same evening, about twelve hours after the assault. He remained unconscious throughout that time and no dying declaration was recorded. A complaint was lodged with the police later that night. The doctor who conducted the post-mortem stated that the probable cause of death was primarily head injury associated with other multiple injuries, and that some stick injuries and an axe injury were identified. Doctors examined the injuries of some accused and found them minor. Eyewitness testimony came from the victim's brother, who was also injured, the victim's son, who witnessed the occurrence, and the mother-in-law of the granddaughter's fiancé, each describing the overt acts of particular accused.
physical_harm: Death of the victim (head injury with multiple injuries); injuries to two eyewitnesses who tried to rescue him; minor injuries to some accused
number_of_offences: 5 charged (ss.302, 147, 148, 337, 504 IPC); 1 finally upheld (s.302 r/w s.34 IPC)
motive: alleged: dispute over the marriage settlement of the victim's granddaughter, with the accused objecting that the match was made to gain support
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PWs 3, 4 and 5; post-mortem evidence of PW-1 attributing head injury to A-7 (axe) and other injuries to A-1 and A-2 (sticks/axe); PW-2's evidence that the accused's injuries were minor
witness_credibility: Related witnesses (brother, son, mother-in-law) found credible; relationship alone not a ground to reject, testimony scrutinised and found free of infirmity; injured witnesses' presence not doubted
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 19.01.1992; trial judgment: 19.07.2003; High Court: 11.04.2005; Supreme Court: 27.09.2012
legal_representation: Accused: Vikas Upadhyay (Crl. A. 246/2008) and Brij Bhusan (Crl. A. 247/2008). State: Sushil Karanjakar
investigation_status: FIR/complaints registered (Crime Nos. 6/92 and 7/92); cases committed to Sessions Court; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Delay in lodging the complaint, no dying declaration recorded, and no explanation for injuries to some accused were raised; the court held none of these affected the prosecution case
appeal_history: Trial court: six convicted under s.302 r/w s.149, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed as to A-1, A-2 and A-7 (s.302 r/w s.34), A-3, A-4 and A-10 acquitted. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Evidence properly appreciated; eyewitnesses were injured; conviction under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC should not be disturbed
defence_argument: Witnesses are relatives of the deceased; FIR delay unexplained; no dying declaration; injuries to accused unexplained, suggesting a free fight, so the prosecution story should be disbelieved
legal_principle_applied: Relatives' testimony is not to be discarded merely for relationship but must be carefully scrutinised; delay, missing dying declaration and minor unexplained injuries do not defeat the prosecution where explained by circumstances; common intention under s.34
precedent_relied_upon: Abdul Rashid Abdul Rahiman Patel and Ors. v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 9 SCC 1
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Kunjumon @ Unni v. State of Kerala
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated for the deceased (Annamma); the defence contended the accused was a total stranger to PW-2 Lidiya
statutory_provisions: IPC s.449; IPC s.397; IPC s.302
weapon: Wall clock (used to strike the victim on the head)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (victim's granddaughter PW-2 and her father PW-1); medical (PW-10, PW-11); recovery of stolen ornaments (PW-13); hostile neighbour witnesses PW-3 and PW-5 placing accused near the house
aggravating_circumstances: Elderly and frail victim dragged from her cot and struck on the head; child threatened and robbed; victim died
mitigating_circumstances: Accused went to the house intending robbery, not to kill; this was why the s.449 conviction was not sustained
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.449 (10 years and fine), s.397 (7 years and fine) and s.302 (life imprisonment); sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed (Crl. A. No. 835 of 2004, judgment 30.10.2007); conviction and sentence upheld
offence_finally_established: IPC s.397 (robbery with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt); IPC s.302 (murder)
neutral_facts: On a day in October 1997, the accused and a companion went to a family's residence intending to commit robbery. While the companion stood guard outside, the accused entered and found the eleven-year-old daughter of the household. He caught hold of her neck, threatened to kill her, and robbed her of a gold chain and two gold ear studs. He then entered a bedroom where the victim, an elderly woman aged about 90, lay on a cot and tried to take her ornaments. When the victim raised an alarm, the accused pulled her down from the cot and struck her on the head with a wall clock. He broke a gold chain from her neck and took two imitation bangles from a bag in an almirah, then left. The girl told her father, and they returned with friends. The victim was taken to a government hospital and then a medical college hospital, where she died nine days after the incident. The treating civil surgeon recorded a forehead injury with suspicion of fracture and eyelid swelling, consistent with a wall clock blow. A forensic doctor attributed death to the head injuries. The girl gave consistent eyewitness testimony corroborating her father. Two neighbours, both declared hostile, admitted seeing the accused near the house that day. The investigating officer recovered the stolen gold ornaments at the accused's instance. No test identification parade was held. The girl identified the accused in court.
physical_harm: Head injuries to the 90-year-old victim (forehead injury with suspected fracture, eyelid oedema, lacerated forehead); victim died on 29 October 1997 from head injuries
number_of_offences: 3 charged; 2 finally upheld (ss.397 and 302); s.449 not upheld
financial_property_loss: Gold chain (about 5.500 grams) and two gold ear studs from PW-2; gold chain of about 5.500 grams from the victim; two imitation bangles taken from an almirah bag
premeditation_planning: No premeditated killing found; the court found the visit was made with a common intention to commit robbery, not to kill
motive: Robbery (accepted by the court)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-2 (victim's granddaughter); PW-1's consistent testimony; medical evidence of PW-10 and PW-11 on cause of death; recovery of gold ornaments at the accused's instance; hostile witnesses PW-3 and PW-5 on presence near the house
witness_credibility: PW-2 found credible as a victim witness; her evidence clear and unambiguous, nothing adverse elicited in cross-examination; six-year delay in recording evidence did not cause memory to fade; she was no longer a child witness
post_offence_conduct: Recovery of stolen gold ornaments at the accused's instance on 24 October 1997; no other post-offence conduct noted
trial_duration: offence: 20 October 1997; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 30 October 2007; Supreme Court: 21 November 2012
legal_representation: Accused: Purnima Bhar; State: Liz Mathew and Sana Hasmi
investigation_status: Investigation completed; charge sheet (challan) filed; trial completed; recovery of ornaments made
procedural_irregularity: No test identification parade held; the Supreme Court found the identification was dealt with in a cursory manner by the trial court and High Court; PW-2's evidence was recorded about six years after the incident
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.449, 397 and 302 IPC. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld. Supreme Court: partly allowed; s.449 conviction set aside, ss.397 and 302 upheld
prosecution_argument: Not separately recorded in the judgment; the court noted that the prosecution's case was that the accused went to the house to commit robbery
defence_argument: No TIP was held, so PW-2's evidence could not be relied on; a child witness's evidence should be carefully scrutinised; the accused had no intention to murder, so the s.302 conviction was improper
legal_principle_applied: Failure to hold a TIP is not fatal, but the trial judge must be circumspect when a stranger is identified in court; victim evidence is given a higher pedestal; murderous intent may be inferred from the act; s.449 requires intent to commit an offence punishable with death
precedent_relied_upon: Sk. Hasib v. State of Bihar, AIR 1972 SC 283; Vaikuntam Chandrappa v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1960 SC 1340; Rameshwar Singh v. State of J&K, (1971) 2 SCC 715; Budhsen v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (1970) 2 SCC 128; Malkhansingh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2003) 5 SCC 746; Vijay @ Chinee v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2010) 8 SCC 191; State of Himachal Pradesh v. Lekh Raj, (2000) 1 SCC 247
sentencing_rationale: Sentence not revisited. The s.449 conviction was set aside because the house trespass was for robbery, not for an offence punishable with death; ss.397 and 302 convictions upheld
judicial_aggravating_factors: Frail, elderly victim dragged from her cot and struck on the head; the court held the accused could not have been unaware that death would result
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: State of Rajasthan v. Girdhari Lal
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304B (dowry death; charge framed under s.304B), with s.498A registered; on appeal, conviction altered to IPC s.306; Evidence Act ss.113A and 113B referred to
evidence_type: Medical (postmortem report and treating doctor's statement); ocular (oral witness testimony on cruelty and harassment); documentary
aggravating_circumstances: Alleged earlier attempt to burn the victim alive (as stated by PW.1); victim died within seven years of marriage by burn injuries
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.304B (dowry death); sentenced to life imprisonment

neutral_facts: The victim was married to the accused and died of burn injuries within seven years of the marriage. The victim's father filed a written complaint the day after the death, alleging that the accused and the accused's family had harassed the victim over dowry demands from the early days of the marriage. He also alleged that the in-laws had earlier tried to set the victim on fire and that neighbours had rescued her. The victim was admitted to hospital with burns all over the body and died during treatment the same afternoon. The postmortem examination recorded extensive burns as the cause of death. A witness stated that the accused used to beat the victim for dowry. The victim's father stated that the accused had beaten and harassed the victim for dowry after the marriage, and had earlier confined the victim in a room and tried to burn her alive by pouring kerosene; family members apologised and assured that it would not recur. The victim's mother testified that the couple visited her village about a month before the death and that the victim asked her to send her father because the accused harassed her. Other witnesses stated that the marriage took place about six or seven years earlier. A case was registered, investigated, and a charge sheet was filed.
physical_harm: Death by extensive burn injuries over the body
number_of_offences: 1 charged; 1 finally upheld (IPC s.306, as altered on appeal)
motive: alleged: cruelty and harassment connected with dowry demands by the in-laws; the Court did not find a specific dowry demand by the accused established
key_evidence_accepted: Postmortem report (Ext.P-6) and doctor's statement (PW.6) on burn death; ocular evidence of cruelty and harassment (PW.1, PW.7, PW.8); marriage date evidence (PW.2, PW.3) showing death within seven years; documentary evidence
witness_credibility: Court relied on ocular and documentary evidence showing cruelty and harassment, but found the dowry-demand statements of PW.1 and PW.7 non-specific as to the accused
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: More than six years undergone before the High Court judgment; High Court directed release if not required in other cases
trial_duration: offence: 10 August 1998; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 14 March 2007; Supreme Court: 7 October 2013

case_title: L. Krishna Reddy v. State by Station House Officer & Ors.
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (parents-in-law of the victim, the husband's parents)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.498A r/w s.34
evidence_type: Statements under s.161 Cr.P.C. of several witnesses and the complainant's further statement; no direct evidence against the parents-in-law discussed
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Refused discharge of the parents-in-law; proceedings to continue to trial
high_court_outcome: Criminal revision allowed; parents-in-law discharged (order dated 18.10.2011, Crl. R.C. No. 761 of 2010)
neutral_facts: The victim, a married woman, was found dead on 26.3.2006 in a hotel room in Puducherry that had been rented by her husband. Her body bore several stab wounds, and the investigation recorded that she had received 11 injuries from a knife. The investigation placed the incident on the evening of 25.3.2006 at about 19.00 hours in that hotel room. The couple had lived apart from the husband's parents, having set up their own separate residence about six months before the death. The victim's husband later died by suicide by hanging, and a separate case was registered in respect of that death. The investigation concluded that the victim's husband, together with his parents, had subjected her to cruelty over a dowry demand and had caused her death. The complainant, the victim's father, said by telephone that the couple had left Hyderabad for Vijayawada. In his further statement he alleged that the parents had planned the killing with the husband because of dowry harassment. The statements of several witnesses recorded during the investigation did not attribute any direct dowry demand to the parents. The parents were not present in Puducherry when the killing took place.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple stab wounds (11 injuries alleged)
premeditation_planning: Not found by the Court against the parents-in-law; planning was alleged by the complainant only
motive: alleged: dowry harassment (the Court noted no direct imputation of dowry demand against the parents-in-law)
key_evidence_accepted: Absence of any direct imputation in witness statements against the parents-in-law; the complainant's sole conspiracy allegation was a bald statement
witness_credibility: Complainant's statements were described as those of an anguished father; the Court did not find the conspiracy allegation sufficient without further linking evidence
post_offence_conduct: Husband committed suicide shortly after the incident, possibly from guilt and remorse; no post-offence conduct of the parents-in-law noted

prosecution_argument: Complainant relied on Stree Atyachar Virodhi Parishad and K. Narayana Rao to urge that the parents-in-law be tried; the Court found these did not support continuing the prosecution
defence_argument: Parents-in-law sought discharge under s.227 Cr.P.C., contending no direct involvement or conspiracy was shown in the charge sheet
legal_principle_applied: Prima facie test under s.227 Cr.P.C.; a bald allegation of conspiracy requires further linking evidence; conspiracy requires an agreement existing at the material time; prosecution that is an exercise in futility should be ended

case_title: Nana Keshav Lagad v. State of Maharashtra
accused_socioeconomic_status: Owned and possessed agricultural land adjacent to the complainant's land; no wealth or class finding otherwise stated
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour (same village) and land rival; prior enmity and dispute over right of way to adjoining agricultural lands
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.324 r/w s.34 (convicted); FIR also cited IPC ss.504, 506, 143, 147, 148, 149 and Bombay Police Act s.37(a) r/w s.135
evidence_type: Eyewitness (two injured/eyewitnesses PW4 and PW5); medical (post-mortem and injury certificates, doctor PW6); recovery of weapons (panch witness PW3); expert/chemical analysis of blood-stained clothing
confession: Admissible portion of the accused's confession was the basis for seizure of cycle chain and stones; the Court did not separately rely on the confession itself
aggravating_circumstances: 19 external and 4 internal injuries to the deceased; group assault with cycle chain and stones; accused reportedly waited on road with intention to assault; injuries to the complainant (11) also noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34 and s.324 r/w s.34; life rigorous imprisonment with Rs.500 fine (default six months) for s.302/34; one year RI with Rs.300 fine (default one month) for s.324/34
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld (judgment dated 16.01.2006 in Criminal Appeal No. 611 of 2003)
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (murder); IPC s.324 r/w s.34 (hurt by dangerous weapon)
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim's family lived in the same village and owned adjoining agricultural land. A dispute existed over the use of a way to reach their fields. On the morning of the incident, the victim and the complainant attempted to reach their field to sow seeds but were obstructed by one of the accused, who abused and threatened them. Later that day, the complainant was told by a neighbour that several of the accused were waiting on a road to assault the victim. The complainant rode a bicycle to the spot and, from about 200 metres away, saw a group beating the victim with a cycle chain and stones while abusing him. The group then turned on the complainant and assaulted him with a cycle chain and stones until a bystander intervened. The complainant found the victim bleeding heavily from the head and with beating marks over the body. The victim was taken to a rural hospital, where he was declared dead. The post-mortem recorded 19 external and 4 internal injuries, all ante-mortem, with death due to shock from haemorrhage. The doctor stated that some injuries were caused by a cycle chain and others by stones, and that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death. The complainant's 11 injuries were certified by the same doctor and attributed to hard blunt objects and a cycle chain. Police arrested the accused, seized blood-stained clothing, and recovered the cycle chain and stones on the basis of information from the accused. Chemical analysis detected human blood on the clothing of the accused and the victim, although the blood group of the accused's sample was inconclusive. A second eyewitness supported the complainant's account. In oral evidence the complainant named fewer assailants than in his written complaint.
physical_harm: Death of the victim (father) from injuries including 19 external and 4 internal injuries; complainant suffered 11 injuries, which were ultimately not serious
number_of_offences: 9 charged (IPC ss.302, 324, 504, 506, 143, 147, 148, 149; Bombay Police Act s.37(a) r/w s.135) per FIR; 2 finally upheld (s.302 r/w 34 and s.324 r/w 34)
premeditation_planning: Court found a coordinated assault with common intention to eliminate the deceased; premeditation not expressly found, though the complaint alleged the accused were waiting on the road to assault the victim
motive: Dispute over right of way to adjoining agricultural lands (enmity); common intention to eliminate the deceased and the complainant
key_evidence_accepted: Complainant PW4's testimony (apart from the two wrongly named assailants); corroborating eyewitness PW5; post-mortem and injury evidence of doctor PW6 linking injuries to cycle chain and stones; expert blood report on clothing; panch witness PW3 on recovery
witness_credibility: PW4 found credible despite wrongly naming two accused, which was admitted fairly; PW5 found to merit acceptance on par with PW4; PW3 panch witness's version found truthfully and fully corroborated despite being alleged a stock witness
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 04.10.2002; trial judgment: 21.08.2003; High Court: 16.01.2006; Supreme Court: 03.07.2013
legal_representation: Accused: Sushil Karanjkar, M.Y. Deshmukh, Nikilesh Kumar, Shrikand R. Deshmukh, Rameshwar Prasad Goyal. State: Shankar Chillarge, Asha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: FIR (CR No.249 of 2002) registered; inquest and arrests made; charge-sheet filed and case committed to Sessions Court; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions Court, Sessions Case No.191 of 2002): convicted and sentenced; High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld; Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Case falls under Section 300 thirdly, established by the doctor's evidence that the injuries caused death; PW5's corroboration, medical evidence and proof of weapons support the conviction
defence_argument: Sole eyewitness PW4 unreliable due to discrepancies (two names omitted); injuries and weapons do not correlate; panch witness PW3 not established; blood finding on shirt not proved by expert evidence; s.34 not attracted
legal_principle_applied: Conviction need not rest solely on uncorroborated injured eyewitness; partial inaccuracy does not warrant rejecting whole testimony where corroborated by medical and other evidence; accused must explain bloodstains on clothing (s.313); s.34 applicable where common intention shown
precedent_relied_upon: Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras, AIR 1957 SC 614 (distinguished, held inapplicable); Abdul Sayeed v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2010) 10 SCC 259 (held inapplicable)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Coordinated vengeance and multiple injuries inflicted to ensure the deceased did not survive
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Manoj and Anr. v. State of Karnataka
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: the victim suspected an illicit intimacy between one accused and his wife, had forbidden that accused from visiting, and threatened to kill him
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.506 r/w s.34 (charged); IPC s.325 (substituted for appellant No.2)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PWs 8, 16, 18); medical (post-mortem); forensic (FSL report on blood on sword and stone); recovery/seizure (site plan and seizures by police)
aggravating_circumstances: Use of a sword; gruesome assault; multiple injuries including a fatal neck injury
mitigating_circumstances: For appellant No.2: his role was limited to throwing a stone; no evidence of intent to kill or pre-concert; no motive attributed to him; long period in jail
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC: life imprisonment and fine of Rs.10,000 each; convicted under s.506 r/w s.34 IPC: one year simple imprisonment and fine of Rs.2,000 each
high_court_outcome: Conviction and sentence under s.302 r/w s.34 affirmed; conviction and sentence under s.506 r/w s.34 set aside
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302) for appellant No.1 (Manoj); grievous hurt (IPC s.325) for appellant No.2
neutral_facts: The prosecution case is that the victim disliked a man visiting his house and suspected him of having an illicit relationship with the victim's wife. The victim had forbidden the man from coming to the house and threatened to kill him if he returned. About two days before the incident the man came again and the victim repeated the threat. On the day of the incident, around noon, the victim was sitting in front of a roadside eatery near a bus stand. Two witnesses had just finished taking tea there and saw a verbal altercation between the victim and two accused, one of whom was the man's father. During the altercation, one accused threw a stone which struck the victim on the head. The victim fell, and the other accused struck him several times with a sword, injuring his neck, head and face. People nearby ran away. Witnesses said the attackers fled believing the victim dead. Witnesses tried to help the victim, who was bleeding heavily, and took him to a police station and then toward a hospital, where he died en route. Police witnesses prepared a site plan and seized items from the spot, including the sword and the stone. The post-mortem found several ante-mortem external injuries, including a frontal bone fracture, a crush injury to the cheek, and a neck wound with a vertebral fracture. The doctor opined the injuries were sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course. The doctor stated that the crush injury could be caused by the stone and the other injuries by the sword. A forensic report found human blood on the blade of the sword and on the stone.
physical_harm: Death of the victim. Ante-mortem injuries: cut wound over right eye with frontal bone fracture; crush injury to left cheek; cut wound at left angle of mouth; wrist wound; neck wound with C2 vertebra fracture
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.506 r/w s.34); 1 finally upheld (s.302 for appellant No.1), with s.325 substituted for appellant No.2
premeditation_planning: Not found; the court noted no evidence of pre-concert between the two accused to kill the victim
motive: Accepted: the victim's suspicion of an illicit intimacy between one accused and his wife. No motive attributed to the other accused, as the prosecution did not allege one against him.
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PWs 8, 18 and 16 on the sequence of events; testimony on prior threats and suspected illicit intimacy; post-mortem evidence; FSL report showing blood on sword and stone; site plan and seizure evidence of police witnesses
witness_credibility: PWs 8, 18 and 16 found reliable and consistent; their testimony survived lengthy cross-examination. PWs 4, 5, 7, 17 and 19 turned hostile and gave no support to the prosecution.
post_offence_conduct: Fled the scene after the assault, believing the victim dead (as stated in PW-18's testimony; not separately found by the court)
custody_duration: Appellant No.2: nearly 3½ years in jail at the time of the judgment. Appellant No.1: not stated.
trial_duration: offence: 30 August 2006; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 15 November 2011; Supreme Court: 5 July 2013
legal_representation: Appellants: H. Chandra Sekhar. State/Respondent: C.B. Gururaj and V.N. Raghupathy.
investigation_status: Case registered; charge-sheet filed; trial completed with 22 prosecution witnesses examined
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.302 and 506 r/w s.34 IPC. High Court: s.302/34 conviction affirmed; s.506/34 set aside. Supreme Court: appeal of appellant No.1 dismissed; appellant No.2's conviction altered to s.325 IPC.
prosecution_argument: Not stated (the judgment records no separate prosecution submissions in the Supreme Court)
defence_argument: Appellant No.2's role was restricted to throwing a stone; nothing showed that the stone was intended to kill or that the assault continued after it; no pre-concert to kill
legal_principle_applied: Murder under s.302 (including via s.34) requires intention to cause death or a shared intention to do so; absent such evidence, liability is limited to the accused's own role, here grievous hurt under s.325. Eyewitness and medical evidence assessed for reliability.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: For appellant No.2: the sentence of nearly 3½ years already undergone was held sufficient given his limited role and conviction altered to s.325 IPC
judicial_mitigating_factors: For appellant No.2: the stone may have triggered the incident but there was no intent to kill; he was involved in an initial altercation; time already served
judicial_aggravating_factors: For appellant No.1: use of a sword to inflict fatal injuries in a gruesome assault
other_sentence_order: Appellant No.2 to be released from custody unless required in another case; fine imposed on appellant No.2 remains unaltered

case_title: Suresh Kumar v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B; IPC s.498-A
evidence_type: Oral testimony of prosecution witnesses on dowry demand and cruelty; FIR; statement under s.313 Cr.P.C.; absence of doctor's evidence on cause of death
aggravating_circumstances: Demand for motorcycle as dowry; beating of victim despite intervention; death within seven years of marriage; cruelty about 15 or 20 days before death
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of s.498-A and s.304-B IPC (death held accidental)
high_court_outcome: State's appeal allowed; acquittal reversed; convicted under s.304-B (7 years RI) and s.498-A (3 years RI and fine of Rs.5,000)
offence_finally_established: Dowry death under IPC s.304-B; cruelty under IPC s.498-A
neutral_facts: The victim was married to the accused in February 1990. The accused was serving in the army and stayed at the matrimonial home only while on leave. The prosecution case was that, soon after the marriage, the accused demanded a motorcycle as dowry and threatened that the victim would not be allowed to remain in the matrimonial home if the demand was not met. Relatives of the victim, including her brother and a village companion, intervened and pacified the accused on more than one occasion. In the days before the victim's death in September 1993, the demand was renewed, the accused harassed the victim and beat her. On 16 September 1993 the accused's brother visited the victim's brother's village and reported that the victim had died after suffering an electric shock. When the victim's brother and others reached the matrimonial village, they learned that the body had already been cremated. Enquiries led the victim's brother to conclude that the victim had been killed for dowry by the accused and the accused's mother. A first information report was lodged on 19 September 1993 and the accused was arrested the same day. The evidence consisted of oral testimony from the victim's brother, a village companion, the victim's father and another witness about the dowry demand and the cruelty, and evidence from the village Sarpanch about the cremation. No doctor who allegedly attended the victim was examined and no medical evidence on the cause of death was produced. The electrocution explanation rested on the accused's brother, who did not testify, and the accused did not mention electrocution in his statement under section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
offence_severity: Minimum 7 years; maximum imprisonment for life (IPC s.304-B(2))
physical_harm: Death of victim by alleged electric shock or electrocution, held not a normal circumstance
motive: Demand for a motorcycle as dowry
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW-4 Gian Singh, PW-5 Mam Chand, PW-6 Sardha and PW-7 Beer Singh on dowry demand and cruelty; High Court finding of cruelty about 15 or 20 days before death; death within seven years of marriage
witness_credibility: Trial court discarded Gian Singh's testimony; High Court and Supreme Court accepted prosecution witnesses' evidence on dowry demand and cruelty; the electrocution theory came only from a witness who did not testify
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: Not stated (arrested on 19 September 1993; duration in custody not given)
bail_history: Bail bond cancelled by Supreme Court; accused directed to be taken into custody to serve remainder of sentence

legal_representation: Accused: R.C. Kohli, S.S. Shamshery, Bhakti Vardhan. State: Kamal Mohan Gupta, Rajeev Gaur Naseem, Mohd. Zahid Hussain, Naresh Bakshi
investigation_status: FIR registered 19 September 1993; accused arrested; charge-sheeted and tried; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Delay in lodging FIR alleged for first time before Supreme Court; rejected. No other irregularity noted
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted. High Court: acquittal reversed, convicted under s.304-B and s.498-A. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld

neutral_facts: A complaint by one member of a society running educational institutions alleged that several persons, acting in collusion with another individual, had prepared fake and fraudulent documents. It was alleged that the signatures of members had been forged to show their participation in general and executive meetings that those members had not attended. A separate application alleged that the accused had fabricated an affidavit bearing forged signatures and filed it before a Deputy Registrar of the society registry. On the basis of that application, a further first information report was registered for offences of cheating, forgery, criminal breach of trust and criminal intimidation. A later complaint by another member of the governing body alleged that twelve persons had conspired to prepare forged documents recording meetings held on different dates, had fabricated the signatures of members, and had filed those papers before the competent authority. The complaint alleged that the purpose was to take the society's property and funds. Members had filed affidavits stating that they had never taken part in the meetings or signed the papers. The investigation proceeded on the basis of these complaints, the application and the affidavits, which formed the material available on the allegations.

case_title: Prashant Bharti v. State of NCT of Delhi
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance
evidence_type: Mobile phone call records, medical examination reports, statements under s.164 CrPC, investigating officer's chargesheet findings
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Charges framed under ss.328, 354 and 376 IPC on 1.12.2008; no verdict or sentence recorded
high_court_outcome: Accused's writ petition to quash FIR dismissed 27.8.2007; victim's writ petition dismissed; revision against framing of charges dismissed 16.1.2009
neutral_facts: The victim, aged 21, had known the accused for about four months. On 15.2.2007 the accused telephoned her at about 8.45 pm and asked her to meet him at Lodhi Colony, New Delhi. When she arrived he drove her around in his car and offered her a cold drink (Pepsi), which she said contained an intoxicating substance. She felt inebriated and alleged that the accused touched her breasts and continued to misbehave despite her objections. She got out of the car, took an auto-rickshaw home and complained to the police on 16.2.2007. A medical examination at AIIMS found no evidence of poisoning. The accused was arrested the same day. On 21.2.2007 the victim made a supplementary statement alleging that, on the assurance of marriage, the accused had physical relations with her at his house on 23.12.2006, 25.12.2006 and 1.1.2007. A medical examination on 21.2.2007 recorded that she had no external injuries and her hymen was not intact. No vaginal smear was taken because more than a month had elapsed, and her clothes were not sent for forensic examination because she had changed them. The police could not recover the drink container, glass or undergarments, and no blood sample was sent for analysis. Mobile phone call records showed that the accused was at Noida and Ghaziabad, including a function from 9.15 pm to 11.30 pm on 15.2.2007, and that no calls were made by him to the victim that day. Her call records placed her at other locations in Delhi and in conversation with friends. A tenancy verification affidavit described her as married. The victim's statement was recorded under section 164 CrPC on 27.2.2007.
offence_severity: Minimum 7 years for s.376 IPC (as stated in the High Court observation quoted in the judgment); maximum not stated
physical_harm: No external injuries; hymen not intact per AIIMS report; no evidence of poisoning; no death
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Mobile phone call details placing the accused in Noida/Ghaziabad and the victim elsewhere on 15.2.2007; divorce judgment and marriage certificate showing the victim was married during the alleged occurrences; the AIIMS medical reports; the investigating officer's chargesheet acknowledging no proof was found
witness_credibility: The court found the victim's assertion of a promise of marriage falsified by her subsisting marriage, and her supplementary allegations and her description of herself as unmarried to police were found false
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: Arrested 16.2.2007; duration of custody not stated
bail_history: Bail granted by Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi on 12.3.2007

case_title: Sahib Hussain @ Sahib Jan v. State of Rajasthan
accused_victim_relationship: Prior dispute: quarrel with deceased Seema on the day of Eid
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence, including extra-judicial confession, recoveries, medical (post-mortem) evidence, motive, and conduct; no eyewitness
confession: Extra-judicial confession made by the accused to PW-4 (a friend); relied on along with other material evidence
aggravating_circumstances: Five deaths including three children; multiple injuries on the bodies
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; sentenced to death
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; conviction upheld; death sentence commuted to life imprisonment with at least 20 years before release and no remission
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 (deaths of five persons)
neutral_facts: On the night of 27 October 2006, at about 10.30 p.m., a resident of the same colony, while walking home, found the accused talking to another resident and heard him say that he had killed a woman, three children and a man. The witness went to the house and found the man lying in a pool of blood outside a room, and the bodies of a young man, the woman and two children inside the rooms. He informed the household's employer by telephone, and a written report was given to police. The man was taken to hospital but died on the way. Post-mortem reports recorded multiple injuries to the bodies, and medical evidence showed all five deaths were homicidal. No eyewitness saw the killings. The second resident said the accused had told him about the incident and that he had changed his clothes and run towards the highway. The accused was said to have had a quarrel with the woman on the day of a festival. After the incident the accused allegedly left the village and boarded a bus to another city. Police stopped the bus, and the accused first gave a false name before giving his true name. On the accused's disclosure statement, a blood-stained axe, clothes and blood-stained chappals were recovered in the presence of two witnesses. Forensic and DNA reports matched blood groups on the chappals, trousers, shirt and axe with those of the deceased.
physical_harm: Death of five persons (Seema, Munna Mawali, Kalu, Isha and Sonu) from multiple injuries
motive: Alleged: quarrel with deceased Seema on the day of Eid; court said the corroborated incident cannot be ruled out
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW-1 and PW-4; extra-judicial confession to PW-4; recoveries of axe, clothes and chappals (PW-2, PW-3); FSL and DNA reports; post-mortem and medical evidence; conduct and false name at arrest
witness_credibility: PW-1 and PW-4 found acceptable with no valid reason to disbelieve; PW-4 found reliable and inspiring confidence; PW-2 and PW-3 recoveries found acceptable
post_offence_conduct: Left village immediately after incident and boarded bus to Delhi; arrested at 2.20 a.m. on 28.10.2006; gave a false name before disclosing true name; no explanation for departure
custody_duration: Not stated (arrest on 28.10.2006 reported; duration of custody not stated)
bail_history: Not stated (appellant was in jail when appealing to Supreme Court)
trial_duration: offence: 27.10.2006; trial judgment: 13.12.2007; High Court: 05.03.2008; Supreme Court: 18.04.2013
legal_representation: Appellant: Pijush K. Roy and Kakali Roy (amicus curiae in the Supreme Court). State: Archana Pathak Dave, Dr. Sumant Bharadwaj, Ankita Chaudhary, Mridula Ray and Milind Kumar
investigation_status: FIR registered (Crime No. 466/2006); post-mortem performed; investigation completed and chargesheet filed; case committed to Sessions Court; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Husband of deceased Seema (Munna) not examined; court held this not fatal to the prosecution case
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, sentenced to death. High Court: conviction upheld, death commuted to life imprisonment with at least 20 years and no remission. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Recoveries, extra-judicial confession, false name at arrest, consistent evidence of PWs 1 and 4, and no denial of absconding in s.313 statement established guilt; High Court justified restrictions on remission
defence_argument: No eyewitness; circumstances not satisfactorily established and no complete chain; FIR doubtful; contradictions on where the accused first disclosed the incident; surrounding households not examined; no reliable independent witness; recoveries doubtful; alternatively, remission restriction unjustified
legal_principle_applied: Conviction on circumstantial evidence where absence of eyewitness is not fatal and circumstances must be fully established; extra-judicial confession may be acted upon if voluntary, true and trustworthy; absconding rules out hypothesis of innocence; minimum fixed term without remission after commutation of death sentence
precedent_relied_upon: Shri Bhagwan v. State of Rajasthan (2001) 6 SCC 296; Prakash Dhawal Khairnar v. State of Maharashtra (2002) 2 SCC 35; Ram Anup Singh v. State of Bihar (2002) 6 SCC 686; Nazir Khan v. State of Delhi (2003) 8 SCC 461; Swamy Shraddananda (2) v. State of Karnataka (2008) 13 SCC 767; Haru Ghosh v. State of West Bengal (2009) 15 SCC 551; Ramraj v. State of Chhattisgarh (2010) 1 SCC 573; Neel Kumar v. State of Haryana (2012) 5 SCC 766; Sandeep v. State of UP (2012) 6 SCC 107; Gurvail Singh v. State of Punjab (2013) 2 SCC 713; Jagmohan Singh v. State of UP (1973) 1 SCC 20; Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684. Sangeet v. State of Haryana (2013) 2 SCC 452 held inapplicable
sentencing_rationale: High Court commutation to life with a minimum of 20 years before release and no remission was upheld in view of the five deaths and the line of Supreme Court decisions fixing minimum terms for serious offences after commutation
judicial_aggravating_factors: Five persons died; offence serious in nature
other_sentence_order: High Court direction (affirmed): not to be released until 20 years served including period undergone; no remission by State or Government of India on any occasion

case_title: Prakash v. State of Rajasthan
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: hostile relations between the victim's family and the accused, arising from a neighbourhood dispute
evidence_type: Circumstantial (last seen in company of accused; recovery of blood-stained clothing on information given; motive)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.302, 364 and 120-B; life imprisonment under s.302 with fine of Rs.5000 each; RI 7 years under s.364 and 7 years RI under s.120-B (with fines)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302), kidnapping (IPC s.364) and criminal conspiracy (IPC s.120-B), as charged and affirmed for the appellants
neutral_facts: The victim, a seven-year-old boy, left home for school one morning in mid-April and did not return. His father searched relatives and the school without success and reported the boy missing to the police the same day. About five days later, the body of a boy was found on a hillock. The body had been partly eaten by animals, the right hand and head were missing, and the father identified the body from the clothes, shoes, socks and school bag. Three witnesses, two goldsmiths and a firewood collector, said they saw the victim in the company of three men, including the accused, on a scooter or walking towards the hillock around midday. The witnesses knew the accused and the victim, and one witness was cross-examined at length without any contradiction of his account. Following information given by one of the accused, a blood-stained pant and shirt were recovered from that accused's house in the presence of two witnesses. A forensic report found the blood on them to be of human origin. The victim's family had a prior dispute with the accused over a neighbourhood incident in which a girl died after consuming poison. One accused had threatened to finish the victim's family. The victim's mother said she saw the accused with a scooter near her house on the day the victim went missing.
physical_harm: Death of the seven-year-old victim; body mutilated, right hand and head missing, partly eaten by animals
motive: Enmity from a neighbourhood dispute over a girl's death by poison and threats to finish the victim's family (accepted by the court as proved)
key_evidence_accepted: Last-seen evidence of PW-3, PW-4 and PW-10; recovery of blood-stained pant and shirt with FSL report of human blood; motive evidence of PW-1 and PW-7
witness_credibility: PW-10 cross-examined at length with nothing disproving his statement; PW-3 and PW-4 did not identify the accused in the identification parade but their assertions were accepted; inconsistencies about the body's condition attributed to villager witnesses and were not held fatal
post_offence_conduct: Not stated for the appellants; blood-stained clothing recovered from a house on information given by A-1, who did not appeal
trial_duration: offence: 15.04.1998; trial judgment: 31.01.2002; High Court: 02.03.2006; Supreme Court: not given
legal_representation: Seeraj Bagga (amicus curiae) for the appellants; Shovan Mishra for the State
investigation_status: Report lodged 16.04.1998; second report 19.04.1998; accused arrested 22.04.1998; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court (31.01.2002): convicted and sentenced. High Court (02.03.2006): appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeals of A-2 and A-3 dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Relied on three circumstances: last seen in company of accused, recovery of incriminating articles on information given, and motive. No separate oral argument recorded in the judgment
defence_argument: Amicus contended that absent direct evidence, any discrepancy suggesting two possible views should give the accused benefit of doubt; counsel also pointed to inconsistencies in witnesses' description of the body
legal_principle_applied: Five golden principles for proof by circumstantial evidence: circumstances fully established and consistent only with guilt, conclusive, excluding every other hypothesis, forming a complete chain
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, (1984) 4 SCC 116; Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra, (1973) 2 SCC 793 (as cited within Sharda)

case_title: Venkatesha v. State of Karnataka
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: the accused blamed the intended target (PW-14, the shop owner and employer of the deceased) for interfering in his marital affairs and threatened to kill him; the deceased was an employee and an unintended victim
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.307, s.427 each read with s.34; Explosive Substances Act 1908 s.3 read with s.34 IPC
evidence_type: Approver (accomplice) testimony; eyewitness and injured-witness depositions; medical evidence; forensic (FSL) evidence; extrajudicial confession evidence via a witness; recovery/investigation evidence (purchase of gelatin sticks, detonators and tape recorder)
confession: Alleged extrajudicial confession by A-1 and A-2 to PW-3 (a relative) that they planted the bomb; the trial court relied on it as independent corroboration. Approver A-3's testimony was also relied on.
aggravating_circumstances: Use of an explosive device in a shop; death of an innocent employee; injuries to two other employees
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC: life rigorous imprisonment and Rs.5,000 fine; s.307 r/w s.34: five years RI and Rs.1,000 fine; s.427 r/w s.34: one year RI; Explosive Substances Act s.3 r/w s.34: ten years RI and Rs.2,000 fine
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentences upheld
offence_finally_established: Murder under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; attempt to murder under s.307 r/w s.34 IPC; mischief under s.427 r/w s.34 IPC; Explosive Substances Act s.3 r/w s.34 IPC
neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that two accused, acting with a third person who later became an accomplice prosecution witness, planned to kill the owner of a hair salon whom they blamed for interfering in one accused's marital troubles. One accused had threatened to kill the owner within a week, and the other joined in that threat. The third person allegedly left a cardboard box containing a tape recorder loaded with explosive at the salon, saying he would return for it. Shortly afterwards, an employee switched on the device, which exploded with a loud sound, damaging the premises. The employee died from his injuries, and two other employees were injured. The prosecution relied on the accomplice's account; the testimony of a relative who said he saw the accused collect the box, pay for it and later hear them admit planting a bomb; the statements of the injured; and a doctor who described the injuries as caused by the blast. Forensic analysis of recovered debris and clothing reportedly detected nitroglycerine, nitrocellulose and ammonium nitrate. Investigators also found that gelatin sticks and detonators had been bought and that a tape recorder had been purchased from a shop.
physical_harm: Death of one employee (the deceased, Shankar); injuries to two other employees (PW-1 and PW-7) from the blast
financial_property_loss: Damage to the shop and several articles; value not stated
premeditation_planning: Yes. The court found the bomb was deliberately planted to kill the owner, with a co-accused deputed to carry the box to the shop and leave it there on a pretext.
motive: Domestic/marital grievance: A-1 blamed the shop owner (PW-14) for interfering in his marital affairs and threatened to kill him; A-2 joined the threat. Accepted by the courts as established.
key_evidence_accepted: Approver PW-2's testimony, corroborated by PW-3's deposition (box handover and confession), PW-1, PW-4, PW-7, PW-8, PW-9, PW-10, PW-11, PW-21 (FSL report of explosive residues) and PW-27 (medical evidence of blast injuries)
witness_credibility: The High Court found PW-3 credible with no reason to implicate the accused falsely; the trial court found the approver's version corroborated and the cross-examination did not discredit the medical and forensic witnesses. The Supreme Court accepted these concurrent findings.
post_offence_conduct: Per the trial court, the accused told witnesses after leaving the box that they had kept a bomb to kill their enemy and threatened them not to disclose it
custody_duration: About 12 years in custody as of 13 March 2012 (per the State's communication noted by the Court)
trial_duration: offence: 2 April 1996; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 16.03.2004; Supreme Court: 8 January 2013
legal_representation: Appellant: Tanuj Bagga Sharma (Amicus Curiae). State: Gurudatta Ankolekar, Azeem A. Kalebudde, V.N. Raghupathy and Sanjay R. Hedge for the respondent.
investigation_status: FIR lodged by PW-1; investigation by CCB police; chargesheet filed; committal after pardon to an accomplice; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted on all counts and sentenced. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: The approver's evidence was uncorroborated in material particulars, so the appellant should be acquitted.
legal_principle_applied: Under s.133 Evidence Act a conviction is not illegal merely on uncorroborated accomplice testimony, but the rule of practice (treated as a rule of law) requires corroboration in material particulars by untainted, credible evidence before convicting on an approver's evidence. Concurrent findings of fact on evidence not perverse, so no interference.

case_title: Chinnam Kameswara Rao and Ors. v. State of A.P. (rep. by Home Secretary)
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: an altercation the previous day (over palmyrah nuts), after which an accused threatened the deceased with dire consequences
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.324 r/w s.34 (charged as s.302 and s.324 per p.2; p.7 refers to s.302 and s.307)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured witness PW-1 and PWs 2, 3, 4, 6); post-mortem; seizure of weapons; circumstantial (prior threat, lying in wait)
aggravating_circumstances: Head injuries to a vital part causing skull fracture; assault continued after the deceased fell; premeditated attack
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted all accused
high_court_outcome: State's appeal partly allowed: acquittal of appellants reversed and convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 and s.324 r/w s.34 IPC; acquittal of A-4 affirmed
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302 r/w s.34); attempt/hurt under IPC s.324 r/w s.34
neutral_facts: On an evening in late April, four men stopped the victim and a second man while they were walking home at a park centre. The previous day, the same parties had quarrelled while the victim and the second man were collecting palmyrah nuts from fields. A shopkeeper in the vicinity intervened and pacified them, though one of the accused allegedly threatened the victim with dire consequences. On the following evening, the accused allegedly confronted the victim and the second man. Three of the accused were armed with stout casuarina sticks; the fourth was unarmed. An altercation followed, and one accused allegedly struck the victim on the head. When the second man intervened, two others allegedly struck him on the head with sticks. Both men fell. The fourth accused allegedly kicked and punched the victim, while the three armed men continued hitting both of them. The assailants then ran away towards the house of one of them, believing both men dead. Four persons were said to have witnessed the incident. The injured were taken to a government hospital, where the victim's statement was recorded. The victim died of his injuries in the early hours of the next day. The investigation included arrest of the accused, post-mortem examination of the body, and seizure of the weapons of offence.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from head injuries including skull fracture; the second man (PW-1) was also injured with bleeding head injuries
premeditation_planning: Yes: court found the attack premeditated and preconcerted, given the prior threat, lying in wait, and fetching hidden sticks
motive: The incident was a sequel to the previous day's confrontation and threat (accepted by the court)
key_evidence_accepted: Depositions of eyewitnesses PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, PW-4 and PW-6; PW-3 as witness to the prior threat; evidence of lying in wait; nature of head injuries
witness_credibility: PW-1 (injured) found credible; trial court erred in rejecting eyewitness testimony over minor contradictions that did not shatter credibility
post_offence_conduct: Fled the scene after believing both victims were dead
trial_duration: offence: 27 April 2003; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 8 February 2011; Supreme Court: 10 January 2013
legal_representation: Appellants: M.S. Ganesh (senior counsel) and T. Anamika. State: D. Mahesh Babu, Mayur Shah, Savita Devi, Suchitra Hrangkhawl, Amit K. Nain, M.B. Shivdu
investigation_status: Case registered on victim's hospital statement; investigation completed (arrests, post-mortem, weapon seizure); charge sheet filed; trial completed with 13 prosecution witnesses and no defence evidence
procedural_irregularity: Section 34 was not in the charge against the appellants; court held no prejudice was shown, so the conviction's legality was unaffected
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted all accused. High Court: appellants' acquittal reversed and convicted (s.302/34 and s.324/34 IPC); A-4 acquittal affirmed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, convictions upheld
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: High Court wrongly re-appraised evidence and reversed acquittal; conviction under s.302/307 r/w s.34 invalid as s.34 was not charged, causing prejudice; no evidence of common intention to murder, so at most s.304 culpable homicide
legal_principle_applied: Appellate court has full power under s.386 CrPC to re-appraise evidence; if the trial court's acquittal was not a reasonably possible view, it may reverse; absence of s.34 charge causes no prejudice unless shown; common intention may be premeditated

State of Karnataka (2007) 4 SCC 415; Krishna Govind Patil v. State of Maharashtra AIR 1963 SC 1413; Darbara Singh v. State of Punjab 2012 (8) SCALE 649; Gurpreet Singh v. State of Punjab (2005) 12 SCC 615

other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Ram Pal @ Bunda v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: the accused had an inimical relationship with the victim's family, stemming from his earlier misbehaviour towards the victim's elder sister and a village panchayat apology; no direct relationship with the victim is described
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.376
weapon: Not stated as a weapon; the victim's neck was wrapped with a blue shawl owned by her, and death was by strangulation
evidence_type: Circumstantial, with medical (post-mortem and forensic) evidence, motive evidence and eyewitness-type testimony of presence at the scene
aggravating_circumstances: Rape and murder of the victim; death by strangulation with contusions on face and chin and abrasions on back
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.302 and 376; sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life and 10 years rigorous imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 686-DB of 2006) dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: On 18 February 2005 at about 6:30 p.m. the victim went to fields near her village to ease herself and did not return. Her family searched but could not find her. During the search the accused was found in the fields. When the victim's mother asked him where her daughter was, he did not respond and ran away from the place. He could not be traced in the village until 21 February 2005, when he was reportedly produced and arrested. The victim's body was found the next morning in daylight in fields belonging to another person, with her neck wrapped in a blue shawl that belonged to her. The family had earlier had a dispute with the accused: some years before, he and a cousin had teased the victim's elder sister on a path, the matter was taken to a village panchayat, and both apologised; the accused was said to have later threatened revenge. Medical examination showed death by asphyxia due to strangulation, ante-mortem and sufficient to cause death. There were multiple abrasions and contusions on the face, chin and back. Forensic examination found blood on the shawl, salwar and underwear of the victim. Human semen was detected on a vaginal swab from the victim. The accused's underwear, taken on his examination after arrest, also showed human semen. The medical evidence indicated the victim had been subjected to sexual intercourse before her death.
physical_harm: Death by asphyxia due to strangulation; multiple abrasions and contusions on face and chin; superficial abrasions on back; victim subjected to sexual intercourse before death
motive: Revenge for the accused's humiliation at the village panchayat over his earlier misconduct (teasing the victim's elder sister in 2002) and the apology he was forced to give
key_evidence_accepted: Medical evidence of death by strangulation and sexual intercourse before death; FSL reports of blood and semen on victim's clothing and vaginal swab and semen on accused's underwear; PW-10's evidence that the accused was present at the scene and ran away; PW-12's evidence of the accused's absence for two days; PW-11's motive evidence, corroborated by PW-10
witness_credibility: PW-10's evidence on the accused's presence at the scene was accepted despite minor variations from her police statement; PW-11's motive evidence was corroborated by PW-10; PW-12's evidence on absence was accepted as the record was not contradicted, despite PW-13 turning hostile
post_offence_conduct: Ran away from the scene without answering the mother's questions and remained absconding for two days; found absent from the village until arrest on 21.2.2005
trial_duration: offence: 18.2.2005; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 07.09.2011; Supreme Court: 11 April 2013
legal_representation: Appellant (accused): R.K. Talwar, David Rao, K. Kaushik, Chander Shekhar Ashri; Respondent (State of Haryana): Kamal Mohan Gupta
investigation_status: Body found after police intimation; accused arrested on 21.2.2005; forensic and medical reports obtained; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted

prosecution_argument: Not stated
