case_title: Indrajit Sureshprasad Bind & Ors. v. State of Gujarat
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband); parents-in-law of the victim
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304B, s.498A, s.306 read with s.114
weapon: Kerosene (poured over the victim's body; self-immolation)
evidence_type: Documentary (letters Ext. 49, Ext. 31, Ext. 44); oral evidence of PW3 and defence witness DW1
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss. 304B, 498A and 306 IPC; sentence not stated in the judgment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction affirmed
neutral_facts: The victim married the accused husband in 2002, and his parents lived with the couple at the matrimonial home in Ahmedabad. On 18 May 2004 the victim poured kerosene over her body and died of burn injuries. Five days later, on 21 May 2004, her brother lodged a complaint with the police. He alleged that the victim had written to him that her husband and in-laws had harassed her for about two years over demands for household items and a colour television, that they used abusive language and beat her, and that they had instigated her to end her life. The brother produced a photocopy of a letter dated 16 February 2004, said to be written by the victim from Ahmedabad, and gave evidence that it was the victim's writing. The defence contended that the victim was at her parents' village in Bihar on that date and produced a postal inland letter bearing dispatch and receipt stamps, together with a witness who had written it, to support this. The brother also produced his own letter of 25 April 2004 to the victim, in which he wrote that after speaking to her on the telephone he was satisfied she was living happily and not being misbehaved with, and referred to sums of Rs.33,000 and Rs.43,000. The police registered an FIR, investigated, and filed a charge sheet.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from burn injuries after pouring kerosene over her body
financial_property_loss: Not applicable (court could not record a definite finding of a dowry demand of Rs.33,000 or Rs.43,000)
motive: alleged: demand for dowry and cruelty/harassment by the husband and his parents; not accepted by the court
key_evidence_accepted: Defence witness DW1's evidence supported by Ext. 44 (inland letter with postal stamps) accepted as making it probable the victim was in Bihar on 16-02-2004; Ext. 31 (letter of 25-04-2004) relied on as showing the victim was living happily and not being misbehaved with
witness_credibility: Court had grave doubts about PW3's account and the authorship of Ext. 49; PW3's own letter Ext. 31 (admitted by him) undermined the cruelty story; DW1's evidence found to be supported by documents
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Appellants on bail at the Supreme Court stage; bail bonds discharged. Earlier bail history not stated
trial_duration: offence: 18-05-2004; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 04-12-2006; Supreme Court: 18-03-2013
legal_representation: Accused: Haresh Raichura, Saroj Raichura, Kalp Raichura, Ranvir Singh, Rajat Vats. State: Hemantika Wahi, Pinky Behara, Shubhade Deshpande
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial held
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss. 304B, 498A, 306 IPC. High Court: conviction affirmed. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, convictions set aside
prosecution_argument: Ext. 31 shows a dowry demand of Rs.33,000 or Rs.43,000 on PW3 in connection with the marriage
defence_argument: Victim was in Bihar, not Ahmedabad, on 16-02-2004, so Ext. 49 is not genuine; victim wanted to stay with her parents and was a minor when married
legal_principle_applied: Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt cruelty or harassment in connection with dowry soon before death (s.304B) and cruelty as defined in the Explanation to s.498A; mere demand of dowry without cruelty is insufficient; abetment requires proof of instigation
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds of the appellants discharged

case_title: R. Shaji v. State of Kerala
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: the victim had an illicit relationship with the accused's wife; the accused had earlier allowed the victim free access to his house and was related to the victim's circle
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.120-B; IPC s.201 r/w s.120-B; IPC s.364 r/w s.120-B
weapon: Chopper (M.O.4); a Maruti van (M.O.5) was used as a vehicle in the crime
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence, including last-seen evidence, motive, recoveries (chopper, skull, van, glove, rope), DNA and post-mortem evidence, and eyewitness testimony of witnesses who saw the accused
confession: Disclosure statement by the accused leading to recovery of the chopper, skull, glove and plastic rope; the court relied on it as the basis of the recoveries. No confession of guilt is recorded.
aggravating_circumstances: Threat to chop the victim into pieces; the victim's body was dismembered and parts were dumped in a lake; the accused was a senior police officer
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.120-B IPC: life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,00,000; s.201 r/w s.120-B: 3 years and Rs. 2,000; s.364 r/w s.120-B: 7 years RI and Rs. 5,000; sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence affirmed
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302 r/w s.120-B); evidence-disappearance (IPC s.201 r/w s.120-B); kidnapping (IPC s.364 r/w s.120-B)
neutral_facts: The victim had developed an illicit relationship with the accused's wife. After the accused learned of it, relatives held a meeting, the matter was apparently settled, and the victim was told to leave the area. A witness said the accused had threatened that if the accused could lay hands on the victim, the accused would chop the victim into pieces. On 15 February 2005 the victim was seen in the company of a co-accused, first at a bar and then at a roadside food stall. Witnesses at the food stall said the accused arrived in a Maruti van with other men, drank coffee, and then followed the motorcycle carrying the victim and the co-accused. An auto-rickshaw driver saw a van parked on a road that night with a man standing beside it, and another driver saw two men take a pillion rider into a van. The victim was not seen again. Between 16 and 19 February 2005, parts of a body, including legs, a torso, hands and a head, were found floating in a lake. The victim's father and others identified the remains, and DNA testing of the parents' samples matched the limbs. A chopper was recovered from the lake on the accused's disclosure, and the accused personally retrieved it. A skull was found after digging at a place the accused showed investigators. A glove and plastic rope were also recovered at the accused's instance. A Maruti van was recovered, and hair found in it matched the victim. A forensic surgeon opined that the chopper could have caused the dismemberment. The serologist could not determine the blood group on the chopper. A witness testified that the accused had borrowed the van and returned it later, and call records between the accused and that witness were proved. A letter purportedly written by the victim was posted at a post office, and a witness saw the accused post it.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by homicide; body dismembered and parts recovered from a lake (legs, torso, hands, head, skull)
premeditation_planning: Found: the accused and co-accused hatched a conspiracy to eliminate the victim; the chopper was made to order and handed over in early January 2005
motive: Accepted by the court: the accused had adequate reason to harbour animosity, as he may well have been unable to tolerate the victim's intimacy with his wife
key_evidence_accepted: DNA report identifying the dismembered body parts; post-mortem findings consistent with use of a chopper; disclosure-based recovery of chopper, skull, glove and rope; recovery of the van with matching hair; last-seen evidence with co-accused; motive; testimony of PW.12 and other eyewitnesses
witness_credibility: PW.12 (prime witness) found credible in part: the High Court's finding that his testimony was disbelieved in toto was held factually incorrect, and his evidence on the accused's conduct was accepted; PW.8 and PW.13 were accepted as knowing the accused; the court accepted the testimony of accomplice-witnesses PW.8 and PW.11 with care and caution
post_offence_conduct: Disclosure leading to recovery of the chopper, skull and van; a letter apparently written in the victim's name was posted to mislead the family (the court also said it became insignificant)
trial_duration: offence: 15/16.02.2005 (victim last seen 15.2.2005; died intervening night 15/16.2.2005); trial judgment: 3.1.2006; High Court: 10.12.2009; Supreme Court: 4.2.2013
legal_representation: Appellant: Dr. S. Gopakumaran Nair, T.G. Narayanan Nair, K.N. Madhusoodhanan. State: R. Basanth, Ramesh Babu M.R., Karthik Ashok, P.V. Dinesh
investigation_status: Investigation completed; accused arrested 24.2.2005; charge sheet filed against five persons; trial proceeded against two; others absconding; two later tried separately
procedural_irregularity: Section 164 CrPC statements of two witnesses were apparently not marked at trial; no test identification parade was held (the court held this immaterial in the circumstances)
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced. High Court: appeal dismissed on 10.12.2009. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Circumstances proved point only to the accused's guilt; no one else could have committed the murder; DNA established the victim's identity; prosecution witnesses had no reason to depose falsely; test identification parade would have been a formality because witnesses knew the accused
defence_argument: No motive; purely circumstantial case with no eyewitness and an incomplete chain; no test identification parade; s.164 statements not exhibited; blood group on the chopper not detected; identification by photograph and brief sighting unreliable; the victim's body identification and DNA process doubtful
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence test (chain complete, excludes other hypotheses); motive as a relevant factor; failure to detect blood group does not break the chain once recovery is made on disclosure; test identification parade has limited significance where witnesses know the accused; quality not number of witnesses; evidence weighed not counted; criminal conspiracy may be proved circumstantially
precedent_relied_upon: Jogendra Nahak (AIR 1999 SC 2565); Assistant Collector of Central Excise v. Duncan Agro (AIR 2000 SC 2901); Prabhu Babaji Navie (AIR 1956 SC 51); Babu v. State of Kerala (2010) 9 SCC 189; Sharad Birdhichand Sarda (AIR 1984 SC 1622); Vijay @ Chinee (2010) 8 SCC 191; Mir Nagvi Askari (AIR 2010 SC 528); Vadivelu Thevar (AIR 1957 SC 614)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Threat to chop the victim into pieces; dismemberment of the body; the accused's position as a senior police officer
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Vipin Jaiswal v. State of A.P.
accused_occupation: Worked at a xerox cum type institute in Nampally (per PW1's evidence)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304B; IPC s.498A
evidence_type: Oral testimony (PW1 father, PW2 cousin, PW4 mother, DW1 appellant); documentary (Ext. 019 chit)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.304B and 498A; sentence not stated in the judgment
high_court_outcome: Acquitted co-accused A2 and A3; maintained appellant's conviction under ss.304B and 498A
neutral_facts: The victim was married to the accused in February 1996. The victim's father alleged that after the marriage the victim was subjected to physical and mental torture by the accused and the accused's family for not getting sufficient dowry. Gold jewellery, silver items, furniture and other gifts were said to have been given at the marriage. On 2 April 1999 the victim's father went to the accused's house with relatives, and he alleged he was abused and physically pushed out. On 4 April 1999 the victim's father was told by telephone that the victim had suffered severe burn injuries and died at the accused's house. An FIR was lodged the same day and the police registered a case and investigated. At trial, the victim's father, the victim's cousin and the victim's mother testified. The father and mother stated that about six months after the marriage the victim reported that the accused had demanded Rs.50,000 to buy a computer for a business. The prosecution witnesses made general allegations of harassment but identified no specific acts of cruelty. The accused gave evidence that, while cleaning the house, he found a handwritten chit bearing the victim's handwriting and signature. The chit stated that nobody was responsible for the victim's death, that the victim's parents and family had harassed the accused, and that the victim was tired of life because of quarrels.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from burn injuries
financial_property_loss: Not applicable (alleged Rs.50,000 demand was not accepted as dowry; alleged marriage gifts worth above Rs.2,50,000 were not a loss found by the court)
motive: alleged: dowry demand of Rs.50,000 for purchasing a computer to start a business (not accepted as dowry by the court)
key_evidence_accepted: Appellant's testimony (DW1) and Ext. 019 suicide chit; evidence of PW1 and PW4 on the Rs.50,000 demand (found not to be dowry)
witness_credibility: Prosecution witnesses PW1 and PW4 gave only general allegations of harassment without specific acts; DW1's account of the chit was not rejected on proper grounds, the court found the lower courts' disbelief was based on imaginary reasoning
post_offence_conduct: Per DW1's evidence (not a court finding), he took the chit to the police station, which refused to receive it
custody_duration: Arrested; released on bail after about one month (per DW1's account); exact custody duration not stated
bail_history: Released on bail; bail bond discharged by the Supreme Court
trial_duration: offence: 4.4.1999; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 11.12.2006; Supreme Court: 13.03.2013
legal_representation: Appellant: A.T.M. Ranga Ramanujam, Prabhakar Sharma, Dipankar Das, Devesh Singh, Shanti Kumar Jaisani, Anu Gupta. State: Mayur R. Shah, D. Mahesh Babu, Suchitra Hrangkhawl, Amjid Maqbool, Amit K. Nain, M. Bala Shivudu
investigation_status: FIR registered on 4.4.1999; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial held
procedural_irregularity: Neither the trial court nor the High Court compared handwriting under s.73 or sought expert opinion under s.45 Evidence Act on the chit
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.304B and 498A. High Court: appellant's conviction maintained; co-accused A2 and A3 acquitted. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction set aside
prosecution_argument: The s.2 Dowry Prohibition Act phrase 'in connection with the marriage' covers the computer demand; PW1, PW2 and PW4 evidence proved dowry demands beyond Rs.50,000; the suicide note should not be believed as the victim was a matriculate; DW1's evidence alone cannot prove the note was written by the victim; cruelty soon before death was proved
defence_argument: The Rs.50,000 demand was for a computer for the accused's own business, not dowry; it is absent from the FIR; the suicide note (Ext. D19) is in the victim's handwriting and its signature matches Ext. D1
legal_principle_applied: Dowry requires a connection with the marriage; to convict under ss.304B and 498A the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt cruelty or harassment soon before death; s.113B presumption depends on this; handwriting may be proved under ss.73 and 45 Evidence Act
precedent_relied_upon: Appasaheb & Anr. v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 9 SCC 721
other_sentence_order: Bail bond furnished by the appellant discharged

case_title: Rohtash Kumar v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.404
weapon: Rope found near the body; death by smothering and throttling
evidence_type: Circumstantial (last seen together, call records, recovery of phone, guest house conduct, FSL hair comparison); medical (post-mortem); recovery memos; oral testimony
confession: No formal confession. Telephone calls from the victim's phone to relatives in which the accused said he had killed her were relied on as evidence. Diary and letter writings were also relied on as admissions of motive.
aggravating_circumstances: Killing of the spouse by smothering and throttling; accused fled, used a fictitious identity, attempted suicide, and made calls to relatives claiming the killing
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302 and s.404; life imprisonment and Rs 5,000 fine under s.302 (one year default); two years RI and Rs 500 fine under s.404; sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed (Criminal Appeal No. 862-DB of 2006, judgment dated 5.2.2009); conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim had married, and the marriage was not approved by the victim's family and was strained. The couple had started divorce proceedings by mutual consent, with the second hearing listed for the following day. On the day before that hearing, the accused visited the hostel where the victim lived and worked. The two spoke for about an hour in the verandah, after which the accused left alone. Later, the victim was found dead among plants in the hostel grounds. The victim's father, who came to the hostel, was told by hostel staff that the accused had visited. A complaint was lodged, and police recovered the body and nearby objects, including a rope. The post-mortem examination found death by asphyxia caused by smothering and throttling, with neck abrasions and fractures of the neck and chest. Calls were later made from the victim's mobile phone to her mother and other relatives, in which the caller said he had killed her and would commit suicide. The accused was traced to a guest house, where he had registered under a fictitious name and address. He tried to end his life there and ran away, leaving a diary, a letter and a wrist watch, which contained writings about his grievances with the victim's family. The victim's mobile phone was later recovered from a shop in another state, following the accused's disclosure, and call records showed it was used after the death. Hair found at the scene was reported as similar to the accused's sample. The accused declined a test identification parade.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by asphyxia from smothering and throttling; neck abrasions, contusions, fracture of thyroid cartilage and tracheal rings, and bilateral clavicle and rib fractures
financial_property_loss: Victim's mobile phone taken by the accused and later recovered; no monetary loss stated
premeditation_planning: Not expressly found; the court noted the accused met the victim just before the divorce date but recorded no finding of planning
motive: Accepted by the court: the accused's feelings of grievance against the victim and her family, drawn from the undelivered letter and the diary suicide note, and marital discord leading to the proposed divorce
key_evidence_accepted: Last-seen evidence of the hostel caretaker; post-mortem findings; call records and calls to relatives; recovery of the victim's phone after disclosure; diary, letter and wrist watch; guest house stay under fake name; FSL hair report; refusal of test identification parade
witness_credibility: Caretaker (PW.8) found independent and reliable, with no reason to doubt her statement. Hostile witness (PW.2) accepted in part where his evidence was consistent with prosecution case. Discrepancies held not material.
post_offence_conduct: Absconded for several days; stayed at a guest house under a fictitious name and address; attempted suicide and fled when chased; made calls to relatives about the killing; phone recovered after disclosure; refused test identification parade
trial_duration: offence: 2.9.2004; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 5.2.2009; Supreme Court: 29.5.2013
legal_representation: Appellant: Dr. Sushil Balwada, Pankaj Bhagat. State: Ramesh Kumar, Manish K. Bishnoi
investigation_status: FIR registered on complaint; investigation, post-mortem and FSL report completed; chargesheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced. High Court: appeal dismissed on 5.2.2009. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Accused was last seen with the victim and left alone just before her death; he fled, used a fake name at a guest house, attempted suicide and left incriminating writings; conduct shows guilt; concurrent findings should not be disturbed
defence_argument: No eye-witness and circumstantial chain incomplete; divorce was to be finalised the next day so no motive; key guard, cook and guest house witnesses not examined; hostile witness evidence unusable; last-seen theory inapplicable; phone recovery far away; material inconsistencies
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain consistent only with guilt; last seen together shifts burden to accused to explain death; motive relevant; s.313 explanation and false explanation as missing link; evidence weighed not counted; hostile and police witness evidence assessed with caution; minor discrepancies ignored
precedent_relied_upon: R. Shaji v. State of Kerala, AIR 2013 SC 651; Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1984 SC 1622; Paramjeet Singh v. State of Uttarakhand, AIR 2011 SC 200; State of Maharashtra v. Suresh, (2000) 1 SCC 471; Nika Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh, AIR 1972 SC 2077; Ganeshlal v. State of Maharashtra, (1992) 3 SCC 106; Trimukh Maroti Kirkan v. State of Maharashtra, (2006) 10 SCC 681; Pradeep Narayan Madgaonkar v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1995 SC 1930
judicial_aggravating_factors: Court described the killing as a heinous crime arising from marital discord; no other aggravating factors weighed separately
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Subodh Nath and Anr. v. State of Tripura
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
weapon: Axe (handle recovered near body), gun, lathi/wooden stick
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-13); corroborating witness (PW-6); inquest report and investigating officer evidence on injuries; recovery of axe handle and sticks; circumstantial evidence
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs.5000 each (default one year)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence maintained
neutral_facts: The victim went out to graze cows and did not return by dusk; the next morning his body was found with injuries in a jungle. The police registered a case, held an inquest, and during investigation a labourer who worked under the victim was apprehended and made a statement implicating two men. The principal evidence is the account of an eyewitness who was grazing cows with the victim in a rubber garden around 2 p.m. At about 4 p.m. the two accused arrived armed with an axe, a lathi and a gun. The first accused struck the victim with the axe; the second struck him with a stick; and the first then took a gun from the jungle and shot him. The eyewitness fled, stating he was afraid because the accused had threatened him with dire consequences if he disclosed the incident. He later told another villager, and subsequently gave a statement to police. A witness stated that around 1.30 p.m. he had seen the victim and the accused grazing cows nearby. The investigating officer's inquest report recorded injuries caused by an axe and a gun. He also recovered the handle of an axe near the body and seized it under a seizure list prepared in the presence of witnesses. Blood-stained wooden sticks and a takkal dao were also found near the body. A charge-sheet was filed against the two accused.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from injuries caused by an axe and a gun
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness account of PW-13; corroboration by PW-6 (presence at grazing site around 1.30 p.m.); Investigating Officer's evidence and inquest report showing axe and gun injuries; seizure of axe handle
witness_credibility: PW-13 found reliable; his flight was explained by fear of the accused; discrepancies among PW-1, PW-2, PW-13 and PW-19 held not material
post_offence_conduct: Accused allegedly threatened the eyewitness with dire consequences if he disclosed the incident; the court accepted that this explained the witness leaving for Cachar
trial_duration: offence: 09.10.1998; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 08.06.2005; Supreme Court: 19.03.2013
legal_representation: Accused: Lalit Chauhan, Somanadri Goud, Kshatrashal Raj, Abhishek Vinod Deshmukh (for Parekh & Co.). State of Tripura: Ritu Raj Biswas, Gopal Singh
investigation_status: FIR registered; inquest held; witness apprehended and s.164 CrPC statement recorded; charge-sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted both under s.302/34 IPC, life imprisonment and fine. High Court: conviction and sentence maintained, appeal dismissed. Supreme Court: appellant no.1's appeal dismissed; appellant no.2's appeal allowed and remitted to the Juvenile Justice Board
prosecution_argument: Appellant no.2 was over 16 and not protected by the 2000 Act, so the conviction should stand; PW-13's evidence was corroborated by PW-6 and by the recovery of the weapons and inquest report; the disclosure-based recovery was relied on under Suresh Chandra Bahri
defence_argument: Appellant no.2 was a juvenile under the 2000 Act as amended (Hari Ram); appellant no.1's conviction rests on the sole, uncorroborated and unreliable eyewitness PW-13, who fled; discrepancies in PW-1, PW-2, PW-13 and PW-19; no recovery of weapon; motive unproved
legal_principle_applied: Discrepancies in witness testimony do not defeat evidence unless material; eyewitness evidence can be accepted if corroborated by material particulars; motive is irrelevant where direct evidence exists; juvenility under ss.7A and 20 of the 2000 Act applies to pending cases
precedent_relied_upon: State of Rajasthan v. Smt. Kalki (1981) 2 SCC 752 (relied on); Hari Ram v. State of Rajasthan (2009) 13 SCC 211 (relied on); Pratap Singh v. State of Jharkhand (2005) 3 SCC 551 (held inapplicable); Badri v. State of Rajasthan (1976) 1 SCC 442 and Lallu Manjhi v. State of Jharkhand AIR 2003 SC 854 (referred to); Suresh Chandra Bahri v. State of Bihar AIR 1994 SC 2420 (referred to)
other_sentence_order: Appellant no.2's case remitted to the Juvenile Justice Board of North Tripura district for disposal under the 2000 Act within four months

case_title: Rakesh and Another v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband); Relative (mother-in-law). Prior dowry-related harassment and demands for money described.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.498A; IPC s.302 r/w s.34
evidence_type: Dying declaration; medical evidence (duty doctor, casualty medical officer, post-mortem); magistrate's testimony; father of victim's testimony; recovery of kerosene stove on disclosure
aggravating_circumstances: Victim beaten mercilessly, including a blow with a leg on the neck before being set on fire; prolonged dowry harassment; accused did not inform victim's parents or seek her transfer to a better hospital
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.498A IPC (RI one year, fine Rs.500 each) and s.302 r/w s.34 IPC (RI for life, fine Rs.2000 each); sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
offence_finally_established: IPC s.498A and IPC s.302 r/w s.34
neutral_facts: The victim had been married to one accused for about eight years and had four children. The victim's family had given dowry at the wedding, but the victim was allegedly harassed for more, including after a sister's wedding about fifteen days before the incident. On the night of 14 May 1998, around 11 p.m., a quarrel took place at the accused's house. It is alleged that one accused placed a leg on the victim's neck and beat the victim, after which the other accused held the victim's hands while the husband sprinkled kerosene and set the victim on fire with a match. A relative was present in the house. The victim was taken to hospital in the early hours of 15 May 1998. On 16 May 1998 a judicial magistrate, after a duty doctor certified the victim fit and conscious, recorded the victim's statement in question-and-answer form, with a toe impression, naming the husband and mother-in-law and describing the dowry harassment. The examining doctor recorded burns over approximately 85% of the body. The victim died of burn injuries on 4 June 1998 at another hospital, and the post-mortem attributed death to burns. Police arrested the husband on 21 May 1998, when he showed doctors burn injuries to his hands; a stove containing kerosene was recovered on his disclosure. The victim's father testified about the in-laws' harassment. A defence witness, a child of the accused, said the fire came from a kerosene stove but admitted the husband was present in the house at the time.
physical_harm: Superficial to deep burns over almost all the body except the legs below the knees (approx. 85%); death from burn injuries
motive: Accepted by the Court: dowry-related harassment and demands for money from the victim's father, including after a sister's wedding
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration recorded by the Judicial Magistrate after the duty doctor certified fitness; doctor's evidence on fitness and burns; Magistrate's evidence; post-mortem evidence of death from burns
witness_credibility: Magistrate (PW-10) and doctor (PW-6) assessed as reliable; alleged wrong names and presence of relatives held not material, as the Magistrate had directed relatives to leave
post_offence_conduct: Accused husband did not get treatment for his alleged hand burns on the day of the incident, only showing them to a doctor on arrest on 21.05.1998; accused did not inform victim's parents
trial_duration: offence: 14.05.1998; trial judgment: 27.09.2001 (conviction) and 28.09.2001 (sentence); High Court: 15.05.2006; Supreme Court: 22.03.2013
legal_representation: Accused: R.N. Kush, S.K. Sabharwal. State: Kamal Mohan Gupta, Mohd. Zahid Hussain
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charges framed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted by the Court; presence of some relatives in the ward during recording was considered and held not to affect the declaration
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Dying declaration was validly recorded after fitness certification; husband's hand burns were no answer since he did not seek treatment on the day; the husband's burns showed doubt about his version
defence_argument: Victim was not fit to make a statement (85% burns), so the dying declaration could not support conviction; husband's burn injuries showed he came to rescue the victim, so it was improbable he set her on fire; alternatively, conviction should be altered to s.304 Part I
legal_principle_applied: Dying declaration acceptable where recording procedure, fitness, and corroborating doctor and Magistrate evidence are satisfied; minor discrepancies in names and presence of relatives are not material; proof beyond reasonable doubt
precedent_relied_upon: None cited in the judgment
sentencing_rationale: Not stated as a separate sentencing rationale; Court declined to alter s.302 conviction to s.304 Part I given the death caused by burns at the accused's instance

case_title: Bhaikon @ Bakul Borah v. State of Assam
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.376
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; corroborative witness testimony (father, brothers, co-villagers); medical (post-mortem) evidence; recovery of stained underwear and FSL examination
aggravating_circumstances: Heinous crime of rape and murder; body dumped in a place surrounded by bushes and shrubs
mitigating_circumstances: Young age (33) and High Court's finding that the case was not rarest of rare
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.302 and 376 IPC; death sentence for s.302; life RI for s.376 with fine of Rs.10,000
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed and conviction confirmed; death sentence altered to life imprisonment (s.302) with fine of Rs.1,000; s.376 sentence altered to 7 years
neutral_facts: According to the prosecution, on the afternoon of 29 March 2000 the victim, a 22-year-old woman, went to a field near an embankment to attend her goats. When she did not return home, her father searched for her along the embankment. While returning, he heard loud laughter from a farm house belonging to the accused. Later he went back to the embankment, shouted for her, and the accused came out of the farm house and looked at him. The father then went down a path and found the victim lying dead on the left side, with a cut injury on her chin and blood oozing from her body. He raised an alarm, and her brother and other villagers gathered. The accused also came to the spot and enquired. The body was taken home, and a Sub-Inspector of Police seized the victim's clothing and prepared a seizure list. The inquest was held and the body was sent for post-mortem. The brother lodged a written complaint at the police out-post, and a case was registered. During investigation, the victim's underwear stained with semen was seized the same day. The accused and an eyewitness labourer were apprehended and interrogated. On the next day, police seized a blue underwear of the accused suspected to have semen stains, a bed sheet, a sporting item and a dao from the farm house. Both underwear items were sent for forensic examination. The post-mortem doctor found death by asphyxia due to throttling, a fractured trachea, bruises on the neck and a cut injury on the chin, and found no spermatozoa in the vaginal smear and no sign of injury on the genital organs. The eyewitness stated that he saw the accused and a companion follow the victim, saw them commit rape and then throttle her, and saw them drag the body into bushes. He said he stayed silent out of fear because both men carried khukris. The victim's father, two brothers and co-villagers gave corroborative evidence about the body and the scene.
physical_harm: Death by asphyxia due to throttling; cut injury over lower chin with cut to mandible; bruises on neck; fractured trachea
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-1; corroborative testimony of PW-2 (father of deceased) and brothers; post-mortem and injury evidence of PW-9; co-villagers' statements
witness_credibility: PW-1 found reliable and independent; trial court found him trustworthy with nothing to falsely implicate his master; his silence explained by fear. PW-2 corroborative; PW-9 injuries support prosecution story
post_offence_conduct: Accused came to the scene of the body and enquired; no other post-offence conduct noted

investigation_status: FIR registered; charge-sheet filed under ss.376 and 302 IPC; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted

prosecution_argument: PW-1's evidence is reliable and corroborated by PW-2 and PW-9; sentence commuted to life imprisonment cannot lead to automatic release after 14 years
defence_argument: PW-1's evidence unreliable; no mark of sexual violence so s.376 conviction unsustainable; after commutation to life the accused should have been released after 14 years
legal_principle_applied: Life imprisonment means imprisonment for the whole of life subject to executive remission under Arts 72 and 161; where death is commuted, remission must be exercised cautiously considering gravity of offence; medical and eyewitness evidence assessed for reliability
precedent_relied_upon: Life Convict @ Khoka Prasanta Sen v. B.K. Srivastava (2013) 3 SCC 425; Mohinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2013) 3 SCC 294; Sangeet v. State of Haryana (2013) 2 SCC 452; Rameshbhai Chandubhai Rathod (2) v. State of Gujarat (2011) 2 SCC 764; Chhote Lal v. State of MP (2011) 8 SCR 239; Mulla v. State of Maharashtra AIR 1961 SC 600; Swami Shraddananda (2) v. State of Karnataka (2008) 13 SCC 767; Sahib Hussain v. State of Rajasthan 2013 (6) Scale 219

judicial_mitigating_factors: Young age of accused (33), as noted by the High Court and not contested by the Supreme Court
judicial_aggravating_factors: Heinous nature of rape and murder and disposal of body in bushes, noted by the Supreme Court while describing the sentence

case_title: Kanhaiya Lal & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: the accused believed the deceased were responsible for the murder of the village leader's son, which led to revenge
weapon: Swords, gandasis (axe-like cutting weapons), sabals, sticks
evidence_type: Eyewitness (informant and relatives), medical evidence, recovery of weapons, site plan and autopsy
confession: None (weapons recovered on information given by accused in custody; not treated as a confession by the court)
aggravating_circumstances: Five deaths; ghastly and brutal assault in the house; High Court found the whole crime was committed in a planned design
mitigating_circumstances: Similarly placed persons given life sentence; accused in custody almost thirteen years; no specific overt acts attributed (High Court)
trial_court_outcome: Six accused sentenced to death (s.302); 11 accused sentenced to life imprisonment under s.302/149; the rest acquitted
high_court_outcome: Partly allowed: death sentences converted to life for several; some accused acquitted by benefit of doubt; convictions of Kanhaiyalal, Naval, Ram Lal and Radhey Shyam s/o Shankar Lal maintained
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 read with s.149 (for the accused whose convictions were maintained)
neutral_facts: On the evening of 28 June 2001, a group of about 25 to 30 persons from the village gathered outside the house where the victims were staying. They were armed with swords, gandasis, sabals and sticks. The group surrounded the house, climbed onto its roof and pelted stones, damaging the roof sheets and tiles. Several of the occupants escaped over a common wall into another room. Around midnight, the informant, his wife, his mother and another woman were made to sit on a neighbouring thatched roof. Shortly afterwards, a further group arrived in a jeep, broke open the door of the informant's house and inflicted blows with swords, gandasis and sticks. Three persons died inside the house. Two others were dragged outside and assaulted on the head, face, hands and feet with gandasis and swords, and both died. The attackers burnt two motorcycles belonging to the victims before leaving. The FIR was lodged at 6.45 a.m. on 29 June 2001. The informant explained that the family was too traumatised during the night to go to the police station. Investigators prepared a site plan, conducted autopsies, seized blood-stained clothing and recorded witness statements. Weapons were recovered on information given by accused persons in custody. The eyewitnesses were the informant and close relatives of the deceased. The defence contended that no independent witness was examined. The motive alleged was suspicion that the victims had killed the son of the village leader, which led to revenge.

financial_property_loss: Two motorcycles taken and burnt (value not stated)
premeditation_planning: Found by the High Court and recorded in the judgment: the crime was committed in a planned design; the Supreme Court described it as revenge for suspected killing
motive: Revenge: the village Sarpanch suspected the deceased of killing his son (court accepted this motive)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of the informant and close relatives describing weapons, assault and injuries; medical corroboration; seized weapons; explained FIR delay
witness_credibility: Relatives scrutinised with care but found reliable and credible; testimony withstood cross-examination in material particulars; minor discrepancies only
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: Almost thirteen years (as stated by the Court)
trial_duration: offence: 28-29 June 2001; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 2 June 2005; Supreme Court: 22 April 2013
legal_representation: Accused: Sushil Kumar Jain, Puneet Jain, Anurag Gohil, Pratibha Jain. State: Imtiaz Ahmed, Naghma Imtiaz, Milind Kumar
investigation_status: FIR registered 29 June 2001 (6.45 a.m.); site plan, autopsy, seizures, statements, weapons recovered; charge-sheet filed and case committed to Sessions; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: 17 convicted (6 death, 11 life), rest acquitted. High Court: partly allowed; death converted to life for several; some acquitted; four convictions maintained. Supreme Court: all appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Not stated (the judgment records the State's counsel appearing but does not set out the State's submissions)
defence_argument: Delay in lodging FIR made the explanation unacceptable and the story embellished; relatives were interested witnesses and no independent witness was examined; witnesses did not specify each accused's role or weapon; innocent persons were implicated
legal_principle_applied: Delay in FIR is not fatal if adequately explained; relatives as witnesses scrutinised with care but not discarded merely for being related; appeal against acquittal interfered with only for compelling reasons; death penalty only in rarest of rare cases
precedent_relied_upon: State of H.P. v. Gian Chand (2001) 6 SCC 71; Ramdas v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 2 SCC 110; Meharaj Singh v. State of U.P. (1994) 5 SCC 188; Kilakkatha Parambath Sasi (AIR 2011 SC 1064); Hari Obula Reddy (1981) 3 SCC 675; Karlik Malhar (1996) 1 SCC 614; Masalti (AIR 1965 SC 202); Jadunath Singh (AIR 1972 SC 116); Sohrab (AIR 1972 SC 2020); Bacchudas (2007) 9 SCC 135; Shera Ram (2012) 1 SCC 602; Bachan Singh (1980) 2 SCC 684; Machhi Singh (1983) 3 SCC 470; Ram Pal (2003) 7 SCC 141

other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Deepak Gulati v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance
statutory_provisions: IPC s.365; IPC s.376
evidence_type: Testimonial (prosecutrix's court deposition and Section 164 statement; father's and investigating officer's deposition); medical officer's deposition; school register proving age; hostile warden's deposition
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Appellant had already served more than 3 years of sentence; the victim was 19, left home voluntarily and made no complaint during the period of intimacy
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.365 and 376; RI 3 years and Rs.2,000 fine (s.365); RI 7 years and Rs.5,000 fine (s.376); sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentences affirmed
neutral_facts: The victim, a 19-year-old student, had known the accused for some time, and the accused had been meeting her outside her school in an attempt to develop intimate relations. On the day in question the accused induced the victim to travel with him to Kurukshetra so that they could get married, and she agreed. En route, the accused took her to a lake, where, according to the prosecution, he had sexual intercourse with her against her wishes, behind bushes. He then took her to Kurukshetra, where she stayed with his relatives for three or four days, during which he allegedly raped her. The accused later threw her out of the house. She went to a university hostel, where the warden became suspicious and questioned her; the victim narrated the incident and the warden informed her father. The victim later met the accused at a temple, where he allegedly persuaded her to accompany him to Ambala to marry. At the bus stand, the victim's father and police officers were present, and the accused was apprehended. The victim's father had lodged a complaint alleging enticement and wrongful confinement. The victim was medically examined, and the medical officer deposed that she had indulged in sexual intercourse and was habitual to it. Her statement was recorded before a Magistrate under Section 164 Cr.P.C. The warden, declared hostile, deposed that the victim had stayed in the hostel without permission. The school register established the victim's date of birth. The investigating officer deposed about the search and apprehension.
physical_harm: No injuries stated; medical officer deposed the victim had indulged in sexual intercourse and was habitual to it
premeditation_planning: Not found against the accused. The Court found an agreed plan to marry in court at Ambala and held there was no basis to show a false promise from the outset.
motive: alleged: the accused obtained the victim's consent to sexual intercourse through a false promise of marriage to satisfy his lust; the Court did not accept this allegation
key_evidence_accepted: The victim's own account, read with the undisputed facts: she left home voluntarily to marry, stayed with the accused, was intimate with him voluntarily, and was apprehended with him at the bus stand; the school register showing her age
witness_credibility: Court noted material contradictions and improvements in the father's and investigating officer's evidence and omission of the lake incident in the Section 164 statement; it relied on the victim's own version as to voluntariness
post_offence_conduct: Not stated as misconduct; per the victim, the accused threw her out after about four days and later persuaded her to go to Ambala; they were apprehended together at the bus stand
custody_duration: More than 3 years of sentence served (exact custody period not stated)
bail_history: Appellant on bail at the time of the Supreme Court's decision; bail bonds discharged. Earlier bail history not stated

defence_argument: Not stated; no one appeared for the appellant, so the Court examined the record

case_title: Karthi @ Karthick v. State Rep. by Inspector of Police, Tamil Nadu
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour (both residents of Achampatti); prior acquaintance in which the accused teased the victim and asked her to marry him; later repeated sexual relations over about six months on a promise of marriage
statutory_provisions: IPC s.376; IPC s.417
evidence_type: Testimonial (victim, victim's brother and father); circumstantial (four village elders on the panchayat; two friends of the accused); medical examination of the victim by a doctor (findings not described in the judgment)
aggravating_circumstances: Forcible first intercourse with the mouth gagged; deception by promise of marriage used to secure silence and then repeated intercourse over about six months
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.376 and 417 by the Assistant Sessions Judge, Virudhunagar; sentence not stated in the judgment
high_court_outcome: Revision petition dismissed (conviction upheld)
neutral_facts: The victim, a young woman, was a neighbour of the accused in the same village. The victim had lost her mother in early childhood and lived with her brother's family, and her father also lived in the house. The accused used to tease the victim and repeatedly asked her to marry him. On one occasion the victim was alone at home while other family members were at a temple. The accused entered the house and asked for sexual intercourse. The victim refused and said intercourse could only take place after marriage. The accused gagged the victim's mouth with the accused's right hand and had sexual intercourse with the victim. Afterwards the accused told the victim not to reveal the incident to anyone, promising marriage while placing a hand on the victim's head. Over about six months the two were intimate repeatedly at different places, and the accused repeatedly said marriage would follow. During a visit to a temple, the accused refused to marry the victim. The victim told the victim's brother and father, who sought the help of village elders. The elders convened a panchayat and summoned the accused, who again refused to marry. The victim then lodged a complaint with the police on 10 October 2003. Prosecution evidence included the testimony of the victim, the victim's brother and father, four village elders who attended the panchayat, two friends of the accused who had met the victim and the accused at the temple, and a doctor who medically examined the victim.
physical_harm: No injury described in the judgment; the victim's mouth was gagged by the accused's hand during the first intercourse
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of the victim, her brother and father; statements of four village elders on the panchayat, which the court called strong circumstantial evidence; statements of two friends of the accused (PW9, PW10) confirming the promise and its withdrawal at the temple
witness_credibility: Court found the victim, her brother and father, the village elders and the two friends consistent and not discredited by cross-examination; the accused could not create any dent in the victim's testimony
post_offence_conduct: Victim disclosed the matter to family and village elders and lodged a police complaint on 10.10.2003; accused surrendered before the Judicial Magistrate on 5.11.2003
bail_history: Released on bail by the Supreme Court vide order dated 4.4.2008; no other bail history stated
trial_duration: offence: not given (complaint 10.10.2003); trial judgment: 30.11.2004; High Court: 18.12.2006; Supreme Court: 1.7.2013
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: R. Balasubrmanian, K.V. Vijayakumar, T.R.B. Siva Kumar. State/respondent: A. Yogesh Kanna, A. Santha Kumaran, B. Balaji
investigation_status: FIR/complaint registered 10.10.2003; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; committed to Sessions Court; trial completed with 16 prosecution witnesses and 12 exhibits
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court (Assistant Sessions Judge, 30.11.2004): convicted under ss.376 and 417 IPC. Appellate court (Additional District and Sessions Judge, Fast Track Court, 1.6.2005): conviction affirmed. High Court (Madurai Bench, 18.12.2006): revision dismissed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Relationship was consensual; no promise of marriage was made; first intercourse was six months before the complaint, so the complaint is an afterthought and the delay in FIR registration creates doubt; following Uday and Zinder Ali Sheikh, each case of consent obtained by deceit must be judged on its own facts
legal_principle_applied: Consent obtained by deceit (false promise of marriage) is not a legitimate defence; a relationship during a subsisting commitment of marriage is not rape under s.376, but becomes so once the promise is refused; delay in FIR does not create doubt where the victim disclosed promptly after refusal and the village elders' panchayat intervened
precedent_relied_upon: Uday v. State of Karnataka (2003) 4 SCC 46 and Zinder Ali Sheikh v. State of West Bengal (2009) 3 SCC 761 (both referred to; relied on by the appellant's counsel)

The accused then issued a cheque for Rs 30 lakh to the complainant, dated 23 February 2012, which was dishonoured for insufficient funds. The complainant alleged that he sold his property and arranged funds to make the payments. case_title: Ganga Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: the defence alleged a quarrel between the accused and the victim's husband; the court rejected this defence. No other relationship stated.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.376
evidence_type: Victim testimony; prior statement to mother-in-law; FIR; medical examination; forensic (FSL) report of semen and spermatozoa on petticoat; seizure evidence
aggravating_circumstances: None noted

neutral_facts: The prosecution case is that the accused approached the victim, a married woman, in an agricultural field at about 6.30 p.m. on 21 December 1987 when she had gone there to relieve herself. The victim alleged that the accused caught hold of her, pushed her to the ground, covered her mouth with one hand, restrained her hands with the other, lifted her petticoat and committed rape on her. She returned home and told her mother-in-law about the incident the same evening. The next day, when her husband returned home, she lodged a complaint at the police station, which was registered as an FIR on 22 December 1987. A doctor who examined her the same evening stated that, as the victim was a married woman habitual to intercourse, no definite opinion could be given on whether she had been subjected to sexual intercourse. No injury was found on her person; the victim explained that she had fallen on her back in a field with a smooth surface where wheat and mustard crops grew. The petticoat and vaginal smear slides were preserved and sent for forensic examination. Police visited the scene on 23 December 1987, seized a blouse, a dhoti and broken bangles, and prepared a site map. The forensic laboratory report recorded spots of semen and spermatozoa on the petticoat. The accused denied having had sexual intercourse with the victim and suggested he had been falsely implicated because of a quarrel with her husband. The victim's mother-in-law denied that suggestion. The victim was not questioned in cross-examination about the seizure of the articles from the field.
