case_title: Barku Bhavrao Bhaskar v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (related to the victim's family); prior dispute over wages between the accused and the victim's father
evidence_type: Circumstantial (last seen together, extra-judicial confession, recovery of blood-stained shirt and body, motive); medical (post-mortem); recovery evidence
confession: Extra-judicial confession made on the way back to the village, stating he killed the child over the wage dispute; treated as circumstance (ii) by the courts below and upheld by the Supreme Court
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.364, 302 and 201 IPC; life imprisonment for s.302; five years RI (stated as s.354); three years RI for s.201; fine with default sentence
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No.1024 of 2001) dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim, a female child of about six years, was the daughter of a man who did masonry work. The accused was related to the victim's family and had worked for the victim's father on occasions. A dispute existed between them over wages the accused had received for work he did not perform. On the day of the incident, a witness saw the accused with the victim at the family home at around 10.30 am, with the child seated on his lap. A shopkeeper later saw the accused buy sweets for the child at about 1.15 pm. When the child could not be found that evening, the family searched the accused's house and a nearby village without success. Another child reported seeing the accused taking the victim away, but that child did not testify. Later the accused was brought back to the village by the victim's father. On the way he reportedly said that if he was not beaten he would tell the truth, and stated that he had killed the child over the wage dispute and hidden her body under stones on a mountain. At his instruction, police and witnesses went to the spot in a jeep, where the body was recovered from under stones and branches. It showed bleeding head and ear injuries, and the child was wearing a school uniform. At the accused's instruction a blood-stained shirt was recovered from under a stone on a road, and it bore blood of the same group as the victim. The accused was physically examined and had no injuries. A post-mortem found head injuries that the doctor considered antemortem and homicidal, with the cause of death being shock from cardio-respiratory arrest due to head injuries.
physical_harm: Death of the victim caused by head injuries: abrasions to face and head, scalp haematoma, skull fracture, and meningeal tears
motive: Wage/payment dispute between the accused and the victim's father (accepted by the courts below and the Supreme Court as proved)
key_evidence_accepted: Last-seen evidence of PW-3 (mother) and PW-7 (shopkeeper); extra-judicial confession; blood-stained shirt recovered at accused's instance with blood of same group as victim; body recovered at accused's instance; post-mortem evidence of PW-6; motive evidence of PWs 1, 4 and 5
witness_credibility: PW-3 found to have no reason to lie; PW-6 doctor's evidence treated as ruling out an accidental fall; motive witnesses' variations found trivial; child witness's silence not held against prosecution
post_offence_conduct: Led police to the body and to the hidden blood-stained shirt; made an extra-judicial confession
trial_duration: offence: 03.12.2000; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 10.02.2006; Supreme Court: 25.07.2013
legal_representation: Appellant: P.C. Aggarwala, Revathy Raghavan. State/Respondent: Sachin J. Patil, Sanjay V. Kharde, Asha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: Complaint lodged at police station; recoveries of body and shirt made; post-mortem conducted; trial completed with conviction
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Doubts whether death was homicidal (suggestion of fall or accident); blood group of accused not tested; last-seen witness PW-7 came to light only through an unexamined person; variations in motive witnesses' versions
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence: the chain of circumstances must be complete and consistent only with guilt, with no missing link
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Sunil Damodar Gaikwad v. State of Maharashtra
accused_occupation: Tailor, employed in a cloth shop
accused_socioeconomic_status: Poor; the Court accepted economic and psychic compulsions arising from abject poverty
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (wife, killed); father of the two sons (killed) and the daughter (injured)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.307
evidence_type: Eyewitness (daughter PW1 and aunt PW4); medical (autopsy by PW3, FSL blood group match); recovery of scissors and clothing; accused's statement to police (Exh. 29)
confession: Statement to police (Exh. 29) admitting the killings, recorded by PW7 and signed by the accused; the Court referred to it and relied on it for the accused's intent and change of heart
aggravating_circumstances: Killing of wife and two sons while asleep with scissors; multiple stab injuries to daughter and attempted suffocation with a pillow; door bolted from outside leaving injured child. Sessions Court and High Court held the case rarest of rare
mitigating_circumstances: Economic and psychic compulsions; abject poverty; son's asthma requiring constant medication; no prior criminal record; reform possible; not a danger to society; change of heart when daughter questioned him; went to police station
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.302 and 307 IPC; death sentence under s.302; life imprisonment under s.307
high_court_outcome: Confirmed death sentence on reference; dismissed the appellant's appeal, confirming conviction and s.307 sentence
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 (murder of wife and two sons); IPC s.307 (attempt to murder daughter)
neutral_facts: In the early hours of the morning on 8 July 2008, while members of a household were asleep in two rooms of a family dwelling, the accused allegedly attacked family members with the separated parts of a pair of sharp scissors. The accused's spouse and two sons were stabbed multiple times and died at the scene. The accused also stabbed the victim, the accused's daughter, multiple times. When the victim asked why she was being hurt, she was told that the whole family had to go and the accused would follow. The accused then gave her water, held her on his lap, and pressed a pillow over her mouth, but she did not die. The accused left her in that condition, bolted the outer door from outside, and went to a police station to report the incident. A neighbouring relative heard the victim calling for help, opened the door and found the deceased lying in pools of blood. The victim was taken to hospital and treated. The post-mortem examination recorded death from haemorrhagic shock with haemothorax due to multiple stab injuries, and the doctor opined that the injuries could have been caused by the scissors. Blood on the accused's clothing matched the blood group of the accused's deceased spouse. The scissors and clothing were recovered on the accused's disclosure, and blood-soaked material was collected from the spot. The accused's statement to the police, recorded at the station, described the killings and gave a reason for them. The investigation included an inquest, a spot panchnama and photographs.
offence_severity: Death or imprisonment for life for murder (s.302); the penalty for s.307 is not stated
physical_harm: Death of wife and two sons from multiple stab injuries; daughter suffered multiple stab injuries to chest, abdomen and hands and was pressed with a pillow, but survived
premeditation_planning: Premeditation not expressly found. The Court accepted that the accused intended to wipe out the whole family, and that his intent changed only after his daughter questioned him
motive: Economic and psychic compulsions from abject poverty, the family's income being insufficient, and stress over his son's asthma treatment
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of the daughter (PW1); aunt's testimony (PW4) on the scene and the victim's statement; medical evidence (PW3); FSL blood group match; recovery of scissors; accused's police statement
witness_credibility: Daughter (PW1) was clear and consistent during investigation and trial; aunt (PW4) corroborated the victim's account; the Court held the evidence established beyond doubt that the accused alone was involved
post_offence_conduct: Bolted the door from outside, went to the police station, and gave a statement admitting the killings
trial_duration: offence: 08.07.2008; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 23.09.2010; Supreme Court: 10.09.2013
legal_representation: Accused: Ramesh Chandra Mishra and Dr. Meera Agarwal. State (Respondent): Sushil Karanjkar and Asha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: FIR registered on the accused's statement; inquest, spot panchnama, recoveries and photographs done; nine prosecution witnesses examined; trial concluded in Sessions Court
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions): convicted under ss.302 and 307; death under s.302, life under s.307. High Court: death sentence confirmed; appeal dismissed. Supreme Court: conviction upheld; s.302 commuted to life; s.307 reduced to 7 years RI
prosecution_argument: Not stated. The judgment does not record the State's submissions in the Supreme Court; the lower courts held the case rarest of rare
defence_argument: Main contention was commutation of the death sentence; the appellant also contended he was not involved in the incident
legal_principle_applied: Life imprisonment is the rule and death the exception (s.354(3) Cr.PC); rarest of rare test with crime and criminal tests; balance sheet of aggravating and mitigating factors; socio-economic compulsions as mitigating factors; judicial comity
precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh (1980) 2 SCC 684; Machhi Singh (1983) 3 SCC 470; Shankar Kisanrao Khade (2013) 5 SCC 546; Dalbir Singh AIR 1979 SC 1384; Ediga Anamma (1974) 4 SCC 443; Sushil Kumar (2009) 10 SCC 434; Gopal Vinayak Godse AIR 1961 SC 600
sentencing_rationale: The case does not fall under the rarest of rare category; the individually inconclusive and cumulatively marginal facts tend towards life imprisonment, which was held to be till the end of the biological life. The s.307 sentence was reduced to 7 years
judicial_mitigating_factors: Economic and psychic compulsions; possibility of reform and rehabilitation; no prior criminal record; not likely to be a menace or danger to society; the accused intended to kill the family out of abject poverty and changed his intent on being questioned by his daughter
other_sentence_order: If the life sentence is remitted or commuted to a specified period (not less than fourteen years under s.433A Cr.PC), the s.307 sentence of 7 years shall commence thereafter

case_title: Ranjeet Goswami v. State of Jharkhand & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
evidence_type: Documentary (school leaving certificate and admission-register records) and oral evidence of the head mistress on age; no eyewitness, medical or recovery evidence on the alleged offences is described
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: The accused was held to be a juvenile on the date of occurrence
trial_court_outcome: JJ Board rejected the juvenility claim on 27.03.2009 and held the accused not a juvenile; no verdict on the charges is stated
high_court_outcome: Criminal Revision allowed; JJ Board order restored and Sessions Judge's order set aside
neutral_facts: The accused was charge-sheeted with offences relating to an incident that occurred on the night of 12/13 April 2008. The accused later surrendered. The judgment does not describe the circumstances of the alleged assault, the identity of the victim, or the manner of any death. The material placed before the court concerned the accused's age on the date of occurrence. A school leaving certificate issued on 10 April 2004 by the then principal of a primary school recorded the accused's date of birth as 10 May 1991. The head mistress of the school identified and recognised the principal's signature on that certificate and gave evidence to that effect. An investigating officer's report indicated that the accused and another person with a similar name were different persons. A medical board was separately asked to assess age and opined that the accused was about 20 years old on the date of occurrence.
physical_harm: Not stated
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: School leaving certificate issued on 10.04.2004 showing date of birth 10.05.1991, proved through the head mistress's evidence identifying the principal's signature
witness_credibility: The head mistress's evidence was unchallenged and the Court accepted it; the Court also noted the investigating officer's report that the two named persons were different
post_offence_conduct: Surrendered on 13.06.2008 after the charge-sheet was submitted
trial_duration: offence: 12/13.04.2008; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 29.10.2010; Supreme Court: 18.09.2013
legal_representation: Accused: Shankar Narayanan (for Gaurav Agrawal). State and respondent: Jayesh Gaurav (for Gopal Prasad), Barun Kr. Sinha, Pratibha Sinha, Aayush Raj (for Rameshwar Prasad Goyal)
investigation_status: Charge-sheet filed; juvenility dispute raised before the JJ Board; case committed to Sessions Court and then directed to the JJ Board
procedural_irregularity: The High Court reversed the Sessions Judge without stating cogent reasons to discard the school leaving certificate
appeal_history: JJ Board: rejected juvenility claim (27.03.2009). Sessions Judge: set aside JJ Board order and directed trial by JJ Board. High Court: revision allowed, JJ Board order restored. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, High Court order set aside and Sessions Judge's order restored
prosecution_argument: The High Court rightly accepted the medical board report, which assessed the accused as about 20 years old on the date of occurrence, because of confusion over the documents produced
defence_argument: The High Court erred in reversing without examining the school admission register, which was properly proved through the head mistress; the medical board report could be considered only if the certificate was discarded for cogent reasons
legal_principle_applied: Where a school leaving certificate is proved and no cogent reason exists to reject it, juvenility is established from it and no medical examination is needed
precedent_relied_upon: Ashwani Kumar Saxena v. State of M.P. (2012) 9 SCC 750 (2012 (10) SCR 540)
other_sentence_order: Accused to be tried only by the Juvenile Justice Board

case_title: AK Devaiah v. State of Karnataka
accused_caste: Kodava community (as stated by the accused)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.498-A, s.304-B; Dowry Prohibition Act s.3, s.4, s.6
weapon: None mentioned (deceased set herself on fire with kerosene)
evidence_type: Oral testimony of PWs 1-3 (sister, brother, sister's husband); medical (post-mortem); recovery of ornaments; inquest statements
aggravating_circumstances: Death within about eleven months of marriage; dowry demand and cruelty alleged and accepted; victim set herself on fire
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of all charges (IPC ss.498-A and 304-B; Dowry Prohibition Act ss.3, 4, 6)
high_court_outcome: State's appeal allowed, acquittal set aside; convicted under IPC ss.498-A, 304-B and DP Act ss.3, 4, 6; 7 years for s.304-B; 5 years and Rs 15,000 fine for s.3 DP Act
offence_finally_established: Dowry death (IPC s.304-B); cruelty (IPC s.498-A); Dowry Prohibition Act ss.3, 4 and 6
neutral_facts: The victim, a woman, was married to the accused in April 1989 and lived in the accused's house, where she also worked for a private company. About three months before her death, the accused and the victim reportedly quarrelled because she had not become pregnant after marriage. The prosecution alleged that before the marriage the accused demanded cash of Rs 15,000 and gold and silver ornaments. Part of the cash was handed over before the wedding and more at the wedding, and all ornaments except one pair of gold bangles were given. The balance was promised after marriage. The prosecution alleged that the accused drank liquor and subjected the victim to mental and physical cruelty over the demand for the balance dowry. In March 1990, about eleven months after the marriage, the victim set herself on fire with kerosene in the house early in the morning. The accused informed the police of the unnatural death. An inquest was held by an executive magistrate, who recorded statements from the victim's blood relatives, and a case was registered. The post-mortem found 97% ante-mortem burns and death due to shock, with no signs of pregnancy. The accused was arrested, and during interrogation he led police to a pawnbroker's shop where the victim's pledged ornaments were recovered. Eleven prosecution witnesses were examined, including the victim's sister, brother and brother-in-law, who deposed about the dowry demand and cruelty.
offence_severity: Minimum 7 years; maximum imprisonment for life (IPC s.304-B)
physical_harm: Death; 97% ante-mortem burns with second and third degree burns over most of the body
financial_property_loss: Alleged dowry of Rs 15,000 cash and gold/silver ornaments; High Court ordered return of Rs 15,000 and the gold ornaments
motive: Demand for balance dowry and cruelty over it (accepted by the court on the evidence of PWs 1-3)
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent testimony of PWs 1-3 on dowry demand and cruelty; post-mortem findings; statutory presumption under s.304-B IPC
witness_credibility: PWs 1-3 found to have consistently deposed; court held the High Court's findings correct and the trial court's acquittal wholly perverse. The defence's interested-witness argument was not specifically addressed
post_offence_conduct: Reported the death to police within hours; ornaments were pledged and later recovered at his instance (as narrated, not separately analysed by the court)
trial_duration: offence: 16-3-1990; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 25.08.2005; Supreme Court: 14.10.2014
legal_representation: Appellant: Rajesh Mahale and Krutin R. Joshi; State of Karnataka: V.N. Raghupathy and Sanjay R. Hegde
investigation_status: Inquest held; suo motu FIR registered; investigation by PW10; charge sheet filed; trial completed; appeals decided by High Court and Supreme Court
procedural_irregularity: None noted by the court; the defence argued that independent witnesses were neither examined nor cited
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted; High Court: State's appeal allowed and accused convicted; Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, convictions upheld
prosecution_argument: PWs 1-3, as close relatives, are competent and natural witnesses with no reason to disbelieve them; dowry was demanded before marriage and the accused coerced the balance demand after marriage; the accused pledged the ornaments
defence_argument: Cash and jewellery were gifts for marriage expenses, not dowry; no dowry custom in the community; PWs 1-3 are interested and inconsistent with their inquest statements; no cruelty soon before death; recovery evidence inadmissible
legal_principle_applied: Dowry death under IPC s.304-B: death by burns or otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of marriage, with cruelty or harassment soon before death linked to a dowry demand; the statutory presumption shifts the onus to the accused to rebut it
precedent_relied_upon: Bansi Lal v. State of Haryana (2011) 11 SCC 359; Thanu Ram v. State of M.P. (2010) 10 SCC 353; Rajesh Bhatnagar v. State of Uttarakhand (2012) 7 SCC 91
judicial_aggravating_factors: None expressly weighed for sentence; court noted the death occurred within eleven months of marriage amid dowry-related cruelty
other_sentence_order: None separately ordered by the Supreme Court; the High Court's direction to return the dowry amount and gold ornaments was not disturbed

case_title: Rajib Ranjan & Ors. v. R. Vijaykumar
accused_occupation: Public servants (Gazetted officers of the Chhattisgarh State Government, as contended by appellants; High Court accepted they are public servants)
accused_victim_relationship: Prior dispute in a tender process: the complainant was a rejected bidder; the accused were officials involved in the tender rejection, and a competing bidder was also an accused
evidence_type: Documentary: tender records, JSEB performance information, General Manager's report, technical experts' report
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Took cognizance of the complaint and issued summons to the appellants (pre-trial; no verdict or sentence)
high_court_outcome: Petitions under s.482 CrPC seeking quashing dismissed; High Court held s.197 not attracted
neutral_facts: The victim's company submitted a bid in response to a state electricity board tender for the design, supply and erection of an ignition system at a thermal power station. The bid was returned without being opened after the tender committee found that the bidder had not furnished a required performance report, despite repeated requests and an assurance to supply it. The board sought performance information from another state electricity board. An official deputed to obtain it reported that the bidder's earlier works were unsatisfactory. The general manager of that other power station reported defects in a scanning system supplied by the bidder, which had adversely affected generation. Technical experts also opined that the bidder was not technically suitable on technical vetting and comparative data. The victim alleged that the accused, together with the successful bidder and another official, conspired to fabricate a performance report cum certificate dated 28 December 2004. The victim alleged the certificate was false, malafide and defamatory, that it was designed to discredit the victim's company and favour the successful bidder, and that it caused the loss of a chance to obtain a contract. The documents available were the tender records, the performance information, the general manager's report and the expert report.
physical_harm: Not stated
financial_property_loss: No money or property quantified; alleged loss of a contract opportunity (Boiler Plant Units, Korba)
premeditation_planning: Not found by the Court; planning and conspiracy to fabricate the certificate was only alleged by the complainant
motive: Court's view of complainant's motive: to give criminal colour to a civil dispute over the rejected tender (alleged motive of complainant; Court did not accept the fabrication allegation)
key_evidence_accepted: Tender committee's pre-qualification rejection, the JSEB officer's report, the General Manager's report of 28.12.2004 on scanning system defects, and the technical experts' opinion; Court held the tender rejection was in discharge of official duties
witness_credibility: No witness credibility assessed; Court found the complainant's forgery allegations an afterthought and not bona fide
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: not given (alleged certificate dated 28.12.2004); trial judgment: not given (cognizance order date not stated); High Court: 03.06.2009; Supreme Court: 14.10.2014
legal_representation: Appellants: Rahul Srivastava, Ram Swarup Sharma. Respondent (complainant) appeared in person. State counsel not stated.
investigation_status: Police declined to register the complaint as a civil dispute; private complaint filed before the Magistrate, registered as C.C. No. 183/07, and cognizance taken
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court (Judicial Magistrate): cognizance taken and summons issued. High Court: quashing petitions dismissed. Supreme Court: appeals allowed, summoning orders set aside, complaint dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Complainant argued the accused conspired and created a false document to reject his claim; sanction under s.197 not required as the charges were conspiracy, cheating, criminal breach of trust and defamation; complainant's legal status was accepted by the Magistrate
defence_argument: Appellants argued that s.197 sanction was mandatory, the complaint disclosed no offence, the complainant lacked locus standi as CEI was not a registered company, and the complaint was an abuse of process after civil remedies failed
legal_principle_applied: Sanction under s.197 CrPC arises only for acts in discharge of official duty, not for criminal conspiracy or fabrication; quashing under s.482 CrPC where proceedings are mala fide, an abuse of process, or convert a civil dispute into a criminal case (Bhajan Lal principles 6 and 7)
precedent_relied_upon: Shambhoo Nath Misra v. State of U.P. (1997) 5 SCC 326; State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335; Indian Oil Corpn. v. NEPC India Ltd. (2006) 6 SCC 736; Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal (2007) 12 SCC 1; also State of Maharashtra v. Dr. Budhikota Subbarao (1993) 2 SCC 567 and G. Sagar Suri (2000) 2 SCC 636 as quoted
other_sentence_order: Complaint dismissed; cognizance and summoning orders set aside; no order as to costs

case_title: O.M. Cherian @ Thankachan v. State of Kerala
accused_occupation: Painter at Delhi at the time of marriage; later employed in Gulf countries
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband and wife)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.498A; IPC s.306
evidence_type: Oral testimony of PWs 1 to 15 (including a neighbour who gave the first information); post-mortem report by PW-4; documentary exhibits P-1 to P-25; material objects MOs 1 to 18; evidence of the accused's leave visits to India
aggravating_circumstances: Alleged ill-treatment and torture of the wife in the matrimonial house; alleged administration of tablets causing a miscarriage in 1993; the wife's suicide by hanging. The Court did not separately weigh these as aggravating factors.
mitigating_circumstances: Accused employed abroad and visited India only four times in eight years; accused made efforts toward mediation scheduled for the day of the wife's death
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.498A IPC: 2 years RI and Rs.5,000 fine (1 year default); convicted under s.306 IPC: 7 years RI and Rs.50,000 fine (3 years default); sentences directed to run consecutively
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed, including consecutive running of sentences
offence_finally_established: IPC s.498A (cruelty) and IPC s.306 (abetment of suicide)
neutral_facts: The accused married the victim in 1988 and they lived in a matrimonial house together with the accused's parents and brother. It is alleged that the accused and other household members ill-treated and tortured the victim. During the marriage the victim had a premature delivery. After a later pregnancy in 1993, it is alleged that the accused gave the victim tablets that caused a miscarriage. A child born to the couple did not survive long. On 23 February 1996 the victim poured kerosene over herself and drank some, which was later cleared away. A mediation meeting had been scheduled for that day, and the victim's relatives and a neighbour were to attend. The victim then died by hanging before the meeting took place. A neighbour gave the first information to the police. The case was first registered as an unnatural death and later altered to offences of cruelty and abetment of suicide. The investigating officer seized documents and material objects, examined witnesses, and laid a charge sheet. A post-mortem examination was conducted. The evidence included oral testimony from fifteen witnesses, documentary exhibits, material objects, and evidence that the accused worked abroad and visited India on leave only four times between 1988 and 1996, the last visit being in January-February 1996. The accused had also made efforts toward mediation to settle the differences.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by suicide by hanging; earlier, the victim poured kerosene on herself and drank some, which was later cleared away
motive: alleged: ill-treatment and torture of the wife in the matrimonial house over marital differences
key_evidence_accepted: Evidence that the accused visited India on leave only four times in eight years, with the last visit in January-February 1996; evidence of mediation efforts scheduled for 23.2.1996
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 23.02.1996; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 27.11.2013; Supreme Court: not given
legal_representation: Appellant: Jayanth Muth Raj and Nishe Rajen Shanker. State of Kerala: Bina Madhavan and Ramesh Babu M.R.
investigation_status: FIR registered as unnatural death (s.174 CrPC), later altered to ss.498A and 306 IPC; post-mortem conducted; charge sheet laid against the accused and others
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.498A and 306 IPC with consecutive sentences. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; sentences ordered to run concurrently.
prosecution_argument: The State supported the views of the courts below that the sentences should run consecutively, relying on Duryodhan Rout v. State of Orissa
defence_argument: Section 31 CrPC gives discretion to order concurrent sentences and the courts below did not exercise it properly; the accused was employed abroad, visited India only four times in eight years, and there could not have been continuous harassment
legal_principle_applied: Under s.31 CrPC the court has full discretion to order concurrent sentences, weighed on the nature of the offences and aggravating or mitigating circumstances, considering the totality of facts; normal rule is not consecutive sentences; s.31(2) limits apply
precedent_relied_upon: Mohd. Akhtar Hussain v. Asstt. Collector of Customs (1988) 4 SCC 183 (considered); Manoj alias Panu v. State of Haryana (2014) 2 SCC 153 (considered); V.K. Bansal v. State of Haryana (2013) 7 SCC 211; Ramesh Chilwal v. State of Uttarakhand (2012) 11 SCC 629; Duryodhan Rout v. State of Orissa 2014 (8) SCALE 96 (cited by State)
sentencing_rationale: Accused's employment abroad and only four visits in eight years, with mediation scheduled on the day of the wife's death, made concurrent running of the sentences appropriate in the totality of circumstances
judicial_mitigating_factors: Accused's absence abroad with only four visits to India in eight years; efforts for mediation scheduled on the day of the wife's suicide
other_sentence_order: Sentences under ss.498A and 306 IPC directed to run concurrently; reference answered that s.31 CrPC leaves full discretion to the court; appeal partly allowed

case_title: Naresh Kumar v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B (dowry death); Evidence Act s.113B presumption discussed
evidence_type: Testimonial evidence of relatives on dowry demands; suicide note (Exhibit P-4); medical evidence; investigation evidence; statutory presumption under s.113B Evidence Act
aggravating_circumstances: Death within 10 months of marriage after repeated dowry demands, threat of divorce, and death by burn injuries
trial_court_outcome: Convicted appellant and co-accused; sentence not stated in this judgment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction of appellant upheld; co-accused mother and brother acquitted
neutral_facts: The victim was married to the accused in July 2000. After the marriage the victim was allegedly harassed for insufficient dowry, and the accused raised a demand for a motorcycle, in addition to demands made by the accused's mother and younger brother. About three months after the marriage the victim telephoned her father about the demands. The victim's father and uncle met the accused and his relatives and asked that the victim not be harassed, but the harassment continued. In April 2001 the victim again complained by telephone. The uncle brought the victim to her parental home, but the next day the accused came, insisted that the victim be sent back, and threatened divorce; the victim was sent with the accused. On 1 May 2001 the victim's family received word that the victim had suffered burn injuries and had been taken to hospital. There, the victim told the victim's father, uncle and brother-in-law that the victim had been beaten and set on fire by the accused and the accused's family members. The victim died of extensive burn injuries. The victim's father lodged the first information report, and an investigating officer conducted the investigation and sent the accused for trial. The prosecution relied on testimony of relatives about dowry demands, medical evidence and investigation evidence. A suicide note stated that nobody should be held responsible and that all doors were closed for the victim. The defence contended that the victim had taken her own life because of pressure from an uncle over parental property, and that relations with the accused were cordial.
physical_harm: Death of victim from extensive burn injuries
motive: Demand for dowry (motorcycle and further dowry) from the victim's family
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent testimony of victim's father, uncle and brother-in-law on dowry harassment soon before death; medical evidence of death by burning; suicide note read in context; s.113B presumption
witness_credibility: Three prosecution witnesses (victim's father, uncle and brother-in-law) found to have specifically and categorically deposed about dowry demands soon before death; their evidence accepted
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 1 May 2001 (death from burn injuries); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 12 March 2013; Supreme Court: 14 November 2014
legal_representation: Appellant: G.C. Shahpuri, Surinder Singh, Balbir Singh Gupta; Respondents (State of Haryana and others): Kamal Mohan Gupta
investigation_status: FIR lodged by victim's father (Exhibit PA/1); investigation completed by SI and accused sent up for trial
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted appellant and co-accused. High Court: conviction of appellant upheld, co-accused acquitted. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Demand of dowry not proved soon before death; suicide note stated nobody should be held responsible and contained no dowry allegation; parity with acquitted mother and brother
legal_principle_applied: Dowry death requires harassment soon before death; suicide note does not exonerate husband; husband's responsibility is higher than other relatives; statutory presumption under s.113B and failure to explain as additional circumstance
precedent_relied_upon: Hira Lal and Ors. v. State (Govt. of NCT) Delhi, 2003 (1) Suppl. SCR 734: (2003) 8 SCC 80 (relied on); Manohar Lal v. State of Haryana, AIR 2014 SC 2555 (referred to and distinguished)
sentencing_rationale: Not stated; concurrent conviction and sentence upheld as no reason to interfere was found

case_title: Om Prakash v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated (the defence alleged enmity, with one accused alleged to be suspected by the victim of spreading news of her abortion; no relationship between accused and victim is described)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.376(2)(g) (rape, as charged under s.376 against two accused); IPC s.109 read with s.107 (abetment of rape, against third accused)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (victim's testimony), corroborative testimony of mother, medical examination, radiological age determination, school certificate
aggravating_circumstances: Victim was about 15 (minor); victim was kept in the house for about an hour; victim was threatened with elimination if she disclosed the incident; offence committed by two accused acting together
trial_court_outcome: Om Prakash and Kartar Singh convicted under s.376(2)(g) IPC, 10 years RI and Rs.10,000 fine each; Chhoti convicted under s.109 IPC, 3 years RI and Rs.10,000 fine
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence of all three accused affirmed (judgment dated 30.7.2008)
offence_finally_established: Rape under s.376(2)(g) IPC (Om Prakash and Kartar Singh); abetment of rape under s.109 IPC (Chhoti)
neutral_facts: On the day of the incident, the victim, aged about fifteen, was alone at home. The victim's mother was away at another village and other family members were not present. One accused came to the house and asked the victim to fetch lassi from the house of another accused and that accused's spouse. When the victim entered that house, two other men already there bolted the door from inside and raped the victim. The victim was held for about an hour and threatened with elimination if the incident was disclosed. The victim did not disclose the incident for about twenty days, until the mother returned from a maternal visit. The victim then told the mother, and the father took the victim to lodge a report at the police station. The report was registered the next day. The investigating officer inspected the spot and recorded the victim's statement before a magistrate under section 164. A medical examination found no external injuries, no injury to the perineum or thighs, and a healed ruptured hymen that admitted one finger easily. A radiological examination assessed the age as between 14 and 16 years. A school certificate recorded a date of birth showing the victim was fifteen at the time. The victim's testimony and the mother's corroborating account of the delayed disclosure were presented.
physical_harm: No external injuries; no injury over perineum or thighs; hymen of healed ruptured type admitting one finger easily; sexual assault confirmed medically
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.376 and s.109 as framed at trial); 2 finally upheld (s.376(2)(g) and s.109)
premeditation_planning: Not stated (the victim was lured to the house on the pretext of fetching lassi; the court did not make an express finding of premeditation)
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Victim's testimony (PW5) and mother's corroborating statement (PW6) on delayed disclosure; radiological age report (PW2); school certificate (PW11) showing date of birth; medical report (PW9); finding that the victim's consent was immaterial due to age
witness_credibility: Victim's and mother's testimony found natural and trustworthy despite lengthy cross-examination; no false implication due to enmity
post_offence_conduct: Accused threatened the victim not to disclose the incident; victim did not disclose for about 20 days
bail_history: Granted bail by Supreme Court: Chhoti on 18.5.2009; Kartar Singh on 20.7.2009; Om Prakash on 16.4.2010. No other bail history stated
trial_duration: offence: not given (victim disclosed the incident to her mother on 12.6.1995, FIR registered 13.6.1995); trial judgment: 16.12.1996; High Court: 30.7.2008; Supreme Court: 14.10.2014
legal_representation: Accused/appellants: Rishi Malhotra and Prem Malhotra. State/respondent: Nupur Chaudhary, Vivekta Singh and Kamal Mohan Gupta
investigation_status: FIR registered 13.6.1995; spot inspected; victim's statement recorded under s.164 CrPC; medical and radiological examinations done; charge-sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted (the 20-day delay in lodging the FIR was held to be sufficiently explained)
appeal_history: Trial court (Additional Sessions Judge, Hissar, 16.12.1996): all three convicted and sentenced. High Court (30.7.2008): appeal dismissed. Supreme Court: all three appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Not stated (the State's submissions are not separately summarised; the Court relied on the trial record and evidence)
defence_argument: Chhoti, being a woman, cannot be convicted under s.376 r/w s.34 or s.109 IPC; mere failure to protect the victim is not abetment (relying on Kulwant Singh and Priya Patel); sentence should be reduced to period already undergone
legal_principle_applied: Abetment under s.107 IPC (third clause: intentional aiding) read with s.109 IPC; a person who aids at the time of the crime is a principal of the second degree; conviction for abetment requires direct involvement or instigation, which the aiding conduct here satisfied
precedent_relied_upon: Kulwant Singh @ Kulbansh Singh v. State of Bihar (2007) 15 SCC 670 (cited by appellants; referred to); Priya Patel v. State of M.P. (2006) 6 SCC 263 (cited by appellants; referred to); Joseph Kurian v. State of Kerala (1994) 6 SCC 535 (as quoted in Kulwant Singh)
sentencing_rationale: Sentence awarded by the trial court and upheld by the High Court found just and proper; no separate reduction granted
other_sentence_order: Accused directed to be taken into custody forthwith to serve remaining sentence

case_title: State of Punjab v. Jagga Singh etc.
accused_occupation: Driver (accused Charanjit Singh, as described in the prosecution case noted by the Court)
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance (defence version, not decided by the Court): accused Charanjit Singh was known to the victim's mother and had worked under the victim's partnership
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.120-B; Arms Act s.25
weapon: Two country-made .303 pistols with live cartridges (firearms)
evidence_type: Eyewitness; fingerprint (latent prints on glass tumblers); medical (autopsy); recovery of pistols, cartridges, scooter and footwear; identification by witnesses
confession: Alleged extra-judicial confession by accused Ranjit Singh to PW9; not relied on because it was uncorroborated and PW9 had no authority to receive it
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: All seven convicted. Two: IPC s.302 (life imprisonment and Rs.2000 fine each) and Arms Act s.25 (two years RI and Rs.1000 fine each). Five: IPC s.302 r/w s.120-B (life imprisonment and Rs.2000 fine each).
high_court_outcome: Allowed appeals of five accused and acquitted them; dismissed appeals of two accused and confirmed their conviction and sentence
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302) and Arms Act s.25 for the two accused; the five acquittals on s.302 r/w s.120-B were upheld
neutral_facts: On the early morning of the occurrence, two visitors who had arranged by telephone the previous evening to be taken to a plot for earthwork came to the victim's house. They were let in, and tea was prepared for them at the victim's direction. The visitors asked the victim to accompany them on his scooter. As he started the scooter, both visitors drew pistols from the folds of their garments and fired at him. He fell onto the scooter. The victim's mother and wife were in the house and witnessed the shooting. The assailants ran away, and the mother heard a vehicle starting on the other side of the road. The mother gave a statement to police, which led to registration of the first information report. The investigating officer called a fingerprint expert to the house. The expert found two glass tumblers on the table, smeared with tea. He lifted fingerprints from them, sealed them in a packet, and sent them to the fingerprint bureau. There, the seal was found intact, and the prints were compared with specimen prints of two suspects taken in the presence of a Judicial Magistrate. The comparison found the questioned prints similar to the specimen prints. The autopsy showed a lacerated wound on the left side of the chest. It had blackening around it and perforated the left lung, the upper part of the heart and the right lung. The doctor opined that death resulted from shock and haemorrhage due to a firearm injury. Police recovered two pistols with live cartridges, two empty twelve-bore cartridges, the scooter and a footwear from the spot.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a firearm wound to the left chest that perforated the lung and heart
number_of_offences: 3 charged (IPC s.302; IPC s.120-B; Arms Act s.25); 2 finally upheld (IPC s.302 and Arms Act s.25 for the two accused)
premeditation_planning: Not found. The Court found no evidence of conspiracy; the visit was arranged by phone the previous evening.
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of the victim's mother and wife; fingerprint evidence from the tumblers matched to two accused; identification of two accused by the eyewitnesses and by the arrest in their presence; autopsy evidence
witness_credibility: The Court found the mother's and wife's testimonies cogent, natural and trustworthy, with no material discrepancy. The alibi-type contention (absence at a wedding) was rejected because they denied the suggestion and the defence led no evidence. The Court found the eyewitnesses' and fingerprint evidence reliable. It discounted PW9 and doubted PW3's presence.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated (witnesses describe the assailants fleeing immediately; the Court made no finding on post-offence conduct)
bail_history: Bail had been granted to accused Surjit Singh; this Court cancelled it. Other bail history not stated.
trial_duration: offence: 10.11.2002; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 17.09.2007; Supreme Court: 17.12.2014
legal_representation: State of Punjab: V. Madhukar, AAG. Accused: counsel listed for the appearing parties without separating the sides (Anvita Kowshish, Mohit Nain, Dhruv A Mohan, Kuldip Singh and others).
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; 25 prosecution witnesses examined; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted by the Court. The defence alleged no identification parade and non-compliance with s.5 of the Identification of Prisoners Act; the Court rejected the latter as devoid of merit.
appeal_history: Trial court: all seven convicted. High Court: five acquitted; two convictions confirmed. Supreme Court: all appeals dismissed; the two convictions and the five acquittals stand.
prosecution_argument: Not stated in detail. The judgment records only that the State's submissions were heard; the State had challenged the five acquittals.
defence_argument: Complaint did not name the accused; no identification parade; false implication; fingerprints taken after the accused were made to hold tumblers in custody; specimen prints not taken before a Magistrate; presence of the eyewitnesses doubtful because they were at a wedding in another village
legal_principle_applied: Eyewitness testimony assessed for cogency and credibility; omission to name accused in the complaint does not defeat identification by the witnesses; fingerprint evidence corroborates; benefit of doubt for the five acquitted accused
precedent_relied_upon: Mohd. Aman and Anr. vs. State of Rajasthan (1997) 10 SCC 44 (distinguished)
other_sentence_order: Bail of accused Surjit Singh cancelled; he is directed to surrender to serve the remaining sentence

case_title: Prem Kumar Gulati v. State of Haryana
accused_occupation: Worked at a flour mill (per his own defence statement)
previous_criminal_record: Not stated (an earlier 2001 criminal complaint was compromised; no conviction recorded)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband Mahender Singh); brother-in-law Prem Kumar Gulati; alleged prior disputes over harassment and the husband's illicit relationship with the brother-in-law's wife
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.498A r/w s.34
evidence_type: Dying declaration (primary); medical evidence (post-mortem and medico-legal); father's and brother's testimony on harassment and prior disputes; investigation/site evidence; defence child witness
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted all three accused under s.302/498A r/w s.34 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs.5,000 under s.302, one year RI and fine of Rs.500 under s.498A (each accused)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; trial court judgment upheld (the header of the HC order gives 09.05.2008 while the text gives 06.09.2008)
offence_finally_established: For main accused Mahender Singh: murder (IPC s.302 r/w s.34) and cruelty (IPC s.498A r/w s.34) upheld. Prem Kumar Gulati acquitted of both.
neutral_facts: The victim, a 28-year-old married woman, was admitted to hospital with extensive burn injuries on the night of 9 December 2003, after kerosene oil was poured on her at her matrimonial home and set alight. Burns covered roughly half her body. Once a doctor certified her fit to give a statement, a Magistrate recorded her statement. She said that at about 9.30 to 10.00 p.m. the accused, a husband, a brother-in-law and the brother-in-law's wife, had poured kerosene oil on her and set her ablaze, and that nobody tried to extinguish the fire. She said the husband had an illicit relationship with the brother-in-law's wife, that she quarrelled with him over it, and that after drinking liquor he beat her with a stick and shoes. Investigators inspected the scene, seized burnt clothing, ash and a kerosene lamp, and obtained post-mortem and forensic reports. The post-mortem doctor attributed death to ante-mortem burns sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature. A medical examiner noted superficial deep burns across the body and said burns from kerosene falling on the head could not be ruled out. The victim's father testified to dowry harassment, earlier divorce proceedings, panchayat settlements and a telephone call a week before the incident seeking to return to her parents' home. The victim's brother supported this account. No eyewitness saw the incident. The defence case was that the burns were accidental, caused by a lamp falling on the victim in the kitchen, and it relied on the testimony of the victim's eight-year-old daughter. Investigators found the brother-in-law and his wife living separately and recorded no specific act by either of them.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from about 50% ante-mortem burns; superficial deep burns all over the body
number_of_offences: 2 charged (s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; s.498A r/w s.34 IPC); 2 finally upheld for main accused Mahender Singh
motive: alleged: husband's illicit relationship with the brother-in-law's wife and dowry-related harassment; the court did not separately decide the motive
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration (found truthful and reliable) and other evidence establishing that the main accused instigated and caused the burning; the dying declaration was not discarded merely for lacking a question-answer form
witness_credibility: The court accepted the dying declaration's reliability and upheld the main accused's conviction. It found the evidence insufficient to link the brother-in-law and his wife to any specific act, and it did not separately assess the defence child witness.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 09.12.2003; trial judgment: 25.04.2006; High Court: 06.09.2008 (header gives 09.05.2008); Supreme Court: 23.09.2014
legal_representation: Accused: Ms. Meenakshi Arora, Sr. Adv., with Jasbir Singh Malik (for S. K. Sabharwal), Adv. State: Roopansh Purohit, AAG, with Ramesh Kumar, Ms. Naresh Bakshi and Daya Krishan Sharma, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered on the basis of the dying declaration; investigation completed; charge sheet against only the main accused; co-accused summoned under s.319 Cr.P.C.; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Brother-in-law and his wife were not charged by police and were added as accused only through s.319 Cr.P.C. summons
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted all three accused. High Court: appeal dismissed, judgment upheld. Supreme Court: main accused's conviction upheld; brother-in-law acquitted
prosecution_argument: The dying declaration alone suffices; it need not be in question-answer form and narrative form is more natural (citing Shariff); the father's evidence is reliable and the deceased was not influenced by him; the brother-in-law and his wife lived in the same building
defence_argument: Brother-in-law's innocence was found during investigation; dying declaration is vague, lacks time of recording and state of mind, and is not in question-answer form; no eyewitness; child witness wrongly disbelieved; motive from past litigation cannot be ruled out
legal_principle_applied: A truthful and reliable dying declaration can be the sole basis of conviction, subject to close scrutiny; it need not be in question-answer form; benefit of doubt for a co-accused where there is no corroboration and no specific act is attributed to him
precedent_relied_upon: Godhu v. State of Rajasthan (1975) 3 SCC 241; K. Ramachandra Reddy v. Public Prosecutor (1976) 3 SCC 618; Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh (1973) 2 SCC 808; Khushal Rao v. State of Bombay (AIR 1958 SC 22, quoted); Harbans Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1962 SC 439); Tapinder Singh v. State of Punjab (1970) 2 SCC 113; Lallubhai Devchand Shah v. State of Gujarat (1971) 3 SCC 767
other_sentence_order: Brother-in-law Prem Kumar Gulati to be released forthwith; the main accused's appeal dismissed

case_title: Sheesh Ram and Ors. v. The State of Rajasthan
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: land dispute and an earlier murder case between the appellants' side and the victim's family
statutory_provisions: IPC s.148, s.302 r/w s.149, s.307 r/w s.149 (as charged/convicted at trial); on final appeal, IPC s.302 r/w s.34 and s.307 r/w s.34 for the appellants
weapon: Axes, a sword, a dhariya and lathis
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured eyewitness PW-5 and three corroborating eyewitnesses); medical evidence (post-mortem/doctor's testimony on cause of death)
aggravating_circumstances: Brutal attack: fatal head injury with axe blows after the victim had fallen, and a second victim attacked with multiple weapons
trial_court_outcome: All accused convicted under IPC ss.148, 302 r/w 149 and 307 r/w 149; sentence for the appellants not stated in the trial court's outcome
high_court_outcome: Four accused acquitted; the appellants' convictions altered to IPC s.302 r/w s.34 and s.307 r/w s.34 with life imprisonment and fines
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (murder of the victim); IPC s.307 r/w s.34 (attempt to murder of the second victim)
neutral_facts: The victim's father and two of his sons were standing by a road when a tractor carrying several men stopped beside them. The men got down and, armed with axes, a sword, a dhariya and lathis, encircled the father and sons. The father and one son ran towards the village. The victim ran in another direction but was chased. One assailant caught hold of him and struck his head with an axe; after he fell, another assailant struck him again with an axe, and a third hit his right hand with a dhariya. According to the doctor who gave evidence, the victim died from haemorrhage and shock caused by the head injury, which damaged the brain and the carotid artery in the neck. The victim's brother was also attacked: he was caught, struck on the left temple with a dhariya and behind the ear with an axe, and hit on the face with a lathi, after which he became unconscious. He received four incised wounds and a fracture of the left parietal bone. The assailants left believing both were dead. The injured brother gave a detailed account of the incident. Two other eyewitnesses, who were related to him, described the same events and were found to be consistent on the main prosecution case. The parties had a prior dispute over land and an earlier murder. The accused examined defence witnesses.
physical_harm: Victim died from haemorrhage and shock due to head injury (injury to brain and carotid artery in neck); second victim suffered four incised wounds, a fracture of the left parietal bone, and unconsciousness
motive: Prior enmity: the appellants' brother Kamal was murdered and the victim's father and some witnesses were facing trial for that murder, giving the appellants a strong motive; the Court did not accept that this led to false implication
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of the injured eyewitness PW-5 Bhagwan Singh, corroborated by PW-2, PW-3 and PW-4; medical evidence on cause of death from PW-12; eyewitness evidence accepted on the main prosecution case
witness_credibility: PW-5 (injured eyewitness) found trustworthy and his evidence not dented on cross-examination; interested (related) witnesses scrutinised with caution and accepted; exaggeration regarding acquitted accused disbelieved but severable from the main case; defence witnesses not believed
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 04/02/1991; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 29.05.2003; Supreme Court: January 29, 2014
legal_representation: Accused/appellants: P.C. Agarwala, Ambuj Agarwal, Chander Shekhar Ashri. State: S.S. Shamshery, AAG, and Milind Kumar
investigation_status: FIR registered on complaint; charge-sheets laid against the accused (appellants' charge-sheet dated 3/2/1993); case committed and tried in Sessions Court
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.148, 302/149, 307/149 IPC. High Court: four accused acquitted; appellants convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 and s.307 r/w s.34 IPC. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, convictions upheld
prosecution_argument: Eyewitness evidence is consistent and reliable; PW-2 and PW-4 are independent; falsus in uno principle does not apply in India so the credible remainder can be relied on (relying on Rizan); enough credible evidence to prove the case
defence_argument: Witnesses exaggerated and implicated the acquitted accused, so the evidence is risky to rely on; falsus in uno falsus in omnibus should apply; eyewitnesses appear tutored and interested; complainant not examined; false implication due to long-standing enmity cannot be ruled out
legal_principle_applied: Evidence of interested witnesses is not always suspect and must be scrutinised with caution; exaggeration severable if it does not change the prosecution story; falsus in uno is only a rule of caution, and the grain can be separated from the chaff
precedent_relied_upon: Balaka Singh v. State of Punjab (1975) 4 SCC 511; Rizan & Anr. v. State of Chhattisgarh (2003) 2 SCC 661
judicial_aggravating_factors: Brutal manner of the killing as noted by the Court
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Badal Murmu and Ors. v. State of West Bengal
accused_socioeconomic_status: Very poor; described as economically weak tribals living in a very poor stratum of society
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: the victim had stolen a hen belonging to one accused, leading to an inimical relation and a panchayat penalty
statutory_provisions: IPC s.148; IPC s.302 r/w s.149 (charged and tried); conviction altered to IPC s.304 Part II
weapon: Lathis (used); tangies (sharp cutting weapons) carried but not used
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-1, PW-3, PW-6, PW-7 including injured witness); medical (post-mortem by PW-9); police statement of first wife
aggravating_circumstances: Fourteen injuries including two rib fractures and haematoma under the scalp; victim tied up before the assault; beaten to death
mitigating_circumstances: Trivial underlying dispute over a stolen hen; no common object to kill shown; sharp weapons available but not used; accused poor tribals; long period in jail (almost 14 years)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.148 and s.302 r/w s.149 IPC; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, IPC s.304 Part II
neutral_facts: A dispute arose after the victim allegedly stole a hen belonging to one of the accused. A community settlement was held and the victim paid a penalty, but the accused were reportedly still unhappy with it. Shortly afterwards, one accused allegedly confronted a witness about the matter and caused bleeding injuries to him, and the witness was examined by a doctor. On the following morning, the victim and this witness were summoned to a courtyard on the pretext of a meeting. On arrival, they were tied to a bamboo pole and a tree. Several accused, armed with lathis and tangies (sharp cutting weapons), allegedly beat the victim with lathis while the witness escaped. The victim was beaten to death. The victim's two wives, who had followed him to the courtyard, witnessed the assault. The first wife gave a statement to the police naming all accused as the assailants, and an investigation followed. The post-mortem doctor recorded fourteen injuries, mostly bruises and abrasions, including two rib fractures and haematoma under the scalp, stated that all injuries contributed to death, and said a blunt object such as a lathi could cause them. The witness, who was related to the victim, named his brother among the assailants. No witness attributed specific blows to specific accused, and the tangies were not used.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; fourteen injuries, mostly bruises and abrasions, plus two rib fractures and haematoma under the scalp
number_of_offences: 2 charged (s.148 and s.302 r/w s.149); 1 finally upheld (s.304 Part II substituted for s.302 r/w s.149; s.148 not separately addressed in Supreme Court)
financial_property_loss: Not applicable (the hen and liquor were a earlier panchayat penalty, not a loss from this offence)
premeditation_planning: Not found; the court held there was no shared common object to kill and the beating arose from a frenzy
motive: Anger over the theft of a hen and the panchayat penalty (court's view)
key_evidence_accepted: Ocular testimony of PW-1, PW-3, PW-6 and PW-7 that the accused assaulted the victim with lathis; post-mortem evidence of PW-9 that the injuries could be caused by a lathi
witness_credibility: Found truthful and having a ring of truth; related to the victim but not shown to have falsely implicated the accused; PW-7 named his own brother as an assailant
post_offence_conduct: Not stated (the quoted conduct concerns PW-7, not the accused)
trial_duration: offence: not given (quarrel on 14/4/1989; assault the following morning); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 20.01.2003; Supreme Court: 5 February 2014
legal_representation: Appellants: Vibha Datta Makhija (learned amicus) and Ruchi Agnihotri. State: Anip Sachthey, Kabir S. Bose, Shagun Matta and Saakaar Sardana
investigation_status: Statement given to Memari Police Station; investigation completed; accused charged and tried
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.148 and s.302 r/w s.149 and sentenced to life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence affirmed. Supreme Court: conviction under s.302 r/w s.149 set aside; convicted under s.304 Part II with sentence of time already undergone
prosecution_argument: Ocular evidence established the case; even if the common object was only to inflict injuries, members of the unlawful assembly knew murder was likely, so all are guilty of murder under s.149
defence_argument: Prosecution not proved beyond reasonable doubt; alternatively, guilt should be only culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s.304 Part II because there was no intention to kill, injuries were superficial, and the accused are poor tribals long in jail
legal_principle_applied: Common object under s.149 must be shown in the peculiar facts; where no individual role or fatal injury is attributed and no intent to kill is shown, murder conviction cannot be sustained and s.304 Part II applies
precedent_relied_upon: Kirti Mahto & Ors. v. State of Bihar 1994 Supp. (2) SCC 569; Molu & Ors. v. State of Haryana AIR 1976 SC 2499; Munivel v. State of Tamil Nadu (2006) 9 SCC 394; Alister Anthony Pareira v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 2 SCC 648; Kashmiri Lal & Ors. v. State of Punjab AIR 1997 SC 393; Sukhdev Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1992 SC 755; Sarman & Ors. v. State of Madhya Pradesh 1993 Supp. (2) SCC 356
sentencing_rationale: Trivial triggering incident; no shared intent to kill; accused's economic and social background; nearly 14 years already in jail; sentence of time undergone under s.304 Part II meets ends of justice
judicial_mitigating_factors: Background of economic and social status; trivial cause of the incident; no shared common object to kill; sharp weapons not used; almost 14 years in jail
other_sentence_order: Accused directed to be released forthwith unless required in any other case

case_title: P.C. Mishra v. State (C.B.I.) & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: PC Act s.7; s.13(1)(d) read with s.13(2)
evidence_type: Trap and arrest during demand and acceptance; co-accused's section 164 CrPC statement; witness examination and record scrutiny during investigation
confession: Statement of co-accused under s.164 CrPC recorded 7.8.1996; described in the background narrative only, not assessed or relied on by the Court for guilt
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted by Special Judge (judgment dated 24.5.2010, as noted in amicus submission); sentence not stated
high_court_outcome: Criminal revision (Crl. M.C. No.3514 of 2008) against rejection of challenge to pardon dismissed
neutral_facts: A written complaint was made that a government official (the accused) had demanded a bribe of Rs 4,000 to settle an appeal the complainant had filed against a tax officer's order. The investigating agency laid a trap. On the day of the trap, the accused and a subordinate reader were caught while demanding and accepting the bribe from the complainant, and both were arrested. During the investigation, witnesses were examined and records scrutinised. It transpired that the subordinate had accepted the bribe money on behalf of the accused. neutral_facts: On 5 November 1990 a man unknown to the victim was looking for her house in a city and asked a passer-by for directions. The passer-by took him to a second woman, who escorted him to the victim's house. At about 1 p.m. a witness saw him at the victim's door. He said a relative was expected to come to the house; the victim replied that the relative had not arrived. That witness left before the man entered the house. That evening the victim did not come to a neighbour's house to watch television. The neighbour sent a child to call her, and the victim said relatives from her village had arrived and she had to cook for them. Another witness saw her alive at about 8.30 p.m. in the company of more than one person. The next day the victim was found dead in her house, with her belongings scattered. At the scene, an expert found chance fingerprints on a plastic cover bearing a bank's name. Later, an expert reported that the accused's fingerprint matched one of them, using a print taken from the accused on a later date. The accused's blood-stained clothes were seized when he was arrested six days after the killing. A blood sample from him could not be tested for blood group. Ornaments were recovered from several people after the accused led police to them, but none was identified as the victim's. A blood-stained steel rod, hidden under a stone slab, was recovered at the accused's instance. No identification parade was held. The relative the accused had mentioned was not questioned by investigators.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by homicide
number_of_offences: 2 charged (murder; theft of cash and ornaments); 0 finally upheld
financial_property_loss: Cash and ornaments alleged to be worth about Rs. 25,000; the ornaments were never linked to the victim
motive: alleged: theft of ornaments
key_evidence_accepted: Accepted only in part: the accused was at best at the house around 1 p.m.; the victim was alive until about 8.30 p.m. with others present; the homicidal death. Fingerprint, blood-group, recovery and identification evidence was not accepted as proving guilt.
witness_credibility: Fingerprint expert's bona fides accepted. Identification witnesses PW-6 and PW-7 were weak (brief, fleeting sighting; identification in court about 4.5 years later). Photographer's evidence on the passbook print was inconsequential.
post_offence_conduct: High Court found absconding after the crime; the Supreme Court did not accept this as proof of guilt. Prosecution case: apprehended on 11 Nov 1990 at about 4.45 p.m.

appeal_history: Trial court (21 Jan 1999): acquitted. High Court (6 Jul 2005): acquittal set aside, convicted. Supreme Court (15 Apr 2014): appeal allowed, accused acquitted.

defence_argument: Photographs did not show the plastic cover, so it was planted later; the fingerprint was taken on 7 November 1990 under a cover-to-hold pretext; the serologist report was not put to him; the ornament identification procedure was improper.
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence requires certainty of each circumstance; mere probabilities are insufficient. Benefit of doubt where the trial court's view is plausible and not perverse. Identification parade not mandatory. Fingerprint evidence needs a proven admitted specimen and a fair procedure.

neutral_facts: On 20 August 2006, at about 2 p.m., the victim, a 17-year-old girl who had taken goats to graze in a forest about half a kilometre from her village, was sitting alone on a footpath when the accused caught hold of her from behind. When she asked why, the accused did not respond. The accused physically abused her body, removed her clothes, made her lie on the ground and committed sexual assault by rape. She raised an alarm but no one came. After leaving, the accused threatened her with consequences if she disclosed the incident. Out of fear she did not tell her parents for several days, but remained tense and distressed. On 2 September 2006 she consumed poison, became unconscious and was taken to several hospitals, finally to a postgraduate institute, where she remained until 10 September 2006. On regaining consciousness she told her father and brother that the accused had raped her on 20 August. A first information report was registered on 11 September 2006, after which she was medically examined. The examining doctor recorded no fresh evidence of bleeding, tear or scratch over the vulva, only a slightly reddened area on the outer mucosa, and noted that the hymen was intact. The doctor also noted that the examination was carried out 21 days after the occurrence. The victim's age was established through a birth certificate, a matriculation certificate and medical age tests. The accused was arrested on 12 September 2006 and a charge sheet was filed. The victim's account was supported by her father and brother.
physical_harm: Victim consumed poison in a suicide attempt, became unconscious and was hospitalised until 10.09.2006; medical examination recorded no fresh bleeding, tear or scratch, and the doctor recorded the hymen as intact
motive: alleged: previous enmity with the victim's family (defence contention; not accepted by the court)
key_evidence_accepted: Victim's testimony of forcible rape; explanation for the 22-day delay in lodging the FIR; victim's immediate account to the doctor, father and brother on regaining consciousness; father's and brother's corroborating testimony; doctor's non-categorical denial of hymen rupture; birth and matriculation records proving minority
witness_credibility: Victim's version found reliable after cross-examination; father and brother corroborated her account; doctor had not categorically denied hymen rupture, so the medical evidence was not decisive
post_offence_conduct: Accused left the place and threatened the victim not to disclose the incident; no other post-offence conduct of the accused is recorded

defence_argument: Accused falsely implicated due to enmity; 22-day delay in FIR unexplained; suicide attempt due to examination fear, not rape; hymen intact per medical evidence; injuries mentioned by victim not recorded by doctor; sole testimony of prosecutrix should not be relied on
legal_principle_applied: Amended s.114-A Evidence Act (presumption of absence of consent) applied impliedly where victim attempted suicide due to trauma of rape; rape held proved even on attempt; delay in FIR adequately explained; medical evidence not decisive where other circumstantial evidence supports prosecution; sole testimony of prosecutrix accepted after cross-examination

neutral_facts: The victim was reported missing around 21 June 1995, and his body was later found floating in a canal, after a chappal was recovered on a path leading to the canal near a bridge. The victim's brother, who had gone searching on a motorcycle, reported seeing a chappal, a saw, two pieces of blade, blood and pieces of meat on the path and the body on the water's surface. A missing-person report was made by the victim's mother, and a first information report was later registered. The prosecution case was that the accused and a co-accused killed the victim on the intervening night of 21/22 June 1995 at the instigation of the victim's wife, with whom the co-accused was alleged to have an illicit relationship, and that the body was thrown into the canal. The accused was alleged to have a grudge over the victim's marriage to the wife and a previous fight with the victim. A family member testified that the victim had been seen with the accused and the co-accused on 21 June 1995. A doctor testified that the victim had been murdered about one week before the post-mortem, which found grievous injuries to the neck and scalp and multiple skull fractures. Recoveries were made on the disclosure statements of the accused and the co-accused: the victim's chappal, and blood-stained shirt and trousers of the accused found in a polythene bag under a bridge. Further blood-stained clothing was recovered hidden near the village. The laboratory reported human blood on the clothes, and blood was also found on a hexa blade and the frame of a saw.

premeditation_planning: Not stated; conspiracy was alleged by the investigation and the s.120B conviction was upheld, but no separate finding on planning is recorded

witness_credibility: Court found discrepancies in inquest report and depositions to be minor; defence had not cross-examined the Investigating Officer or ASI on them, and the court relied on the witnesses' evidence
post_offence_conduct: Blood-stained clothes concealed near the village were recovered on the appellant's own disclosure statement; the appellant gave no explanation for the deceased's whereabouts in his s.313 statement

neutral_facts: Some twenty years after an earlier family dispute, which had caused enmity between two families, a group of seventeen persons, including the two accused, allegedly assembled with the common object of killing the victim. On the night of 30 July 1999, the victim was sleeping on a cot outside his house. The assailants allegedly encircled him and inflicted indiscriminate cuts over his body with an aruval, causing instant death. The victim's two sons intervened to save him and were also injured. After the attack the assailants ran away. The matter was first reported to a police station whose jurisdiction did not cover the place of occurrence. An inspector went to the scene that night and recorded the statement of the victim's wife, and a first information report was registered the next morning. The post-mortem examination recorded fifteen incised wounds, mainly on the neck, chest, shoulder, arm and hand. The victim's two sons were also treated for cut injuries. The victim's wife testified that she had known both accused for a long time because they were closely related, and that she recognised them even though it was dark, relying on a street light and electricity supply at the scene. One injured son initially did not support the prosecution but, when examined, named the two accused as taking part in the attack. A wireman from the electricity board gave evidence that power was supplied at the scene at the relevant time. Recoveries were made on the basis of the accused's disclosure statements.

neutral_facts: On the evening of 2 March 1991, the victim, a medical practitioner, was attending patients in a clinic when two unidentified youths shot the victim from point-blank range, and the victim died. A report of the incident was lodged the following day. During the investigation, several witnesses who had heard about the occurrence from the victim's wife and daughter were examined. The post-mortem examination recorded two bullet wounds, one on the right side of the face near the outer corner of the eye and one on the left side of the neck just below the ear, and gave shock and haemorrhage from the bullet injuries as the cause of death. The victim's daughter had been with the victim at the clinic and was an eyewitness, while the victim's wife was slightly away from the scene. The eyewitness gave a statement to the investigating officers about two years and eight months after the incident. He stated that he had been threatened by a co-accused. His acquaintance with the accused was a fortnight old when he accompanied the accused and another person to the clinic, where the other person went inside pretending to be a patient. He asserted that the accused fired at the victim, who fell and died. The accused was arrested about eight years after the incident, following the eyewitness's statement. The victim's wife and daughter were not examined as witnesses.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from two gunshot wounds (right side of face near outer angle of right eye; left side of neck below the ear)

motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Post-mortem evidence establishing homicidal death from firing at point-blank range. The eyewitness testimony of PW-14 was not accepted as reliable.
witness_credibility: PW-14 (eyewitness): found thoroughly and wholly unreliable because of the two years eight months delay, the implausible threat explanation, and the implausibility of silence after witnessing the shooting. Wife and daughter, the most natural witnesses, were not examined and no explanation was given.

The body lay on its side with multiple injuries from a sharp-edged weapon, blood was on the ground nearby, and the victim's car was missing. The victim's brother lodged a first information report and a post-mortem was conducted. The post-mortem surgeon recorded seven injuries, opined that death resulted from shock and haemorrhage, and stated that a kirpan could have caused the injuries. A co-accused, held by another police force in a separate matter, made statements implicating two other men. His first statement named a different accomplice who had taken only the watch and briefcase, and the car was recovered on his disclosure. In a later statement he named the two men, saying one took the briefcase and the other the watch. Following disclosures, the two men were arrested and a briefcase and wrist watch were recovered. The victim's wife identified the items as belonging to her husband, stating that the watch bore initials. The victim's brother testified that three men arrived at the victim's house shortly after the victim left, asked for him, and gave their names. No footprints were found in the kutcha area where the body lay, and no other evidence placed the two men near the scene.
