case_title: Pargan Singh v. State of Punjab & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Stranger (the assailants were unknown to the complainant and other persons)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.307, s.397, each read with s.34
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PW-2 injured eyewitness, PW-3 complainant); medical evidence (postmortem and injury reports); extra-judicial confession (PW-1)
confession: Extra-judicial confession made to PW-1 (Pradhan of the mohalla). Accepted by the courts below and not disturbed by the Supreme Court, but treated as a weak type of evidence needing corroboration; the Court relied mainly on the two eyewitnesses.
aggravating_circumstances: Shooting of the victim's companion who was killed; firing at a bystander who tried to stop the robbery, causing serious injury; robbery of cash during the attack
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.302, 307 and 397 IPC r/w s.34; life imprisonment and Rs.50,000 fine under s.302; 10 years RI and Rs.25,000 fine under s.307; 10 years RI under s.397; sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld (judgment dated 13.12.2012)
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302 r/w s.34); attempt to murder (IPC s.307 r/w s.34); robbery-related offence under IPC s.397
neutral_facts: On 25 March 1999, the victim and a companion withdrew four lakh rupees in cash from a bank and rode two-wheelers back toward their office. Near a market, a black scooter carrying two men approached from behind. The pillion rider fired a pistol at the victim, who fell from the scooter. The two men snatched the money bag, which also contained a cheque book, and turned back. When the companion tried to stop them, the pillion rider fired at him, injuring him. The assailants then fled on the scooter with the money bag. The victim died from a gunshot wound to the back, with severe haemorrhage and injury to vital organs. The companion received multiple gunshot wounds to the shoulder, neck, face and tongue and lost consciousness. The complainant, who was present, reported the incident promptly to the police, and officers visited the spot and recorded the death and injuries. The assailants were unknown to the complainant and the companion. Police could not trace the culprits for several years. In July 2006 a special team was formed, and police received information identifying the accused. A local resident, described as the Pradhan of his mohalla, stated that the accused had confessed to him. The accused were arrested at a naka in August 2006 when they were seen riding a scooter. The accused declined a test identification parade. The eyewitnesses later identified the accused at trial.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a gunshot wound to the upper back with severe haemorrhage and injury to vital organs; the companion suffered multiple gunshot wounds to the shoulder, neck, face and tongue, with serious injury
financial_property_loss: Rs.4 lakhs in cash withdrawn from the bank (money bag snatched), plus a cheque book
motive: alleged: robbery of the cash bag (Rs.4 lakhs) withdrawn from the bank
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-2 (injured eyewitness) and PW-3 (complainant); extra-judicial confession to PW-1, corroborated by the two eyewitnesses; medical evidence of ante-mortem gunshot injuries
witness_credibility: The Court found PW-2 and PW-3 credible: their accounts were consistent and PW-2, as an injured witness, had a higher degree of credibility; PW-1 was a respectable Pradhan with no axe to grind
post_offence_conduct: Accused declined a test identification parade without any stated reason; no other post-offence conduct such as absconding is noted by the Court
custody_duration: Not stated (arrested 07.08.2006; duration of custody not stated)
trial_duration: offence: 25.03.1999; trial judgment: 25.09.2008; High Court: 13.12.2012; Supreme Court: 05.09.2014
legal_representation: Accused: Shreepal Singh (for Pargan Singh) and Shiv Kumar Suri (for Harminder Singh), with others listed as counsel for the appellants; State: V. Madhukar, AAG, with Anvita Cowshish and Kuldip Singh for the respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered on the complainant's statement; site inquest and seizures made; culprits not traced for years; accused arrested in August 2006; challan filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions Judge, Kapurthala): convicted; High Court: appeal dismissed; Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, convictions upheld
prosecution_argument: The eyewitnesses PW-1 and PW-2 are credible; PW-2 is an injured eyewitness; 90 seconds was enough to observe and remember the assailants; PW-1 is an independent witness; the claim that faces were shown at the police station was never pleaded earlier
defence_argument: The prosecution story is suspect; PW-2 was shown the accused at the police station before the test identification parade, so the parade had no purpose; the witnesses were unknown and the incident lasted only about 90 seconds, so identification after 7 years is unreliable; the accused were falsely implicated
legal_principle_applied: Eyewitness identification after a long gap depends on the circumstances of observation (duration and trauma); an injured witness's testimony needs higher credibility; extra-judicial confession is weak and needs corroboration; conviction may rest on credible eyewitnesses alone
precedent_relied_upon: Balwinder Singh v. State of Punjab, (1995) Supp (4) SCC 259 (on extra-judicial confession)
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Raju @ Devendra Choubey v. State of Chhattisgarh
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (step mother-in-law) for accused no. 1, with prior domestic dispute; no evidence of prior animosity for accused nos. 2 and 4
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34 and s.120B (printed as '1208' in the judgment)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (child witness PW-21); recovery (knife, hair from deceased's grip, bloodstained cloth); medical (post-mortem); test identification parade and in-court identification

trial_court_outcome: All accused convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 and s.120B IPC; life imprisonment and Rs. 1,000 fine each, default 3 months additional rigorous imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; conviction of all accused confirmed (judgment dated 17.09.2010)
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 read with s.34 for accused nos. 1, 2 and 4 (conviction upheld); accused no. 3 acquitted
neutral_facts: On 25 November 2003 the victim was found dead in the courtyard of a family house. The victim had been married into the household in July 2003. The prosecution case was that the step mother-in-law of the victim, who was annoyed with the victim over a domestic dispute, engaged three other persons to kill the victim. The only eyewitness was a thirteen-year-old domestic servant living in the house. According to the witness, one assailant held the victim while another stabbed the victim three to four times with a knife in the courtyard. The step mother-in-law was present in the passage, and a further person stood outside the house. After the assault, the assailants threatened the witness not to disclose anything. The witness was then taken to the terrace by the step mother-in-law and told to say that thieves had committed the crime. The step mother-in-law then began shouting and lay down near the victim. The victim's husband, returning from his clinic, found the servant weeping and the victim dead, and the step mother-in-law unconscious nearby. A First Information Report was lodged the same evening. Post-mortem examination recorded fourteen incised wounds, neurogenic and haemorrhagic shock as the cause of death, and a two-month pregnancy. Investigators seized a bloodstained knife, a hair found in the victim's grip, bloodstained cloth of the victim and of the step mother-in-law, and cement mortar. Three accused were arrested on 29 November 2003 and one on 22 December 2003. The witness identified the accused in test identification parades held within about a fortnight and four days of arrest, and identified them again in court.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by neurogenic and haemorrhagic shock; 14 incised wounds (including neck and chest), punctured lungs; victim was carrying a two-month fetus
number_of_offences: 1 offence (murder, s.302) charged with s.34 and s.120B as modes of liability; 1 finally upheld (for accused nos. 1, 2 and 4)
premeditation_planning: Yes. Court found the accused engaged paid killers with a single mission to kill the victim
motive: alleged: annoyance over domestic dispute with the victim; PW-1 deposed that accused no. 1 opposed the victim's marriage to her son because she wanted her daughter to marry him
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of child eyewitness PW-21; recovery of knife from accused no. 2 corroborating his account; identification parade and in-court identification of accused; hair found in deceased's grip; post-mortem findings
witness_credibility: PW-21 (child witness) found reliable: no reason to lie, no grudge or ulterior motive, presence in house natural; tutoring contention rejected as the period between arrest and identification parade was not inordinate
post_offence_conduct: Accused no. 1 asked the witness to conceal the truth and blame thieves; accused no. 2 threatened the witness not to disclose; all accused fled the scene
bail_history: Accused no. 3 was on bail (bail bonds cancelled on acquittal); otherwise not stated
trial_duration: offence: 25.11.2003; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 17.09.2010; Supreme Court: 21.08.2014
legal_representation: Appellants: P.C. Agrawala, Dr. Rajesh Pandey, Mahesh Pandey, Priyanka Pandey, Mridula Ray Bhardwaj, Revathy Raghavan, Vidya Dhar Gaur. Respondent (State): Atul Jha, Sandeep Jha, Dharmendra Kumar Sinha
investigation_status: FIR registered 25.11.2003; inquest, post-mortem, seizures and arrests completed; test identification parades held; charges framed and trial conducted with 32 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: all four convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 and s.120B, life imprisonment. High Court: conviction of all confirmed. Supreme Court: appeals of accused nos. 1, 2 and 4 dismissed; accused no. 3 acquitted
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: PW-21 was a tutored witness influenced by police, so his evidence needed close scrutiny and corroboration; delayed test identification made in-court identification unreliable; accused no. 3 merely stood outside and did not act as guard
legal_principle_applied: Child witness evidence assessed for reliability; corroboration by earlier identification is a safe rule of prudence where witness is a stranger to accused; common intention and conspiracy are matters of inference and benefit of doubt goes to accused
precedent_relied_upon: Relied on: Baliya v. State of M.P. (2012) 9 SCC 696. Referred to: Budhsen v. State of UP (1970) 2 SCC 128; Suresh Sakharam Nangare v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 9 SCC 249; Jai Bhagwan v. State of Haryana AIR 1999 SC 1083; Ramashish Yadav v. State of Bihar (1999) 8 SCC 555. Distinguished: Subash and Shiv Kumar v. State of UP (1987) 3 SCC 331; Mohd. Abdul Hafeez v. State of Andhra Pradesh AIR 1983 SC 367

neutral_facts: On the anniversary of the couple's marriage, the accused and a co-accused were allegedly present in the house where the accused and the victim lived. It was alleged that the accused poured kerosene oil on his wife and set her on fire. She was taken to a mission hospital and then transferred to a medical college hospital, where she died of burn injuries. The victim's brother lodged the first information report, and the police investigated and filed a charge-sheet. The doctor who performed the autopsy opined that death was caused by shock from ante mortem flame burns covering about 90% of the body surface. At the hospital, a doctor examined the victim and recorded her statement that her husband had poured kerosene oil on her and ignited it, and a nurse attending her supported that account. A person who accompanied the victim's brother to the hospital testified that the victim had said in their presence that her husband had set her on fire. Neighbours heard a commotion and saw the victim near the gateway, as did a son of the accused from an earlier marriage. A maid servant present at the time could not be examined. Hair of the victim sent for chemical examination showed no smell of kerosene.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock due to ante mortem flame burns over about 90% of body surface (dermo-epidermal severity)
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declarations to PW-6 doctor and PW-7 nurse that the husband poured kerosene oil and set her on fire, corroborated by PW-1 (brother) and PW-8; autopsy evidence
witness_credibility: PW-6 and PW-7 had no prior contact with the victim, were not related to her and were not interested witnesses; their evidence was treated as very important and the Sessions Court found PW-6 true
post_offence_conduct: Not stated

case_title: Pradeep Kumar v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B (dowry death); IPC s.498-A (cruelty)
weapon: Kerosene used to set the victim on fire; no weapon mentioned
evidence_type: Dying declaration; medical (post-mortem) evidence; oral testimony of mother and father; magistrate's testimony; letter from victim to father
aggravating_circumstances: Death by burns within nine months of marriage; soon-before-death cruelty and harassment over dowry demand
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.498-A and s.304-B by Sessions Judge, Kamal (judgment 1 August 1997); sentence amount not stated
high_court_outcome: Revision/appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence affirmed (judgment 3 February 2010)
offence_finally_established: Dowry death under IPC s.304-B; cruelty/harassment under IPC s.498-A
neutral_facts: The victim was married to the accused on 20 June 1995. On 1 March 1996, about nine months after the marriage, she suffered burn injuries. Her statement, recorded by a Chief Judicial Magistrate on 2 March 1996 after a medical fitness endorsement, had two parts. The first part described an accident in which a kerosene stove burst while she was preparing tea. The second part alleged that the accused had been pressing her to bring Rs. One lakh from her parents and had threatened to kill her. It further alleged that the accused had tried to hang her, had earlier tried to burn her at night, and at about 5.30 a.m. had doused her from behind with kerosene and set her alight. She stated that the first part had been tutored by the accused. A First Information Report was registered on the basis of that statement. The victim died on 12 March 1996. The post-mortem examination found superficial to deep burns over most of the body, excluding the face, scalp, both legs, feet and part of the left upper arm. The doctor recorded that the cause of death was ante mortem burns. He agreed that kerosene poured from behind would leave burns on the back, and that a stove burst would ordinarily have affected the face and scalp, which were not burnt. The victim's mother testified that the victim had told her of quarrels over a demand of Rs. One lakh for a piggery farm. The victim's father testified to the same demand and to physical abuse. A letter from the victim to her father demanding Rs. 5,000 was also in evidence. The accused was reported to have donated blood, but the victim died despite it. The case was then converted to a dowry-related offence and a charge sheet was filed.
offence_severity: Maximum: imprisonment for life; Minimum: seven years imprisonment (IPC s.304-B). For s.498-A the judgment states imprisonment up to three years and fine.
physical_harm: Superficial to deep burns over most of the body; death from ante mortem burns on 12 March 1996
premeditation_planning: Not stated; the court recorded the dying declaration's account of an earlier night-time attempt but made no express finding of premeditation
motive: Demand for dowry of Rs. One lakh (for piggery farm) from the victim's parents, with harassment and threats to force compliance; accepted by the court
key_evidence_accepted: Second part of the dying declaration; evidence of the victim's father (PW-8); post-mortem evidence (PW-7) that burns were ante mortem; mother's (PW-6) evidence of dowry demand
witness_credibility: Court accepted the father's evidence and the second part of the dying declaration as reliable; the first part was found tutored by the accused
post_offence_conduct: Not stated (court did not separately find post-offence conduct; the prosecution case alleged the accused tried to save her)
bail_history: Not stated; Supreme Court cancelled the bail bond

neutral_facts: The victim alleged that the accused, a neighbour known to her, asked her to sit in his car at a bus stand around 1997-98. She initially refused but got in. The accused then drove to an uninhabited place, beat her and had sexual intercourse with her against her wishes, threatening her not to disclose the incident. The victim alleged that about a month later the accused repeated the act at a hotel and told her he had taken her photographs. case_title: State of Maharashtra v. Ramlal Devappa Rathod

neutral_facts: The victim was attacked at a village temple by a large group of villagers at about dawn, after prayers, and was struck with a sword. The accused, part of the crowd, chased him from place to place, including to the homes of relatives, where relatives and others were also assaulted. The attackers removed roof tiles and tin sheets to reach him, dragged him into a field and assaulted him with swords, axes and a sattur. Houses in the area were damaged and some set on fire, and documents, gold ornaments and cash were taken or burnt. Family members took the victim to hospital, where he was found dead. The post-mortem recorded multiple chop and incised wounds, skull fractures and sub-dural haematoma, with the cause of death given as hemorrhage and shock due to multiple chop wounds with head injury. The victim's brother lodged a complaint naming thirty-four persons and attributing overt acts to some. The spot panchnama recorded blood stains at the temple, the well, a road and the houses. After disclosure statements by several accused, blood-stained weapons were recovered the day after the incident. At trial, most eye-witnesses, including close relatives, were declared hostile on identity. The sole eye-witness, the victim's wife, described the incident in stages and identified specific accused. Her account was said to be supported by the medical evidence and other material.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple chop wounds, skull fractures and brain injury; post-mortem recorded 13 external wounds and internal head injuries
number_of_offences: 11 charged (ss.147, 148, 302, 307, 324, 326, 395, 427, 435, 436, 452 r/w 149); 10 finally upheld for six accused (s.395 not among the convictions)

key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of sole eye-witness PW12 (victim's wife), including the nine stages of the incident and identification of six accused; medical evidence; spot panchnama; recovery of blood-stained weapons on disclosure statements (supported by investigating officer PW18); damage to houses
witness_credibility: PW12 found natural, consistent and reliable; her failure to be present earlier explained by a warrant, and lack of physical injuries not fatal to her account. Hostile witnesses' reluctance attributed to intensity of incident
post_offence_conduct: Disclosure statements leading to recovery of blood-stained weapons the day after the incident; Court treated it as a relevant circumstance
trial_duration: offence: 30.04.2000; trial judgment: 06.10.2001; High Court: 22.06.2006; Supreme Court: 29.09.2015
legal_representation: Appellant (State of Maharashtra): Shankar Chillarge, Sonia Shankar Chillarge, Aniruddha P. Mayee. Respondents: Meenakshi Arora, Mahima, Anjani Kumar Jha, Vinay Naware, Dr. R.R. Deshpande, Yuvraj Gaikwad
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation, spot panchnama, post-mortem, recoveries and charge-sheet against thirty-four persons; trial completed

appeal_history: Trial court: 8 convicted (life under s.302 r/w 149). High Court: acquitted all 8. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; convictions of 6 (A-1, A-2, A-3, A-12, A-29, A-30) restored; acquittal of A-7 and A-10 confirmed
prosecution_argument: Sole eye-witness testimony (PW12) is reliable and corroborated; reliance on Masalti was not called for; High Court's assessment was erroneous

In October 2009 he emailed the synopsis to a friend, who was seeking a comedy film story for the son of a film director. The friend forwarded the synopsis by email to another person, describing it as just an idea, on 15.10.2009. The friend received no reply. Later the complainant saw promotional material for a film titled "Desi Boyz". He alleges that this title infringes copyright in his title. He has not seen the film and cannot say whether any part of his story was used. The accused state that their film was released on 25.11.2011 and was based on a story written by another author under a written agreement dated 02.09.2009 and paid for by cheque. case_title: Narender Singh & Ors. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute (old enmity recorded in the FIR crime details form; this is the prosecution's recorded motive, not a finding on the relationship)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w ss.148 and 149 (conviction); charged also under IPC ss.147 and 294
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured eyewitness and corroborating eyewitnesses); medical evidence (MLC and post mortem); documentary records (FIR, crime details form, express report); recovery of weapons; Section 27 disclosure statements

high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 666 of 2000) dismissed; conviction and life sentence confirmed
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 r/w ss.148 and 149
neutral_facts: On the night of 27 June 1997, around 10:00 p.m., the victim, who was a village sarpanch, was sitting and talking with two other persons near a hotel in the village, with street lights on and a chimney burning nearby. Several men arrived at the spot. One carried a sword, another a farsa, another an axe, and the rest lathis. The man with the sword, while abusing the victim and saying he could not escape that day, struck the victim on the head, causing bleeding. Another assailant then struck the victim's head with the farsa, and a third struck the head with an axe, after which the victim fell. Others struck with lathis. Witnesses pleaded for the victim to be spared, and the assailants left after warning the victim not to contest against them in future. The injured eyewitness went to the police station about one kilometre away, and a first information report was registered at 10:45 p.m. The investigating officer visited the scene at 11:10 p.m. and prepared the crime details form. The injured eyewitness was sent for medical examination, completed by 1:30 a.m. The post mortem recorded eight injuries on the body, four of them grievous. The body was taken to the hospital by 7:30 a.m. the next day. Witnesses who came on hearing shouts corroborated the account. The accused were arrested on 28 June 1997, weapons were seized on 29 June 1997 at their instance, and disclosure statements were recorded. The express report was received by the magistrate only on 30 June 1997.
physical_harm: Death of the deceased from head and body injuries (eight injuries, four grievous, from sword, farsa, axe and lathis); the injured eyewitness also sustained injuries
motive: alleged: old enmity (as recorded in the crime details form); the court did not separately decide the motive
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of injured P.W.3 and P.W.6, corroborated by P.Ws. 7 and 11; MLC of P.W.3 (Exhibit P1) and Exhibits P1A and P1B; post mortem evidence of P.W.10; weapons recovered at the appellants' instance; arrest and seizure records; crime details form and contemporaneous FIR documents
witness_credibility: P.W.3 (injured eyewitness) found cogent in every respect; his presence and injuries held established by the doctor's evidence; P.W.6 supportive; P.W.10's evidence found to fully support the prosecution; the court relied on the Bhajan Singh principle that an injured witness's testimony is accorded special status
post_offence_conduct: Arrested on 28 June 1997; weapons recovered at their instance on 29 June 1997; the accused left the place of occurrence after warning the victim
trial_duration: offence: 27 June 1997; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 7 September 2006; Supreme Court: 29 September 2015
legal_representation: Appellants: Tripurari Ray, Dhirendra Singh Parmar, Suresh Kumar Sharma, Rajinder Singh, Susheel Tomar, Ms. Abha R. Sharma (Advocates). State: Arjun Garg, Manish Yadav, Mishra Saurabh (Advocates)
investigation_status: FIR registered at 10:45 p.m. on 27 June 1997; investigating officer visited scene; medical examination and post mortem conducted; arrests 28 June 1997; seizures 29 June 1997; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Delay in forwarding the Express Report under s.157 CrPC to the Illaka Magistrate (received 1:20 p.m. on 30 June 1997); the court held it caused no serious prejudice
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 r/w ss.148 and 149 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Arrest, seizure and Section 27 statements established involvement; the delay in the Express Report caused no prejudice; eyewitness account and medical evidence were clinching; the FIR was registered in time and the Express Report was sent through a constable on 27 June 1997
defence_argument: FIR was ante-dated; injured witness P.W.3's injuries were fake and his presence doubtful; eyewitness Ranganath Sharma was not examined; unexplained delay in forwarding the Express Report; omissions in the crime details form and other documents; weapons not linked to the injuries; minor infirmities
legal_principle_applied: Delay in sending the report to the Magistrate is not fatal unless prejudice is shown; evidence of an injured eyewitness is accorded special status; contemporaneous documents and other corroborating evidence can cure non-mention in a statutory form; minor discrepancies do not impinge on the judgment

other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Sat Parkash v. State of Haryana and another

neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused kidnapped a girl of about fifteen from the lawful guardianship of her father in Ganaur on 7 June 1992, with intent that she be forced into illicit intercourse, and raped her in that area and at other places. Her date of birth was admitted as 5 November 1976. The victim was later found at the accused's residence. On 12 June 1992 it was alleged that the victim was administered poison and died, with the accused's relatives alleged to have concealed her at their house. The accused also made an attempt to commit suicide along with the victim; the victim died in that attempt while the accused survived. A note said to have been written by the victim just before the attempt was produced. In it she stated that she had left home of her own free will, that she loved the accused, and that she was taking her own life. No other evidence was produced showing that the accused enticed her away. The prosecution produced no evidence that sexual intercourse had taken place with the victim.

case_title: Shim Singh v. State of Uttarakhand
accused_occupation: Not stated by the court. Defence counsel said Shim Singh was a vehicle driver and Aan Singh a chowkidar in P.W.D.
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband, appellant No.1); other appellants were the husband's brothers and a brother's wife (in-laws of the deceased)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B; IPC s.498-A; Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 s.3 and s.4; Evidence Act s.113-A and s.113-B (presumptions)
weapon: Poison (organo chloro insecticide and ethyl alcohol found in viscera); fire (victim's body burnt)
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence; medical evidence (autopsy and viscera chemical report); oral evidence of relatives and village head
confession: Admissions under s.313 CrPC to the marriage date and unnatural death only; not a confession of the offence; not treated as such by the court
aggravating_circumstances: Death within about five months of marriage; 90% burns; poison found in viscera; death at in-laws' house; prior complaints of dowry-related taunts and torture
trial_court_outcome: Appellants 1 and 2 convicted under s.304-B IPC (life imprisonment); all four convicted under s.498-A IPC (rigorous imprisonment; term stated as one year at p.5 and three years at p.7) and DPA ss.3-4 (three months' RI and fine); sentences concurrent

neutral_facts: The victim married the accused in May 1997. About five months later, on 26 September 1997, the victim died at the matrimonial home. The village head reported the unnatural death by telephone to the sub-divisional magistrate. The body was found with about 90% burn injuries. The accused, including the victim's husband, his brothers and his brother's wife, told the village head that the victim had set herself on fire. Post-mortem examination by two doctors could not ascertain the cause of death from external examination, so the viscera were preserved. Chemical examination of the viscera detected organo chloro insecticide and ethyl alcohol. The victim's brother, father and uncle testified that the victim had complained of taunts and torture over dowry. One witness said that at a post-marriage ceremony an accused complained that the marriage expenses had not been recovered. The victim had complained to the family twice about dowry demands. The victim's brother said no dowry demand was made before the marriage. The defence contended that the victim had swallowed poison and then set herself on fire. Police investigated, and a charge-sheet was filed against all four accused.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; 90% burn injuries (skin deep); poison found in viscera

premeditation_planning: No explicit finding of premeditation; court noted only that the accused had the opportunity to administer poison
motive: Dowry demand: cruelty and harassment for dowry accepted by the court; alleged: resentment over unrecovered marriage expenses
key_evidence_accepted: Post-mortem and viscera report; oral evidence of relatives (PW-1, PW-2, PW-3) on dowry taunts and the durgun incident; victim's two prior complaints; death within five months of marriage; s.313 admissions; death in accused's house; opportunity to administer poison
witness_credibility: Court accepted the relatives' testimony on dowry demands as cogent and consistent; defence points that no dowry demand was made before marriage and no prior police report was lodged were rejected
post_offence_conduct: Accused informed the village head of the death and said the victim had set herself on fire; court found that failure to take the victim to hospital was inconsistent with innocence

case_title: Sanjeev v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance: the two drank liquor together before the altercation; no other relationship described
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged; conviction set aside); IPC s.304 Part I (conviction substituted)
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence; extra-judicial confession; medical evidence; recovery of blood-stained clothes; forensic blood-group report; witness saw accused fleeing

aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden altercation after mutual drinking leading to a scuffle; act treated as covered by Exception 4 to s.300
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs.5,000 (default two further months)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence under s.302 affirmed

neutral_facts: On the night of 11 January 2000, the victim was last known to be travelling from a town toward his village after an outing. Around 10 p.m., the victim's brother saw the accused near a tubewell and a bus stand, running away with blood-stained clothes; the brother identified the accused in vehicle headlights and did not then know of any killing. The next morning the victim's wife reported that he had not returned home. The family searched and found the victim's body near a water-supply tubewell, lying in a pool of blood, with wounds on the forehead, nose and eyebrows; his shirt, sweater and slippers lay some distance away. Police recorded the body's location, took possession of the body, a blood-stained brick and clothing, and prepared an inquest. A post-mortem recorded multiple injuries, including contusions on the back, a large chest swelling with fractured ribs and blood in the chest cavity, and lacerated wounds on the forehead and above the right eye; the examining doctors stated that these injuries were sufficient to cause death. In the early hours of the next day the accused attended a government hospital, where a doctor recorded a superficial incised wound on the back of the left forearm with a corresponding cut in the shirt. Later, a witness stated that the accused had told him that on the earlier night he had quarrelled with the victim after both drank liquor and had struck him with a brick. On disclosure by the accused, police recovered blood-stained clothes concealed in a wooden box in the accused's house. Forensic analysis found the same blood group ('O') on the recovered clothes and on the victim's clothing.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple head, chest and body injuries; accused had a superficial 22 x 0.2 x 2 to 0.5 cm incised wound on the left forearm
number_of_offences: 1 charged; 0 finally upheld as charged (s.302 set aside; s.304 Part I conviction substituted)
premeditation_planning: No premeditation found; act treated as committed in a sudden fight in heat of passion
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Chain of circumstances: witness saw accused fleeing blood-stained; medical record of forearm wound; extra-judicial confession to PW-12 corroborated by PW-13; recovery of blood-stained clothes; forensic blood-group match
witness_credibility: Court found no reason to disbelieve the chain of circumstances and the PW-12 confession, which was corroborated by PW-13's medical evidence; no defence explanation for the accused's injury
post_offence_conduct: Seen fleeing blood-stained toward a bus stand; sought medical treatment for forearm wound; blood-stained clothes concealed in a wooden box at home; disclosed the incident to PW-12
custody_duration: Appellant said to be in jail; duration not stated
trial_duration: offence: 11.1.2000 (intervening night of 11-12 January 2000); trial judgment: 3.10.2002; High Court: 24.05.2011; Supreme Court: 19.02.2015
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: J.P. Tiwari, Sanjeev Bansal, Praksh Kumar Singh; State/respondent: Nupur Choudhary (for Kamal Mohan Gupta)

defence_argument: Circumstances do not complete the chain; no eyewitness; no motive, so the accused could not be said to be the only person who could have committed the crime

case_title: Dr. Vinod Bhandari v. State of M.P.
accused_occupation: Managing Director of a medical institute (Shri Aurbindo Institute of Medical Sciences, Indore)
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.420, s.467, s.468, s.471, s.120B; MP Manyata Prapt Pariksha Adhiniyam 1937 s.3(d), s.1, s.2/4; IT Act s.65, s.66 (as listed in FIR; not confirmed as framed charges)

neutral_facts: The prosecution alleges a conspiracy to secure admission to undergraduate medical courses for candidates who had not earned places on merit. The scheme allegedly involved copying during a state professional entrance test, with some high-scoring persons seated among candidates so they could supply correct answers. Blank answer sheets were allegedly later filled in with correct answers by officials, and a model answer key was reportedly copied and passed to candidates one night before the examination. Each candidate reportedly paid several lakh rupees to middlemen, who shared the money with officials. The accused is alleged to have received money from candidates through a general manager of an institution connected with the accused, who handled admissions. During investigation, the general manager made a disclosure that led to the recovery of money and documents, including a seizure of cash. Seized material included a list of candidates sponsored from the accused's institution, electronic data from an examination board office, documents and activity charts from that board, and memoranda of other accused persons. A statement recorded under the criminal procedure code by a parent of a candidate said the accused had asked him to meet the general manager and pay a sum for admission, which he could not pay. The investigation involved a large number of accused persons, a substantial number of whom had been arrested, with further charge sheets pending.

neutral_facts: The victim, a married woman living in a joint household with her husband and his parents and relatives at Morbi, was found hanging from a ceiling fan at the marital home on 23 March 2000. A family member of the accused telephoned the victim's father, who worked at a bank in Rajkot, to come to the house. The police were informed, and an assistant sub-inspector visited the scene, recorded a statement from the accused's family member, and initially registered the death as accidental. The investigation was then taken over by an inspector. The victim's father arrived later that day and suspected foul play, noting that the accused had repeatedly demanded dowry and that none of them were present at the house when the death occurred. A complaint was lodged and an FIR registered for offences relating to cruelty, dowry death and abetment of suicide. The body was cut down and sent for post-mortem examination. Several witnesses were examined. The victim's father, elder sister and grandfather testified that the victim frequently complained of mental torture and harassment by the accused for bringing insufficient dowry. A close friend of the victim testified that the victim had told her of such harassment. Photographs of the body and the inquest panchnama were placed on record. The accused had absconded for some weeks before surrendering at the police station.

case_title: Dhirendra Kumar @ Dhiroo v. State of Uttarakhand
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity arising from an earlier altercation over an alleged night-time knocking at a household member's door
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302

neutral_facts: On the evening of 1 April 1983, the victim was struck with a stone at about 8.30 pm in a village. About four days earlier, during a festival, the victim had visited the accused's home. Later that night the accused came to the victim's household to assault the victim, alleging that the victim's family had been involved in an incident of knocking at the door of a woman in the accused's household at night with evil intention. Family members intervened, preventing the accused from dragging the victim out, and the accused left with a threat. The victim did not return home that night. The next morning a witness said he had seen the victim with the accused at about 7.30 pm, and two eyewitnesses said they saw the accused beating the victim with a stone at about 8.30 pm. Another witness said he had seen the two together just before the incident. The victim's body was later found near a riverbank. The post-mortem recorded that the face and head were flattened, with multiple irregular lacerated wounds, a disfigured face, pulverized skull and mandible bones, and brain matter flowing from the wounds. The death was attributed to shock and haemorrhage from ante-mortem injuries which could have been caused by a stone between 8 and 9 pm. The accused was examined and had three injuries to the face, which the doctor said were caused by a hard blunt object or friction about a day earlier. The accused said he had been falsely implicated because of complaints he had made against local officials.

case_title: Kiriti Pal v. State of West Bengal
accused_occupation: Not stated (described only as posing as a teacher; a school official said no teacher of that name worked there)
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance (friendship and intimacy; A-1 frequently visited and was allowed to stay at the victim's residence)

evidence_type: Circumstantial (last seen evidence, conduct, recovery of weapon, call records); medical evidence; witness testimony

neutral_facts: The victim, a widow who ran a beauty parlour, had become acquainted with one of the accused, and the two developed a close friendship; that accused frequently visited the victim's home and sometimes stayed overnight there. On an evening in November, the victim left home as a pillion rider on the motorcycle of that accused, telling a tenant she was going to a school function. The tenant later saw the accused return alone around 10 to 10:30 p.m. and, when asked about the victim, was told the victim was engaged with someone and would be brought back later. A school official testified that no function had been scheduled at that school on that date. The next morning the victim's body was found in an isolated jungle about 25 km from the residence, with the neck tied by one end of a saree whose other end was tied to a tree. The post-mortem found lacerated head wounds sufficient to cause death, and an injury consistent with forcible intercourse. Investigators arrested the accused, and on the basis of a confessional statement by one accused a motorcycle was seized. Recoveries of an improvised pipe gun with wooden butts were made from near a river and the jungle, and blood was detected on the butts. Call records showed numerous calls between the accused, and a notebook belonging to a co-accused contained a coded number of one accused. A witness testified that one accused threatened him and another witness not to disclose anything to the police.

neutral_facts: At about 9.30 p.m. on the evening in question, the victim and a companion were riding a scooter near a sweet-meat shop when several persons attacked them. The rider lost control and both fell. The attackers then assaulted the victim: some stabbed him repeatedly with knives, while others beat him with iron rods. One attacker tried to stab the companion but missed, and another stabbed the companion in the left arm. The companion escaped and hid in a nearby office. Two persons returning from work saw the incident and took the injured victim to a government hospital. The companion also returned to the scene and was taken to hospital, where his statement was recorded and a case was registered. The victim was later moved to another hospital. A magistrate recorded the victim's dying declaration after confirming through the treating doctor that he was conscious; the declaration named several attackers. The victim died three days after the attack. The post-mortem examination found five stab injuries at different parts of the body and attributed death to multiple stab wounds. The investigating officer later arrested several suspects and recovered four knives and two iron rods on their instructions. The prosecution case was that the victim had been attacked because he had been a witness in an earlier murder case in which one of the attackers had been an accused.

neutral_facts: On a morning in January 1984, a group of men including the accused came to the house of the victim's family armed with lathis, a farsa and handmade bombs. They began abusing the family and threatened that they would not leave the family alive. One of the accused allegedly hurled a handmade bomb at a family member, causing leg injuries, and another accused threw a handmade bomb onto the chest of the victim, who suffered serious burn and laceration injuries. Other accused used lathis, and a farsa was used to injure a woman on her hand. The victim, who was declared brought dead at hospital, was the subject of a post-mortem examination, which recorded extensive burns and lacerated wounds on the chest and hand and found the death homicidal, caused by an explosive substance. Several family members who were present were also injured and were examined by a doctor, and their injuries were proved by medical reports. The complainant lodged a First Information Report shortly after the incident. The investigating officer prepared a spot map, collected bloodstained soil, and seized the lathis, the farsa and the handmade bombs at the instance of the accused. Several other persons who were present were not examined as witnesses. The accused gave a version that the complainant's side had confined a man who later died.

witness_credibility: Court found injured related eye witnesses reliable, consistent with each other on material particulars, supported by medical evidence and FIR; minor contradictions treated as natural and insignificant

case_title: Santosh S/O Shankar Pawar v. State of Maharashtra
accused_socioeconomic_status: Poor (the judgment states the couple lived in poverty)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (FIR initially registered under s.307 IPC, later altered to s.302)
weapon: Kerosene poured from a lamp, and a lighted matchstick thrown on the victim
evidence_type: Dying declaration; oral eyewitness-type testimony of family members (PW2, PW3); medical evidence (post-mortem, doctor's fitness certificate); panch witness evidence on kerosene lamp
aggravating_circumstances: Death within three months of marriage (bride burning); suspicion of infidelity; no provocation for pouring kerosene; victim set ablaze

high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: The victim had been married to the accused only a short time before the incident, and the couple lived in a rented house near the victim's parental home. Both earned a living through daily wage work. On the morning of the incident, the victim went out to answer a call of nature and, on returning somewhat late, was questioned by the accused, who suspected her of infidelity. Despite her attempts to explain, the accused began assaulting her with fists and kicks. He then poured kerosene from a nearby lamp over her and set her ablaze. Her saree caught fire and she ran towards the accused, whose hands were burnt. When she screamed for help, the accused poured water on her. Neighbours and her parents gathered and she was taken to hospital. On the way, she told her mother, sister-in-law and a neighbour what had happened. The neighbour testified only that she said the accused had beaten and kicked her, and did not support the account of kerosene. A sub-inspector recorded her statement at the hospital, on which a First Information Report was registered. After a doctor certified her mental fitness, an executive magistrate recorded a dying declaration naming the accused as the person who poured kerosene and set her on fire. She succumbed to burn injuries on 12 September 2005. The post-mortem found death due to shock and septicaemia caused by 60% burn injuries. A panch witness spoke to a kerosene lamp prepared in an empty liquor bottle in the house. The accused's defence was that the fire was accidental and that he had tried to extinguish it.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock and septicaemia due to 60% burn injuries; accused's hands also burnt
premeditation_planning: No premeditation or planning found; court held absence of premeditation did not reduce the offence, given the clear act of setting the victim ablaze
motive: Suspicion of the victim's infidelity after she returned late from answering nature's call
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration (Ex.1) recorded by the executive magistrate after doctor's fitness certificate (PW6); oral evidence of PW2 (mother) and PW3 (sister-in-law); post-mortem evidence (PW8)
witness_credibility: PW2 and PW3 found reliable and corroborative; PW1 did not support the kerosene account, but the court still accepted the dying declaration and family testimony as not to be doubted
post_offence_conduct: Accused poured water on the victim only when she screamed; court viewed this as an attempt to cloak guilt, not as remorse
trial_duration: offence: 4.9.2005; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 02.02.2012; Supreme Court: 21.04.2015
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: Shashi Bhushan Kumar. State/respondent: Sushil Kranjkar, Dharmendra Kishor, Aniruddha P. Mayee
investigation_status: FIR registered on victim's statement (s.307); altered to s.302 on death; autopsy, inquest and chargesheet completed; trial held
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, life imprisonment and fine Rs.1000. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed (SLP notice limited to nature of offence)
prosecution_argument: Pouring kerosene and throwing a lighted matchstick showed intention to cause death; conviction under s.302 was correct
defence_argument: Fire was accidental; accused rushed to extinguish it and was burnt; no premeditation or intent to kill; relied on Kalu Ram to reduce the offence
legal_principle_applied: Intention to kill distinguishes murder from culpable homicide; absence of premeditation does not reduce murder where the act of setting ablaze is clear; clause (iv) of s.300; concurrent findings not disturbed unless perverse
precedent_relied_upon: Kalu Ram v. State of Rajasthan (2000) 10 SCC 324 (held inapplicable); Satya Narayan Tiwari v. State of UP (2010) 13 SCC 689 (referred); Dhananjay Shanker Shetty v. State of Maharashtra (2002) 6 SCC 596 (referred)

neutral_facts: On a morning in September 1996, near a cycle stand inside a college campus, a group of seven accused, some armed with lathis, knives and khukris, approached two students standing there. They asked the victim and a second student to withdraw their names from a college election. When both refused, the accused assaulted them with their weapons. The victim was struck on the back, neck and face, then ran from the spot, became entangled in wire fencing near a nearby building, and fell. Several accused chased him there and attacked him again with sticks. The second student suffered a head injury. About three hundred students gathered. The victim was taken to hospital and died the next day. The second student lodged a written complaint at a police station, and the shirt he wore was seized. A medical officer examined both injured persons. The victim's frontal bone was found fractured and a lung ruptured; the second student's injuries were consistent with sticks. Eyewitnesses named all the accused and described their individual roles. One witness who had been present gave differing accounts to police and in court. The weapons were not recovered, and a blood-stained shirt was recovered six days after the incident.

neutral_facts: The complainant, who owns a theatre, alleges that he advanced a loan of five lakh rupees to the accused on 20 May 2006 to support the production of a Tamil film, and that she promised to repay it on the film's release. When repayment was not made, the accused issued a cheque for five lakh rupees, drawn on a State Bank of Mysore branch, on 16 January 2007. The complainant presented the cheque through his bank on the same day. The bank returned it on 18 January 2007 with the remark 'Stop Payment'. The complainant then sent a legal notice on 27 January 2007 to the accused's office and residential addresses. The residential notice was duly received, while the office notice was returned marked 'Absent-Information delivered'. The accused did not pay or respond. The accused's position is that she was only a name lender to a film distribution firm run by her husband. She denied taking any loan and said the cheque was an old security cheque given in 1999 against an earlier loan, which the complainant had supposedly misplaced and later misused. The cheque bore a printed date of 1999 on its leaf, though it was filled in with the 2007 date. The cheque and the signature on it were not disputed.

neutral_facts: The victim was riding home from work on a bicycle at about 8:00 p.m. on the evening of the incident, with his younger brother following about 10 to 15 feet behind. At a spot in front of a house, one man stopped the victim by catching his bicycle and poured petrol over him, and another man set him alight with a matchstick. The victim began burning and ran from the spot. A group of persons surrounded him, shouting that he should be beaten, burned and not allowed to escape. One member of the group threw a burning tyre onto him, and another threw a sword at him as he ran. The victim ran to a neighbouring house, where the fire was put out. The brother ran home to alert the family, and relatives came to the scene before the victim was taken to hospital. Before dying, the victim gave two statements, one recorded at the hospital by a police officer and one recorded by an Executive Magistrate after a doctor certified he was conscious. Both named the persons involved and described the group's role and an earlier enmity with the main assailants. The brother testified as an eyewitness. The post-mortem recorded burns over about 90% of the body and an incised wound on the back of the chest. The victim died the following day. neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused had a long-running dispute with the victim's family over the sale of a plot of land and the flow of irrigation water from a distributary, and that they demanded that the land be transferred to them and later demanded money for letting water flow. On the evening of the incident the victim was returning home when the accused allegedly caught hold of him, tied his hands behind his back, threw chilly powder on his face and assaulted him with a club of stones and a stick, causing injuries to the head and other parts of the body. The victim's brother and mother said they witnessed the assault from a nearby field. The brother said he moved to intervene but his mother dissuaded him. After the assailants left, the brother and mother went near the injured man but returned home. Later they went back to the field with the victim's father, who found the victim with his hands still tied, a leg injury and his eyes burning from chilly powder. The father went to lodge a report at a police post. A Sub-Inspector arrived at about 10.00 p.m. in a police jeep and recorded a written complaint from the brother as the first information, in which the victim was described as dead. The brother was then directed to untie the victim's hands, and the victim was taken to hospital, where he was found to have died on the way. The investigating officer later destroyed the report he had received about the incident after the brother's statement was recorded on the spot. A charge-sheet was filed against the accused.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from injuries to the head and other parts of the body; also a broken/fractured leg and eyes affected by chilly powder
number_of_offences: 1 charged (s.302 IPC r/w s.34); 0 finally upheld

case_title: Om Prakash v. Union of India & Ors.
accused_victim_relationship: Co-worker: both served in the same army unit; the judgment describes no prior enmity beyond the farewell-party altercation
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged); IPC s.304 Part II (conviction), with s.34 referred to in the headnote
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence; eyewitness-type testimony about the room and departure; medical evidence; recorded statement under Rule 23 of the Army Rules
confession: Police-station confession to Army officers: not relied on. Statement recorded under Rule 23 (Exh. 36): relied on as voluntary and proved
aggravating_circumstances: Altercation at party; drunken state; alone in room with deceased; left by rear door; presence at police station at odd hour; absence from fall-in parade
trial_court_outcome: General Court Martial convicted under IPC s.304 Part II (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) and sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Writ petition in Delhi High Court transferred to Armed Forces Tribunal, which treated it as an appeal under s.15; no separate High Court decision on merits stated
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, IPC s.304 Part II
neutral_facts: At a farewell party at an army unit's barracks, drinks were served. The accused became involved in a heated argument with a senior non-commissioned officer, who slapped the accused. The accused then fought with and abused that officer and also abused the victim, a fellow soldier, who had tried to intervene. An officer intervened and directed two junior soldiers to escort the accused to his living barracks. Later, the victim was found lying on the floor of the room, bleeding from the mouth and nose, with a stab wound to the chest. The accused was found lying on a bed in the same room. Witnesses testified that no one other than the accused and the victim had been present in the room, and that the accused had been seen leaving quietly through the rear door. The accused was absent from the morning fall-in parade. At about 1.30 to 2 a.m., the accused surrendered at a nearby police station and said he had stabbed a person with a knife. Unit officers went to the station, and the accused confessed to stabbing the victim. The forensic surgeon who conducted the autopsy found two ante mortem injuries, one a deep stab wound to the chest that could have caused death. The knife was not recovered. A statement the accused gave during a summary of evidence under the army rules, describing a scuffle and saying he stabbed the victim to free his neck, was proved through the officer who recorded it, with a supporting witness. The adjutant lodged an FIR and the accused was handed to military police.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a stab wound to the chest (3 x 2 cm, deep to chest cavity); a second injury was a linear abrasion on the back of the chest
number_of_offences: 1 charged (IPC s.302); 1 finally upheld (IPC s.304 Part II)
premeditation_planning: Not found. The GCM found no intention to kill but knowledge that death was a likely consequence; the Supreme Court did not address premeditation
motive: alleged: altercation and quarrel at the farewell party while intoxicated, with the victim intervening
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony that only the accused and the victim were in the room; that the accused left by the rear door; that the accused was absent from the fall-in parade; surrender at the police station; autopsy evidence of a knife wound; the Rule 23 statement (Exh. 36) proved through PW30 and corroborated by CW2
witness_credibility: Minor discrepancies did not damage the testimony; the witnesses stood firm under roving cross-examination; the evidence read in entirety was found reliable
post_offence_conduct: Left the room quietly by the rear door; was absent from the fall-in parade; surrendered at the police station around 1.30 to 2 a.m. and disclosed the stabbing to officers; gave no explanation for his presence there
trial_duration: offence: 3 April 2006; trial judgment: GCM order dated 24.2.2007; High Court: not given (writ W.P.(C) No.7266 of 2009 transferred to AFT); Supreme Court: July 09, 2015
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: Mohit Kumar Shah. Respondents (Union of India): R. Balasubramaniam, Amarendra Bal, Vikas Malhotra, B.V. Bairam Das and Anil Katiyar
investigation_status: FIR lodged by the adjutant; accused handed to military police; GCM proceedings initiated; 31 prosecution witnesses examined
procedural_irregularity: None noted

prosecution_argument: Ample material established the chain of circumstantial evidence; minor discrepancies did not matter; non-recovery of the knife was immaterial; the Rule 23 statement was corroborated; the accused's petition under s.164 admitted use of a knife in self-defence
defence_argument: The police-station confession was inadmissible; the Rule 23 statement was legally unsound; discrepancies and hearsay undermined the evidence; the knife was not recovered; others were present in the room; presence was doubtful; relied on Ravindran and Rumi Bora Dutta

high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: The victim lived in a joint family with a spouse and in-laws after marriage and had a young daughter. Within about two years of marriage, the victim was allegedly tortured by the spouse and in-laws over demands for dowry and for work performance, and was driven out of the matrimonial home. The victim repeatedly left and stayed at shelters and other places, and was returned to the matrimonial home after mediation by relatives. The victim reported demands for Rs.20,000 and filed a maintenance claim, which went unpaid, and lodged a criminal complaint alleging cruelty and dowry harassment. Several witnesses, including the victim's paternal uncle, that uncle's wife, the victim's brother, a social worker and neighbours, testified that the victim was regularly taunted and physically harassed, that the victim was seen sleeping at odd places, and that heated quarrels took place. One witness said the victim came to him for help, claiming the in-laws were trying to kill her, and had burn marks on her hands. On the day of the incident, the victim ran out of the house calling for help, and one in-law described the condition as epileptic fits. The victim was later found to have consumed poisonous tablets. The accused were in the house at the time and took the victim to hospital when the condition became critical. In a dying declaration, the victim stated the tablets were taken by mistake, and the examining doctor recorded that the victim was stable and conscious enough to give a statement. The victim died. A relative lodged a complaint with the police, after which the scene was examined in a panchanama, witness statements were recorded and the accused were arrested.

physical_harm: Death of the victim after consuming poisonous tablets; earlier beatings and burn marks branded on her hands

motive: Cruelty and dowry-related harassment by in-laws, accepted as proved by the Court; the Court did not find that this cruelty led to suicide or abetment

post_offence_conduct: Accused took the victim to hospital and the son was called once the mother-in-law realized the gravity of the situation; the Court treated this as showing no abetment

bail_history: Not stated (appellants sought enlargement on bail; no bail order described)

neutral_facts: The victim, who is blind and illiterate, lived in her family home with her brothers after her mother left. The accused, a friend of one of the victim's brothers, began visiting the house and talking with the victim. The prosecution case is that about a year before the incident the accused came to the house when the victim was alone, said he loved her and would marry her, and wanted intercourse. The victim tried to avoid it because she was blind, but she submitted after being assured of marriage and support. The accused then came to the house whenever the victim was alone and had intercourse with her. When the victim became pregnant and asked him to marry her, he stopped visiting. The incident was disclosed to the victim's father, who called a village Panchayat. There the accused admitted having had intercourse with the victim but refused to marry her and left. The prosecution's case is that, though blind, the victim could recognise the accused by voice and touch. The matter was investigated, the victim was medically examined, and a charge-sheet was filed. Prosecution witnesses included the victim, a doctor who gave the medical examination report, a radiologist whose X-ray examination estimated the victim's age at approximately 18 years, and persons who attended the Panchayat. The victim testified that she recognised the accused by his voice, that he committed intercourse with her on the pretext of marriage, and that he stopped visiting after she became pregnant. She also testified that the Panchayat was held after she disclosed the incident.
physical_harm: No physical injury recorded in the judgment; victim became pregnant as a result of the intercourse
premeditation_planning: No explicit finding of premeditation; the Supreme Court described the conduct as malicious and fraudulent, using a promise of marriage to commit rape
motive: alleged: sexual gratification obtained through a promise of marriage
key_evidence_accepted: Overall evidence considered by both courts, including the victim's testimony (PW-1), medical evidence, radiological age evidence and Panchayat evidence; the Supreme Court found no infirmity
witness_credibility: Not separately discussed; the Supreme Court said it meticulously examined the two courts' findings and held guilt proved beyond reasonable doubt
post_offence_conduct: Admitted intercourse before the Panchayat, refused to marry, and stopped visiting the house after the victim became pregnant

neutral_facts: The complainant, the wife of one of the accused, lodged a first information report alleging that her husband, his parents and his sisters harassed her in connection with dowry. She alleged that a demand of Rs 10 lakh had been made and that she would be harassed and tortured if it was not met. The couple had a daughter born in 2000 and lived together in Pune until October 2001, when the complainant left the matrimonial home. In March 2002 she attempted to enter her parents-in-law's house in Lucknow. A first investigating officer filed a closure report finding no substance in the allegations and attributing the dispute to personal differences. On the complainant's protest, further investigation was ordered, and a second officer again recommended closure, noting that the dowry demand rested only on oral statements without independent evidence. A third officer's closure report stated that the complainant had written an email claiming dowry had been demanded, and recorded that maintenance and a bank draft had been provided. Later, a fourth officer, carrying out investigation after the earlier reports, filed a charge sheet under the cruelty and dowry provisions against the husband, his parents and his sisters. The complainant's family was described in the reports as well-to-do; no independent witness to the alleged demand was identified in the earlier reports.

neutral_facts: On a Saturday afternoon in August 1995, the victim was sitting in a pandal set up for a festival, talking with a person who was the decoration contractor for the pandal. Two unknown persons entered the pandal from a road, were allegedly escorted by three other persons, and opened fire on the victim, firing many bullets into his head, chest and other parts of his body at point blank range. The firing created commotion in the pandal. The contractor tried to run, was hit by a bullet and fell down. The assailants escaped. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead on arrival. The first information report was lodged about an hour and a quarter later by an eyewitness who said he saw the incident from the first floor gallery of a building abutting the pandal. Five eyewitnesses later gave evidence, including the injured contractor. Several witnesses said they identified suspects in test identification parades, which were held roughly a year or more after the incident. The prosecution also relied on recovery of a weapon and a ballistic report. The post-mortem report recorded no injury on the victim's forehead, and the victim had been attacked from behind.

evidence_type: Eyewitness (father of victim), medical evidence, investigation witnesses
aggravating_circumstances: Armed group; large number of injuries (ten sharp-edged injuries plus lathi blows); death on the spot
trial_court_outcome: Convicted all six accused; for appellants: life imprisonment and fine of Rs.5,000 each (default 3 months SI) under s.302 r/w s.149; RI one year under s.148 r/w s.302
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction affirmed for remaining five accused (one accused acquitted by High Court for benefit of doubt)
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302 r/w s.149); IPC s.148 r/w s.302
neutral_facts: The victim's father reported that the victim had gone to a village gathering place and, when he did not return, went with two others to search for him. Near a veterinary hospital they saw the victim confronted by several men, some armed with lathis and others with swords. The men said the victim should be taught a lesson for having an evil eye on the women of the accused's family. The attackers struck the victim with sword blows to the head, hand and face and with lathi blows, and inflicted injuries on the hands, stomach, waist and chest, then fled. The victim died at the scene. The First Information Report was lodged early the next morning, about seven hours after the incident. A doctor's medical examination recorded ten sharp-edged injuries and lathi contusions and bruises on the back, right side, front chest and both arms. The victim's father was an eyewitness to the beating. He stated that he became unwell for about two hours after the victim's death, which explained the delay in lodging the report. The defence contended that the victim had tried to molest a woman and was beaten by villagers. Two named witnesses were not examined. Eleven prosecution witnesses were examined, including investigating and medical witnesses.
physical_harm: Death on the spot; ten sharp-edged injuries and multiple lathi contusions and bruises
number_of_offences: 2 charged (as reflected in convictions; separate charge framing not stated); 2 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Not found by the court; court noted the accused came armed
motive: alleged: victim had an evil eye on the women of the accused's family
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness account of the victim's father (PW5), corroborated by medical evidence of Dr. Naresh Dahiya (PW7)
witness_credibility: Father-eyewitness (PW5) found reliable and truthful; no enmity; delay in FIR satisfactorily explained; no inherent improbabilities
post_offence_conduct: Fled from the scene after the beating (as narrated in FIR; court did not separately comment)
trial_duration: offence: 4.7.2003; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 06.08.2009; Supreme Court: 25.02.2016
legal_representation: Accused: Pushpinder Singh, Kumar Kumkay, Aruneshwar Gupta, Amarjit Singh Bedi (Advs.). State of Haryana: S.U.K. Sagar, Vishwa Pal Singh, Naresh Bakshi, Rao Ranjit (Advs.)
investigation_status: FIR registered 5.7.2003; investigation completed; 11 prosecution witnesses examined; 8 defence witnesses examined
procedural_irregularity: Two named witnesses not examined; court held adverse inference depends on facts and was not warranted; no unfair trial found
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted six accused. High Court: affirmed convictions of five, acquitted one. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Ocular evidence of PW5 is supported by medical evidence; conviction proper; non-examined witnesses were won over by the accused; defence evidence considered
defence_argument: False implication; victim tried to outrage a woman's modesty and was beaten by villagers; belated FIR; adverse inference for non-examination of two named witnesses; version of a related and chance witness not acceptable (Bahal Singh)
legal_principle_applied: Reliable ocular evidence corroborated by medical evidence sustains conviction; adverse inference for non-examination depends on facts; fair trial assessed on facts of each case
precedent_relied_upon: State of U.P. v. Jaggo alias Jagdish, AIR 1971 SC 1586; Bahal Singh v. State of Haryana, AIR 1976 SC 2032
