case_title: Raju Devade v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour; former romantic partner (love affair). The victim had asked the accused to marry her.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (case initially registered under IPC s.307); Evidence Act 1872 s.32 (dying declarations)
weapon: Kerosene oil and a burning match-stick
evidence_type: Dying declarations (police-recorded oral statement treated as dying declaration; Executive Magistrate's dying declaration; a later Executive Magistrate's statement); brother's evidence (PW 4); medical evidence (autopsy, about 72 per cent burns)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction maintained
neutral_facts: The victim, an 18-year-old, was alone at home in the late evening on 4 March 1989. The victim's parents had gone out, and the victim's brother and sister had gone to watch an evening movie. At about 9.30 pm the brother returned and found the victim on fire in bushes near the house. He smothered the flames with a quilt and took the victim on a push-cart to the Rural Hospital, where no doctor was available. A waterman and a maid-servant cleaned the wounds and administered intravenous saline. A police sub-inspector arrived at once and recorded an oral statement from the victim, which bore the victim's thumb impression. In it the victim said the accused, with whom the victim had a love affair and who the victim said had made the victim pregnant, had been asked to marry the victim that evening. The victim said the accused then poured kerosene on the victim and set the victim alight with a match-stick. On the police requisition, an Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration at the hospital in the presence of two hospital employees, and the victim put a thumb impression on it. The victim was then moved to a district hospital. On 5 March 1989 another Executive Magistrate recorded a different statement, attributing the burns to a falling chimney lamp while the victim slept. That statement had no thumb impression. The victim died on 9 March 1989. A medical officer conducted the autopsy and recorded about 72 per cent burns. The defence case was that the burns were accidental.
physical_harm: Death from burn injuries (about 72 per cent burns); victim died 9 March 1989
motive: Accused's unwillingness to marry the pregnant victim after a love affair, after the victim repeatedly asked him to marry her (accepted from PW 4's evidence and the dying declarations)
key_evidence_accepted: Police-recorded oral statement and the Executive Magistrate's dying declaration (same account, implicating the accused); PW 4's evidence on the motive; autopsy and doctor's evidence that death was from burns; rejection of the chimney-accident theory
witness_credibility: Court accepted that the police sub-inspector had no reason to implicate the accused; accepted PW 4's evidence on motive; did not expressly assess PW 5's non-support of the panchnama
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 04.03.1989; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 13.04.2007; Supreme Court: 29.06.2016
legal_representation: Appellant: Kumar Parimal and Ms. Praveena Gautam (Advocates). State/respondents: Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar (Advocate).
investigation_status: FIR (case No. 63/89) registered; oral statement recorded; Executive Magistrate requisitioned; seven prosecution witnesses and one defence witness; trial completed; charge converted to s.302 IPC
procedural_irregularity: First dying declaration recorded without a doctor's certificate; Rural Hospital had no trained medical staff; third dying declaration not in question-answer form and lacked thumb impression. Court held none of these fatal.
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions Judge): convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction maintained (13.04.2007). Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: State supported the High Court and Sessions Judge: the first two dying declarations were properly relied on with cogent reasons, and there were valid reasons for rejecting the third.
defence_argument: Inconsistent dying declarations required caution; the third declaration exonerated the accused; PW 4 was an interested witness with contradictions and omissions; no independent witness; the victim could not give the accused's surname; the death was accidental (falling chimney lamp); PW 5 did not support the panchnama; the marriage claim conflicted with PW 4.
legal_principle_applied: Each dying declaration must be considered independently on its own merit and cannot be rejected because of the contents of another; the court must decide which reflects the true state of affairs. Non-question-answer form does not by itself defeat reliability. Where declarations conflict, the court looks for corroboration and may lean toward the first.
precedent_relied_upon: Bhupan v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2002 (2) SCC 556; State of Punjab v. Parveen Kumar, 2005 (9) SCC 769; Sudhakar v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2012 (7) SCC 569; Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, 2006 (13) SCC 130; Prem Kumar Gulati v. State of Haryana, 2014 (14) SCC 646; Nallam Veera Stayanarayana v. Public Prosecutor (cited in Sudhakar, as quoted in the judgment)
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: S.P.S. Rathore v. C.B.I. & Anr.
accused_occupation: Senior police officer (on deputation as Director (Vigilance & Security), BBMB)
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance: the accused was founder/president of the tennis association (HLTA) in which the victim was an enrolled member, and he called her to his office
statutory_provisions: IPC s.354 (outraging modesty of a woman); FIR also cited s.509; s.306 addition was set aside
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PW-13), corroborated by other witnesses; documentary (Memorandum); handwriting expert opinion (disputed); enquiry statements
aggravating_circumstances: Accused was a very senior police officer; victim was an unmarried minor girl (about 15)
mitigating_circumstances: Old age; health ailments; responsibility for unmarried daughter with congenital heart disease; past meritorious service; prolonged trial
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.354 IPC; sentenced to 6 months RI and fine of Rs. 1,000
high_court_outcome: Criminal revision dismissed (01.09.2010); Sessions court had enhanced sentence to 1.5 years RI on 25.05.2010
offence_finally_established: IPC s.354 (outraging modesty of a woman)
neutral_facts: The victim, a 15-year-old girl, was an enrolled member of a lawn tennis association whose office was in a garage of a house owned by the accused, who was the association's president and a senior police officer. The accused had told the victim's father that he would arrange special coaching for her at the association, and he asked that she come to his office. On the day in question, the victim and a companion went to the office at the accused's request. The accused asked the companion to fetch the coach, and she left the room. On returning, the companion saw the accused holding one of the victim's hands while his other arm was around her waist and he was pulling her towards his chest to embrace her, while the victim tried to push him back with her free hand. On seeing the companion, the accused released the victim and sat down. The companion later found the victim crying and the victim described what had happened. The two girls initially decided not to tell their parents, fearing the accused's position. On a later date the victim disclosed the incident to her parents, and a memorandum describing the incident, signed by the victim and others, was submitted to state authorities. A state official conducted an enquiry and recorded statements. The victim's signature on the memorandum was disputed, and a handwriting expert was examined; several witnesses testified that they saw the victim sign it. The victim's father testified that the accused had visited him on an earlier day, asked that the victim not be sent abroad, and asked that she come to his office; the companion's account was consistent with this. The ball picker and the coach were not examined. A formal FIR was later registered and the investigation was carried out by the CBI, which filed a charge-sheet.
physical_harm: No injury described; forcible holding and embracing of the victim while she tried to push the accused away
premeditation_planning: Not found as premeditation; the court inferred the requisite culpable intention (knowledge/intent to outrage modesty) from the sequence of events
motive: alleged: intent to molest the victim, per the victim's account; the defence alleged rivalry between tennis associations, which the court found unsupported
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-13 on the molestation; PW-15's account of the accused's earlier visit and summons, corroborating PW-13; statements of PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, PW-4 and PW-15; the Memorandum and witness identification of the victim's signature
witness_credibility: PW-13 found reliable, consistent and corroborated; withstood cross-examination; no reason to depose falsely; the court also found the other witnesses independent and not shown to be inimical
post_offence_conduct: Per the complainants' account, the accused had left for Chandigarh when they went to his office on 14.08.1990; not a court finding
bail_history: Bail allowed by the Supreme Court by order dated 11.11.2010 on special leave petition; no other bail history stated
trial_duration: offence: 12.08.1990; trial judgment: 21.12.2009; High Court: 01.09.2010; Supreme Court: 23.09.2016
legal_representation: Appellant: K.V. Viswanathan, Sr. Adv., with Ms. Priyanjali Singh, Dhananjay Ray and Mehul M. Gupta (Advs.). Respondents: Ms. Vibha Datta Makhija, Sr. Adv. (for CBI), with Rajiv Nanda, Ajay Sharma and others; Vikas Mehta for respondent no. 2
investigation_status: FIR No. 516 of 1999 registered at PS Panchkula under ss.354 and 509 IPC; investigation by CBI; CBI charge-sheet dated 16.11.2000 under s.354 IPC
procedural_irregularity: Delay in registering a case: the enquiry report recommending a case (1990) was not acted upon by the State government, and the FIR was registered only in 1999 after High Court and Supreme Court orders. Court found the 6-day delay in complaining to the SHO explained
appeal_history: Trial court (21.12.2009): convicted s.354, 6 months RI and Rs. 1,000 fine. Sessions (25.05.2010): accused's appeal dismissed; CBI and complainant's enhancement appeals allowed, sentence raised to 1.5 years RI. High Court (01.09.2010): revision dismissed. Supreme Court (23.09.2016): conviction upheld, sentence reduced to period undergone
prosecution_argument: Occurrence proved by PW-13's unimpeachable eyewitness testimony, corroborated by PW-15 and others; signatures on Memorandum proved by witnesses present, handwriting expert evidence weak; Memorandum not manipulated; non-examination of ball picker and coach draws no adverse inference; enquiry officer competent and his statements admissible under s.157; rivalry irrelevant
defence_argument: Act impossible in a garage office with people present; prosecution story false and framed by complainant side and senior officers; victim's signature forged; 'Sathi Khiladi' planted; no police complaint lodged; enquiry without jurisdiction; IAS lobby rivalry; ball picker and coach not examined; witness improvements and discrepancies
legal_principle_applied: Essential ingredients of s.354 IPC (woman assaulted; criminal force used; force used intending to outrage modesty); intention/knowledge may be inferred from circumstances; a single truthful, consistent eyewitness suffices; uncorroborated handwriting expert evidence is weak; adverse inference only where evidence is withheld; delay explained by social context
precedent_relied_upon: Vidyadharan v. State of Kerala (2004) 1 SCC 215; Tarkeshwar Sahu v. State of Bihar (2006) 8 SCC 560; Mobarik Ali Ahmed v. State of Bombay AIR 1957 SC 857; Smt. Bhagwan Kaur v. Shri Maharaj Krishan Sharma (1973) 4 SCC 46
sentencing_rationale: Given the accused's old age, physical condition and health ailments, the court held it not expedient to send him back to jail and reduced the sentence to the period already undergone as a special case
judicial_mitigating_factors: Old age and physical condition of the accused, with the other factors cited (health ailments, daughter's illness, past service, prolonged trial)
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Jamnadas v. State of M.P.
accused_occupation: Businessman (shopkeeper), per the defence version; the Court did not separately find this
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (Manoj, husband); in-laws (father-in-law Jamnadas, mother-in-law Dhanwantari)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (conviction for appellants); charged also under IPC s.201, s.304-B and s.498-A, with the latter heads ending in acquittal
weapon: Hard and sharp object (knives and scissors were sent for examination)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW1-PW5 saw body being thrown); circumstantial chain; medical (autopsy and PW15 testimony); forensic (blood stains in house, blood on nails of co-accused)
aggravating_circumstances: Brutal murder of a young bride within six months of marriage; body cut into two pieces and dumped in a park
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of murder with common intention (IPC s.302/34); life imprisonment and fine of Rs.5000 each (default one year rigorous imprisonment); other charges ended in acquittal
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld (judgment dated 23.8.2012)
offence_finally_established: Murder with common intention (IPC s.302 r/w s.34)
neutral_facts: The victim, a young woman married about six months earlier, lived in the house of the accused together with her husband, father-in-law, mother-in-law, a brother-in-law and a minor sister-in-law. On 16 September 2006 the police control room received a call that a middle-aged woman on a scooty had thrown two bundles wrapped in bed sheets into a park, with blood stains visible. Four men near the park had earlier seen a bundle with blood spots, and later saw a woman on an activa throw another packet and leave. The bundles contained the victim's body, which had been cut into two pieces. The autopsy recorded twelve ante mortem injuries, including defence wounds on the hands, and post-mortem cuts dividing the body. Death was due to shock and haemorrhage from multiple injuries. The medical evidence indicated that one person alone could not have inflicted them. Police searching the accused's house found blood stains, which were sampled. Blood was found on the fingernails of the mother-in-law but not on the nails of the husband or father-in-law. The accused's family claimed that the victim had gone to a relative's place and never returned home. No report of a homicidal death was lodged by the accused. Police registered a case against unknown persons and later filed a charge sheet against the four family members.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by shock and haemorrhage from twelve ante mortem injuries; body cut into two pieces post-mortem; defence wounds on hands
number_of_offences: 4 charged (s.302 r/w s.34, s.201, s.304-B, s.498-A); 1 finally upheld (s.302 r/w s.34)
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness evidence of PW1-PW5; autopsy report and PW15 testimony; blood stains in the house; blood on the mother-in-law's nails; the accused's false explanation under s.313 CrPC
witness_credibility: PW1-PW5 accepted as seeing the body being thrown; PW32 (minor sister-in-law) declared hostile and given no role; autopsy and PW15 evidence accepted as reliable
post_offence_conduct: No police report of the homicidal death lodged; false explanation given in statements under s.313 CrPC that the victim had gone to a relative's place and was missing
custody_duration: Not stated (arrest on 19.9.2006 only; duration not given)
trial_duration: offence: 16.09.2006; trial judgment: not given (sentence order dated 24.8.2009); High Court: 23.08.2012; Supreme Court: 29.06.2016
legal_representation: Accused: Sushil Kumar Jain, Sr. Adv. with others; State of M.P.: C.D. Singh, Sandeepan Pathak and others
investigation_status: FIR/crime registered 17.9.2006 against unknown persons; house searched and blood samples taken; charge sheet filed against four accused; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302/34 (life). High Court: appeals dismissed (23.8.2012). Supreme Court: appeals of the two accused dismissed; mother-in-law's SLP withdrawn
prosecution_argument: Section 106 Evidence Act applies because the facts are within the accused's special knowledge; the defence story is a blatant false plea completing the chain
defence_argument: Right to silence (Selvi) bars adverse inference; alibi that the accused were in the shop; no blood on appellants' nails; no specific evidence against them; Tomaso Bruno and Rajkumar cited
legal_principle_applied: Five-point circumstantial evidence test (Sharad Birdhichand Sarda); s.106 Evidence Act lighter burden for offences inside a house; false explanation as additional link; common intention
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda (1984) 4 SCC 116; Trimukh Maroti Kirkan (2006) 10 SCC 681; Kuldeep Singh (2000) 5 SCC 7; Rumi Bora Dutta (2013) 7 SCC 417; Suresh v. State of Haryana (2015) 2 SCC 227; State of W.B. v. Mir Mohammad Omar (2000) 8 SCC 382
judicial_aggravating_factors: Brutal murder of a young bride, body dismembered and disposed of; multiple injuries requiring more than one assailant
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Randhir @ Randhir Pal & Ors. v. State of Haryana
accused_caste: Brahaman (described for Randhir (A2) and Shiv Narain (A8); the judgment also describes Lakhmi Ram (A7) as Brahaman by caste)
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity: the alleged motive was an earlier murder (of Prem s/o Baru, 30.8.2001) in which the victim was allegedly involved; appellants are relatives of that deceased
statutory_provisions: IPC s.148, s.302, s.342, s.452 read with s.149; Arms Act (charged against Satpal A1 only, not the appellants)
weapon: Country-made pistol, knives and gandasas (axes), alleged as carried by the six assailants inside the shop
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony of two brothers of the deceased; complaint/FIR; site plan Ex.PC and rough sketch map
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.148, 302, 342, 452 read with s.149 (sentence not stated in judgment)
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 715 DB/2004) dismissed; conviction upheld
neutral_facts: On the morning of the occurrence, the victim was at a shop with his two brothers. According to a complaint lodged the same day, six men entered the shop carrying a country-made pistol, knives and axes. One of them fired a shot that struck the victim in the chest, and others struck the victim with axes and a knife on the face, shoulder and ear. The assailants then left the shop. The complaint further alleged that five other men stood outside the shop and in the street, preventing people from entering the shop and passersby from moving along the street. The complaint was converted into a First Information Report. Two of the victim's brothers testified as eyewitnesses. One brother described the five men as armed with lathis and pitchforks and said they stopped three named persons from approaching the shop. Those three persons were not named in the original complaint and were not recorded during the investigation. The other brother said he had gone to his field to call for help and returned with those same persons. The victim died from his injuries. A site plan marked the positions of the five men outside the shop. The prosecution case placed the motive in an earlier killing involving a relative of the victim.
physical_harm: Victim died; fatal gunshot to the chest and axe and knife injuries to face, shoulder and ear (alleged)
number_of_offences: 4 charged (ss.148, 302, 342, 452, each read with s.149); 0 finally upheld for these appellants
motive: alleged: revenge for the earlier murder of Prem s/o Baru (30.8.2001), in which the victim was allegedly involved
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness accounts (PW7, PW8) that the five appellants were not involved in the assault inside the shop and caused no injuries; FIR did not say the appellants were armed; State's concession that none of the five participated inside the shop
witness_credibility: PW7's added account of persons being stopped was an afterthought, not in the FIR, and was demolished by PW8's statement; found doubtful and not fully established
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Appellants were on bail at the Supreme Court stage; bail bonds discharged on acquittal
trial_duration: offence: 26.11.2002; trial judgment: 23.7.2004; High Court: 18.9.2009; Supreme Court: 06.10.2016
legal_representation: Accused: V. Giri, Sr. Adv., with Mrs. Kawaljit Kochar, Ms. Krishna Parkhari, Ms. Kusum Chaudhary (Advs.). State: Anish Kumar Gupta, AAG, with Chandra Shekhar Suman, R. K. Rajwanshi, Ms. Deepshikha Bharati, Dr. Monika Gusain (Advs.)
investigation_status: FIR registered on same-day complaint; site plan Ex.PC prepared; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Persons allegedly stopped from entering or passing were never examined during investigation or trial; new names added later at trial, not in FIR
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted; High Court: appeal dismissed 18.9.2009; Supreme Court: appellants acquitted (benefit of doubt); co-accused's SLP dismissed 22.2.2010
prosecution_argument: Appellants' positions were shown in the site plan Ex.PC at points J and K; the State disputed that their position was absent from the rough sketch map
defence_argument: Appellants were not alleged to have entered the shop, assaulted the deceased, been armed or caused injuries; the named persons were an afterthought; motive was enmity and family members were roped in
legal_principle_applied: Benefit of doubt: where involvement cannot be established with certainty, accused are acquitted
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds discharged

case_title: Ram Autar & Ors. v. State of U.P.
previous_criminal_record: No. The evidence showed the appellants had no infamous criminal background.
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour (accused resided next door); distant relative (descended from a common ancestor, grandfathers were real brothers); prior dispute over cattle trespass and crop damage.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged, with ss.147/149; s.148 against one accused); finally convicted under IPC s.304 Part I read with ss.147, 148, 149
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; medical (post-mortem); forensic (blood-stained earth and chemical analyst report); sketch map of scene
aggravating_circumstances: Joint lethal attack by several accused using a firearm and lathis; the prosecution alleged an exhortation by a co-accused to eliminate the deceased.
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden quarrel on the spur of the moment; deceased contributed to escalating tension; no prior criminal record; incident occurred in 1982, more than three decades earlier.
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.302, 147, 148 and 149 IPC; life imprisonment for s.302 IPC and other sentences.
high_court_outcome: Conviction under ss.147/148/149 upheld; s.302 conviction altered to s.304 Part I; sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and Rs.5000 fine (default two months simple imprisonment).
offence_finally_established: IPC s.304 Part I read with ss.147, 148 and 149
neutral_facts: The victim's cattle allegedly strayed into the fields of neighbouring residents in the morning and damaged a standing crop. The neighbours abused the victim, who drove the cattle back home. In the early afternoon, the victim was sitting in his compound with his brother, a second witness and a third witness, when a dispute broke out between him and neighbours who lived next door over the same issue. The exchanges grew heated and the neighbours, including the accused, allegedly closed in on the victim. On being urged by another neighbour to eliminate the victim, one of the accused allegedly fetched a gun and fired at the victim, who fell injured. The other accused then allegedly struck him with sticks. The victim's brother and two witnesses who tried to intervene were allegedly stopped by the gun being pointed at them. The victim died at the spot. The first information report was lodged at about 3.15 p.m. the same day. Investigation included an inquest, a sketch map of the scene, and collection of blood-stained earth, which a chemical analyst found to be human blood. Three eyewitnesses testified to the sequence of events and identified the accused. The post-mortem doctor recorded firearm wounds on the head, chest and right upper arm, multiple abrasions and contusions, and death from shock and haemorrhage. The doctor also recorded simple lacerated or incised wounds and contusions on some of the accused. The defence contended that the accused had been attacked while escorting cattle and that one of them fired in self-defence.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from firearm wounds to head, chest and right upper arm, with multiple abrasions and contusions; death due to shock and haemorrhage.
number_of_offences: 4 charged (ss.302, 147, 148, 149 IPC); 4 finally upheld (s.304 Part I, ss.147, 148, 149 IPC)
premeditation_planning: Court found no premeditation or prior concert; the incident arose on the spur of the moment.
motive: Dispute arising from the victim's cattle trespassing into the accused's fields and damaging the crop, escalating into an afternoon altercation (the Court found no common object to eliminate the deceased).
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-1, PW-2 and PW-4; post-mortem evidence of PW-5; sketch map and blood-stained earth with chemical analyst report corroborating the place of occurrence; rejection of the self-inflicted-injury defence explanation.
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses found consistent and cohesive, identified the accused and gave detailed sequential accounts; concurrent findings of the courts below accepted.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 04.04.1982; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 10.06.2016; Supreme Court: 28.11.2016
legal_representation: Accused: Dr. J. P. Dhanda, Ms. Raj Rani Dhanda, Vineet Dhanda, N. A. Usmani, Mohd. Shahid Hussain. State: Ravi Prakash Mehrotra, V. S. Shukla, Vibhu Tiwari.
investigation_status: FIR registered at about 3.15 p.m.; inquest and sketch map completed; charge-sheet filed; charge framed; trial completed.
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.302, 147, 148, 149 IPC (life for s.302). High Court: ss.147/148/149 upheld; s.302 altered to s.304 Part I; 10 years RI. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; sentence under s.304 Part I reduced to 7 years RI.
prosecution_argument: Eyewitness testimony proved the accused formed an unlawful assembly, intending to eliminate the deceased, and jointly launched a lethal attack including a firearm; conviction should not be interfered with and the sentence was lenient.
defence_argument: Accused were attacked while escorting the cattle and one fired in self-defence; no premeditation or pre-concert; the High Court sentence was unduly harsh and should be scaled down.
legal_principle_applied: Absence of premeditation, prior concert or common object to kill; sudden quarrel on the spur of the moment with loss of self-control, supporting culpable homicide (s.304 Part I) rather than murder; contribution of the deceased to escalation considered.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: Singular facts and circumstances: sudden quarrel, no premeditation, no criminal background, and more than three decades since the 1982 incident.
judicial_mitigating_factors: Spur-of-the-moment incident with loss of self-control; deceased obdurately refused to withdraw and contributed to escalation; no infamous criminal background; over three decades elapsed since 1982.
other_sentence_order: Trial Court directed to take necessary follow-up steps to ensure the appellants serve the sentence; other sentences affirmed.

case_title: Jose @ Pappachan v. The Sub-Inspector of Police, Koyilandy & Another
accused_occupation: Former police constable who resigned from state police service in about 1997 and went to Saudi Arabia; occupation at the time of the incident not stated
accused_socioeconomic_status: Defence claimed financial distress prompted his move abroad and that he remitted money for family sustenance (defence claim; the Court said the remittance records were not impeached)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34; IPC s.498A read with s.34 (cruelty charge, accused acquitted)
weapon: Alleged: nylon/plastic rope for strangulation and saree as ligature for hanging; the Court did not treat homicidal hanging as decisively established
evidence_type: Circumstantial (no eyewitness); medical (post-mortem); recovery (nylon rope and bangle pieces from under a cot); oral testimony on discovery of the body and last seen circumstances
aggravating_circumstances: Alleged by prosecution: extra-marital relationship and plot to eliminate the wife; the Court did not find these established
mitigating_circumstances: Defence evidence of an affectionate marriage, letters from the victim and remittances to the family; the Court relied on these in favour of the accused
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; sentenced to life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 10,000; acquitted under s.498A IPC; co-accused acquitted of all charges
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 668 of 2008) dismissed; conviction under s.302 IPC sustained
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim had been married for several years and had two sons. The accused had earlier left police service and worked abroad for a period, sending money home. On the evening of the incident, the accused and the victim returned from a short spiritual retreat. The victim was sent home with the accused's son while the accused went looking for labourers. Later that evening, the accused's brother suffered an epileptic attack at a tea shop, and the accused asked two men to fetch the brother's medical papers from the house. They found the front door open, a lamp lit, and no response from the victim. On entering, they found the victim hanging from a hook in the work area by a saree, with movements, and they raised an alarm. Others arrived, and the saree was cut with a knife and the body brought down. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead. The prosecution alleged that the accused smothered and strangled the victim with a plastic rope and then hanged her. A nylon rope and broken glass bangles were recovered from under a cot in the dining room, away from the hanging site. The chemical report found no blood on the rope, and the hairs on it could not be attributed to a sex. The post-mortem doctor recorded pressure abrasion on the neck, a fracture of the hyoid bone, and forehead and facial injuries, but could not say whether death was from suicidal or homicidal hanging. The accused's account was that two unknown persons pushed the accused down on the way home that evening. Three witnesses gave statements at the inquest, and were re-examined nearly four years later, shortly before the charge-sheet was submitted.
physical_harm: Death by hanging (cause disputed between suicide and homicide); swelling and dried blood on forehead and nose, facial contusions, pressure abrasion on neck, fracture of left greater horn of hyoid
number_of_offences: 2 charged (s.498A and s.302, both read with s.34); 0 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Not found by the Court; prosecution alleged the accused plotted to eliminate the victim
motive: alleged: to eliminate the wife to legalise the accused's extra-marital relationship; the Court held the plea that he deserted the family for that reason was not borne out definitively
key_evidence_accepted: Account of the three witnesses who found and brought down the body, as to its essence; unchallenged post-mortem expositions that homicidal hanging was not established; authenticity of the victim's letters and remittance records; the son's testimony (found credible)
witness_credibility: Prosecution witnesses PW1, PW6 and PW7: variations held inconsequential, but re-examination after nearly four years with no reason given was noted. Defence witness DW1 (son): courts below rejected him, but the Court found that reasoning unacceptable and held him credible. The doctor (PW20) was categorical that he could not say suicidal or homicidal
post_offence_conduct: Accused cut the saree, helped bring the body down and took the victim to hospital; his earlier conduct was somewhat unusual but the Court held it did not irrefutably establish culpability
custody_duration: Arrested on 21.9.2000; total duration in custody not stated; released forthwith if not required in any other case
trial_duration: offence: 19.9.2000 (alleged); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 21.11.2012; Supreme Court: 03.10.2016
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: Mr. Basant R., senior counsel, with Raghenth Basant, M. F. Philip and others. State/respondents: Mr. G. Prakash, with Jishnu M. L., Mrs. Priyanka Prakash, Mrs. Beena Prakash, Manu Srinath and Nishe Rajen Shonker
investigation_status: FIR lodged 20.9.2000 by PW1; investigation completed and charge-sheet filed; case committed to Sessions Court and tried; prosecution examined 25 witnesses
procedural_irregularity: Key prosecution witnesses (PW1, PW6, PW7) were re-examined about four years after the incident, shortly before charge-sheet submission, with no reason given; the Court noted this as undermining the prosecution
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment and Rs. 10,000 fine; acquitted under s.498A. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside, accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: Circumstantial evidence proves strangulation with a nylon rope and hanging with a saree; the accused's failure to rush home and arranging transport for his brother is unusual conduct; the victim was last seen with the accused; the son's evidence is partisan; motive was to remove the wife to continue an illicit relationship
defence_argument: No eyewitness and no complete chain of circumstances; the death was suicide; medical evidence did not establish homicidal hanging; the son's evidence was wrongly discarded; the witnesses were re-examined after four years; the marriage was affectionate and the accused remitted money; the 498A acquittal and co-accused's acquittal undercut the case
legal_principle_applied: Suspicion cannot replace proof; the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; for circumstantial evidence the facts must be consistent only with guilt and exclude innocence; benefit of doubt goes to the accused; no burden shifted under s.106 Evidence Act without persuasive evidence of presence
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; R. Rajendran Nair v. State of Kerala (1998) SCC (Crl.) 254; Sujit Biswas v. State of Assam (2013) 12 SCC 406; Dhan Raj @ Dhand v. State of Haryana (2014) 6 SCC 745
other_sentence_order: Direction to release the accused forthwith if not required in any other case

case_title: Gurpal Singh v. State of Punjab
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (brother of the informant, who was shot at); prior land dispute between the brothers; the deceased was a friend of the informant's son
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.307 (charged). Final conviction under IPC s.304 Part I and s.307
evidence_type: Eyewitness; medical; recovery (gun and cartridges); site plan; cartridge shells recovered from spot
aggravating_circumstances: Firing at several persons within sight, causing one death and several injuries
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden uncontrollable anger; root cause of incident and events that unfolded; twelve-year lapse since occurrence
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302 (life imprisonment, fine Rs.5,000) and s.307 (five years RI, fine Rs.2,000); sentences concurrent; co-accused acquitted
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 378-DB of 2004) dismissed; conviction and sentence affirmed
offence_finally_established: IPC s.304 Part I (culpable homicide not amounting to murder); IPC s.307 (attempt to murder)
neutral_facts: Two adjacent households, whose members were brothers, had a long-running dispute over land. On the day in question, the son of one household was working in the fields when the accused hurled abuses at him. The son returned home upset and complained to his father. The father went to the rooftop of his house and called the accused over. The accused came with his own son. When the father asked why the accused had abused his son, the accused replied angrily that he was justified and would continue. The accused then ran downstairs, fetched a double-barrelled 12-bore gun and fired at the father, striking him on the side of the head. It was alleged that the accused's son urged the firing. Hearing the commotion, the father's wife and two friends of the son rushed to the rooftop. The accused fired at them. One friend was struck in the abdomen and died, the father's wife was struck in the abdomen, and the other friend was struck in the mouth and head. The injured were taken to hospital, where the friend who was struck died. The accused and his son then fled. In the investigation, the 12-bore gun loaded with two live cartridges was recovered from the accused, and four cartridge shells were recovered from the spot. The site plan prepared by the investigating officer matched the eyewitnesses' account of the place of occurrence. The eyewitnesses included the father and the injured. The medical evidence showed injuries on the deceased and the injured compatible with the weapon used.
physical_harm: Death of one friend (Jatinder Singh); gunshot wound to the informant's head side; gunshot injuries to the informant's wife (abdomen) and to Lakhwinder (mouth and head)
number_of_offences: 2 charged; 2 finally upheld (s.302 modified to s.304 Part I; s.307 upheld)
premeditation_planning: Not found. Court held the firing followed an uncontrollable fit of anger and did not show intention to eliminate any person.
motive: alleged: lingering land dispute between the brothers, with the abuse of the informant's son as the immediate trigger
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of the informant and injured witnesses; recovery of the 12-bore gun with live cartridges from the accused; four cartridge shells recovered from the spot; site plan; medical evidence compatible with the weapon
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses, including the informant, found consistent, coherent and convincing, and trustworthy; family relationship plea rejected
post_offence_conduct: Fled the scene after the firing (as alleged in the prosecution account; not separately found by the court)
trial_duration: offence: 06.07.2002 (judgment also refers to the occurrence as being of the year 2004 at page 5); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 01.10.2008; Supreme Court: 02.12.2016
legal_representation: Appellant: Yatinder Singh, Senior Advocate (Amicus Curiae), with Arijeet Singh and Ms. Aprajita Anvita, Advocates. State: Saurabh Ajay Gupta, AAG, with Ms. Naresh Bakshi, Saurabh Singhal and Nishant Bishnoi, Advocates.
investigation_status: FIR registered on the informant's statement; investigation completed; charge-sheet laid under ss.302 and 307 IPC; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial Court: convicted under ss.302 and 307 IPC, sentenced. High Court (Criminal Appeal No. 378-DB of 2004): dismissed; conviction and sentence affirmed. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; conviction converted to ss.304 Part I and 307 IPC; sentence reduced to period undergone.
prosecution_argument: Injured eyewitness testimony, supported by medical evidence, proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt; concurrent findings of the lower courts should not be disturbed
defence_argument: Prosecution failed to prove the charge; the co-accused's acquittal undermines the case; eyewitnesses are related and partisan; in the alternative, even if accepted, no murder or attempt to murder was proved and the sentence should be reduced
legal_principle_applied: Evaluation of eyewitness reliability and medical corroboration; acquittal of co-accused does not bear on the appellant's guilt; distinction between intention to kill and knowledge of likely fatal consequences, leading to s.304 Part I
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: Singular facts, root cause of the incident, sequence of events, uncontrollable anger, lack of intention to eliminate, and the twelve-year lapse since the occurrence, taken together meet the ends of justice
judicial_mitigating_factors: Overpowered by uncontrollable anger; root cause and sequence of events; time lag of twelve years since the occurrence
other_sentence_order: Appellant to be set at liberty forthwith unless required in any other case

case_title: Harpal Singh @ Chhota v. State of Punjab
accused_occupation: Municipal Councillor (appellant Sukhmeet Singh); occupation of other appellant not stated
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance (appellant Sukhmeet Singh, a Municipal Councillor known to the victim without personal intimacy); appellant Harpal Singh unknown to the victim before the incident; otherwise Stranger
statutory_provisions: IPC s.364A, s.395, s.412, s.471, s.120B; Arms Act s.25 (Harpal Singh only)
weapon: Revolver (.32 bore, victim's licensed revolver) and country-made pistol with live cartridge; victim's cash, cell phone and car keys taken at gunpoint
evidence_type: Eyewitness (victim); father's testimony on ransom calls; recovery evidence on disclosure statements; lender testimony identifying marked currency notes; call details (held inadmissible); finger print expert evidence
confession: Disclosure statements by accused leading to recoveries, relied on as admissible under s.27 Evidence Act; no confession to police described
aggravating_circumstances: Victim held captive about two days, chained, blindfolded and drugged; repeated threats to kill victim and family; ransom demand of Rs. 5 crores later pursued
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under the charged sections (IPC ss.364A, 395, 412, 471, 120B; Arms Act s.25 for Harpal Singh); sentences ranging from one year to life imprisonment with fine, running concurrently
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
offence_finally_established: Conspiracy and abduction for ransom under IPC s.364A, s.395, s.412, s.471 and s.120B; Arms Act s.25 for Harpal Singh
neutral_facts: The victim, who was involved in real estate, was contacted by phone by a caller offering a land deal, and over several weeks the callers built his confidence in the proposal. On the morning of the planned meeting, the victim went to the site in his own car. Several men arrived in a Honda City car; one pointed a revolver at him, his cell phone, car keys and cash were taken, his face was covered, his mouth was taped and his hands were tied, and he was forced into the dicky of the Honda City car. For about two days he was held captive and moved between places. He was chained, blindfolded and given drugs, and he heard his captors address each other by nicknames. The captors repeatedly phoned his father demanding ransom, first Rs. 5 crores and later Rs. 1 crore, threatening that the victim and family would be killed if it was not paid. The father raised money from several lenders, some of whom had marked packets of notes with initials. Money was thrown from a moving train as instructed, and the victim was released. Police registered an FIR, arrested the accused and, on their disclosure statements, recovered cash, firearms, the Honda City car, and the victim's driving licence and tape from the car's dicky. Telephone call records were collected, but no certificate was obtained for them. No identification parade was held. The victim identified the accused in later testimony.
physical_harm: No specific injuries recorded; victim's hands and feet chained, mouth taped, blindfolded and drugged during captivity; no death
number_of_offences: 13 charged (11 IPC sections plus Arms Act ss.25 and 27 per charge-sheet); 5 IPC sections finally upheld for both appellants (s.364A, s.395, s.412, s.471, s.120B), plus Arms Act s.25 for Harpal Singh
financial_property_loss: Ransom of about Rs. 1 crore paid in two bags thrown from a train; Rs. 15,000 cash, licensed revolver and cell phone taken from victim
premeditation_planning: Yes: court found a conspiratorial build-up through the land-deal lure and deliberate timing of the abduction
motive: Extortion of ransom (court accepted)
key_evidence_accepted: Victim's testimony (identification and captivity account); father PW2's account of ransom calls; disclosure-based recoveries of cash, firearms, Honda City car and victim's driving licence; lender testimony and PW14's identification of marked notes
witness_credibility: Victim's evidence found truthful and substantially unshaken by cross-examination; father's evidence of ransom calls detailed; lenders' testimony not lightly ignored
post_offence_conduct: Disclosure statements led police to recovery sites (cash, firearms, Honda City car); no absconding by appellants noted
trial_duration: offence: 09.01.2008; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 21.04.2014; Supreme Court: 21.11.2016
legal_representation: For appellants: R. Basant and Subromaniam Prasad (senior advocates); for State: V. Madhukar, AAG
investigation_status: FIR registered 11.01.2008; charge-sheet laid; 27 prosecution witnesses examined; trial completed; no TIP held
procedural_irregularity: No s.65B(4) certificate for call details, which were held inadmissible; no test identification parade held; no independent witness present at Harpal Singh's disclosure statement
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced; High Court: appeals dismissed, conviction and sentence sustained; Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Evidence taken as a whole proves the abduction-for-ransom conspiracy beyond reasonable doubt; recoveries and cash linkage support guilt; no interference warranted
defence_argument: Harpal Singh's complicity unproved; call details inadmissible without s.65B certificate; no TIP; victim did not name him in earlier statements; recoveries unconnected; Sukhmeet Singh alleged political vendetta and that cash belonged to his father's land sale
legal_principle_applied: Conspiracy elements (agreement as act, intention as mens rea; unity of object suffices); s.27 Evidence Act recoveries admissible; s.65B(4) certificate mandatory for electronic records; omission to name accused at first instance not fatal
precedent_relied_upon: Relied on: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014) 10 SCC 473; Pullukuri Kotayya v. King Emperor AIR 1947 PC 67; Bodhraj @ Bodha v. State of J&K (2002) 8 SCC 45. Referred to: Ferozuddin Basheeruddin v. State of Kerala (2001) 7 SCC 596; Mir Nagvi Askari v. CBI (2009) 15 SCC 643; Mohd. Amin v. CBI (2008) 15 SCC 49
other_sentence_order: Registry directed to transmit original record to the Trial Court

case_title: Ramesh and Others v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (Ramesh is the husband); other accused are the husband's younger brother Suresh, Suresh's wife Saroj and the mother-in-law Prem; prior physical abuse and dowry-related harassment alleged
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.34; IPC s.498A
evidence_type: Dying declaration recorded by Judicial Magistrate; medical evidence (MLR, doctor's fitness endorsement, autopsy); recovery of kerosene container; oral evidence of brother (PW-4), father (PW-3, hostile)
confession: No confession relied on. Disclosure statement by Ramesh (Ex.PM) led to recovery of a kerosene container; the Court did not rely on it as a confession.
aggravating_circumstances: Prior assault (victim allegedly thrown into a well a year earlier) and repeated dowry-related beatings, as described in the dying declaration
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of all charges by the Sessions Court
high_court_outcome: Appeal against acquittal allowed; all four convicted. s.302/34 IPC: rigorous imprisonment for life and fine Rs.10,000 (1 year in default); s.498A/34 IPC: two years RI and fine Rs.2,000 (six months in default)
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302 read with s.34); cruelty by husband and relatives (IPC s.498A read with s.34)
neutral_facts: The victim, a married woman, was sleeping in the matrimonial house in the early hours of 20 September 1999 when the accused persons came to her room. According to the victim's statement, the husband and his younger brother had earlier beaten her. Two other family members held her arms, the husband sprinkled kerosene on her and the brother lit a matchstick, setting her ablaze. Neighbours extinguished the fire. The accused persons took the victim to a hospital, where she was found to have about 100% burns. The attending doctor certified that she was fit to make a statement. A judicial magistrate then recorded her statement in the presence of the medical officer, and the doctor again certified that she remained fit during the recording. The victim died within a few hours. A post-mortem found the burns to be ante mortem and sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course. Following a disclosure by the husband, police recovered an empty plastic kerosene container. The victim's father and brother, examined as witnesses, did not support the prosecution account. The brother said the husband had been with him at his house on the night of the incident and that they learned of the burns at about 4 a.m. Hospital records showed that the husband had brought the victim to hospital and had her admitted. The victim's statement also alleged years of dowry demands and repeated beatings by the in-laws.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from about 100% burn injuries; the post-mortem opinion was that the burns were ante mortem and sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.302 and s.498A, each with s.34); 2 finally upheld
motive: alleged: continued dowry demands (money, scooter, buffalo) by the husband and in-laws, as stated in the dying declaration
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration recorded by the Judicial Magistrate (PW-11) with the doctor's fitness certificates before and after recording; medical officer present during recording; hospital records showing the husband brought and admitted the victim; post-mortem evidence of ante mortem burns
witness_credibility: Magistrate PW-11 found credible; his cross-examination answer read out of context. PW-4 (brother) found to have been won over by the accused and his evidence discarded as false in view of hospital records. PW-3 (father) turned hostile; the Court attributed the hostility to a culture of compromise.
post_offence_conduct: The husband and other accused took the victim to PGIMS, Rohtak and got her admitted, per hospital records and the defence case
trial_duration: offence: 20 September 1999; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 30 May 2014; Supreme Court: 22 November 2016
legal_representation: Accused: Praveen Kr. Aggarwal, Upendra Pratap Singh, Sanjay Jain (Advocates). State: Jagdeep Kr. Sharma, Gyanendra Kr., Vishwa Pal Singh (Advocates).
investigation_status: FIR registered (No. 254, 28 September 1999); investigation completed; charge sheet under s.173(2) Cr.P.C. filed; case committed to Sessions Court
procedural_irregularity: Trial court gave no weight to the doctor's fitness certification, gave no reasons for disbelieving the Magistrate, and did not discuss whether precautions were taken in recording the dying declaration
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted. High Court: acquittal set aside and all four convicted (30 May 2014). Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld.
prosecution_argument: The incident occurred in the matrimonial house, the statement was recorded after the victim reached hospital, and the authorities were satisfied she was fit to give it, so there was no reason to discard it.
defence_argument: The acquittal should not have been disturbed since two views were possible; the husband was with PW-4 on the night, showing he was falsely implicated; a victim with 100% burns could not give a statement, so the doctor's certificate should not be believed.
legal_principle_applied: Appeal against acquittal: the appellate court may reappreciate evidence but must find the acquittal perverse or against settled law before interfering. Dying declaration: admissible and reliable if the declarant was in a fit state of mind and it was voluntary; a declaration made to a competent Magistrate with no animus stands on a higher footing; burn percentage alone is not determinative.
precedent_relied_upon: Sanwat Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1961 SCR (3) 120); Govindaraju @ Govinda v. State by Sriramapuram PS (2012) 4 SCC 722; Jai Karan v. State of N.C.T. Delhi (1999) 8 SCC 161; Rambai v. State of Chhattisgarh (2002) 8 SCC 83; Kushal Rao v. State of Bombay (1958 SCR 552); Vikas v. State of Maharashtra (2008) 2 SCC 516; Krishna Mochi v. State of Bihar (2002) 6 SCC 81; Zahira Habibullah v. State of Gujarat (2006) 3 SCC 374; Sakshi v. Union of India (2004) 5 SCC 518; State v. Sanjeev Nanda (2012) 8 SCC 450
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Kuna @ Sanjaya Behera v. State of Odisha
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (the accused persons are related as nephew and aunt; the co-accused appears to be the deceased's wife, but the appellant's exact relation to the deceased is not expressly stated)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.203 r/w s.34 (acquitted on s.203)
weapon: None mentioned for the killing (strangulation by hands); rope used to suspend the body
evidence_type: Eyewitness (sole eyewitness); medical (post-mortem); circumstantial/motive evidence; testimony of witnesses to disclosures (PW5, PW6, PW8)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100 (default 30 days RI); acquitted under s.203 IPC
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; conviction and sentence under s.302 r/w s.34 affirmed; acquittal under s.203 affirmed on State's appeal; co-accused left free to seek premature release
neutral_facts: The victim was found hanging by a rope from the roof of a shed adjacent to the victim's house, and the victim's brother reported the death to police as unnatural. The sole eyewitness, a relative of both the victim and the accused, testified that on the night of the incident he returned from a village video show with the accused, who had been drinking. He said that when the victim was returning from relieving himself, the accused struck the victim twice from behind, sat on the victim's chest and pressed the victim's neck, while the co-accused covered the victim's mouth until the victim suffocated. He stated that the accused then tied a rope around the victim's neck and suspended the body from the shed roof, and threatened him with death if he disclosed the incident. He said the events lasted about an hour and that he raised no alarm. He disclosed the incident to three other persons about three days later. The investigating officer's spot map recorded no source of light in the locality. The post-mortem examination found death was due to asphyxia from constriction of the neck and not hanging by rope. The prosecution also relied on the victim's mother's evidence that she had rebuked the accused persons for secret talks between them. The case was initially registered as unnatural death and converted to murder six days later on the basis of disclosures by the eyewitness and three others.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by asphyxia from constriction/pressing of the neck; external injuries described as abrasions
number_of_offences: 2 charged (s.302 r/w s.34 and s.203 r/w s.34); 0 finally upheld
motive: alleged: illicit/extra-marital relationship between the accused persons; not proved by the Supreme Court, which held the High Court's inference of motive flawed
key_evidence_accepted: No evidence accepted as a sufficient basis for conviction. The Court accepted the Trial Court's analysis rejecting the motive and treated PW5, PW6 and PW8 as not substantive. The medical evidence was noted as conforming to PW1's manner of narration but was not considered safe to base a conviction on.
witness_credibility: Sole eyewitness PW1 found wholly unacceptable: related to both parties, admittedly intoxicated, silent during an hour-long incident despite 150-200 nearby residents, and unexplained delay in disclosure. PW5, PW6 and PW8 derived knowledge from PW1 and were not substantive. PW3's evidence on motive was found flawed.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated (the Court noted PW1's three-day delay in disclosure, which it found unexplained; the accused were arrested after the disclosures)
trial_duration: offence: 19/20.2.2000 (intervening night); trial judgment: 26.1.2001; High Court: 07.11.2007; Supreme Court: 17.11.2017
legal_representation: Accused (appellant): Krishnan Venugopal, Sr. Adv., with Shivendra Singh, Ms. Deepanshi Ishar, Dharmendra Kumar Sinha, Advs. State (respondent): Shibashish Misra and Ms. Sylona Mohapatra, Advs.
investigation_status: Initial report of unnatural death (20.2.2000); formal FIR registered 26.2.2000 under ss.302/203/34 IPC; inquest, spot map, seizure of rope and post-mortem done; charge-sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Delay in converting the case to murder (six days) and in the eyewitness's disclosure (three days); the Court treated these as weakening the prosecution case
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted s.302 r/w s.34 (life), acquitted s.203. High Court: appeals dismissed, conviction affirmed, s.203 acquittal affirmed. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, appellant acquitted.
prosecution_argument: PW1's sole eyewitness testimony is coherent and consistent and corroborated by medical evidence; PW2 and PW12 support the discovery of the body; PW1 with PW3 proves the illicit relationship as motive; delay explained by threat; Gulam Sarbar cited that ocular evidence matching medical evidence supports conviction
defence_argument: PW1's evidence is unbelievable: intoxicated, silent for an hour, no lighting shown, presence doubtful; delay in FIR and disclosure; PW5, PW6, PW8 are hearsay; injury descriptions inconsistent; illicit relationship not proved
legal_principle_applied: A conviction may rest on a single eyewitness if reliable (quality, not number, of evidence); motive is important where the case rests on circumstantial evidence; proof standard under s.3 Evidence Act (prudent man test); benefit of reasonable doubt
precedent_relied_upon: Anil Phukhan v. State of Assam (1993) 3 SCC 282; Ramji Surya Padvi v. State of Maharashtra (1983) 3 SCC 629; State of A.P. v. Patnam Anandam (2005) 9 SCC 237; Gulam Sarbar v. State of Bihar (2014) 3 SCC 401; Mahamadkhan Nathekhan v. State of Gujarat (2014) 14 SCC 589; Lokeman Shah v. State of West Bengal AIR 2001 SC 1760; M. Narsinga Rao v. State of A.P. 2001 Crl.L.J. 515 (approved); Vijayee Singh v. State of U.P. (1990) 3 SCC 190
other_sentence_order: Appellant ordered set at liberty if not required in connection with any other case

case_title: Vijendra Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: accused's family was in enmity with the victim's uncle (PW-1) over a earlier murder case; victim was PW-1's nephew and all belonged to the same village
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34
weapon: Gun/pistol (fatal gunshot); co-accused carried ballam and lathi
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PWs 1-3), medical evidence (post-mortem), recovery of cartridges from spot, investigation documents (panchanama, sketch map)
aggravating_circumstances: Accused went armed with lathi/ballam alongside co-accused armed with gun; murder by gunshot
mitigating_circumstances: Appellant Vijendra was a juvenile (16 years 3 months 10 days) on the date of offence
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; rigorous imprisonment for life
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and life sentence affirmed
neutral_facts: The victim, a student, stayed overnight in a shed at a tube-well in a field, where electric light was available for his studies. At about 7.30 p.m., two relatives of the victim, carrying meals for him, met a third villager who wanted to irrigate his fields, and the three walked to the tube-well together. Near the tube-well they heard the sound of a gunshot from inside the shed. They hurried to the spot and saw four men come out of the shed. Two carried pistols, one carried a ballam and one carried a lathi. On seeing the witnesses, the men ran away. The witnesses found the victim lying dead in a pool of blood. They identified the men by an electric bulb on the shed roof and by torchlight. A report was prepared on the spot with the help of the victim's uncle and an FIR was lodged at the police station the same night. Investigators recorded witness statements, prepared a panchanama and sketch map, and collected blood-stained and unstained earth and two cartridges from the spot. The post-mortem found eight gunshot entry wounds on the right side of the neck and no blackening or scorching around the wound. The doctor opined that death was caused by gunshot injury. There was enmity between the accused's family and the victim's uncle's family arising from an earlier murder case in which the uncle had faced prosecution.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from gunshot injuries; eight entry wounds on right side of neck
premeditation_planning: No premeditation or pre-arranged plan found; court held common intention may be formed on the spot, and the group's intention to go to the shed was established
motive: Alleged: revenge over the earlier murder case in which the victim's uncle had faced prosecution; the court noted that PWs 1-3 deposed about this previous enmity
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PWs 1-3 (identification, weapons carried, presence at spot, victim lying in blood); cartridges recovered from spot; doctor's evidence that death was from gunshot injury
witness_credibility: PWs 1-3 found trustworthy and reliable; related witnesses not treated as interested; PW-3 not discredited as a chance witness; cross-examination elicited nothing to discredit them
post_offence_conduct: Accused fled the scene on being seen; all accused except Dhani Ram later surrendered before the Court; Dhani Ram was arrested later
custody_duration: Vijendra remained in custody beyond the maximum juvenile confinement period; exact duration not stated
trial_duration: offence: 26.03.1979; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 13.05.2009; Supreme Court: 04.01.2017
legal_representation: Accused: Mukesh K. Giri, Advocate. State: R. K. Dash, Senior Advocate, with Ms. Archana Singh and others
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial held and completed in Sessions Court
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: appeals dismissed (appeal abated for Dhani Ram, who died). Supreme Court: Mahendra's appeal dismissed; Vijendra's conviction sustained but released as juvenile
prosecution_argument: Conviction under s.34 supported; non-examination of witnesses does not affect the prosecution case; Vijendra's juvenility conceded and compensation suggested

State of Gujarat (1976) 4 SCC 640; Suresh Sakharam Nangare (2012) 9 SCC 249; Jai Bhagwan (1999) 3 SCC 102; Hari Obula Reddy (1981) 3 SCC 675; Rana Pratap (1983) 3 SCC 327; Hari Ram (2009) 13 SCC 211

case_title: Suresh Singhal v. State (Delhi Administration)
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: a dispute over the sale of property, with the deceased acting as the property dealer
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 and s.304 read with s.34
weapon: Revolver (.32 bore Smith & Wesson), fired at the deceased; the weapon used by the appellant could not be determined by ballistics
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (conflicting versions), medical evidence on range of shot, ballistic and recovery evidence
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden fight in heat of passion; shot fired in private defence after being strangled; no premeditation; no undue advantage taken
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.302 and 304 r/w s.34 for the deaths of both brothers; sentence not stated in the judgment

neutral_facts: The incident occurred in the afternoon at the office of a third person, which had been arranged as a meeting to settle a dispute over the sale of a property, through a property dealer, between the accused and one of the victims. The victim, his two brothers and a witness were already present when the accused arrived with his father and another man. Witnesses gave two versions of what followed. One witness said that as soon as the deceased got up, the accused took out a revolver and fired at him, after which the accused's father also fired at the victim's brothers. Another witness said that the three brothers and the accused were involved in a scuffle in which the deceased and his brothers tried to strangulate the accused. The accused then reached for his revolver, the deceased released him and turned to run, and the accused fired. The bullet entered below the right shoulder of the deceased from the back and did not exit. A doctor stated that the shot was fired from a distant range, with no blackening, tattooing or charring. Seven bullets were fired and no empty cartridge cases were found at the scene. evidence_type: Eyewitness (complainant's and witnesses' statements), medical (MLR and injury chart), recovery of weapons and vehicles, call detail records, CCTV footage

trial_court_outcome: Framed charges including s.307 IPC; no trial verdict or sentence stated

neutral_facts: The victim, a practising advocate, was in a car with his brother and an employee when about ten to twelve men attacked it. The assailants were reported to be armed with swords, daatars, a baseball bat and similar weapons. They smashed the front, back and driver's side windows of the car. The victim, seated inside, was struck on the head and bent away, suffering a blow to his right arm. The victim's brother opened the car door to escape, was struck on the head, and suffered finger injuries when he raised his hands to protect himself. He was then chased and injured further. Bystanders gathered after shouting, and the assailants left in their vehicles. The brother drove the injured men to hospital. Medical examination recorded that one injury to each of the two men was grievous and caused by a sharp-edged weapon, with other injuries simple. The employee sustained four simple injuries. During investigation, eleven persons were arrested and the weapons and vehicles used were recovered at their instance. Call detail records and CCTV footage from a nearby bank were analysed. The complainant alleged that the attack was carried out at the instance of a person against whom he had instituted several cases.
physical_harm: Complainant: 11 injuries including two grievous, hospitalised 12 days. Brother: three injuries, one grievous. Employee: four simple injuries. No death.
number_of_offences: 9 charged; 0 finally upheld (s.307 charge restored for trial; no conviction stands)

key_evidence_accepted: Complainant's statement and witness statements recorded under s.161 Cr.P.C. in the charge-sheet; medical report showing grievous sharp-edged injuries
witness_credibility: No credibility finding made; Court treated the statements and medical report as supporting the ingredients of s.307 at the framing stage
post_offence_conduct: Alleged in complainant's statement: assailants fled the spot in their cars with weapons after people gathered. Not a court finding.

case_title: Charandas Swami v. State of Gujarat & Anr.
accused_occupation: Temple functionaries: Accused 1 was Assistant Kothari; Accused 2 informally assisted him; Accused 3-5 were henchmen of Accused 1 and 2
accused_socioeconomic_status: Accused 1 and 2 had large unexplained cash and investments found at their residence; no other class or wealth finding stated

neutral_facts: The victim, the newly elected chairman of a temple trust board, had proposed transferring a senior temple official and his associates, who feared exposure of financial irregularities. The victim was last seen on a afternoon in a blue car with one of the accused, leaving the temple premises. Witnesses who initially said they saw the victim leave the temple later turned hostile, though the court weighed their admissible parts together with other testimony. According to the prosecution, the accused took the victim to another temple complex, where a call girl was procured through a co-accused, the victim was sedated and then strangled. Cellular records showed a co-accused in contact with the person who brought the woman. A burnt, unidentified body was later found in a ditch in a neighbouring State the next day. Following a disclosure by one of the accused, the body was identified through a key tied with cotton thread matching the victim's room lock, gold dental caps, and DNA comparison with a blood sample from the victim's sister. A post-mortem recorded death by asphyxia from strangulation and homicide. The car used was later found burnt in a garage, and an insurance claim for it was rejected after a surveyor found no accidental or mechanical cause for the burning. A disclosure by another accused led police to the crime location, where a panchnama recorded the discovery of the room and of tablets.

The accused's bank returned them on 05 April 1991 with the endorsement 'Refer to drawer', and the complainant's bank intimated the dishonour on 08 April 1991. case_title: A Kattukulangara Madhavan (Dead) thr. LRs v. Majeed & Ors.
accused_victim_relationship: Political rival (members of opposing political parties); no personal relationship described
statutory_provisions: IPC s.143, s.147, s.148, s.341, s.323, s.302 r/w s.149 (charged); finally s.326 r/w s.149 for convicted accused
weapon: Knife (MO.1) used by one accused for stab wounds; sticks and a reaper used by others
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PW3, PW4); medical evidence (post-mortem certificate and stab injury findings)
aggravating_circumstances: Death from multiple injuries, including a stab wound to the left chest cavity; attack linked to political rivalry
mitigating_circumstances: Incident occurred in 1993; other accused caused simple injuries on non-vital parts with sticks
trial_court_outcome: Convicted A1, A2, A4, A14, A15, A18 under s.302 r/w s.149 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment; acquitted A5-A13, A16, A17
high_court_outcome: Acquitted A3, A14, A15, A18 of s.302/149; altered A4's conviction to s.324/149 with 1 year; upheld acquittal of A5-A13, A16, A17

neutral_facts: On the evening of 10 March 1993, a group gathered at a road junction where an opposing political party had a presence, searching for supporters of that party travelling in passing buses. The victim was travelling in a stage carriage bus that stopped at the junction. Several persons boarded the bus, pulled the victim out, and took him to the front of the bus, where he was attacked. One of the attackers inflicted a stab wound on the back of the left side of the victim's chest and then two more stab wounds. When the victim tried to stand up, the other attackers beat him with a reaper and sticks. The victim was later found unconscious and bleeding on the road margin and was taken to hospital, where he was declared dead. The informant's statement was recorded at midnight and a first information report was registered. The autopsy recorded 26 injuries, with the cause of death given as multiple injuries to the chest. A stab wound of about 7.5 cm entered the left chest cavity and was stated to be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. An independent resident who was travelling in the same bus described the attack, and another resident who lived nearby gave evidence naming further participants. A knife was identified in evidence. The informant, another eyewitness and the bus driver turned hostile, and several attesting witnesses to the seizure also turned hostile.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple injuries (26 injuries), including stab wounds to the chest; other attackers caused simple injuries on non-vital parts

premeditation_planning: Not found as planned murder; court found the assembly gathered and searched for rival party workers in buses, and rejected the High Court's view that absence of plan to murder negated common object
motive: Political rivalry between opposing parties (accepted by the Court)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness PW3 (independent, vivid account, naming stab attackers); eyewitness PW4 (named A3, A14, A15, A18 and their involvement); post-mortem and stab injury findings; identified knife
witness_credibility: PW3 independent and believed by both lower courts; PW4 believed by Trial Court and should not have been limited to corroboration; PW5 and PW6 disbelieved by lower courts
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 10.03.1993; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 05.09.2005; Supreme Court: 30.03.2017
legal_representation: For accused: Siddharth Luthra, Sr. Adv. (with others). For complainant/appellant: Basant R., Sr. Adv. For State of Kerala: G. Prakash, Advocate
investigation_status: FIR registered (FIR No. 95 of 1993); investigation considered perfunctory by complainant, who filed a private complaint
procedural_irregularity: None noted by the Supreme Court; High Court rejected defence objection to unexplained FIR delay and delayed reaching Magistrate

High Court: acquitted A3, A14, A15, A18 of s.302/149; A4 reduced to s.324/149 (1 year); acquittals of others upheld. precedent_relied_upon: Lalji v. State of U.P. (1989) 1 SCC 437; State of UP v. Dan Singh (1997) 3 SCC 747; Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra (1973) 2 SCC 793

judicial_mitigating_factors: Lapse of time since 1993 incident; simple injuries on non-vital parts caused by sticks
