case_title: Mukesh & Anr. v. State for NCT of Delhi & Ors.
accused_occupation: Bus helper/cleaner (Akshay); bus driver (Mukesh, per the judgment's account of the bus crew)
accused_socioeconomic_status: Poor/ordinary background (stated by the accused in their affidavits; not a court finding)
previous_criminal_record: Not stated (accused claimed no criminal antecedents in affidavits; court made no finding)
accused_victim_relationship: Stranger (no prior connection between the accused and the victim is described)
weapon: Iron rods (two), inserted into the victim's private parts; bodily assault with hands and kicks
evidence_type: Dying declarations (three); eyewitness testimony of the victim's friend; medical evidence; DNA and fingerprint analysis; odontology (bite mark) report; CCTV footage; recovery of articles on disclosure statements; test identification parade
confession: None relied on; disclosure statements were used only for recoveries under s.27 Evidence Act
aggravating_circumstances: Gang rape in a moving bus; anal and oral sex forced; iron rods inserted into private parts causing intestinal perforation and sepsis; bite marks (10); victims robbed; victims thrown from bus in cold winter night; attempt to run them over; destruction of evidence
mitigating_circumstances: Poverty and rural background; aged parents and young children; conduct in custody; claimed reformation; young age (as argued); no criminal antecedents (claimed)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of all charges; death sentence under s.302 IPC; life imprisonment for s.120B and s.376(2)(g); terms of years for other offences; sentences ordered to run concurrently
high_court_outcome: Conviction affirmed; death penalty confirmed for all four
offence_finally_established: Criminal conspiracy (s.120B); murder (s.302 r/w s.120B); gang rape (s.376(2)(g) r/w Explanation 1, per Banumathi J.) and other convicted offences upheld as trial court found
neutral_facts: On the night of 16 December 2012 the victim and a male friend boarded a chartered white bus at a bus stand in South Delhi. Six occupants were inside. After the bus moved, its lights were switched off. The friend was held down and beaten with iron rods, while the victim was taken to the rear of the bus and raped repeatedly by several men in turn, including anal and oral sex. Iron rods were inserted into her vagina and rectum. Her belongings and the friend's were robbed. Both were then thrown from the moving bus, and the bus was turned to run over them. The victim suffered severe internal injuries and died of sepsis with multiple organ failure in Singapore on 29 December 2012. Investigators recovered the bus, CCTV footage of the bus near the dumping spot, and blood-stained iron rods. DNA profiles from blood on the rods and on clothing matched the victim and the friend. A bite-mark comparison linked two accused to bite marks on the victim. Articles belonging to the victim and friend were recovered on the accused's disclosure statements. The victim gave several statements in hospital, including a later one written in gestures and writing, naming the accused.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from sepsis and multi-organ failure after multiple internal injuries (intestinal perforation, rectal and vaginal tears, bite marks); friend suffered head and body injuries
number_of_offences: 12 charged (IPC ss.120B, 365, 366, 307, 376(2)(g), 377, 396, 302, 395, 397, 201, 412); 11 finally upheld (s.396 was charged but not convicted)
financial_property_loss: Cash of Rs.1,000, mobile phones, debit and credit cards, watches, rings, shoes, clothing and a purse taken from the friend and the victim
premeditation_planning: Court found a concert/agreement formed once the victim and friend boarded; no separate premeditation finding beyond this
motive: Sexual gratification and sadistic pleasure (as found by the court from the conduct)
key_evidence_accepted: Three consistent dying declarations (including one by gestures and writing); eyewitness PW-1 testimony; medical and OT records; DNA reports linking accused and blood on rods to victim; odontology report linking two accused; CCTV footage and bus identification; fingerprint report placing one accused in the bus; recovery of victim and friend's articles
witness_credibility: Friend-eyewitness found credible; injuries lent assurance of presence; omissions in FIR held not fatal; injured-witness testimony given greater weight
post_offence_conduct: Attempted to run over the victims; washed the bus; burnt clothing; divided the loot; one accused fled when police approached the bus (Ram Singh); accused led police to recoveries
custody_duration: Approximately four years (per the court's reference to custody by early 2017)
trial_duration: offence: 16 December 2012 (night of 16/17 Dec 2012); trial judgment: 10.09.2013; High Court: 13.03.2014; Supreme Court: not given
legal_representation: Accused: M.L. Sharma and A.P. Singh (with associates); amici curiae Raju Ramachandran and Sanjay R. Hegde. State: Sidharth Luthra, Sr. Adv.
investigation_status: FIR registered 17.12.2012; investigation completed; chargesheet filed 03.01.2013; supplementary chargesheet 04.02.2013; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Amicus argued s.235(2) CrPC was not effectively complied with on sentence; court itself gave the accused opportunity by affidavits. Overwriting of date on a forwarding note was found insignificant
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, death sentence. High Court: conviction affirmed, death confirmed. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Crime falls in rarest of rare category; devastation of social trust warrants death penalty; conviction on conspiracy and gang rape based on dying declarations, scientific and recovery evidence
defence_argument: Investigation flawed and biased; FIR delayed and crafted; PW-1 unreliable and improved his version; dying declarations tutored; DNA and bus evidence planted; plea of alibi; mitigating circumstances warranting commutation
legal_principle_applied: Conspiracy inferred from circumstances; gang rape joint liability (s.376(2)(g) Explanation 1); dying declaration reliability; DNA reports accepted unless absolutely dented; s.27 recoveries; rarest of rare doctrine; s.235(2) hearing
precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684; Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) 3 SCC 470; Pulukuri Kottaya v. Emperor AIR 1947 PC 67; Laxman v. State of Maharashtra (2002) 6 SCC 710; Atbir v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi (2010) 9 SCC 1; Dagdu v. State of Maharashtra (1977) 3 SCC 68; Ram Jag v. State of U.P. (1974) 4 SCC 201
sentencing_rationale: Gruesome gang rape, insertion of iron rods, and callous abandonment of victims in cold night shock the collective conscience; aggravating circumstances outweigh mitigating ones; life imprisonment held inadequate
judicial_mitigating_factors: Considered (family circumstances, young age, conduct in jail, reformation prospects) but held outweighed by aggravating factors
judicial_aggravating_factors: Brutality and diabolic manner of the crime; sadistic conduct; use of iron rods; bite marks; disposal of victims in cold night; attempt to kill by running them over; destruction of evidence; shock to collective conscience
other_sentence_order: Trial court recommended compensation under s.357A CrPC to victim's heirs; Supreme Court permitted accused affidavits on sentence and gave gender-justice recommendations (Banumathi J.)

case_title: Rajndawar v. High Court of Delhi
accused_victim_relationship: Advocate and client (professional engagement)
statutory_provisions: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 s.2(c) read with ss.10 and 15; Constitution of India Art.215
evidence_type: Complainant's unilateral allegations; Bar Council order dated 30.09.2006; affidavit filed by the accused
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Accused complied with the direction to refund the money; Disciplinary Authority completely absolved the accused
trial_court_outcome: Not applicable: the Additional Sessions Judge made a reference to the High Court and did not decide guilt; no sentence imposed at that level
high_court_outcome: Accused held guilty of criminal contempt; fine of Rs. 2,000 under the Contempt of Courts Act and suspension from practice for two months under Article 215
neutral_facts: The victim was facing trial in a separate criminal case and had engaged the accused, an advocate, to defend him in that matter. The victim later complained that the accused had charged professional fees of about Rs. 7.05 lakh, had provided no active assistance in the case, and had withdrawn from representing him. The victim sought a refund of at least Rs. 6 lakh. The accused maintained that appropriate fees had been charged for professional services actually rendered, and that the sums received were not for any other purpose. The Bar Council of Delhi examined the complaint. Its findings were that the accused had withdrawn from the engagement without sufficient cause and had not refunded the unearned part of the fee, but that the matter did not involve misconduct such as misrepresentation, deliberate receipt of money by falsification or false assurances. The victim did not seek disciplinary action and confined the prayer to a refund. The Bar Council held that a refund of Rs. 4 lakh was justified, with no interest payable.
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: 1 charged (criminal contempt under s.2(c) read with ss.10 and 15); 0 finally upheld
financial_property_loss: Complainant alleged fees of Rs. 7.05 lakh were charged; refund of Rs. 6 lakh sought; Bar Council ordered refund of Rs. 4 lakh, which the accused complied with
motive: alleged: dispute over fees charged and the accused's withdrawal from the case
key_evidence_accepted: None accepted as proof of guilt; the court relied on the Bar Council order absolving the accused of misconduct and on the non-compliance with procedural safeguards
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Complied with the direction to refund money
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 02.01.2007; Supreme Court: 26.07.2017
legal_representation: Accused (appellant): K. V. Vishwanathan, Sr. Adv., with Ashok Mathur, Ms. Nidhi Agrawal, Sameer Dawar, Dhananjay Ray, Advs. Respondent: C. K. Sucharita, Adv. (no State counsel named)
investigation_status: Complaint examined by the Bar Council of Delhi; order dated 30.09.2006
procedural_irregularity: Accused was not given an opportunity to adduce evidence or cross-examine the complainant; procedural safeguards were not followed
appeal_history: Trial court (Additional Sessions Judge): made reference to High Court, no decision on guilt. High Court: guilty of criminal contempt; fine Rs. 2,000 and two-month suspension. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Conviction rested on the complainant's unilateral version; the accused was not allowed to adduce evidence or cross-examine the complainant; appropriate fees were charged for services rendered
legal_principle_applied: In contempt proceedings the contemnor must be given an opportunity to establish innocence; conviction cannot rest solely on unproved allegations
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
judicial_mitigating_factors: Accused had complied with the refund direction; disciplinary authority completely absolved the accused; procedural safeguards not followed
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: S. Subbulaxmi v. Kumarasamy & Ors.
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (accused are the victim's brother-in-law and other close relatives, including the father-in-law's family); prior enmity over a land dispute
weapon: Iron rod and twigs (cart twigs); stabbing also alleged
evidence_type: Eyewitness (complainant and others), medical (post-mortem, wound certificates), recovery of weapons and clothing, chemical analysis, FIR and complaint documents
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted; A1 life imprisonment under s.302; A2 and A3 life imprisonment under s.34 r/w s.302; all three three years RI under s.506(11); sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction and sentence set aside; all three accused acquitted
neutral_facts: A land dispute between closely related families had strained relations after the victim cultivated land that had been leased to a relative. On the evening of 15 September 1994, the victim's wife, while cutting grass in her field, saw the three accused working in a nearby field and heard them say they would not spare the victim because he had beaten a relative. The accused left the field carrying an iron rod and twigs, and the wife followed them to a place where a relative was sitting injured on the road and the victim was standing nearby. The prosecution case was that one accused struck the victim on the head with an iron rod and stabbed him on the cheek, while the others beat his legs and hands with twigs. The accused then threw their weapons away and left. The victim was taken to a government hospital by the wife and another person and was declared dead. A post-mortem recorded six serious bleeding injuries to the scalp. Police registered a complaint from the wife and, separately, a case based on the injured relative's statement. Bloodstained iron rod, twigs and earth were seized. The accused were arrested on 17 September 1994 from a bus-stand, when blood-stained clothing worn by one accused was seized. All material objects were sent for chemical analysis.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; six serious bleeding injuries on the scalp per post-mortem; alleged stab wound to cheek and blows to legs and hands
motive: Land dispute and strained relations over leased agricultural land (the court noted the dispute existed; it did not find the accused guilty of the attack)
key_evidence_accepted: No prosecution evidence was accepted as proving guilt. Court accepted the close relationship and land dispute, and relied on the wound certificate (Ext. D1) and the thumb-impression discrepancy as undermining the prosecution account.
witness_credibility: Complainant wife (PW1) found not reliable; investigating officer's conduct (PW9, PW11) found suspicious; DW2's statement to police found doubtful; doctors' depositions contradictory
post_offence_conduct: Arrested 17 September 1994 at a bus-stand; blood-stained dhoti and shirt of A2 seized. Court found it unbelievable that A2 wore the same blood-stained clothes until arrest.
trial_duration: offence: 15 September 1994; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 22 March 2005; Supreme Court: 6 July 2017
legal_representation: Appellant (complainant): Jayant Muth Raj, Ms. Malavika J., C. K. Sasi. Respondents (accused): M. Karpaga Vinayagam, Sr. Adv., R. Nedumaran, S. Syed Mahaboob, M. Yogesh Kanna, Ms. Nithya, Ms. Maha Lakshmi, Partha Sarathi. No separate State counsel named.
investigation_status: FIR Crime No. 398/94 registered on complainant's statement; second case Crime No. 399/94 registered on injured relative's complaint and dropped after the accused in it died; trial held
procedural_irregularity: Unexplained interpolation changing time of occurrence in FIR; delayed registration of complaints (12:30 am and 2:00 am); investigation continued against a dead accused; thumb impression taken without valid reason; no doctor's certificate before recording injured relative's statement
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced. High Court: conviction set aside, all accused acquitted. Supreme Court: complainant's appeal against acquittal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Eyewitness testimony is unimpeachable; place of occurrence, weapon recovery and chemical analyst report establish guilt; injuries on DW2 explained and corroborated; time interpolation does not affect case; High Court judgment perverse
defence_argument: Two FIRs were fabricated and the investigation was partisan; deceased attacked DW2 so accused acted in self-defence; DW2 never gave a complaint; time of incident changed; prosecution story fabricated and tainted
legal_principle_applied: Prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; where the defence alleges fabricated or tampered records and two incidents, courts must test the true version; High Court had compelling and substantial reasons to interfere with conviction
precedent_relied_upon: Cited by parties: Sadhu Saran Singh v. State of UP (2016) 4 SCC 357; Hare Krishna Singh v. State of Bihar (1988) 2 SCC 95; Appabhai v. State of Gujarat (1988) Suppl. SCC 241; State of AP v. Punati Ramulu AIR 1993 SC 2644; Ashish Batham v. State of MP (2002) 7 SCC 317; Joginder Singh v. State of Haryana (2014) 11 SCC 335. Court's own reasoning applies no precedent expressly.
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: State of Haryana v. Krishan & Anr.
accused_occupation: Contractors holding the licence to run a country liquor vend
accused_victim_relationship: Vendor-customer only: the victims bought liquor from the accused's vend; one witness knew the vendor personally. No other prior connection described.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.120B; IPC s.328 r/w s.120B; Punjab Excise Act 1914 s.61(1)(a)
weapon: None mentioned (liquor adulterated with methyl alcohol, used as poison)
evidence_type: Medical (post-mortem, chemical examiner, eye examinations); eyewitness/victim and relative statements; recovery of bottles and records; documentary (licence, seized records); conduct evidence (destruction of stock)
aggravating_circumstances: Mass deaths (36) and permanent blindness (44); greed for quick money; destruction of remaining stock after the tragedy came to media attention; knowledge of methyl alcohol toxicity
trial_court_outcome: Convicted (Krishan and Som Nath) of IPC s.302 r/w s.120B: life imprisonment and Rs.10,000 fine each; s.328 r/w s.120B: 5 years and Rs.5,000 fine each; Excise Act s.61(1)(a): six months RI and Rs.1,000 fine; sentences concurrent. Other accused acquitted.
high_court_outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions of the respondents set aside (acquittal); State directed to pay Rs.2,00,000 to heirs of each of 36 deceased and Rs.1,50,000 to each person rendered blind
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 r/w s.120B (murder by conspiracy); IPC s.328 r/w s.120B; Punjab Excise Act s.61(1)(a), as restored from the trial court
neutral_facts: In December 1980, a large number of people who had bought country liquor from a single licensed liquor vend in a village and consumed it fell seriously ill. Thirty-six of them died and forty-four lost their eyesight permanently. Post-mortem examinations of the deceased found methyl alcohol in their viscera. Doctors who examined the surviving victims attributed their loss of vision to intake of methyl alcohol. Statements made by the victims immediately after they fell ill, and by close relatives of the deceased, consistently identified the vend as the source of the liquor. Police produced and sealed bottles of the liquor from victims, and after the accused were interrogated they recovered empty bottles and corks used for preparing and storing the liquor. The vend's records were seized and were found to have been forged. The prosecution case was that the accused, as contractors of the licensed vend, adulterated liquor with methyl alcohol and sold it through their agents, knowing its toxic effect. After the tragedy received media coverage, the accused's staff were said to have thrown remaining bottles into a river and canal. Some bottles recovered from the canal were not tested for methyl alcohol, and the investigation was criticised for lapses.
physical_harm: 36 deaths from methyl alcohol poisoning; 44 persons permanently lost eyesight. (Para 14 of the judgment elsewhere refers to 44 deaths, which conflicts with the other figures.)
number_of_offences: 4 charged/convicted (IPC ss.302, 328, 120B; Punjab Excise Act s.61(1)(a)); 4 finally upheld by restoration of trial court conviction
premeditation_planning: Yes: Court described the sale as planned and found the respondents knew the liquor contained methyl alcohol and its consequences
motive: Greed for quick and easy money (accepted by the Court)
key_evidence_accepted: Post-mortem and chemical examiner reports showing methyl alcohol; 25+ doctors' identical opinion on causation; contemporaneous victim and relative statements that liquor came from the respondents' vends; testimony of PW-43, PW-44, PW-81, PW-220, PW-225; recovery of sealed bottles and forged vend records; seizure of the licence record; conduct in throwing away stock
witness_credibility: Medical witnesses found credible and consistent; contemporaneous statements of victims and relatives accepted as reliable
post_offence_conduct: Respondents and staff threw remaining stock into river/canal after the tragedy became publicised; Court treated this as supporting evidence
trial_duration: offence: December 1980 (deaths between December 1 and December 4, 1980; FIR dated December 2, 1980); trial judgment: August 18, 2000; High Court: May 09, 2006; Supreme Court: June 09, 2017
legal_representation: For the State (appellant): Sanjay Kumar Tyagi, Addl. AG, Dilip Pratap, Kamal Mohan Gupta. For the respondents: R. S. Sodhi, Sr. Adv., Harpreet Singh Sandhu, Satyapal Khushal Chand Pasi, Ms. Aparna Rohatgi Jain, Mahesh Kasana, S. K. Dhingra
investigation_status: FIR registered (FIR No. 211, Police Station Kalanwali/Baragudha); investigation completed; 48 persons sent up for trial; charge framed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Lapses by police in investigating with the required vigour; no State inquiry into how spurious liquor was sold; High Court noted bottles recovered from canal were not sampled (Supreme Court treated this as a lapse but relied on other evidence)
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted Krishan and Som Nath, acquitted others. High Court: appeal allowed, convictions set aside, compensation directed. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed, High Court acquittal set aside, trial court conviction restored.
prosecution_argument: Not stated in detail; the judgment records only that the parties argued the appeal limited to the High Court's acquittal of the respondents. The State's position was that the conviction should be restored.
defence_argument: Arguments recorded are those made before the High Court: no evidence of conspiracy; no evidence of respondents' involvement or knowledge; no proof that victims consumed liquor from the respondents' vends; no evidence the methanol was supplied by or with consent of the respondents
legal_principle_applied: Contemporaneous statements admissible and relevant under s.7 Evidence Act; cause of death established by medical evidence; individual culpability can be shown without a proved s.120B conspiracy; knowledge of toxic consequences brings the case within s.300 fourthly IPC
precedent_relied_upon: Joseph Kurian Philip Jose v. State of Kerala (1994) 6 SCC 535 (referred to by trial court and High Court); Fakhruddin v. State of M.P., AIR 1967 SC 1326 (relied on by High Court, referred to)
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable: the Supreme Court gave no separate sentencing reasoning and restored the trial court's sentence
judicial_aggravating_factors: Greed for quick money; exploitation of gullible, rustic villagers; scale of deaths and blindness; destruction of evidence after the tragedy
other_sentence_order: Respondents directed to surrender to undergo the trial court's sentence. High Court's compensation directions (Rs.2,00,000 per deceased heir; Rs.1,50,000 per blinded person) not interfered with; amounts already disbursed.

case_title: Siddaling v. The State, through Kalagi Police Station
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband and wife)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.498-A; IPC s.306 (finally upheld). Trial court also convicted under IPC s.304-B r/w s.34, s.306 r/w s.34 and Dowry Prohibition Act ss.3, 4, 6; High Court acquitted on the other offences.
evidence_type: Oral testimony of family witnesses (victim's father, mother and two brothers); documentary evidence (panchayat agreement dated 22 June 2002)
confession: Admission recorded in the panchayat agreement dated 22 June 2002 that the accused was living with another woman; relied on by the Supreme Court
aggravating_circumstances: Suicide within four months of marriage; accused continued the relationship after the panchayat agreement; suicide within three months of the panchayat
trial_court_outcome: Accused convicted under IPC ss.498-A, 304-B r/w 34, 306 r/w 34 and Dowry Prohibition Act ss.3, 4, 6; sentence for the trial court not separately stated
high_court_outcome: Appeal partly allowed: conviction under ss.498-A and 306 IPC maintained; acquitted of other offences; co-accused father acquitted of all charges
offence_finally_established: IPC s.498-A (cruelty); IPC s.306 (abetment of suicide)
neutral_facts: The victim was married to the accused and, within four months of the marriage, died by jumping into a well in the village. The prosecution alleged that the victim took this step because of harassment over an alleged dowry demand and cruelty, the accused being involved in a relationship with another woman. The prosecution relied on oral evidence from the victim's father, the victim's mother and two brothers, each of whom stated that the accused had a relationship with another woman. A further document was produced: an agreement executed before a village panchayat dated 22 June 2002, in which the accused admitted living with another woman, and which was seen by the victim. Under that agreement the accused agreed to sever the relationship and to live with the victim at the victim's house. The witnesses stated that the accused continued the relationship after the agreement, which, according to the prosecution, caused mental agony to the victim. The victim died within three months of the panchayat meeting.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by suicide (jumped into a village well)
number_of_offences: 7 charged (IPC ss.498-A, 304-B, 306; Dowry Prohibition Act ss.3, 4, 6); 2 finally upheld (IPC ss.498-A and 306)
motive: Accepted by the Court: the accused's continued relationship with another woman caused psychological imbalance and mental agony to the victim, leading to suicide
key_evidence_accepted: Oral testimony of PW-1, PW-6, PW-10 and PW-22 that the accused continued his relationship with another woman; panchayat agreement dated 22 June 2002 recording the accused's admission
witness_credibility: Court relied on the consistent statements of these four family witnesses; no specific credibility analysis recorded
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 17 September 2002; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 27.06.2007; Supreme Court: 09 August 2018
legal_representation: Accused: Girish Ananthamurthy and Mrs. Vaijayanthi Girish, Advocates. State: Joseph Aristotle S. (senior counsel) and Ms. Anitha Shenoy, Advocates
investigation_status: Trial completed with conviction; FIR and charge sheet not described in the judgment
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted on multiple counts. High Court: partly allowed; conviction under ss.498-A and 306 IPC maintained, other offences acquitted. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld and sentence not reduced
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: No mens rea or active/direct act inciting suicide, so s.306 not made out (relying on Gurucharan Singh); plea for leniency in sentence
legal_principle_applied: Abetment involves a mental process of instigation or aiding; facts must be carefully assessed to decide whether cruelty induced the victim to commit suicide; the accused's illicit relationship could create psychological imbalance negating s.306 defence
precedent_relied_upon: Randhir Singh v. State of Punjab (2004) 13 SCC 129 (relied on for abetment); Gurucharan Singh v. State of Punjab (2017) 1 SCC 433 (cited by the appellant)
sentencing_rationale: Suicide within four months of marriage and within three months of the panchayat made leniency misplaced; not a fit case to reduce the sentence
judicial_aggravating_factors: Suicide within four months of marriage and within three months of the panchayat convened over the accused's relationship
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Jagjit Singh v. State of Punjab
accused_socioeconomic_status: Described as an average family, less well off than the victim's sister's family; the appellant contended he earned Rs.3000/- per month.
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B (dowry death); Evidence Act s.113-B (presumption); IPC s.406 (accused acquitted at trial); IPC s.498-A (referred to, no separate conviction recorded)
evidence_type: Oral testimony (victim's father, elder sister, PCO operator, PCO witness); medical (post-mortem opinion on time of death); circumstantial (proximity of alleged cruelty to death)
aggravating_circumstances: Alleged beatings, taunting and expulsion from home over demand for a Maruti car or Rs.2 lakh; alleged beating the night before death, if believed
mitigating_circumstances: Appellant's father contributed to the victim's continued higher education; father acquitted at trial
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.304-B; sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment; acquitted under s.406 IPC; no separate s.498-A conviction recorded
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction under s.304-B affirmed; sentence reduced from 8 years to 7 years RI
neutral_facts: The victim was married to the accused in January 1998 and died within about three years of the marriage, along with her young child, by drowning in a river. The prosecution case was that after the marriage the accused and other in-laws repeatedly beat and taunted the victim for bringing insufficient dowry and demanded a Maruti car or two lakh rupees. The victim's father testified that the victim told him about the maltreatment and that he gave the victim a fixed deposit receipt for thirty thousand rupees and spoke to the accused by phone. The victim's elder sister testified that on 16 February 2001 the victim visited her home, wept, complained of cruelty and said the accused had beaten her the previous night after she tried to stop him abusing her father; the victim's daughter was present. The same day the victim telephoned her father from a public call office, saying she had been maltreated, thrown out of the house, and would not be allowed back without a car or two lakh rupees. The operator at the call office and another witness saw the victim weeping during the call but could not hear the conversation. The post-mortem doctor estimated that about twelve days had elapsed between death and the post-mortem, placing the death on 16 or 17 February 2001. The victim's body and the child's body were found secured together with one chunni. The FIR was lodged on 17 February 2001.
physical_harm: Death of the victim and of her child by drowning in a river
number_of_offences: 3 charged (IPC s.304-B, s.406, s.498-A); 1 finally upheld (s.304-B)
motive: Alleged demand for dowry in the form of a Maruti car or Rs.2 lakh; the court treated this as cruelty in connection with dowry demand if the testimony is believed
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of the victim's father about the 16.02.2001 phone call; testimony of the elder sister about the victim's visit and the previous-night beating; PCO operator's evidence that the victim was weeping; PCO witness seeing the victim weeping; post-mortem opinion on time of death
witness_credibility: Trial court had the demeanour advantage and its view was affirmed; the Supreme Court would not reappraise credibility; the testimony was accepted 'if he is to be believed (In fact, two courts have)'
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 16.02.2001/17.02.2001 (death); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 27.02.2015; Supreme Court: 26.09.2018
legal_representation: Appellant: Dr. J.P. Dhanda, Ms. Raj Rani Dhanda, Vineet Dhanda, N.A. Usmani, K.P. Singh, Gopi Chand (Advs.); State: Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Ms. Manadakini Singh (Advs.)
investigation_status: FIR lodged 17.02.2001; post-mortem conducted 28.02.2001; charge sheet not stated; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.304-B, 8 years RI. High Court: conviction affirmed, sentence reduced to 7 years RI. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Neighbour witnesses (defence DW6 and DW8) should not be relied on; the evidence of PW1 and PW3 shows proximity in time between the alleged acts and the death
defence_argument: No cruelty or dowry demand established; the victim's death was attributed to taunts by her sister (PW3); the appellant financed the victim's education and the father-in-law financed her education

case_title: State of Himachal Pradesh v. Raj Kumar
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (brother-in-law of the deceased); prior dispute, as the accused frequently quarrelled with and assaulted her
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; s.201 read with s.34
evidence_type: Circumstantial (principal); medical autopsy evidence; testimony of son (PW-1) on the beating and the accused taking the victim away; motive evidence of PW-15
confession: Investigation recorded a confession on 27.08.2007 leading to recovery of a lady shirt; the Court did not rely on it in its reasoning
aggravating_circumstances: Accused beat the deceased and took her away; did not report her missing; no explanation for her death; prior assault on her and frequent quarrels
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC and s.201 read with s.34 IPC; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction and life sentence set aside (accused acquitted)
neutral_facts: The victim, a woman whose husband had died about eleven years earlier, lived in a joint family house with her son, her daughter and the accused, her brother-in-law. On the evening of 23 August 2007, the accused came to the house in a drunken state, abused the victim and her children and threatened to kill them. An elderly woman in the house took the son into an adjoining room and bolted it from outside, and sent the daughter to the house of the victim's maternal uncle. From the room's window, the son heard the victim crying out and saw the accused taking her towards the house of another person. Hours later, the accused opened the door and told the son that the victim had run away, and told him to tell the maternal uncle the same. Under threat from the accused and another person, the son told the uncle so. The uncle came to the house in the early hours of 24 August, and the son and uncle reported the victim missing at the police station. On 25 August the uncle received a call that the victim's body was hanging from a tree in a forest. The body was found hanging from a pine branch, a plastic rope tied around the neck. The autopsy surgeon found death due to haemorrhagic shock from a ruptured spleen, with anti-mortem injuries suggesting gagging, and found hanging was after death. The accused was taken into custody on 25 August. His confession on 27 August led to recovery of a lady's shirt from a room under construction. The sister-in-law testified that the victim had told her of ill-treatment by the accused, including an earlier beating and a compromise, and that the accused was a chronic drunkard. The accused did not report the victim missing to the police and gave no explanation for her death.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; haemorrhagic shock from ruptured spleen and anti-mortem injuries suggesting gagging; hanging was post-mortem
motive: Accepted by the Court on PW-15's evidence: frequent quarrels and assaults on the deceased, a land dispute over property Swami wanted to give to her, and greed for a fixed deposit of Rs.1,20,000 due to the deceased
key_evidence_accepted: PW-1's evidence of the beating and the accused taking the victim away; PW-15's motive evidence; PW-24's autopsy finding of homicide; the accused's failure to report her missing; his absence of explanation; the last-seen circumstance; FSL finding of no poison
witness_credibility: PW-1 (son) found cogent, natural and trustworthy; trial court's view that he was trustworthy upheld; High Court wrongly doubted him on alleged improvements. Omission of two names in his first statement explained by trauma and fear
post_offence_conduct: Told the son the victim had run away; did not report her missing to police or the maternal uncle; gave no explanation for her death
custody_duration: Not stated (taken into custody on 25.08.2007; duration not given)
trial_duration: offence: 23.08.2007; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 19.08.2014; Supreme Court: 08.01.2018
legal_representation: For the State (appellant): D. K. Thakur, AAG, Shariq Ahmed, Varinder Kumar Sharma, Advs. For the accused (respondent): Jose Abraham, Ruchir Batra, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR No.250 of 2007 registered; investigation completed; chargesheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 and s.201 r/w s.34 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal allowed, conviction set aside. Supreme Court: State's appeal allowed, conviction and life sentence affirmed
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Suggested that the deceased consumed poison and committed suicide; the Court rejected this as FSL found no poison. Submissions before the Supreme Court not recorded
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence test (cogent proof, conclusive circumstances, complete chain, consistent only with guilt); s.106 Evidence Act burden on the inmate to explain; last-seen-together circumstance
precedent_relied_upon: Trimukh Maroti Kirkan v. State of Maharashtra (2006) 10 SCC 681; State of Rajasthan v. Kashi Ram (2006) 12 SCC 254; Ganesh Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2002) 1 SCC 731; State of Maharashtra v. Suresh (2000) 1 SCC 471; State of Tamil Nadu v. Rajendran (1999) 8 SCC 679

case_title: Atul Thakur v. State of Himachal Pradesh etc.
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance (friends who had gathered for a drink party; trial court noted cordial relations and no enmity, as quoted by the Supreme Court)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.201 read with s.34 (charged); s.304 Part II (conviction finally upheld)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-11, PW-12); recovery of knife at accused's instance; nature of injuries attributed to the knife; telephone call corroborated by PW-2 (father)
aggravating_circumstances: Six knife blows on different parts of body; use of knife; victim unarmed (relied on by High Court, held not decisive by Supreme Court)
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden fight in heat of passion; no premeditation; no intention to cause death; offered water and took victim to hospital; stayed until last rites
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.304 Part II IPC; rigorous imprisonment 5 years and fine Rs.10,000, default 1 year further RI
high_court_outcome: Appeal against conviction dismissed on facts; conviction altered to s.302 IPC (life imprisonment with fine); co-accused acquittal affirmed
offence_finally_established: IPC s.304 Part II (culpable homicide not amounting to murder)
neutral_facts: On a night in late July 2011, a group of friends gathered at a house for a drink party arranged at the behest of the victim, a 22-year-old man. During the gathering the victim, while smoking, blew smoke into the face of the accused. The accused objected that the victim was junior in age and should not smoke in the accused's presence. A sudden physical fight followed, and the accused struck the victim with a knife six times on different parts of the body. Two friends who were present as eyewitnesses testified that, after realising the victim was badly injured, the accused offered water and took the victim to hospital with other friends. The accused stayed at the hospital until the victim died. The accused also telephoned the victim's father and asked him to come to the hospital. Eyewitnesses stated that doctors did not give immediate treatment but insisted on first calling the father. Police received a telephone message about a quarrel near a tunnel and an injured person being taken to hospital. The Station House Officer recorded the statement of the victim's father under section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The knife was recovered at the accused's instance, and the nature of the injuries was attributed to the same knife. Four persons who had gathered at the house were proceeded against, and three of them were later separated from the case. The victim died from the knife injuries.
offence_severity: Not stated (judgment records only the respondents' submission that s.302 carries life imprisonment)
physical_harm: Six knife wounds on different parts of the body; victim died
number_of_offences: 2 charged (s.302; s.201 read with s.34); 1 finally upheld (s.304 Part II)
premeditation_planning: No premeditation or planning found; act was sudden and in heat of passion
motive: Sudden quarrel after victim blew cigarette smoke into accused's face (accepted by the Supreme Court as the trigger; trial court had found no proven motive)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-11 and PW-12 on sudden fight and aftermath; recovery of knife at accused's instance; nature of injuries matching the knife; PW-2 corroboration of the telephone call
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses PW-11 and PW-12 found reliable and present throughout; concurrent findings on their evidence upheld; PW-2 corroborates the telephone call
post_offence_conduct: Offered water, took victim to hospital, stayed there, and telephoned the victim's father to come to the hospital
custody_duration: Per appellant's counsel: 7 years 3 months 24 days served as on 24 November 2017, including remission of 1 year 2 months 6 days
trial_duration: offence: 27.07.2011 (night of incident; telephone message 28.07.2011); trial judgment: 31.12.2014; High Court: 01.04.2016; Supreme Court: 19.01.2018
legal_representation: Accused: Aditya Dhawan, Ms. Kiran Dhawan, Chander Shekhar Ashri. State/respondents: D. K. Thakur (AAG), Shariq Ahmed, Ms. Taiba Khan, Ajay Marwah
investigation_status: FIR-equivalent statement recorded under s.154 CrPC; investigation completed; four persons sent for trial
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted s.304 Part II, 5 years RI and Rs.10,000 fine. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction altered to s.302 (life with fine). Supreme Court: partly allowed; s.304 Part II with 10 years RI and Rs.10,000 fine
prosecution_argument: Guilt supported by evidence; High Court rightly held the offence to be murder under s.302 given the repeated knife blows; appeals devoid of merit
defence_argument: Contradictions in eyewitness evidence; genesis of offence doubtful; involvement not proved beyond reasonable doubt; at best Exception 4 to s.300 (s.304 Part II); sentence already undergone
legal_principle_applied: Exception 4 to s.300 IPC: sudden fight, heat of passion, no premeditation, no undue advantage or cruel manner; number of wounds and use of knife not decisive; court must take an overall view
precedent_relied_upon: Surain Singh v. State of Punjab (2017) 5 SCC 796
sentencing_rationale: Trial court's five-year sentence gave no special reasons; nature of offence, trivial reason for anger, knife use and multiple blows do not warrant light punishment; 10 years with fine meets the ends of justice
judicial_mitigating_factors: Sudden fight; heat of passion; no premeditation; no undue advantage or cruel manner; no intention to cause death
judicial_aggravating_factors: Nature of offence; trivial reason for anger; use of knife; multiple blows
other_sentence_order: Entitled to set off under s.428 CrPC

case_title: Shajahan v. State rep. by Inspector of Police
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.457, s.395, s.396, s.302 r/w s.34 (s.396 r/w s.34 on which conviction rests)
weapon: Jute rope (used for strangulation); accused not armed per court

neutral_facts: On the intervening night of 13/14 November 2002, at about 1.30 a.m., several men allegedly planned to rob a pawn broking shop whose owner is named as the complainant. One accused allegedly held the legs of the victim, who was sleeping inside the shop, while another allegedly sat on his chest, tied a jute rope around his neck and strangled him to death. The others allegedly robbed jewellery of about 4.788 kg of gold and 5.595 kg of silver, valued at about Rs.12,00,000. The shop sweeper found the victim dead on the morning of 13 November 2002 and informed the owner, who lodged a complaint with the police. During the investigation, one accused was arrested and, on his confession, a sum of money and jewellery were recovered; further confessions led to recoveries of jewellery from several locations, including a jewellery shop and houses. On 6 February 2003, at about 1.30 a.m., two accused on a two-wheeler were intercepted by police; they ran but were caught, and jewels were recovered from a cover on the petrol tank. The shop owner and several persons who had pledged jewels identified the recovered items, and the shop's registers recorded the pledges. Two witnesses to the arrests turned hostile on identifying the accused, but the investigating officer gave evidence of the arrests and recoveries.
offence_severity: Death or imprisonment for life (as stated in the judgment); minimum not stated

key_evidence_accepted: Evidence of PW-15 and PW-17; recovery of jewels identified by PW-1 and PWs 7 to 14; pawn registers corroborating pledges; evidence of IO PW-37 on arrests and recovery of jewels from the two-wheeler
witness_credibility: PWs 21 and 22 turned hostile on identification but their evidence on the two-wheeler and recovery was read with PW-37; hostility did not affect the case. PW-1's evidence corroborated by registers
post_offence_conduct: Accused Basheer and Shajahan ran when intercepted by police and were caught

case_title: Kavita Chandrakant Lakhani v. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Prior intimate relationship (acquaintance/partner); relationship known to both families
statutory_provisions: IPC s.366 (discharge sought; not maintainable); charge sheet under ss.363, 342, 324, 354, 323, 506(II); charges framed 13.06.2012 under ss.342, 324, 323, 354
evidence_type: Eyewitness (watchman); complainant's testimony/statements (FIR and later supplementary statement)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Sessions Judge discharged accused of s.366 (also 363 and 506(ii)) on 04.07.2007; the earlier ACMM order of 03.10.2006 had refused discharge and committed the case
high_court_outcome: Criminal Writ Petition No. 3766 of 2012 dismissed on 06.05.2013 (discharge order upheld)
neutral_facts: The victim and the accused had been in a relationship known to both families. After a birthday party attended by both and their friends, the accused offered to drop the victim at a venue for dinner but instead drove the victim to the accused's home. When the victim refused to leave the car, the accused pulled the victim out forcibly, carried the victim into the house and placed the victim on a bed. According to the victim, the accused first declared love and asked why the victim was not marrying the accused, then beat the victim with the hands and a waist belt and struck the victim's head against a wall, causing injuries. A watchman witnessed the victim being pulled from the car. At about 2 a.m. the accused's father returned home and the victim was taken home. A complaint was lodged on 12 September 2003 describing these acts. A week later, on 19 September 2003, a further statement added allegations that the accused removed the victim's clothes and touched the victim inappropriately. The victim explained the omission by embarrassment. A charge sheet was filed on 30 March 2004 under sections of the Penal Code covering abduction, wrongful confinement, hurt, outraging modesty and criminal intimidation.
offence_severity: Imprisonment up to 10 years and fine (s.366); minimum not stated
physical_harm: Injuries to the victim from beating with hands and belt and head striking wall (extent not stated)
number_of_offences: 6 charged (ss.363, 342, 324, 354, 323, 506(II)) plus s.366 discharge sought; 0 finally upheld (no conviction; trial pending)

witness_credibility: Victim's later molestation account not believed: delay and unexplained omission made it an afterthought; primary allegations accepted as evident on record

case_title: Bhaskarrao & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour/acquaintance; alleged prior quarrel over Rs.50 with Accused No. 4 (alleged, not proved). PW1 said their relationship was cordial.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.147, s.148, s.452 r/w s.149, s.302 r/w s.149, s.506; SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act s.3(i)(x) (as charged/alleged)
weapon: Sticks, axe, sword and iron pipe
evidence_type: Eyewitness (related witnesses), circumstantial, medical (post-mortem), recovery of weapons and clothing, motive
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted all accused tried (accused 1 to 15) of all charges; no sentence
high_court_outcome: Reversed acquittal and convicted all appellants except accused 6 (dead). Sentences: 2 years for ss.147, 148, 452; life imprisonment and Rs.5,000 fine each for s.302 r/w 149; 6 months and Rs.500 fine for s.506 (sentences concurrent)
neutral_facts: On the evening of 19 June 1995, an altercation reportedly took place between the victim and one of the accused over a sum of money, near a grocery shop in the village; the victim was said to have slapped that accused during the scuffle. Later that evening, a group of about sixteen persons, armed with sticks, a sword, an axe and an iron pipe, allegedly entered the victim's house, dragged him out, and assaulted his hands and legs. The assault allegedly continued while he was dragged along the road and to a field, where his right palm was reportedly cut off. The victim's wife, who witnessed part of the incident, reportedly hid in a cattle shed for about two hours before informing a neighbour, and a complaint was lodged the following day. The victim's body was found in a field on 21 June 1995 without the right palm, which was found at some distance. Several witnesses, most of them related to the victim or to one another, gave statements about the number of assailants, the lighting, and the sequence of events, and their accounts differed on several points. The witness who recorded the complaint said the earlier quarrel was not mentioned in it. A panch witness for seizure of clothing did not support the prosecution, and weapons recovered at the instance of the accused were found to have no bloodstains on chemical analysis. The post-mortem doctor opined that death resulted from heavy blood loss due to amputation of the hand, with no injury to vital organs. No test identification parade was held.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from blood loss due to amputation of the right hand/palm; incised wounds to wrist, forearm and leg; no injury to vital organs
number_of_offences: 6 charged (IPC ss.147, 148, 452 r/w 149, 302 r/w 149, 506; SC/ST Act s.3(i)(x)); 0 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Not found; the Court held an intention to kill and unlawful assembly were not established
motive: alleged: earlier quarrel over Rs.50 in which the deceased slapped Accused No. 4 (not proved); alleged caste-based motive also not proved
key_evidence_accepted: Court relied on the post-mortem opinion that death was from blood loss due to amputation, the chemical report showing no bloodstains on recovered weapons, and the contradictions in the evidence. No eyewitness account was accepted as proving the amputation or the identity of assailants.
witness_credibility: Witnesses were related and their evidence was scrutinised with caution. PW1 showed many improvements and FIR omissions, and her account of the quarrel was hearsay. PWs 2, 3 and 5 contradicted each other on the number of accused. PW4 made improvements. PW11 and PW13 (panch) did not support the prosecution, PW6 could not identify his signatures, and PW7's medical evidence did not corroborate the case.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: About three years before enlargement on bail (as noted by the Court)
bail_history: Accused were enlarged on bail at some stage (date not stated); bail bonds discharged by Supreme Court order
trial_duration: offence: 19 June 1995; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 21 December 2013; Supreme Court: 26 April 2018
legal_representation: Accused: V.V.S. Rao, Sr. Adv. (for Accused No. 8); Ms. Anagha S. Desai (for Accused Nos. 2, 7, 9, 10 to 14); Dharmendra Kumar Sinha (for Accused Nos. 1, 3, 4, 5); also Varun Mathur, Tadimalla Baskar Gowtham, Subodh K. investigation_status: FIR/complaint registered (Crime No. 72 of 1995, 20 June 1995); investigation completed; charges framed against accused 1 to 15; trial held

appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted all accused (1 to 15). High Court: reversed acquittal and convicted all except accused 6 (dead). Supreme Court: appeals allowed, High Court order set aside, trial court acquittal restored.
prosecution_argument: Minor discrepancies were given undue importance; the accused in pursuance of a common object dragged the deceased and assaulted him with sticks, axe and sword; PW1 tried to save him; the High Court correctly assessed the evidence.

case_title: Chandra Bhawan Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (Tribhuwan Singh was the victim's husband); Relative (Chandra Bhawan Singh was brother-in-law and Makoi Devi mother-in-law); prior dowry harassment by in-laws
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.201; Dowry Prohibition Act s.4 (charged)
evidence_type: Circumstantial (principal basis); medical (post-mortem, gunshot injuries); recovery (gun); ballistic report; oral testimony of the victim's brother (PW-1) on dowry demand
aggravating_circumstances: Seven gunshot injuries on the victim; death inside the in-laws' house; sustained dowry demands and harassment
trial_court_outcome: Jwala Singh acquitted; Tribhuwan Singh convicted under IPC s.302/34, life imprisonment and Rs 5000 fine; Chandra Bhawan Singh convicted under IPC s.302/34 (life) and s.201 (five years RI), concurrent; Makoi Devi convicted under s.302/34 (life)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed for Tribhuwan Singh and Chandra Bhawan Singh, conviction and sentence confirmed; appeal allowed and Makoi Devi acquitted
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (both appellants); IPC s.201 (Chandra Bhawan Singh)
neutral_facts: The victim was married and lived in the household of her in-laws, which included her husband, mother-in-law and brother-in-law. Family members of the victim alleged that the in-laws harassed her for failing to bring a motorcycle as dowry. Because of the harassment she returned to her parents' house. About three days later, two of the accused brought her back to the in-laws' house. On 18.03.1984 the victim was found dead inside that house, having suffered gunshot injuries, and her body lay in the courtyard. A first information report was lodged the same day by one of the accused, stating that the victim had committed suicide by gunshot. A separate report was registered on the basis of a complaint by the village headman. The victim's brother also lodged a report that day alleging that all four accused had killed her because their dowry demand was not met. The accused were arrested on 19/20.04.1984. A gun was recovered from the house on the instance of one accused. The post-mortem examination found that the victim had been murdered. Ballistic experts examined the weapon, and statements were recorded from the accused and other witnesses. The police filed the charge sheet on 09.06.1984.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by gunshot; seven gunshot injuries on the body
number_of_offences: 3 charged (IPC s.302/34, IPC s.201, DP Act s.4); 2 convictions finally upheld for Chandra Bhawan Singh (IPC s.302/34 and s.201); 1 finally upheld for Tribhuwan Singh (IPC s.302/34)
motive: Dowry demand (motorcycle) and harassment of the victim by the in-laws, accepted by the Court
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW-1 (victim's brother) on dowry demand and harassment; medical evidence of multiple gunshot injuries; DBBL gun use; the seven circumstances relied on by the High Court; the appellants' failure to explain under s.313 CrPC; Tribhuwan Singh's unproved alibi
witness_credibility: PW-1 (victim's brother, complainant) found natural, consistent and without material contradiction; his evidence accepted. Defence suicide story found wholly unbelievable on the record
post_offence_conduct: Chandra Bhawan Singh lodged the first FIR claiming suicide, which the Court found false and intended to divert police attention; both accused gave no explanation under s.313 CrPC; Tribhuwan Singh's alibi was not proved
trial_duration: offence: 18.03.1984 (date victim found dead; date of death not separately stated); trial judgment: 07.05.1986; High Court: 20.05.2014; Supreme Court: May 01, 2018

procedural_irregularity: None noted
