case_title: Sunita v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (cousin of the victim's husband); alleged property-related dispute; the appellant had filed a suit claiming the estate of the victim's co-accused relative, as noted by the court
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302
evidence_type: Circumstantial: last-seen testimony of two witnesses; DNA identification report; extra-judicial confession; recovery of scooty on disclosure
confession: Extra-judicial confession to PW-12 (brother-in-law of the victim's father); not relied on, held untenable
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of murder (IPC s.302) by Additional Sessions Judge, Karnal; sentence not stated
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction upheld (25.03.2008)
neutral_facts: In the early morning of 4 January 2004, a fire was reported in a conical storage structure for cow dung cakes located in an open field in a village. Police found a partly burnt human body in the structure, and a post-mortem recorded it as a female body. Flesh and bone samples were sent for expert opinion. DNA testing of bones and tissue matched the blood samples of the victim's parents, establishing the identity of the deceased. The FIR was lodged in June 2004, after the DNA report. One witness, a relative of the victim's family, stated he saw the accused walking with the victim and her two young children toward a village on the afternoon of 3 January 2004, and later that night saw the accused riding a scooty with a gunny bag on its footrest. Another witness stated he saw the victim with her two children at the accused's house at about 5 pm on 3 January 2004. Both witnesses were shown to have a dispute with the accused over an estate claim. The victim's children were later found at a welfare organisation. An extra-judicial confession was allegedly made to a relative of the victim's family. Police recovered the scooty on the basis of a statement by the accused. The victim's cause of death and the place of death were not established.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; body partly burnt in a storage structure; cause and place of death not established
premeditation_planning: Not found. The court recorded the prosecution's planned-visit story but did not accept that the offence was proved to be premeditated
motive: Not identified (alleged: the accused feared the victim's father would give his property to the victim; court found the primary motive not made out)
key_evidence_accepted: DNA report establishing the death and identity of the deceased; at best, a last-seen inference, which the court held insufficient alone
witness_credibility: Court found the two last-seen witnesses inimical to the accused (estate suit), and found the height discrepancy and the implausibility of carrying a body on a scooty undermined the first witness; statements not reliable without corroboration
post_offence_conduct: Disclosure statement leading to recovery of a scooty; no blood mark or other evidence that it was used in disposing of the body
bail_history: Not stated for earlier stages; bail bonds discharged on acquittal
trial_duration: offence: 3/4 January 2004; trial judgment: 13 January 2006; High Court: 25 March 2008; Supreme Court: 30 July 2019
legal_representation: Appellant: Shaurya Sahay, Amit Kumar, Advocates. State of Haryana: Raj Singh Rana, Pankaj Kumar Singh, Sanjeet Paliwal, Avisek Minj, Vishwa Pal Singh, Advocates
investigation_status: Investigation completed; FIR lodged 15 June 2004 after DNA identification; accused tried
procedural_irregularity: No missing report lodged; FIR lodged about five months after the incident; court held the High Court erred in applying s.106 of the Evidence Act
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted (13.01.2006), sentence not stated. High Court: appeal dismissed (25.03.2008). Supreme Court: appeal allowed; accused acquitted (30.07.2019)
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Prosecution story unbelievable and contradictory; last-seen witnesses inimical due to the estate suit; height discrepancy; impossible to ride a scooty with a body on the footrest; PW-5's statement not corroborated; Satpal ruling applies
legal_principle_applied: Section 106 Evidence Act explanation arises only after the prosecution discharges its initial onus; last-seen evidence is weak alone and needs corroboration; chain of circumstances must be complete
precedent_relied_upon: Satpal v. State of Haryana (2018) 6 SCC 610; Asar Mohammad v. State of U.P. 2018 SCC OnLine SC 2179 (which applied Padala Veera Reddy v. State of A.P. 1989 Supp (2) SCC 706 and Mulakh Raj v. Satish Kumar (1992) 3 SCC 43)
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds discharged; accused to be set at liberty if not wanted in any other case

case_title: Jagdish and another v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour/acquaintance; prior enmity/dispute (animosity over love letters written by the son of the second appellant to the daughter of PW-1, and earlier police cases between the parties)
weapon: Lathis, gandasi and guns (as alleged); the two appellants were armed with lathis
evidence_type: Eyewitness (solitary, PW-1); medical evidence (post-mortem injury findings); FIR; earlier police records of enmity
aggravating_circumstances: Assault by a group of 13 persons at night; eleven injuries including a bone-deep head wound and incised wounds (as alleged in the prosecution evidence)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted three accused; sentence not stated in the judgment
high_court_outcome: Acquitted one accused (Ishwar); upheld convictions of the two appellants
neutral_facts: The victim and the accused lived in the same locality and knew each other. Animosity existed because the son of one accused had written love letters to the daughter of the prosecution's eyewitness. An earlier altercation on 20 May 1995 led to police cases against both sides, and a further incident followed on 12 June 1995. On 16 June 1995, at about 9.00 p.m., the victim was returning from the eyewitness's house when the assault is said to have taken place. The prosecution alleged that thirteen persons surrounded the victim at night and attacked with lathis, gandasi and guns. The solitary eyewitness, a woman, said she was accompanied by her husband, her sister-in-law and another person, and that all of them moved away out of fear. Later, the eyewitness and her sister-in-law went to a police station about a kilometre away at about 3.00 a.m. to lodge the first information report, while the husband and the other person remained at home. The report made generalised allegations against all thirteen accused, while the eyewitness's later account attributed specific blows to each. The victim sustained eleven injuries, including a bone-deep wound to the head with damage to the brain, lacerated wounds, and a linear incised wound caused by a sharp weapon. One accused was said to have struck the victim's head with a lathi.
physical_harm: Death of the deceased; eleven injuries including a bone-deep wound to the right parieto-occipital region with damage to the brain, lacerated wounds and a linear incision from a sharp weapon
motive: alleged: animosity arising from love letters written by the son of the second appellant to the daughter of PW-1, with earlier police cases between the parties
key_evidence_accepted: Medical evidence of eleven injuries, accepted as indicating a mob assault; the Court did not accept the eyewitness account as reliable enough to sustain conviction
witness_credibility: PW-1 (sole eyewitness) severely doubted: FIR generalised, court statement more specific, delayed police visit, enmity; PW-8 wrongly treated as eyewitness by High Court, his presence disbelieved by Trial Court
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Not stated (judgment only directs that bail bonds be discharged if the accused were on bail)
trial_duration: offence: 16.06.1995; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 18.07.2008; Supreme Court: 06.08.2009
legal_representation: Appellants: S. R. Singh, Senior Advocate, with Ram Naresh Yadav and others; State: Deepak Thukral and Dr. Monika Gusain, Advocates
investigation_status: FIR lodged at about 3.00 a.m.; of 13 accused only six charge-sheeted; two tried by juvenile court; seven summoned under s.319; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Prosecution gave up two witnesses without examining them; High Court erred in treating PW-8 as an eyewitness without discussion
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted three accused. High Court: acquitted one (Ishwar), upheld the two appellants' convictions. Supreme Court: appellants acquitted, High Court order set aside
prosecution_argument: PW-1 and PW-8 were eyewitnesses; appellant no.2 gave the fatal lathi blow to the head and appellant no.1 also assaulted the deceased; street light present; PW-1's sister-relationship with the deceased does not make her evidence doubtful (Khem Karan)
defence_argument: Acquittal of co-accused bars conviction under s.149; High Court wrongly applied s.34 without charge; no common intention; PW-1 and PW-8 were not eyewitnesses; alternatively the case falls under s.304 Part II (Dalip Singh, Sakharam Nangare)
legal_principle_applied: A conviction on a solitary eyewitness is sustainable only if reliable, cogent and convincing with surrounding circumstances; such evidence requires heightened scrutiny; false implication must be considered
precedent_relied_upon: State of Rajasthan v. Bhola Singh, AIR 1994 SC 542 (relied on); Lallu Manjhi v. State of Jharkhand, (2003) 2 SCC 401 (relied on); Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1953 SC 364, Sakharam Nangare v. State of Maharashtra, (2012) 9 SCC 249, and Khem Karan v. State of U.P., (1974) 4 SCC 603 (referred to)
other_sentence_order: Appellants to be released forthwith unless required in any other case; bail bonds discharged if on bail

case_title: Rameshwar and another v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Political or land rival / prior enmity: appellant No.1 had a rivalry with the deceased; no relationship stated for appellant No.2
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (convicted accused). FIR also registered under IPC ss.452, 147, 148, 302 r/w s.149 and MP Dakaiti Act ss.11, 13; Dakaiti Act charges failed
weapon: Farsa (axe); firearms (rifle and a .12 bore gun)
evidence_type: Eyewitness; medical (post-mortem); recovery (cartridges, plastic pieces, axe)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted both appellants under IPC s.302 r/w s.34; life imprisonment and Rs.5,000 fine each; Dakaiti Act charges failed; all other accused acquitted
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction under s.302 r/w s.34 and life sentence affirmed
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (appellant No.2 only); appeal of appellant No.1 dismissed as abated on his death
neutral_facts: On the day in question, the victim had finished a meal at home, and then stepped into the courtyard to drink water. One accused, who had a rivalry with the victim, came into the courtyard carrying an axe. Several other accused stood at the door of a neighbouring house; some were armed with rifles and one with a stick. The first accused urged the others to kill the victim and then struck the victim with the axe. The victim ran out of the courtyard, but four men at the neighbouring door caught hold of the victim. The victim's mother came to shield the victim and was injured near her ear when she tried to take the axe away. The accused armed with a rifle fired at the victim, and the shot hit the victim's back, causing the victim to fall. The first accused is said to have taken a gun from a third accused and also fired at the victim. When villagers arrived, all the accused fled the spot. The post-mortem found one circular gunshot wound of 1.5 cm on the back, in the middle of the spine, with a fractured spinal bone and five pellets recovered from the spinal cord; the doctor opined that this injury was sufficient to cause death. The investigating officer seized a .12 bore cartridge, an empty cartridge and two plastic pieces smelling of gunpowder under a seizure memo. Eyewitnesses, including the victim's wife, father and two neighbours, gave consistent accounts that the rifle-armed accused was present. The first accused was arrested and, on his statement, an axe was recovered. None of the witnesses could say which part of the victim's body was hit by the shot fired by the third accused.
physical_harm: Victim died of a gunshot wound to the back (1.5 cm circular hole, fractured spinal bone, five pellets in spinal cord); victim's mother injured near her ear
premeditation_planning: Not expressly found as premeditation; the court found a shared common intention acting in concert between the appellants
motive: alleged: prior rivalry between appellant No.1 and the deceased
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent eyewitness evidence of PWs 1, 2, 6 and 7 placing appellant No.2 at the scene armed with a rifle; post-mortem evidence of a single gunshot injury to the back; seizure of cartridges and gunpowder-smelling plastic pieces
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses PWs 1, 2, 6 and 7 found consistent on appellant No.2's presence; contradictions on who fired were held not to matter given s.34
post_offence_conduct: Fled from the spot when villagers came (prosecution narrative); appellant No.1 arrested on 23.04.1984
trial_duration: offence: 08.01.1984; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 25.06.2008; Supreme Court: 16.08.2019
legal_representation: Appellants: Nagendra Rai, Sr. Adv., with Rajesh, Advs. State: Rahul Kaushik, Ms. Bhuvneshwari Pathak, Ms. Shilpi Satyapriya Satyam, Siddharth Chakravorty (for Mrs. Swarupama Chaturvedi), Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered (Crime Case No.08/84); appellant No.1 arrested and axe recovered; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: both appellants convicted under s.302 r/w s.34, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction affirmed. Supreme Court: appeal of appellant No.2 dismissed; appeal of appellant No.1 dismissed as abated on his death
prosecution_argument: Oral eyewitness evidence and other evidence support the conviction; the High Court rightly affirmed it; PW-1's FIR statement is corroborated by PWs 6 and 7
defence_argument: No prior concert or meeting of minds shown for s.34; eyewitness depositions (PWs 1, 2, 6, 7) are inconsistent and contradictory, so the conviction is unsustainable
legal_principle_applied: Section 34 IPC requires (i) common intention among several persons to commit a particular crime and (ii) that, in furtherance of it, the crime was actually committed by them; a participant armed and acting in concert can be convicted with aid of s.34 even if another fired the fatal shot
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
other_sentence_order: Appellant No.2 directed to surrender within six weeks to serve the remaining sentence, failing which he is to be taken into custody

case_title: Mahesh Kumar v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (the accused was the victim's husband)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B; Evidence Act s.113-B (presumption, considered)
weapon: Poison (organophosphorus pesticide, as alleged by the State)
evidence_type: Oral testimony (father PW3 and brother PW4); documentary (letters Ex.PF/1, Ex.PK/1, Ex.PG/1; memorandum Ex.PE/1); investigation records
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Protracted trial of more than 15 years (noted by High Court when reducing sentence)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.304-B IPC; sentence of ten years
high_court_outcome: Conviction affirmed; sentence reduced from ten years to seven years (co-accused mother-in-law acquitted on appeal)
neutral_facts: The victim married the accused in May 1991. The victim's father alleged that after the marriage the victim was mistreated by her husband, father-in-law, mother-in-law and sister-in-law because they demanded dowry. The father said he gave dowry beyond his means, gave a gold chain about a year after the marriage, and paid cash sums on later occasions, but the in-laws continued to demand money and beat the victim. The victim had written letters about the harassment. In February 1994 the victim's father was informed that the victim had died in hospital, and he alleged that the in-laws had administered poison. A first information report was lodged the next day against four family members, who were arrested. The prosecution relied on the oral statements of the victim's father and brother and on several letters written by the victim, including one to her father about the in-laws and the gold chain, one to a brother-in-law saying her husband beat her daily, and one about her mother-in-law's dislike of her cooking. A written memorandum dated January 1992, said to record a settlement executed by the in-laws before panchayat members, was also relied upon, though no panchayat member was examined. The death was attributed to organophosphorus pesticide poisoning.
offence_severity: Minimum 7 years; maximum imprisonment for life
physical_harm: Death of the victim in hospital on or about 08.02.1994, alleged to be caused by poison
financial_property_loss: Alleged dowry payments: gold chain and Rs.1,000 and Rs.2,000 in cash; alleged further demand of Rs.5,000 (allegations only, not court findings)
motive: alleged: demand for dowry by the in-laws; the Supreme Court held this demand was not proved
key_evidence_accepted: No evidence accepted as proving a dowry demand or soon-before cruelty; the Court found the oral statements of PW3 and PW4 insufficient and the letters did not support the prosecution
witness_credibility: Statements of PW3 (father) and PW4 (brother) held insufficient without independent evidence, which was available but not examined; no express finding of dishonesty
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Not stated during trial; bail bonds discharged on acquittal
trial_duration: offence: not given (death reported 08.02.1994); trial judgment: 12.12.1995; High Court: 21.01.2009; Supreme Court: 07.08.2019
legal_representation: Appellant: D. N. Goburdhan, Adv. State: Shekhar Raj Sharma and Vishwa Pal Singh, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR lodged 09.02.1994; investigation completed by IO Assim Khan; all four accused arrested; charge sheet filed and case committed to trial court
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.304-B, ten years. High Court: conviction affirmed, sentence reduced to seven years. Supreme Court: conviction set aside and accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: The victim died within seven years of marriage by unnatural death (organophosphorus pesticide), and the evidence showed continuous cruelty over dowry
defence_argument: Essential ingredients of s.304-B not proved; letters do not relate to dowry demand; the gold chain demand was too remote to be soon before death; no evidence of demand soon before death
legal_principle_applied: Section 304-B requires proof of dowry-related cruelty or harassment soon before death, with a proximate nexus to death; the s.113-B presumption arises only after this initial proof
precedent_relied_upon: Satvir Singh v. State of Punjab (2001) 8 SCC 633; Hira Lal v. State (Govt. of NCT), Delhi (2003) 8 SCC 80; Sakatar Singh v. State of Haryana (2004) 11 SCC 291; Major Singh v. State of Punjab (2015) 5 SCC 201
other_sentence_order: Conviction set aside; accused set at liberty unless involved in another case; bail bonds discharged

case_title: Fainul Khan v. State of Jharkhand and Another
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity: raised by the defence as ground for false implication; the court held the enmity irrelevant
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured witnesses P.W.7 and P.W.8); injury reports; testimony of the officer-in-charge (P.W.11)
aggravating_circumstances: Unlawful assembly; some members armed with spears; deceased surrounded to prevent escape
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302/149 (life imprisonment), s.323/149 and s.147 (varied terms), sentences concurrent
high_court_outcome: Not stated (High Court of Jharkhand judgment dated 28.05.2009; outcome not described in this judgment)
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 read with s.149 (murder); IPC s.323 read with s.149 (hurt); IPC s.147
neutral_facts: On the evening of 1 November 1983, a group of men armed with spears and lathis surrounded the victim and another man who were walking together. The accused surrounded both men, and one accused struck the victim on the head with a lathi. The victim fell to the ground, and when he tried to stand up, he was struck by two accused with spears. The victim later died. The second man, an injured eyewitness, was struck on the face, head and hand with a lathi by one accused. A resident of the locality, also an injured eyewitness, was struck on the head by one accused and on the thigh by another during the same incident. A further witness said he reached the scene only after hearing the commotion, when the victim was already lying on the ground. Both injured witnesses said they were taken to hospital with the victim, where their injuries were examined. One injured witness showed scars from his injuries while testifying. The officer-in-charge of the police station testified that he requested the injury reports of the witnesses, which were then made available to him before he filed the charge sheet. The first information report was lodged by the second injured witness at the hospital.
physical_harm: Death of the victim after assault with lathis and spears; injuries to P.W.7 (head, right hand, thigh) and P.W.8 (face, head, hand)
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Ocular evidence of injured eyewitnesses P.W.7 and P.W.8; evidence of P.W.11 (officer-in-charge) on injury reports and charge sheet; scars noticed by the trial judge
witness_credibility: Injured eyewitnesses P.W.7 and P.W.8 found credible; no lacunae in P.W.8's evidence; P.W.6 not accepted as an eyewitness; P.W.11 not discredited in cross-examination
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Appellants were on bail; bail bonds cancelled and they were directed to surrender to serve the remaining sentence
trial_duration: offence: 01.11.1983; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 28.05.2009; Supreme Court: 04.10.2019
legal_representation: Accused: Sidharth Luthra, Sr. Adv. with others. State: Anil K. Jha with others
investigation_status: FIR lodged by P.W.8 at hospital; injury reports obtained on request; charge sheet filed; trial held
procedural_irregularity: Section 147 charge framed against only four of the accused (held inadvertent, no prejudice); s.313 questions alleged to be casual and perfunctory (held no prejudice)
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.302/149, 323/149, 147 IPC. High Court: judgment dated 28.05.2009 (outcome not stated). Supreme Court: appeals dismissed

case_title: Imrat Singh & Ors. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute (court noted enmity between the two sides; victim had a lot of enemies)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.148; IPC s.302 r/w s.149
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PW-10, PW-11); last-seen testimony (PW-6, PW-7); site plan; police investigation record
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.148 and 302 r/w s.149 IPC; life imprisonment for murder, two years RI under s.148, fine Rs.25,000 (default three years RI)

neutral_facts: On 25 May 1994 at about 2 pm, the victim was allegedly beaten with lathis by a group of five accused at a place called Brar Khora, near a path between two villages. Two villagers walking nearby stated that they saw the beating. They said they asked the accused why the victim was being beaten, were threatened, and ran away. They went to their village and later to the police station, where a report was lodged after police visited the spot. Another witness stated that the victim had been called away by one of the accused with an offer of liquor, and a different witness gave a different invitation, offering mutton. A further witness said he was told that one accused and another person had beaten the victim. The victim's body was later found in a jungle or river area, and the witnesses differed on who first reported the death in the village. A site plan was prepared, and the witnesses named as having signed it denied doing so. The victim was reported to have had several enemies, and there was enmity between the two sides. Several persons who were named in the statements, including police personnel and villagers, were not examined as witnesses. The defence disputed the reliability of the eyewitness and last-seen accounts.
physical_harm: Death of the victim (Gajraj Singh) from beating with lathis, as alleged by the prosecution
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: None relied on for conviction; Court found eyewitness (PW-10, PW-11) and last-seen (PW-6, PW-7) evidence doubtful due to contradictions
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses PW-10 and PW-11 found unreliable: prepared witnesses, contradictory on attending circumstances, improving statements over time; PW-15 and PW-10 versions totally different
post_offence_conduct: Not stated

case_title: Ramji Singh & Ors. v. State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Political rival (village Pradhan election); prior dispute over cultivation of a plot; relations strained, belonging to different groups. No family relationship between the accused and the victim is described.
statutory_provisions: IPC ss.147, 148, 149, 302, 449 (charged); s.452 IPC also recorded in the FIR
weapon: Firearms (two guns, three shots each fired by two accused); axes; pitchfork (kanta); lathi
evidence_type: Eyewitness (two eyewitnesses); medical (post-mortem); documentary (written complaint/FIR); scribe witness; site plan; ballistic/seized guns (not proved)
aggravating_circumstances: Armed group of six attacking in broad daylight; two accused used guns; threats to bystanders to prevent intervention.
trial_court_outcome: All six accused acquitted.
high_court_outcome: Appeal by the State allowed; trial court acquittal set aside; accused Ramji Singh (A-2), Laxman Singh (A-4) and Lala Ram (A-5) convicted under ss.147, 148, 302/149 IPC and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life and fine of Rs.10,000 each; appeal against A-1, A-3, A-6 abated on their death.
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 r/w s.149 (murder by unlawful assembly), with s.147 and s.148 IPC
neutral_facts: The prosecution case is that the victim had a dispute with one of the accused over the cultivation of a plot of land, which led to an exchange of abuses and threats that the victim would be killed. Later the same day, around noon, the victim sat on a cot in the courtyard of another villager's house while the victim's uncle went to get an agricultural implement repaired. The uncle heard a noise and returned to find six accused standing outside the house, armed with a lathi, two guns, two axes and a pitchfork. One accused allegedly directed that the victim be killed. Two accused fired three shots each from the entrance of the house, two others struck the victim with axes, and another struck with a pitchfork. The victim died on the spot. Other villagers arrived, and the accused threatened them before running away. The uncle dictated a written complaint immediately afterwards. It was scribed by a teacher who reached the spot around 12:45 pm, and was taken to the police station and registered as a first information report. The post-mortem doctor recorded six firearm entry wounds, several incised wounds and firearm exit wounds, and opined that death occurred between 12 and 12:30 pm. The investigation included a site plan and the seizure of guns. The ballistic report was not proved. Two eyewitnesses gave evidence supporting the prosecution account.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from six firearm entry wounds, axe and pitchfork injuries (incised wounds) and firearm exit wounds.
number_of_offences: 5 charged (ss.147, 148, 149, 302, 449 IPC); 3 finally upheld for the appellants (ss.147, 148, 302/149 IPC)
motive: alleged: dispute over cultivation of a plot of land and rivalry arising from village Pradhan election; the court assumed enmity existed but did not decide motive.
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of two eyewitnesses (PW-1 and PW-2), corroborated by the scribe (PW-4); the written complaint recorded immediately after the occurrence and the FIR based on it; medical evidence matching firearm and sharp-edged injuries and time of death.
witness_credibility: The eyewitnesses' statements were almost identical with no major contradictions; PW-2 may have slightly improved his version but the core remained intact; enmity and interest did not make them unreliable; PW-4 found to be independent and not discredited.
post_offence_conduct: Threatened bystanders not to interfere and fled the scene.
trial_duration: offence: 17.06.1982; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 30.04.2014; Supreme Court: 11.12.2019
legal_representation: Appellants: Rajiv Dutta and Sidharth Luthra, Sr. Advs., with others. State of UP: Ms. Sansriti Pathak and Krishnanand Pandeya, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered (Crime No.66/82); investigation completed; charge sheet filed against all six accused; trial completed in Sessions Court.
procedural_irregularity: Delay in compliance with s.157 CrPC not proved and noted as not fatal; ballistic report not proved and bullets not all sent for examination (court held this did not discredit eyewitnesses).
appeal_history: Trial court: all accused acquitted. High Court: acquittal set aside; three appellants convicted under ss.147, 148, 302/149 IPC, life imprisonment. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Trial court's view was perverse; medical and ocular evidence consistent; FIR time correctly recorded; all material witnesses examined.
defence_argument: Medical evidence renders eyewitness presence doubtful; contradictions in witnesses; witnesses related to deceased and interested; FIR ante-timed; material witnesses not examined; ballistic report not proved.
legal_principle_applied: Enmity between parties is not by itself sufficient to discredit eyewitnesses; each case decided on its own evidence; site plan is not to scale and cannot fix exact directions; ocular evidence corroborated by medical evidence prevails over investigative lapses.
precedent_relied_upon: Meharaj Singh (L/NK) v. State of U.P., (1994) 5 SCC 188 (cited by appellants; held inapplicable)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Attack by six heavily armed persons, two with guns, in broad daylight; threats to bystanders intimidating witnesses.
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab
accused_occupation: Servant (accused Darshan Singh, employed at the house of accused Avtar Singh); other accused's occupation not stated
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (mother of accused Avtar Singh; accused Swaran Kaur is his wife and accused Jagmohan Singh his son); Darshan Singh was a servant in Avtar Singh's house; prior dispute over unpaid lease money for inherited land
statutory_provisions: Penal Code 1860 s.302 (other sections not stated)
weapon: Dupatta (ligature around neck); folding iron chair (kursi) used as a blow; acid poured on the face; aluminium phosphide insecticide detected in the body
evidence_type: Extra-judicial confession; medical (postmortem and chemical examination); recovery (acid bottle, folding chair, motorcycle); circumstantial (motive, conduct after death, last-seen sighting); identification of body by clothing
confession: Extra-judicial confession made before PW-16 by accused Swaran Kaur, Jagmohan Singh and Darshan Singh, describing the dupatta, chair blow and acid; relied on by the trial court and the High Court, and the Supreme Court relied on it for Darshan Singh, supported by medical evidence and recovery of the chair
aggravating_circumstances: Face disfigured by acid poured with intention to avoid identification; accused not available in the village after the death and did not attend cremation or prayer ceremony
trial_court_outcome: Convicted Jagmohan Singh, Swaran Kaur and Darshan Singh; acquitted Avtar Singh; sentence not stated
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; conviction upheld (Criminal Appeal No. 612-DB of 2007, judgment dated 19.02.2009)
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302) as charged; accused Swaran Kaur died during the appeal
neutral_facts: A decomposed body was found inside a jute bag in a field beside a bypass road, with maggots around it. The face had been disfigured by acid, so the body was identified only from its clothing by two sons-in-law of the victim. A dupatta was wrapped around the neck with two turns. The postmortem found a fracture of the hyoid bone, an irregular wound over the left chest, and fractures of the sixth and seventh ribs. The chemical examination detected aluminium phosphide insecticide in intestinal samples and phosphine in decomposed organs. A small telephone diary was found in the undershirt pocket of the body. A witness reported seeing a man and a woman on a TVS motorcycle at about 5:30 am on 22 March 2005 carrying a gunny bag; he could not identify either person. The victim had inherited land from a deceased son and leased part of it to the accused for a yearly rent, but the lease money was not paid, and the victim complained of this to a village sarpanch. After the body was identified, police could not trace the accused in the village. Later, a witness stated that one accused had confessed to him in detail, describing a dupatta, a blow with a chair and acid poured on the face. A bottle of acid was recovered from a house on the basis of a disclosure, a folding iron chair was recovered from another house, and a motorcycle was recovered.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; face disfigured by acid; fracture of hyoid bone; irregular wound over left chest; fractures of 6th and 7th ribs; aluminium phosphide poisoning noted in postmortem opinion
number_of_offences: 1 charged (murder, IPC s.302 per headnote; separate charges not listed); 1 finally upheld
financial_property_loss: Unpaid lease money for the victim's land (lease at Rs.4,000 per bigha; only Rs.1,000 paid)
premeditation_planning: No premeditation finding stated; court found acid was poured with intention to avoid identification of the body
motive: Dispute over lease money for land the victim inherited from her deceased son; accused Avtar Singh had not paid the lease, which the court accepted
key_evidence_accepted: Extra-judicial confession before PW-16 (for Darshan Singh) corroborated by postmortem findings and recovery of the folding chair; postmortem findings of hyoid fracture and two dupatta turns; recovery of acid bottle on disclosure; photographs showing acid disfigurement; lease dispute and PW-11 and PW-13 evidence; absence from village and non-attendance at cremation; last-seen sighting of a man and woman on a TVS motorcycle
witness_credibility: Court accepted PW-11 (Sarpanch) and PW-13 (son-in-law) on lease dispute and absence of accused; PW-14 could not identify accused but his sighting of a man and woman on a TVS motorcycle was held relevant; the court did not separately assess PW-16's reliability beyond corroboration by medical evidence and recovery
post_offence_conduct: Accused not found in the village after the occurrence; did not attend cremation or the prayer ceremony held after one week; acid bottle concealed in house and recovered on disclosure; folding chair concealed in house and recovered on disclosure; motorcycle concealed and recovered
bail_history: Accused Swaran Kaur released on bail by the Supreme Court on 4 October 2010; no other bail details stated
trial_duration: offence: not given (last seen 22 March 2005; FIR 28 March 2005); trial judgment: 23 May 2007 / 26 May 2007; High Court: 19 February 2009; Supreme Court: 06 December 2019
legal_representation: Accused (appellants): D. P. Singh, Ms. Sonam Gupta, Ms. Ishita Jain, Sanjay Jain, Advocates. State: Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Ms. Mandakini Singh, Ms. Ashima Mandla, Ms. Anupriya, Advocates
investigation_status: FIR lodged 28 March 2005; body recovered and postmortem done; arrests and recoveries made; investigation completed and accused sent for trial (charge sheet not expressly mentioned)
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted Jagmohan Singh, Swaran Kaur and Darshan Singh, acquitted Avtar Singh. High Court: appeals dismissed, 19 February 2009. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed; Swaran Kaur died during pendency; Darshan Singh and Jagmohan Singh to surrender
prosecution_argument: Last-seen evidence of a man and woman on a TVS motorcycle is relevant even without identification; motive was proved through the Sarpanch and the son-in-law; extra-judicial confession need not always be corroborated (Ram Lal)
defence_argument: Chain of circumstances incomplete; last-seen evidence rejected; extra-judicial confession is weak evidence; no motive attributable to the accused; poison not administered or recovered and inconsistent with strangulation; hyoid fracture does not necessarily mean strangulation
legal_principle_applied: Chain of circumstances test; extra-judicial confession may support conviction, with corroboration by medical or recovery evidence; post-offence conduct and motive as circumstances
precedent_relied_upon: Ram Lal v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2018 SCC OnLine SC 1730), quoted by the court; Ajay Singh v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 12 SCC 341, S. Arul Raja v. State of Tamil Nadu (2010) 8 SCC 233, Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116 and Devi Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2019 SCC OnLine 39) referred to in arguments
judicial_aggravating_factors: Acid disfigurement of the body to avoid identification; accused's absence from the village and non-attendance at cremation and prayer ceremony
other_sentence_order: Darshan Singh and Jagmohan Singh directed to surrender to undergo the remaining sentence

case_title: Suraj Jagannath Jadha v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (conviction); s.300 fourthly considered; Exception 4 to s.300 and s.304 Part II considered as alternative
weapon: Kerosene poured as accelerant and a lit match-stick; no weapon mentioned
evidence_type: Dying declaration (recording conversation between victim and accused); no other evidence discussed in the judgment
aggravating_circumstances: Victim set ablaze while trying to run away; accused fully conscious of consequences; no provocation; no proven inebriation
mitigating_circumstances: None noted by the court; defence alleged intoxication and that accused poured water to save victim, both rejected
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; sentence not stated in judgment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction under s.302 IPC confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim was the accused's wife. According to the prosecution's account, after abusing and assaulting the victim, the accused poured kerosene on her person and set her ablaze. The victim was trying to run out of the house to save herself and was attempting to open the latch of the door when the accused, coming from behind, threw a lit match-stick on her and set her on fire. The incident is recorded in a dying declaration by the victim, which describes a conversation between the victim and the accused at the time. According to that declaration, after the victim came out of the room making noise, the accused poured water on her. The defence said the accused was under the influence of liquor at the time, that he poured water to try to save the victim, and that he was himself injured in the process. The State submitted that the victim was pregnant, about 18 to 20 weeks, at the time. The victim died from burns.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from burns after being set ablaze with kerosene
number_of_offences: 1 charged (s.302 IPC as stated); 1 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Not found as premeditation; court held the act was conscious and deliberate, and that its spur-of-the-moment nature does not reduce culpability (adopting Santosh)
motive: Not identified (State's submission describes abuse and assault before the act; no motive found)
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration, especially the account of the conversation between victim and accused, relied on to find the accused was conscious
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Accused poured water only after the victim screamed for help; treated as an attempt to cloak guilt and not mitigating (quoting Santosh, applied by the Court)
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 09.10.2018; Supreme Court: 13.12.2019
legal_representation: Appellant: Sushil Karanjkar, Nikhilesh Kumar, K. N. Rai. State: Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar, Anoop Kandari
investigation_status: Not stated
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC; High Court (Criminal Appeal No. 723 of 2013): appeal dismissed, conviction confirmed; Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Kalu Ram distinguished as accused not highly inebriated; pouring kerosene and lighting match are intimately connected; s.300 fourthly applies; later water-pouring was an attempt to cloak guilt; victim was pregnant
defence_argument: No intention to kill; accused intoxicated; poured water to save victim and was injured; Kalu Ram applies so conviction should be altered to s.304 Part II
legal_principle_applied: Intoxication is not a defence unless it renders accused incapable of forming intention; s.300 fourthly applies to act imminently dangerous to cause death; Exception 4 not applicable absent evidence of high inebriation; later water-pouring not mitigating
precedent_relied_upon: Santosh v. State of Maharashtra (2015) 7 SCC 641 (relied on); Bhagwan Tukaram Dange v. State of Maharashtra (2014) 4 SCC 270 (relied on); Kalu Ram v. State of Rajasthan (2000) 10 SCC 324 (distinguished)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Accused fully conscious of consequences; act done while victim was trying to escape; no proven high inebriation
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Anokhilal v. State of Madhya Pradesh
previous_criminal_record: Yes - earlier conviction (judgment dated 21.10.2010) for committing carnal sex with a small boy
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour
evidence_type: Circumstantial (last-seen evidence), eyewitness-type last-seen testimony of Kirti Bai, DNA and forensic (FSL) reports, injury evidence
aggravating_circumstances: Victim a nine-year-old girl; brutal rape; throttling; body dumped in a field; accused exploited the victim's trust; prior conviction for a sexual offence (as noted by the High Court)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.363, 366, 377, 376(2)(f) and 302 r/w POCSO s.6; death sentence (s.302); seven years RI each for ss.363, 366, 377; life imprisonment (s.376(2)(f)); fine Rs.1000 each
high_court_outcome: Death sentence confirmed and other sentences upheld; appeal (Criminal Appeal No.748 of 2013) dismissed and reference (No.4 of 2013) answered in favour of confirmation
neutral_facts: A nine-year-old girl was reported missing in the evening of 30 January 2013 after a neighbour of her family had sent her to buy a bidi from a shop; she did not return. Her body was found in an open field the next day. The investigation recovered hairs from the victim's fist and skin from under her fingernails, which were reported to belong to the accused. Semen found on the victim's pyjamas was reported to be the accused's, and blood found on the accused's underwear was reported to be the victim's. The victim's body bore numerous injuries and marks of throttling, and she had been sexually assaulted. A witness, Kirti Bai, stated that the victim was seen alive with the accused at a time close to the incident. After the incident the accused was not seen, and he was arrested on 4 February 2013. Investigation was completed and a charge-sheet was filed, and the case proceeded on the basis of this evidence.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by throttling; rape and carnal sex; numerous injuries on the body
premeditation_planning: Found by the High Court (not decided by the Supreme Court): accused followed the victim with a premeditated mind
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court made no finding on the merits of the evidence; it noted that the DNA report formed the foundation of the High Court's discussion and that the High Court relied on last-seen evidence and DNA/FSL reports
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Absconded after the incident (as noted by the High Court)
custody_duration: In detention since 04.02.2013; total duration not stated
trial_duration: offence: 30.01.2013 (missing report lodged; trial court notes incident occurred midnight 30-31 January); trial judgment: 04.03.2013; High Court: 27.06.2013; Supreme Court: 18.12.2019
legal_representation: Appellant: Sidharth Luthra, Senior Advocate (for the Supreme Court Legal Services Authority), with Amicus Curiae; State: Varun Chopra, Deputy Advocate General
investigation_status: FIR registered 30.01.2013; body found 01.02.2013; accused arrested 04.02.2013; charge-sheet filed 13.02.2013; charges framed 19.02.2013; trial concluded 04.03.2013
procedural_irregularity: Amicus Curiae appointed on the same day charges were framed, with no time to study the record or meet the accused; 13 witnesses examined within seven days; accused examined under s.313 CrPC before complete evidence; trial concluded within a fortnight without awaiting FSL/DNA reports
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, death sentence (04.03.2013). High Court: death sentence and other sentences upheld; appeal dismissed (27.06.2013). Supreme Court: convictions and sentences set aside; de novo consideration directed
prosecution_argument: The evidence pointed to the accused's guilt without doubt, so the conviction recorded by the courts below was correct and called for no interference
defence_argument: Amicus Curiae was appointed on the day charges were framed, with no sufficient opportunity to study the matter or interact with the accused; the trial was unfair and prejudicial
legal_principle_applied: Right to free legal aid under Art. 39-A and Art. 21 requires real and meaningful assistance, with counsel given sufficient time to prepare; expeditious trial must not compromise fairness
precedent_relied_upon: Bashira v. State of U.P., [1969] 1 SCR 32 (relied on); Mohd. Hussain alias Julfikar Ali v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2012) 9 SCC 408; Hussainara Khatoon (IV), (1980) 1 SCC 98; Ambadas Laxman Shinde (2018) 18 SCC 788; Imtiyaz Ramzan Khan (2018) 9 SCC 160; V.K. Sasikala (2012) 9 SCC 771 (referred to)
other_sentence_order: De novo consideration by the Trial Court; counsel may address whether charges should be amended, whether prosecution witnesses should be recalled, and whether expert evidence is needed on FSL and DNA reports; matter listed on 18.02.2020 for other related issues

case_title: Mahadevappa v. State of Karnataka rep. by Public Prosecutor
accused_occupation: Police constable (posted at Police Station, Kaladagi)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse
statutory_provisions: IPC s.498-A; IPC s.302
weapon: Kerosene oil (poured on the victim and ignited); no separate weapon mentioned
evidence_type: Ocular testimony of family and relative witnesses; medical (post-mortem and doctor's evidence); forensic (FSL report and kerosene bottle recovery); circumstantial; victim's oral statements to father before death
aggravating_circumstances: Repeated demands for money, ill-treatment and assault over the marriage; death by burning within seven years of marriage; accused alone present at the time
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of all charges (ss.498-A and 302 IPC) on 31.05.2000
high_court_outcome: State's appeal allowed; acquittal reversed; convicted under ss.498-A and 302 IPC; sentenced to life imprisonment
offence_finally_established: Cruelty/dowry-related offence under s.498-A IPC and murder under s.302 IPC
neutral_facts: The victim, a woman married to the accused in June 1994, died in October 1995 from severe burn injuries, about seventeen months after the marriage. The accused, a police constable, lived with her at his posting. Over the marriage the accused was said to drink alcohol heavily, often arriving at the victim's parents' house drunk, and repeatedly demanded money from the victim and her parents, at one stage insisting she bring several thousand rupees from her family. He also beat and ill-treated the victim, including while intoxicated. The victim's father and mother, a brother-in-law and a relative each described these incidents in evidence, saying the victim had complained to them and that her parents had sent money on two occasions. The victim also wrote a letter to her father describing ill-treatment. When the victim's mother and a sister-in-law visited the accused's house, the accused allegedly abused them and beat them with shoes. On the day of the incident, around 8 a.m., only the victim and the accused were in the house. Evidence showed that the victim had been doused with kerosene and set alight in the kitchen, and a bottle of kerosene lay in the room. Broken bangles were found in the room. The post-mortem and forensic reports showed kerosene on the body and burns heavier on the upper body, including a burnt blouse. The accused's explanation was that the victim's nylon sari caught fire accidentally while she was boiling water on the oven. At the hospital the victim told her father that the accused had poured kerosene on her and set her on fire, and she died that evening. The father lodged a complaint the same day. The investigating officer recorded statements, arranged the post-mortem, obtained the forensic report and filed a charge-sheet.
physical_harm: Death from severe burn injuries after the victim was doused with kerosene and set on fire
financial_property_loss: Rs.2,000 sent to the accused by the victim's father (per father's testimony); further demands of Rs.4,000-5,000 not met
motive: Repeated demands for money from the victim and her parents, which the court accepted
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent evidence of the victim's father (PW-1), mother (PW-4), brother-in-law (PW-5) and relative (PW-17) on cruelty and demands; post-mortem and FSL reports; doctor's evidence (PW-6); kerosene bottle in room; broken bangles; kerosene smell on body; burns concentrated on upper body
witness_credibility: Four witnesses found consistent on material issues despite lengthy cross-examination; parents held to be the most natural and material witnesses with no reason to lie
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 02.10.1995; trial judgment: 31.05.2000; High Court: 03.01.2007; Supreme Court: 07.01.2019
legal_representation: Accused: Mallikarjun S. Mylar, Manjunath, Ms. Umme Salma, Ms. E. R. Sumathy (Advs.). State: Joseph Aristotle S., Mrs. Priya Aristotle, Shiva P., Ms. Aruna Hannah Dutta, Ms. Anitha Shenoy (Advs.)
investigation_status: FIR registered same day; statements recorded; post-mortem and FSL report obtained; charge-sheet filed; case committed to Sessions Court
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions Judge, 31.05.2000): acquitted. High Court (03.01.2007): acquittal reversed, convicted under ss.498-A and 302 IPC, life imprisonment. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld
prosecution_argument: State argued the Sessions Judge failed to appreciate the evidence and that the High Court rightly found both dowry demand and murder proved
defence_argument: No case for reversal of acquittal and the Sessions Judge's view should be restored; the death was accidental (sari caught fire while boiling water on oven); witnesses turned hostile so the prosecution case should be discarded
legal_principle_applied: Cruelty under s.498-A (Explanations (a) and (b)) assessed from evidence of repeated harassment and demands; homicidal versus accidental death decided on circumstantial evidence and absence of plausible explanation; hostile witnesses do not affect case where other evidence proves it
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
judicial_aggravating_factors: Repeated cruelty and demands for money from the start of the marriage; death by burning within seven years of marriage; accused was the only person present with no plausible explanation
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Digamber Vaishna & Anr. v. State of Chhattisgarh
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated (court found acquaintance between accused and victims not shown)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.394 r/w s.34
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence: child witness testimony, s.27 recoveries, fingerprint report, FSL/hair report, alleged robbery motive, last seen together
confession: Section 27 disclosure statements by the accused leading to recoveries (motorcycle, cash, anklet, shirt); the Court did not treat them as a confession and found the recoveries unreliable
aggravating_circumstances: Five women killed by strangulation (as found by the trial court); the Supreme Court weighed no aggravating factor
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302/34 IPC and sentenced to death; convicted under s.394/34 IPC and sentenced to RI for ten years with fine of Rs.500 (default one month RI)
high_court_outcome: Death reference confirmed; criminal appeals dismissed; death sentence affirmed
neutral_facts: Five women living in one house were found dead on 17 December 2012, with some bodies in a courtyard and others in a room. A relative who was alerted by a child living in the house went to the scene and saw blood from the nose and mouth of the victims and marks of injury on their necks. A post-mortem examination found that all five died of asphyxia due to strangulation, and the deaths were homicidal. The investigating officer prepared a site map and seized a glass whisky bottle, a torch, six strands of black hair from one victim's hand, two white buttons, blood-stained soil and a woollen shawl. Fingerprints lifted from the bottle were reported to match one accused. A forensic report found a shirt button and the buttons from the scene to be similar, and a hair report identified only human hair. Following statements made by the accused, a motorcycle, a sum of cash and a silver anklet were recovered, and one accused's shirt was seized. The prosecution alleged that the killings were committed during a robbery. A child witness said that the accused had come to the house the previous night and that, in the early morning, she had found the door locked from outside. She identified the accused as the persons she had seen with the victims. A witness heard of the accused's visit only through a telephone call, and a motorcycle witness gave conflicting descriptions. The gold ornaments and pearl necklace on the victims' bodies were recorded in the site plan.
physical_harm: Death of five women by asphyxia due to strangulation
number_of_offences: 2 charged (s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; s.394 r/w s.34 IPC); 0 finally upheld
financial_property_loss: Not established: cash (Rs.3000 and Rs.2600 recovered) and a silver anklet were alleged to be stolen, but no theft was proved
motive: alleged: robbery (the Court found this motive unsubstantiated)
key_evidence_accepted: None accepted as sufficient to convict; the Court found the chain of circumstances incomplete, including the child witness identification, recoveries, fingerprint and hair evidence, and last seen evidence
witness_credibility: Child witness PW-8 found unreliable: not an eyewitness, inconsistent, contradicted by PWs 1, 3 and 10, and her identification uncorroborated. PW-9 evidence was hearsay-based. PW-2 and the seizure memos were contradictory, and the motorcycle colour evidence unreliable.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 16.12.2012 (last seen together) and 17.12.2012 (bodies found); trial judgment: 14.05.2014; High Court: 30.04.2015; Supreme Court: 05.03.2019
legal_representation: Appellants: S. Nagamuthu, Senior Advocate, with Himanshu Agarwal, Ankita S., Ayush Raj Singh, Veerapan P. and Pyoli, Advocates. State: Atul Jha, Sandeep Jha and Dharmendra Kumar Sinha, Advocates.
investigation_status: FIR registered (Crime No.430/12, Police Station Bilaigarh); investigation completed; chargesheet filed; trial completed with 14 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: Key witness Anita not examined without explanation; three other children present not examined; fingerprint expert and sample-taker not examined; articles left at scene after lifting prints; unexplained delay in reporting the crime
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, death sentence under s.302/34 IPC. High Court: death sentence confirmed, appeals dismissed. Supreme Court: appeals allowed, accused acquitted.
prosecution_argument: Supported the judgments of the courts below and prayed for dismissal of the appeals; no specific arguments recorded
defence_argument: Unexplained delay in reporting; child witness PW-8 uncorroborated and unreliable; s.27 recoveries (motorcycle, articles) unconnected and unreliable; PW-9 testimony hearsay; fingerprint report unreliable; last seen evidence insufficient
legal_principle_applied: Burden of proof on prosecution; suspicion cannot replace proof; circumstantial evidence chain must be complete (Jaharlal Das conditions); where two views are possible, the view favourable to the accused is adopted; child witness evidence needs corroboration as prudence; s.27 requires relevant discovery; last seen together requires close proximity
precedent_relied_upon: Jaharlal Das v. State of Orissa (1991) 3 SCC 27; Varkey Joseph v. State of Kerala 1993 Suppl (3) SCC 745; Sujit Biswas v. State of Assam (2013) 12 SCC 406; Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh (1973) 2 SCC 808; Panchhi v. State of U.P. (1998) 7 SCC 177; State of U.P. v. Ashok Dixit (2000) 3 SCC 70; State of Rajasthan v. Om Prakash (2002) 5 SCC 745; Alagupandi v. case_title: Shiv Shankar Prasad Singh v. The State of Bihar
accused_occupation: Government employee of the Food Corporation of India depot: AG-III (in charge of receipt of consignments) for Shiv Shankar Prasad Singh; Depot Incharge for Ramdeo Prasad
accused_victim_relationship: Employees of the complainant organisation (Food Corporation of India); co-workers at the depot

neutral_facts: The victim organisation, a food corporation, alleged that a depot in-charge and other staff conspired with a transporter and a contractor to misappropriate urea fertiliser bags during March 1980. A complaint dated December 1981 led to registration of a first information report, which initially referred to 540 bags. Wagons carrying fertiliser were placed at a railway station for unloading, and delivery was signed for in the delivery book on 24 and 25 March 1980. The prosecution alleged that 500 bags were handed over to a representative who signed gate passes for two trucks, each said to carry 250 bags to the depot. The accused responsible for receipt at the depot gate register and the in-charge who maintained the godown registers were said to have entered the arrival of these bags, although the bags were never delivered. The investigation concluded that the entire 1040 bags were misappropriated. Evidence included depositions of the two truck owners, the drivers and a cleaner, who stated that one truck was diverted to a different location and the other was never used for carrying fertiliser. The gate register, arrival tally book, daily receipt register and godown stock register were examined, together with a chart prepared in October 1982 showing delivery of the 500 bags. A government document examiner, an audit assistant manager, a physical verification officer and the investigating officer also testified. Defence evidence came from a retired assistant depot manager.

neutral_facts: On the night of 10 July 1988, the victim, an army officer, and a colleague visited a hotel on the main road in Ahmednagar. The prosecution alleged that a quarrel broke out at the hotel between the accused and the two visitors, and that chilli powder was thrown into the eyes of the visitors, after which they ran out. The victim was allegedly chased by the accused and assaulted with a gupti, a knife-type weapon, and fell on the road. A beat constable on patrol nearby stated that he saw the accused chase and assault the victim, and that the accused was wearing a black sando banian and a lungi. The constable took the victim by rickshaw to the police station and then to the civil hospital. At the hospital, a Special Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration from the victim around midnight, in which the victim described the assailant's clothing. An offence was registered on that basis. The accused was arrested in the early hours of the following day, and blood-stained clothing, a vest and a lungi, was seized from him, along with a gupti recovered on his information. Chemical analysis found the blood group on the clothing matched the victim's blood group. The victim died on 23 July 1988 and the investigation was extended to a homicide offence. The prosecution examined 14 witnesses. Two independent witnesses and the panch witnesses to the seizure did not support the prosecution. The medical evidence was said to be consistent with the eyewitness account.

neutral_facts: On a day in March 1998 at about 5.30 pm, the victim was riding a motorcycle with two companions when a group of four men stopped it near a lane. One of the men asked the victim to get down to talk. When the victim got down, one attacker struck the victim on the back with a lathi. The victim ran toward a lane to escape. Two other men allegedly caught hold of the victim's arms, and the accused who had the pistol fired at close range at the victim's face, killing the victim instantly. Three eyewitnesses, two of them the victim's companions on the motorcycle and one nearby, described these acts consistently. The defence alleged no eyewitness was present. The post-mortem found a gunshot wound to the left eye and brain, with gunpowder in the eyes, and nine other injuries on the back, arms, chest and head. The doctor opined that the shot was fired from about one foot away. Following a disclosure, a country-made pistol was recovered from a house. Forensic examination found the pistol operative, but the barrel marks on the bullet were insufficient for decisive matching. The FIR was registered at a police station on the same day at 6 pm, and an inquest was conducted at the scene.

neutral_facts: The accused sought to take the wife of the victim as a third wife, and over time tried to separate the couple through gifts, financial help and interference in their personal lives. On 01.10.2001 the victim and his wife were abducted and released the same day, and a separate complaint was lodged about that abduction. On 26.10.2001 the wife and victim were taken in a vehicle from Tirunelveli, accompanied by several co-accused. At a culvert on the way, co-accused alighted from a following vehicle and took the victim away, and the accused reportedly instructed them to finish him off. The victim's body was found on 31.10.2001 in a forest area near Kodaikanal, decomposed, and was buried as unidentified. The wife said she was under surveillance and could not file a complaint earlier. Investigation included a confession by one accused who led police to the body and a recovery of the body on that basis; recovery of a wallet and gold chain from another accused's house; identification of the body by the wife and family from photographs, clothes, belongings and a scar on the waist; a superimposition test by an expert; post-mortem findings of death by throttling and a broken hyoid bone; handwriting comparison of hotel records; and petrol pump bills showing the vehicle refuelled en route to Kodaikanal. The victim was last seen with the accused.

In August 2010 the victim was given a sub-contract on payment of a caution deposit of Rs 1,00,000, made through two cheques credited to the firm's account on 30 August 2010. The victim performed data-entry work from September to December 2010, valued at Rs 8,50,000. For that work the accused issued two cheques: dated 1 November 2010 for Rs 2,00,000 and 18 December 2010 for Rs 2,50,000. When the victim presented them through the victim's bank, both were returned unpaid for insufficient funds, and the victim requested payment of the dishonoured amounts with later months' dues. In February 2011 one accused transferred Rs 1,00,000 into the victim's account and promised to pay the balance. Later, a managing partner issued two further cheques, dated 30 May 2011 and 19 July 2011, each for Rs 2,00,000. The first was returned unpaid on 30 May 2011. After the accused assured the victim that both would be honoured on re-presentation in July 2011, the victim presented them; both were returned unpaid on 14 July and 20 July 2011 for insufficient funds. The victim alleges the accused then avoided contact. A notice of demand was issued on 1 August 2011, and no payment followed.

neutral_facts: A written complaint by a housing development director in November 2000 led to an FIR alleging a fraud on a housing authority concerning a flat allotted to the victim. The prosecution case was that several housing authority employees, together with property dealers and a special power of attorney holder, acted on a request purportedly made by the allottee to reduce the flat's cost, and that the original fixed deposit receipt and refund application were found removed or misplaced from the file. The FIR further alleged that a refund cheque of Rs.2,22,263 was withdrawn through a savings bank account opened at a bank branch with a forged signature of the allottee. The investigation later alleged that the accused, then a branch manager at that bank, opened a savings account in the allottee's name in connivance with others, in order to encash the cheque dated 7 January 2000. The prosecution relied on a forensic handwriting report dated 30 December 2002 comparing the signature on the account opening form with the accused's specimen signatures. That report stated that a definite opinion could not be given on the remaining items on the materials available. A further report was later sought from a government examiner of questioned documents, which, according to the submissions recorded, expressed an opinion that the signature on the account opening form tallied with the accused's specimen signatures.
