legal_principle_applied: Section 197 applies only to a public servant not removable from office save by or with the sanction of the Government; if not met, the official-duty question need not be examined. Magistrate must avoid conclusive opinion on investigation evidence before final trial
precedent_relied_upon: K.Ch. Prasad v. J. Vanalatha Devi (1987) 2 SCC 52 (relied on); Parkash Singh Badal v. State of Punjab (2007) 1 SCC 1; Inspector of Police v. Battenapatla Venkata Ratnam (2015) 13 SCC 87; Devinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2016) 12 SCC 87; N.K. Ganguly v. CBI (2016) 2 SCC 143; S.P.S. Rathore v. CBI (2017) 5 SCC 817 (referred to)
other_sentence_order: Observations in the CMM order of 03.12.2014 that the accused forged the signatures and that an act of forgery by a public servant is not official duty are deleted; no other order

case_title: Nagji Odha Vji Kumbhar & Anr. v. State of Gujarat
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: land and right-of-way dispute; complainant party had obtained an injunction in a civil suit
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.324 (r/w s.34)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured witnesses PW-3 and PW-4); medical (PW-2 and PW-10 injury evidence; post-mortem report)
aggravating_circumstances: Multiple stab wounds on the chest, a vital part, of both deceased; attack by seven to eight armed persons on unarmed victims
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; life imprisonment; no separate punishment under s.324
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 234 of 1990) dismissed on 24.10.2008; conviction under ss.302 and 324 maintained
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (murder of two persons); IPC s.324 conviction maintained
neutral_facts: On the night of 1 July 1987, at about midnight in a village, a group of men confronted two victims over a long-running dispute about a right of way over land. The accused group was said to be armed: one man carried a spear, another an axe, and others sticks. Both victims were stabbed and struck and died at the spot. Two men present, including the complainant, were injured and were examined by a doctor, whose evidence recorded their wounds. The complainant's statement formed the basis of the first information report, lodged at 7 AM the next morning. Post-mortem examination of the two victims recorded stab wounds to the chest, including wounds to the lungs, consistent with the oral evidence that both had received stab wounds. The accused, arrested later in July, also had injuries examined by the same doctor. Their account was that the victims' side, nine in number, had attacked them, and the investigating officer testified that one accused was lying bleeding at the scene. The injured eyewitnesses described the attackers as armed with spears and other weapons. The accused's first account, lodged as a cross-complaint, stated that the victims were not armed.
physical_harm: Death of two victims from stab wounds to the chest (lungs, vessels and trachea cut); injuries to both accused, including head wounds, cut and bone-deep wounds and fractures
number_of_offences: 2 charged; 2 finally upheld (s.302 and s.324; no separate sentence under s.324)
premeditation_planning: Not expressly found; the court rejected the spur-of-the-moment plea because of multiple wounds on vital parts
motive: alleged: dispute over right of way to the deceased (the court did not decide motive)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of injured witnesses PW-3 and PW-4 (attack by armed appellants); PW-2 and PW-10 injury evidence; post-mortem report corroborating stab wounds
witness_credibility: Injured eyewitnesses PW-3 and PW-4 accepted as reliable; their presence not seriously disputed; medical report corroborates their account. The Investigating Officer's account that one accused lay bleeding was held not to merit consideration
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: Defence submitted more than 11 years of actual imprisonment; the appellants were arrested on 17 July 1987
trial_duration: offence: 1 July 1987; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 24.10.2008; Supreme Court: 23 April 2019
legal_representation: Accused: Ravi Prakash Mehrotra, Ankit Agarwal, Ms. Deepti R. Mehrotra (Advocates). State of Gujarat: Ms. Jesal Wahi (for Ms. Hemantika Wahi), Advocate
investigation_status: FIR registered 2 July 1987; accused arrested 17 July 1987; investigation completed and trial conducted; cross-case FIR under separate trial
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, life imprisonment. High Court: conviction maintained on 24.10.2008 (Criminal Appeal No. 234 of 1990). Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Relied on injured eyewitness statements (PW-3, PW-4) and medical evidence (PW-2, PW-10, post-mortem) to establish armed attack by the accused; the judgment records no separate State submissions
defence_argument: Deceased side were aggressors; accused injured while protecting their land, so acted in private defence; alternatively, the act was on the spur of the moment without pre-meditation, so conviction should be under s.304 Part II; relied on Jangir Singh
legal_principle_applied: Private defence unavailable where the victims were unarmed; the right cannot justify harm beyond what is necessary; a plea of spur-of-the-moment killing fails where multiple wounds are inflicted on vital parts
precedent_relied_upon: Jangir Singh v. State of Punjab, 2018 (15) SCALE 88 (Criminal Appeal No. 2499 of 2009) – distinguished
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable (the court upheld the trial sentence without separate sentencing reasoning)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Multiple injuries on vital parts (chest) of the deceased
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Rambir v. State of NCT, Delhi
accused_socioeconomic_status: Not stated (judgment records only that the appellant's counsel was appointed by the Delhi High Court Legal Services Committee)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband and wife)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.34 (as cited in FIR); conviction under IPC s.302, modified to s.304 Part II
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (son), last-seen evidence (PW-9), witness corroboration (PW-17, PW-18), scene evidence (PW-15 found body with saria)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden fight, no premeditation, act in heat of passion, manner not extremely cruel
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed (judgment dated 11.10.2017); conviction under s.302 and life sentence confirmed
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, IPC s.304 Part II (Exception 4 to s.300)
neutral_facts: On the intervening night of 31 August and 1 September 2010, the accused is alleged to have strangled the victim, his wife, on the rooftop of a residential premises in Delhi, causing her death. The primary eyewitness was the couple's son, who testified that he saw the accused strangling his mother with an iron rod (saria) after she had taken money from the accused's wallet. The son's account was the central prosecution evidence. A police sub-inspector, the first officer to reach the scene, found the victim's body on the terrace along with a saria, an empty liquor bottle and a plastic glass. A worker in the workshop on the premises testified that he saw the accused leaving the premises in the morning of 1 September 2010. Two further prosecution witnesses confirmed the accused's presence at the scene. The case was registered as an FIR on 1 September 2010 under sections 302 and 34 of the Penal Code. The investigation and trial relied on these eyewitness, last-seen and scene-based evidence, together with the recovered rod.
physical_harm: Death of victim by strangulation with a saria
number_of_offences: 1 charged (s.302 IPC, with s.34 cited in FIR); 1 finally upheld (s.304 Part II IPC, conviction modified)
premeditation_planning: No premeditation found; the court held the saria was picked up on the spur of the moment
motive: Sudden quarrel after the victim took money from the accused's wallet (court accepted incident arose in a sudden fight)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-7 (son); corroboration by PW-9 (last seen leaving), PW-17 and PW-18 (presence), and PW-15 (scene and saria)
witness_credibility: High Court found PW-7, PW-9, PW-17 and PW-18 credible and reliable; Supreme Court accepted PW-7's account as the basis for finding a sudden fight
post_offence_conduct: Accused seen leaving the premises at about 6:30 a.m. on 1 September 2010 (PW-9); no other conduct noted
trial_duration: offence: 31.08.2010 and 01.09.2010 (intervening night); trial judgment: 19.07.2012; High Court: 11.10.2017; Supreme Court: 06.05.2019
legal_representation: Appellant: Shikhil Suri, Shiv Kumar Suri (Advocates). State: Ms. Pinky Anand, ASG, with Ashok Panigrahi, P. S. Sudheer, Ms. Kirti Dua, B.V. Balaram Das (Advocates)
investigation_status: FIR registered 01.09.2010; 18 prosecution witnesses examined; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, life imprisonment (23.07.2012). High Court: appeal dismissed (11.10.2017). Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; conviction modified to s.304 Part II, 10 years' simple imprisonment
prosecution_argument: Clear murder proved by four witnesses; compressing the neck with a saria cannot be an act committed in a fit of anger; strangulation with a saria is an extremely cruel act, so Exception 4 is rightly negated
defence_argument: Sudden quarrel in a fit of anger under influence of liquor; no intention to kill; all four ingredients of Exception 4 to s.300 IPC are met, and the High Court's finding on two ingredients runs contrary to evidence
legal_principle_applied: Four ingredients of Exception 4 to s.300 IPC; strangulation is not extreme cruelty unless barbaric, torturous and brutal
precedent_relied_upon: Surinder Kumar v. Union Territory, Chandigarh (1989) 2 SCC 217 : [1989] 1 SCR 941
sentencing_rationale: Act committed in sudden fight and heat of passion without premeditation and not extremely cruel, so Exception 4 applies; conviction reduced to s.304 Part II with 10 years' simple imprisonment
judicial_mitigating_factors: Sudden quarrel; no premeditation; act in heat of passion; manner not extremely cruel
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Asim Shariff v. National Investigation Agency
accused_victim_relationship: No prior enmity; prosecution admitted there was no animosity between the accused and the victim. No other relationship described.
evidence_type: Circumstantial and documentary evidence (call data records, bank account details, seized banner, disclosure report, purse letter); recovery evidence. Prosecution's evidence as described by the parties, not tested by the Court.
confession: Alleged confession by accused no. 4 (prosecution submission only); not evaluated or relied on by the Court.
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Discharge application under s.227 CrPC dismissed; charges framed against the accused. No verdict; trial not concluded.
high_court_outcome: Writ petition under Arts. 226/227 and s.482 CrPC dismissed; trial court's order affirmed.
neutral_facts: On 16 October 2016, around midday, the victim was with several friends near a medical store when a pillion rider on a motorcycle attacked him with a sharp-edged machete, striking the right side of his neck, and then fled. The victim was declared dead on arrival at hospital. According to the prosecution, the victim was dressed in uniform during a march organised by an association that day, and his throat was cut in a single blow. The case was first registered as a murder by local police, and four persons were arrested within weeks. A fifth person, the accused, was arrested later. The investigation was then taken over by a national investigating agency, which alleged that the accused and four co-accused conspired to kill members of that association. The prosecution relied on call data records showing frequent telephone contact between the accused and co-accused before and after the incident, bank account details, and a seized banner bearing the photographs of all the accused. It also relied on a disclosure leading to a letter listing earlier killings, and on an allegation that the accused had organised indoctrination classes about eight to nine months earlier that the co-accused attended. One co-accused was alleged to have named the accused as the mastermind. The accused denied any personal animosity toward the victim and said nothing incriminating had been recovered from him.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a throat wound caused by a single blow with a machete (as alleged by the prosecution).
premeditation_planning: Prima facie conspiracy found for charge-framing only. The Court did not finally determine premeditation; this is for trial.
motive: alleged: conspiracy to kill members of a particular association (RSS) and create fear among the public
key_evidence_accepted: Charge-sheet material showing the accused's position in the organisation and frequent telephone/mobile contact with co-accused before and after the incident. Accepted only as prima facie material.
witness_credibility: Not assessed; the Court left the truth and veracity of the evidence to trial.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: Arrested 2 November 2016; total period in custody not stated.
trial_duration: offence: 16 October 2016; trial judgment: 2 January 2018 (order on discharge application; para 21 gives 12 January 2018); High Court: 22 November 2018; Supreme Court: 1 July 2019
legal_representation: Accused: Kamini Jaiswal, Abdul Rahiman, Shereef K.A., Rani Mishra, Jatinderpal Singh (Advocates). State/NIA: Aman Lekhi, ASG, with Shraddha Deshmukh, Kanu Agrawal, B. V. Balaram Das (Advocates).
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation transferred to NIA; charge sheet filed against five accused; charges framed by the trial court.
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: discharge dismissed and charges framed. High Court: writ petition dismissed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Section 15 UAP Act covers individual acts and terrorist gangs, and s.20 does not require the organisation to be scheduled. The victim was attacked in uniform during a procession, with no animosity. Evidence included PFI membership, a seized banner, phone contacts, a disclosure report, indoctrination classes, and an alleged confession by a co-accused.
defence_argument: Charges based on suspicion; no incriminating material recovered; the prosecution failed to adduce evidence against the accused; the Navaratri date allegation was false; no co-accused was a member of a banned organisation, so the UAP Act charge was not sustainable.
legal_principle_applied: Under s.227 CrPC the judge may sift and weigh evidence only to decide whether a prima facie case or grave suspicion exists. If two views are possible and one shows only suspicion, discharge is warranted. No mini-trial.
precedent_relied_upon: Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal (1979) 3 SCC 4; Sajjan Kumar v. CBI (2010) 9 SCC 368; State v. S. Selvi (2018) 13 SCC 455; Vikram Johar v. State of UP (2019) 6 SCALE 794
other_sentence_order: Observations made only for disposing of the appeal and do not prejudice the trial; trial to proceed independently. Appeal dismissed.

case_title: Sardar Ali Khan v. State of Uttar Pradesh through Principal Secretary Home Department & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance of the victim's late father; civil dispute (prior dispute) over the sale of the plot
evidence_type: Not stated
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Accused stated to be about 87 years old; complaint lodged about four years after the civil suit

neutral_facts: The accused states that they bought a plot of land from the victim under a sale deed executed in late December 1993 and registered in early January 1994. The victim died in December 1997, and his heir later obtained mutation of the inherited property in November 1998. In August 2008 the heir filed a civil suit seeking cancellation of the sale deed. The suit alleged that the deed was obtained falsely and fraudulently by the accused and the accused's brother, who made use of the victim's acquaintance. The civil suit did not allege impersonation or forgery of signatures. The accused had separately filed a civil suit against the heir seeking an injunction over constructions on the plot. In April 2012 the accused's brother lodged a complaint alleging that the heir had stolen the original sale deed from the mutation file. In September 2012 the heir lodged a criminal complaint against the accused and the brother alleging forgery and impersonation, about four years after the civil suit was filed. According to the accused, the heir also signed the sale deed as a witness. The material before the authorities consisted of the registered sale deed and the civil and criminal pleadings. A case was registered at the police station on the criminal complaint.
physical_harm: Not stated
financial_property_loss: Not applicable (no money loss stated; plot No.102 is the disputed property)

witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Not stated

case_title: Shri Satish Kumar & Anr. v. State of Himachal Pradesh & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour (one accused's house was in front of the victim's daughter's house); prior land dispute with one accused, alleged by the prosecution and not proved
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; Arms Act s.25; Arms Act s.27
weapon: Single barrel gun (licensed to one accused's father) with empty and live cartridges
evidence_type: Circumstantial; recovery on disclosure statements; forensic science report; post-mortem; telephone call; testimony of hostile witnesses
confession: Disclosure statements of two accused (linked to recovery of body and gun); not relied on because the recovery in pursuance of them was not proved
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: All accused acquitted (benefit of doubt)
high_court_outcome: Complainant's appeal allowed; acquittal set aside; all accused convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC and Arms Act ss.25 and 27
neutral_facts: The victim left home in the morning, saying he would visit a relative in a nearby village and then report for duty. He did not return by evening, and his mobile phone was switched off. The next morning the victim's daughter was told by a forest guard that he had not reported for duty. She then telephoned a person who lived opposite her house and asked for a contact number at the village. At about 7:15 am on the following day, the police received a telephone call from one of the accused reporting that the victim had died of a gunshot. A police team went towards the place of occurrence. Later that day the victim's daughter gave a statement naming two accused as the shooters, saying she had learned this from police when they came to the village. The police took the two accused, two local witnesses and the daughter to a forest about two kilometres from the house. There the victim's body was found, along with a bag and two pellet marks on nearby bushes. Both accused were said to have made disclosure statements in the presence of the two witnesses, leading to the body and a single-barrel gun with cartridges being recovered; the gun was licensed to a third person and was found at his house. Forensic examination reported that a cartridge had been fired from the gun and that gunshot residue on the victim's clothes indicated distant firing. The post-mortem found multiple perforated gunshot wounds and recorded death from cardio-respiratory failure and hypovolemic shock due to gunshot injury. Both witnesses to the disclosure statements later denied in cross-examination that any such statement was made in their presence. The investigating officer's accounts of when the death became known were said to be contradictory, and no call records were produced to verify the telephone call. The alleged motive was a land dispute with one of the accused.
physical_harm: Death from multiple gunshot wounds (perforated wounds to body; cardio-respiratory failure and hypovolemic shock)
motive: alleged: land dispute with one accused (Satish Kumar); the court held the prosecution failed to prove any motive and the alleged motive had no foundation
key_evidence_accepted: None relied on for conviction. The court noted only that the forensic report showed the gun was used in the crime, which did not establish which accused fired
witness_credibility: Witnesses to disclosure statements (PW-2, PW-3) turned hostile and were not trustworthy; investigating officer's statements were contradictory; the daughter's first statement recorded at 12.45 pm naming the assailants was doubtful; evidence did not inspire confidence
post_offence_conduct: One accused allegedly telephoned police at 7:15 am reporting the death; disclosure statements and recoveries allegedly followed, but the court found the telephone call unverified and the recoveries not proved
custody_duration: Not stated (arrest on 22 December 2009 noted; duration of custody not given)
bail_history: Not stated (bail bonds were furnished; no grant or refusal details given)
trial_duration: offence: 21 December 2009 (deceased left home; death reported 22 December 2009); trial judgment: 30 November 2012; High Court: 20 September 2016; Supreme Court: 2 March 2020
legal_representation: Accused: Ruchi Kohli, Babita Yadav, Amit Sharma, Srishti Mishra, R. C. Kohli (Advocates). State: Upasana Nath, Abhinav Mukerji, Radhika Gautam (Advocates)
investigation_status: FIR No. 218 registered 22 December 2009; post-mortem, forensic examination and recoveries carried out; trial completed with acquittal
procedural_irregularity: Investigating officer gave contradictory statements; police did not verify the telephone call; the FIR's account of cause of death suggested the body was known before recovery; disclosure-based recovery not proved
appeal_history: Trial court: all accused acquitted (30 November 2012). High Court: complainant's appeal allowed, acquittal set aside, accused convicted (20 September 2016). Supreme Court: appeals allowed, convictions set aside, acquittal restored (2 March 2020)
prosecution_argument: Not stated (State's submissions before the Supreme Court are not recorded; the judgment records the High Court's reasoning that post-mortem and forensic reports showed use of the gun and that recoveries corroborated the disclosure statements)
defence_argument: Case rested wholly on circumstantial evidence not meeting the required chain; prosecution witnesses gave contradictory statements, so the truthfulness of the prosecution case was doubtful
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain consistent only with guilt; an appellate court may interfere with acquittal only if the trial court's findings are perverse or not possible on the evidence

other_sentence_order: Bail bonds discharged; all accused to be set at liberty if not wanted in any other case

case_title: Chhota Ahirwar v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (the victim is a cousin of the main accused and a relative of the accused); prior land dispute and enmity between the accused and the victim
statutory_provisions: IPC s.307 read with s.34
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured complainant PW-3 and eyewitness PW-4); medical (PW-8); investigating officer (PW-7); hostile witnesses PW-5, PW-9 and PW-10
confession: None relied on. An alleged confession by the main accused to PW-9 and PW-10 was denied by them and was not relied on
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Accused neither carried arms nor opened fire (not in dispute)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.307/34 IPC; sentenced to five years' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.1000
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 1050 of 1994) dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: On 22 October 1992 at about 11 a.m., a quarrel broke out between the accused and the victim over the victim's cultivation of land that the accused had been given for cultivation. The two had a pre-existing land dispute, and the victim was related to a co-accused, who was also related to the accused. The accused stopped the victim on his way to the field and told him not to cultivate the land. The argument grew heated with raised voices, and about 50 to 60 villagers gathered. A co-accused, cycling past, stopped and intervened. The victim told him not to interfere and to go home. The co-accused took a country-made pistol from his trouser pocket, pointed it at the victim, and fired. The victim was struck by splinters on the forehead near his eye, on his lips and on his shoulder, and bled. The victim testified that the accused urged the co-accused to kill him; an eyewitness testified that the accused told the co-accused to beat the victim. A medical officer said the injuries were caused by firearm splinters. After the firing the co-accused fled and the accused followed him. The victim lodged a report at a police chowki, a case was registered, and the investigating officer examined the victim and eyewitnesses and seized blood-stained clothing. Several witnesses did not support the prosecution.
physical_harm: Injuries to forehead near eye, lips and shoulder from pistol splinters, with bleeding; no death
premeditation_planning: No premeditation or prearranged plan found; the main accused's intervention was by chance and any words attributed to the accused were on the spur of the moment
motive: alleged: land dispute and enmity between the accused and the victim over cultivation of land
key_evidence_accepted: PW-5's account that the main accused intervened, took out a pistol and aimed it at the complainant, corroborated by PW-3 and PW-4; the main accused's firing noted as some evidence
witness_credibility: Notable discrepancies between PW-3 and PW-4 on the accused's role raised serious doubts on their accuracy, given enmity and family disputes; PW-5, though hostile, not rejected entirely; PW-3 admitted omitting instigation from his police statement
post_offence_conduct: Prosecution case only: after the firing the main accused fled and the accused followed him; the court made no finding on this
trial_duration: offence: 22 October 1992; trial judgment: 26 August 1994; High Court: 5 November 2008; Supreme Court: 6 February 2020

procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.307/34 IPC. High Court: appeal dismissed. Supreme Court: appeal allowed and accused acquitted

case_title: Ex-Gunner Virender Prasad v. Union of India & Anr.
accused_occupation: Gunner (soldier) in the Signals Corps, Indian Army
accused_victim_relationship: Co-worker (same army unit); described as on good terms
statutory_provisions: Army Act 1950 s.69 (civil offence of murder, contrary to Ranbir Penal Code s.302)
evidence_type: Oral testimony of 15 witnesses including a psychiatrist; the judgment does not detail the other evidence
confession: Extra-judicial confession to senior authorities after surrender; the Supreme Court did not expressly rely on it
aggravating_circumstances: Victim shot while asleep; a complete magazine of rifle ammunition was fired
mitigating_circumstances: Posted in Kashmir when terrorism was at its peak; immediate surrender and explanation of delusion; excellent jail conduct

neutral_facts: The accused was a gunner in a signals corps unit and was posted to a radar post, having reported there in May 2003. The victim, a radar operator from the same regiment, was on good terms with the accused. On the date of the incident the accused shot the victim while the victim was asleep. The accused said the shooting happened in the belief that a militant attack was under way and that he had no control over his senses at the time. A complete magazine of rifle ammunition was fired, and the victim died as a result. Immediately afterwards the accused came out of the tent, surrendered to senior authorities and confessed guilt. Police registered a case and submitted a challan, but at the request of army authorities the case, the challan and the seized items were handed over to the army for trial. Fifteen witnesses, including a psychiatrist, were examined.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from gunshot wounds
premeditation_planning: Not found; the judgment does not address premeditation. The accused's account was that he acted in a delusion.
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: The Court Martial's findings of fact, as confirmed by the Armed Forces Tribunal, including the finding of guilt for murder
witness_credibility: Not stated

case_title: State of Rajasthan v. Mehram & Ors.
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/land dispute: dispute over use of an unrecorded passage through the accused's fields; the victim's side had repeatedly entered those fields despite objections.
statutory_provisions: Charged/tried: IPC s.148, s.302, s.324/149 (accused No. 5 convicted at trial). High Court: s.326 IPC. Supreme Court: s.304 Part I and s.148 IPC.
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-5, 6, 7, 8, 11); medical (post-mortem and injury reports); recovery (blood-stained lathi, blood-stained clothing); spot inspection report and site plan
aggravating_circumstances: Accused were the aggressors, hid in bushes armed with lethal weapons and attacked on the complainant party's arrival; single fatal blow to the head with intention to kill.
mitigating_circumstances: Grave and sudden provocation from repeated unauthorised entry on the accused's fields; the provocation was not invited by the accused party; accused had simple injuries.
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.148, 302, 324/149 IPC; life imprisonment and Rs.100 fine for s.302; six months' simple imprisonment for s.148 and s.324/149 each.
high_court_outcome: Appeal partly allowed: s.302 conviction converted to s.326 IPC; s.148 conviction maintained; sentence reduced to period already undergone (about five months); Rs.50,000 compensation.
offence_finally_established: IPC s.304 Part I; IPC s.148
neutral_facts: A dispute existed between two family groups over use of an unrecorded passage that ran through fields owned by some of the accused and that the victim's group used to reach its own land. Earlier, a similar obstruction had been settled through local intervention. On the day of the incident, a quarrel broke out between a member of the victim's group and one of the accused over the passage, and the parties dispersed. At sunset, the complainant, a member of the victim's group, was walking alone towards the village when several men came out from behind a thicket of bushes near a pond and surrounded him. Some carried sharp-edged weapons and others carried sticks. One of the men allegedly swung a sharp-edged weapon at the complainant, who raised his hand and was wounded on the palm. Other members of the victim's group then arrived from their fields. One of them caught hold of the weapon, and the victim allegedly was struck on the head from behind with a sharp-edged weapon by one of the accused and fell. Beatings from both sides followed until other villagers intervened, after which the assailants ran away. The victim died of the head wound. Prosecution evidence included eyewitness depositions of several persons from the victim's group, the post-mortem report describing a deep incised wound to the head with the underlying bone and brain membranes cut, injury reports for both sides, the first information report lodged that night, a spot inspection memo and site plan, and recovery of a blood-stained lathi and blood-stained clothing of the injured and deceased.
offence_severity: Not stated for s.302 (charged offence). Judgment states that s.326 IPC carries imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and fine.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a single deep incised head wound (bone and brain membranes cut); complainant-side injury to palm; superficial injuries to accused No. 5.
number_of_offences: 3 charged against accused No. 5 (ss.148, 302, 324/149 IPC as convicted at trial); 2 finally upheld (s.304 Part I and s.148 IPC)
premeditation_planning: Court found accused had assembled with lethal weapons and waited in hiding for the complainant party to arrive; no separate finding of premeditated planning to kill.
motive: Court accepted: provocation from repeated unauthorised entry on the accused's fields. Trial court also found a revenge motive (alleged: revenge over the way dispute).
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-11 corroborated by PW-5, 6, 7, 8; post-mortem and injury reports; spot inspection report; recovery of blood-stained lathi and clothing; findings that accused were aggressors.
witness_credibility: Prosecution witnesses' evidence accepted as truthful by the trial court and not disturbed; Supreme Court found High Court's reasoning flawed when it departed from that evidence.
post_offence_conduct: Accused ran away after other villagers intervened (as recorded in the FIR and headnote).
custody_duration: Approximately five months (period already undergone per High Court sentence); exact custody period not stated.
bail_history: Bail bonds cancelled; accused directed to surrender within six weeks of relaxation of COVID-19 lockdown. Earlier bail grant or refusal not stated.
trial_duration: offence: 14.08.1981; trial judgment: 21.7.1982; High Court: 05.11.2007; Supreme Court: 06.05.2020
legal_representation: For State (appellant): Dr. Manish Singhvi, Sr. Adv., with D.K. Devesh and Milind Kumar. For accused (respondent): Sushil Kumar Jain, Sr. Adv., with H.D. Thanvi and Rishi Matoliya.
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; case committed to Sessions Court in February 1982; full trial completed with 14 prosecution witnesses.
procedural_irregularity: High Court's cryptic judgment applied a wrong assumption of provocation and private defence, and it imposed sentence for s.326 equal to time served; Supreme Court disapproved this approach.
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted ss.148, 302, 324/149 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: s.302 converted to s.326, sentence reduced to period undergone. Supreme Court: partly allowed; convicted s.304 Part I and s.148; 10 years' simple imprisonment.
prosecution_argument: State sought restoration of the s.302 conviction and life imprisonment for accused No. 5; appeal pursued against him only, on nature of offence and sentence.
defence_argument: Accused could challenge conviction without a formal appeal; incident was sudden due to provocation; blow was in private defence, so no intention to cause death; benefit of doubt; old age and health; if excessive private defence, benefit should go to accused.
legal_principle_applied: Where accused are aggressors, the right of private defence does not arise, so excess of private defence cannot be considered; s.300 exceptions (grave and sudden provocation) assessed to decide between s.304 Part I and Part II.
precedent_relied_upon: Chandrakant Patil v. State through CBI (1998) 3 SCC 38; Sumer Singh v. Surajbhan Singh (2014) 7 SCC 323; State of Rajasthan v. Ramanand (2017) 5 SCC 695 (accused's right to challenge conviction); Gottipulla Venkatasiva Subbrayanam (1970) 1 SCC 235, Deo Narain (1973) 1 SCC 347, Subramani (2002) 7 SCC 210, Gajey Singh (2009) 11 SCC 414 (cited by defence; Court did not dilate on them).
sentencing_rationale: High Court's sentence of about five months was inadequate given the nature and gravity of the offence and the background of the case; a ten-year term was imposed for s.304 Part I.
judicial_mitigating_factors: Grave and sudden provocation from repeated unauthorised entry on the accused's fields; provocation not invited by the accused party; single blow.
judicial_aggravating_factors: Fatal blow to a vital part of the victim's head with intention to cause death; accused was the aggressor; age plea rejected.
other_sentence_order: Compensation of Rs.50,000 to next of kin of deceased (if not already paid); set-off of period undergone under s.428 Cr.P.C.; bail bonds cancelled; surrender ordered.

case_title: Amar Singh v. The State (NCT of Delhi)
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute (alleged by the defence): the defence said the victim had been accused of murdering the father of accused Inderjeet Singh. The Court did not accept this.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.506; Arms Act s.25 and s.27 (charged against accused Inderjeet Singh); conviction under Arms Act s.27 for Inderjeet Singh
evidence_type: Eyewitness (sole remaining eyewitness, PW-1); medical (post-mortem and MLC); recovery (knife and hockey sticks)
confession: Disclosure statements led to recovery of the knife and hockey sticks; the Court did not rely on them as a confession
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34 and sentenced to life imprisonment with fine of Rs.5000 each; accused Inderjeet Singh also convicted under Arms Act s.27 and sentenced to one year rigorous imprisonment, concurrent
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld (judgment dated 09.05.2014)
neutral_facts: On the night of the incident, the victim was walking on foot with his two brothers toward a taxi stand in a market area at about 10 pm. Three men attacked the victim. Two were said to have struck him with hockey sticks and one with a knife. When the brothers tried to help, the attackers brandished their weapons and threatened to kill anyone who intervened. The victim collapsed and the attackers fled. After some time a police PCR van took the victim to a hospital, where he was declared brought dead. The post-mortem examination recorded around fifteen antemortem injuries caused by a sharp-edged weapon. The cause of death was given as shock from multiple antemortem injuries. Police recovered a knife and hockey sticks following statements by the accused persons. A medical clinic was located nearby. The hospital record initially listed the victim as unknown and recorded a head constable as the person who brought him in. The brothers said the attack lasted about five minutes. The sole eyewitness account came from one brother; the other brother and a third witness did not support the prosecution account at trial. The recovered knife had a broken, blunt tip. The doctor was not shown the knife to comment on whether it could cause the injuries.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock due to multiple antemortem injuries (about 15 injuries, including sharp-edged stab and incised wounds)
number_of_offences: 4 charged (IPC s.302, s.506, Arms Act s.25 and s.27; IPC s.34 is a common-intention provision); 0 finally upheld
motive: Not identified. Alleged by the defence: the victim's brothers had a motive to falsely implicate the accused because the victim was accused of murdering the father of accused Inderjeet Singh. The Court did not decide this.
key_evidence_accepted: The Court relied on the post-mortem finding of cause of death, but did not accept the eyewitness account or the MLC/recovery evidence as reliable
witness_credibility: PW-1 (sole eyewitness) found not wholly reliable and not shown to be present, given his unnatural conduct and the timing discrepancy. PW-11 and PW-5 turned hostile. The MLC (PW-17) entries cast doubt on the brothers' presence at the hospital.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 03.08.1990; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 09.05.2014; Supreme Court: 12.10.2020
legal_representation: Accused: Dushyant Dave, Senior Advocate (with others listed). State: Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, ASG
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial completed with 27 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: Investigating officer did not show the recovered knife to the doctor; the MLC entries (name recorded as unknown, head constable as the person who brought the victim in, 'and brothers' added) were noted as irregular
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed (09.05.2014). Supreme Court: appeals allowed, accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: Concurrent findings of guilt rest on a reliable eyewitness; hostile witness evidence can be relied on in part; investigation lapses do not make the case doubtful where direct evidence is corroborated by medical evidence
defence_argument: The incident was inherently improbable; PW-1's conduct was unnatural, making his presence doubtful; the conviction rests on an uncorroborated sole eyewitness; the knife with a broken tip could not have caused the injuries; the victim's brothers had a motive to falsely implicate
legal_principle_applied: A sole eyewitness may be relied on if wholly reliable (Evidence Act s.134), but where doubts exist the Court insists on corroboration; unnatural conduct, medical discrepancy and investigative lapses can make conviction unsafe; benefit of doubt to accused
precedent_relied_upon: Kartarey v. State of U.P. (1976) 1 SCC 172; Ishwar Singh v. State of U.P. (1976) 4 SCC 355 (relied on). Also Sunil Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2003) 11 SCC 367 and Selvaraj v. State of Tamil Nadu (1976) 4 SCC 343 (referred to)
other_sentence_order: Release of appellants forthwith unless required in any other case

statutory_provisions: IPC s.307; Arms Act s.27
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; medical (MLR and doctor); forensic/ballistic (CFSL report); recovery of pistol at arrest
aggravating_circumstances: Pistol aimed at the complainant's face after a threat to kill; accused was intoxicated; loaded service pistol used

neutral_facts: On 10 July 1999, the victim, an advocate, was sitting in his residential office dictating to his stenographer, with his clerk present. At about 5:30 pm, the accused, a police constable, entered the office in an inebriated condition, claiming to be a beat officer, and asked for water. After drinking the water, the accused pulled out his service pistol, pointed it at the victim and said he would kill ten people that day. The accused asked the victim to stand with raised hands and directed the clerk and stenographer to leave the room. The accused then moved around the table towards the victim and pulled the lever to ready the weapon. The victim lunged and pushed the accused's hand upward, and a bullet struck the ceiling. No one was injured. The accused tried to fire again, but a bullet fell from the pistol. Household members entered and raised an alarm, and the accused fled, leaving a wireless set behind. Police arrived within about 10 to 15 minutes and arrested the accused nearby with the pistol still in hand. A medical examination recorded that the accused was under the influence of alcohol; the accused declined to give urine or blood samples. A forensic report found that the cartridge recovered from the office was fired from the accused's pistol. The stenographer testified that he saw the shot fired through a mesh door, and the clerk testified to the accused's drunken state and to hearing the shot. The victim testified to the sequence of events.
physical_harm: No injury caused to the complainant or any other person
premeditation_planning: Not found. Court said no planning was proved, suggesting the act may have been impulsive
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Ocular evidence of complainant (PW-2) and stenographer (PW-4) that the accused pointed and fired the pistol; medical report and testimony of doctor (PW-7) on intoxication; CFSL ballistic report linking the cartridge to the accused's service pistol; PW-13 evidence on semi-automatic firing mode
witness_credibility: Complainant and PW-4 found categorical and corroborated by medical and ballistic evidence; minor inconsistencies not material; defence version found incredulous; absence of motive did not make the eyewitness account untrustworthy
post_offence_conduct: Fled the office, leaving wireless set and scooter behind; found nearby by police with pistol still in hand; declined to give urine or blood samples
custody_duration: Sentence already undergone: 3 months and 19 days (per court; custody period not separately stated)
bail_history: On bail at the Supreme Court stage; bail bonds discharged. Earlier bail history not stated

legal_representation: Appellant: Jasbir Singh Malik and Ms. Usha Nandini V (Advocates). State: Manpreet Singh Doabia, Anil Kumar and Sudarshan Singh Rawat (Advocates)

prosecution_argument: Concurrent findings of fact limit interference under Art.136; no substantial question of law arises; conviction should stand

legal_principle_applied: s.307 IPC requires intention or knowledge to cause death plus an overt act, injury not necessary; absence of motive not fatal; limited Art.136 interference with concurrent findings; post-1988 s.27 Arms Act requires contravention of s.5 or s.7; proportionality in sentencing
precedent_relied_upon: Relied on: State of M.P. v. Saleem @ Chamaru (2005) 5 SCC 554; Bipin Kumar Mondal v. State of West Bengal (2010) 12 SCC 91. Also cited: Shivaji Genu Mohite (1973) 3 SCC 219. sentencing_rationale: Sentence was disproportionate to the offence given the mitigating factors, so it was reduced to the period already undergone
judicial_mitigating_factors: No motive or planning (possible impulsive act); no injury caused; long passage of time with clean record before and after; unblemished service record apart from this incident; suspension in 1999 and dismissal in 2007 treated as social sanction
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds discharged; s.27 Arms Act conviction and sentence set aside

case_title: Jaikam Khan v. The State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Relative: Momin Khan was a son of the deceased father and brother of the deceased Shaukeen Khan; Jaikam Khan was a first cousin; Sajid was a nephew of Momin Khan. Prior dispute over management of a brick-kiln and its accounts involving Momin Khan and the family.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; Arms Act s.25/4
weapon: Knives (knife, chhuriyan and a daav recovered by the police)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony of two interested, related witnesses; recovery of weapons and clothes; arrest evidence; site plans; FIR; forensic and fingerprint material (not relied on)
confession: Alleged confession by the accused recorded in the arrest-cum-recovery memo (Ex Ka-49); not relied on beyond facts distinctly discovered under s.27 Evidence Act
aggravating_circumstances: Six persons killed with knives, including a woman, a child aged about 8 and elderly parents
trial_court_outcome: All four accused convicted under IPC s.302/34 and sentenced to death; accused 1, 3 and 4 also convicted under Arms Act s.25/4 with three years RI and fine of Rs 5,000
high_court_outcome: Appeals of accused 1, 3 and 4 dismissed and death sentence confirmed; accused 2 (Nazra) acquitted
neutral_facts: On the evening of 23 January 2014, around 8.30 pm, six members of one family were attacked and killed with knives at their house in a village. The prosecution case is that four persons, including the accused, entered the family compound carrying knives. According to the prosecution, the victims were killed in the courtyard, the verandah, rooms in the middle portion of the house and an upstairs room. Two relatives of the victims who were present in the house said they hid and watched the attack; their accounts formed the main eyewitness evidence. Villagers gathered after the incident. The surviving relatives went to the police station to lodge a written report and a first information report was registered. The investigating officer prepared site plans on the basis of information given by the witnesses. Later that night police arrested three of the accused at a crossroads and recovered knives from a room and from open fields near the house, following statements attributed to the accused. Blood-stained clothes were later recovered from another house. Forensic science reports were obtained. A fingerprint expert report and a dog squad report were not placed on record, and no independent villager witness was examined.
physical_harm: Six persons killed by knife assaults; injuries not described in detail in the judgment
premeditation_planning: Not found by the Supreme Court; the trial court's finding of a pre-planned crime was held to be conjecture
motive: alleged: dispute over management and accounts of a brick-kiln between Momin Khan and the deceased father, brother and PW-1. Court held no motive proved against accused 3 and 4 and no strong motive proved against accused 1
key_evidence_accepted: Court accepted only that the two eyewitnesses could at most have seen the assault on some of the deceased; it did not accept the eyewitness account as sufficient alone, and rejected the clothes recovery and the s.27 recoveries
witness_credibility: PW-1 and PW-2 are interested and related witnesses, neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable; their version is hard to reconcile with the site plans and they could not have seen all assaults. Investigating officer admitted their hideouts were not recorded in the site plan
post_offence_conduct: Prosecution alleged the accused fled through the rear gate, returned and changed clothes; the court found this a mystery and gave no weight to it
trial_duration: offence: 23 January 2014; trial judgment: 2 January 2016; High Court: 18 May 2018; Supreme Court: 15 December 2021
legal_representation: Accused 1: Smt. Nitya Ramakrishnan, Senior Counsel; Accused 3 and 4: Shri Dama Seshadri Naidu; PW-1 (appellant against acquittal of accused 2): Shri Anant Agarwal; State of Uttar Pradesh: Shri Vinod Diwakar, AAG
investigation_status: FIR registered on PW-1's complaint; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: No independent villager witnesses examined; fingerprint expert report and dog squad report not placed on record; the trial court's reasoning was criticised as conjectural
appeal_history: Trial court: all four convicted under s.302/34 IPC and sentenced to death. High Court: accused 1, 3, 4 appeals dismissed and death sentence confirmed; accused 2 acquitted. Supreme Court: appeals of accused 1, 3, 4 allowed; PW-1's appeal against acquittal of accused 2 dismissed
prosecution_argument: Concurrent findings of conviction should not be disturbed; absence of kitchen and bathroom in site plans is not fatal; eyewitness testimony corroborated by the FIR; discrepancies not fatal to ocular evidence; accused gave no explanation under s.313
defence_argument: Eyewitnesses are interested and related; site plans omit kitchen and bathroom; independent witnesses not examined; no call made on mobile phones and C.D.Rs rejected; recoveries of clothes and weapons farcical; no motive for accused 3 and 4; no reasons for death sentence
legal_principle_applied: Interested witnesses scrutinised with care and corroboration required where neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable; non-examination of independent witnesses leads to adverse inference; s.27 admits only information distinctly relating to discovery; motive relevant where eyewitnesses are not wholly reliable; prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt
precedent_relied_upon: Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras (1957) SCR 981; State of Rajasthan v. Teja Singh (2001) 3 SCC 147; Joydeb Patra v. State of West Bengal (2014) 12 SCC 444; State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh (1974) 3 SCC 277; Anand Ramachandra Chougule v. Sidarai Laxman Chougala (2019) 8 SCC 50; Piara Singh v. State of Punjab (1977) 4 SCC 452 and Anil Phukan v. State of Assam (1993) 3 SCC 282 (referred); Pulukuri Kottayya v. King Emperor AIR 1947 PC 67 (referred)
other_sentence_order: Release of accused 1, 3 and 4 forthwith if not required in any other offence; PW-1's appeal against acquittal of accused 2 dismissed; court deprecated the manner in which the trial court and High Court dealt with the death sentence

case_title: Achhar Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour; prior enmity/dispute (alleged land dispute, prior litigation and social boycott of the complainant's family)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.452 (Budhi Singh); IPC s.452, s.326, s.323 (Achhar Singh)
weapon: Axe (used by both appellants); other accused had sickles, spears and sticks
evidence_type: Eyewitness; medical (post-mortem and injury evidence); recovery (axe and house articles); FIR
aggravating_circumstances: Axe blow to the head of an elderly victim, with knowledge that it would in all probability cause death
trial_court_outcome: All accused acquitted by Additional Sessions Judge, Mandi, giving benefit of doubt (24.02.1998)
high_court_outcome: Acquittal of the two appellants set aside; Budhi Singh convicted under ss.302 and 452 IPC (life imprisonment with fine); Achhar Singh convicted under ss.452, 326 and 323 IPC (five years RI with fine); acquittal of the other five accused upheld
offence_finally_established: Budhi Singh: IPC s.302 (murder) and s.452 (house trespass). Achhar Singh: IPC s.452, s.326 (grievous hurt by dangerous weapon) and s.323 (hurt).
neutral_facts: On a night in February, the complainant's family had returned home from a wedding function in a nearby village with food. At about 8 pm, while the family was eating, a group of villagers came to the house, shouted for the complainant and his father to come out, and began pelting stones. The family retreated and bolted the door, but the group broke it open and entered the house armed with axes, sickles, spears and sticks. It is alleged that one accused struck an elderly relative of the complainant on the head with an axe, causing death on the spot, and that another accused struck the complainant's father with an axe, causing him to faint. Other assailants beat the complainant with sticks, and he escaped to the roof. Some bystanders intervened and the attackers left. The complainant walked through the night to the police station and lodged a First Information Report the next morning. Police recovered sticks, a blood-stained stone, glass splinters, pieces of wood, broken door pieces, a broken bulb and blood-stained soil from the house, and an axe from one accused. Blood marks were also found on a path outside the house. The post-mortem found one fatal sharp-edged head injury, which the doctor said could have been caused by the recovered axe. The injured man had incised wounds on the face and back of the skull and a facial bone fracture, which the doctor said could be caused by an axe. The complainant, his wife and his father gave consistent eyewitness accounts of the attack.
physical_harm: Death of the elderly victim from a single fatal sharp-edged head injury (axe); injured male with incised wounds on face and posterior skull, facial bone fracture, and other grievous and simple injuries
number_of_offences: 7 charged (IPC ss.147, 148, 452, 506, 323, 302, 326, framed against the accused persons collectively); 4 finally upheld (IPC ss.302, 452, 326, 323 across the two appellants)
financial_property_loss: Property damage to the house (broken door, windows, utensils); no monetary value stated
premeditation_planning: Not stated. The High Court noted no common intention to kill was suggested; premeditation was not addressed.
motive: alleged: land dispute (purchase of the complainant's land) and prior litigation; social boycott of the complainant's family
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent eyewitness testimony (P.W.1, P.W.11, P.W.12) that the appellant Budhi Singh gave the fatal axe blow and Achhar Singh attacked with an axe; post-mortem report; doctor's testimony; axe recovery; recoveries from the house corroborated by P.W.14 and P.W.16
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses exaggerated but their core account was consistent and matched the medical evidence; exaggerations were separable from truth; no reason shown to falsely implicate; trial court erred in discarding the evidence
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Bail bonds cancelled by the Supreme Court; grant of bail earlier not described
trial_duration: offence: 23.02.1996; trial judgment: 24.02.1998; High Court: 12.05.2010 and 27.05.2010; Supreme Court: 07.05.2021
legal_representation: Appellants: J.S. Attri and R. Basant (Senior Advocates) with others. State: Abhinav Mukerji, AAG.
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed against seven persons; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted by the Supreme Court (the High Court considered and explained the delay in lodging the FIR)
appeal_history: Trial court: all acquitted (24.02.1998). High Court: acquittal of two appellants set aside and convictions recorded; acquittal of the other five upheld. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed, High Court convictions maintained.
prosecution_argument: Relying on Sheikh Hasib and Dharma Rama Bhagare, the FIR is not substantive evidence; witnesses' credibility is not affected by relationship or minor discrepancies or exaggerations (Kishan Chand, Leela Ram); inconsistent evidence against one accused cannot benefit another (Gangadhar Behera, Prabhu Dayal)
defence_argument: Trial court's view was a possible view and interference required perversity (Murugesan, Aruvelu); witnesses exaggerated and falsely implicated; medical evidence showed only one head injury; axe recovered from public place; blood trail outside the house; police arrival timing; no reason for the appellant to attack neighbours on his daughter's wedding day
legal_principle_applied: Presumption of innocence is doubled after acquittal; appellate courts show self-restraint and interfere only for perversity, but the High Court may re-appreciate evidence fully; exaggeration must be separated from falsity; benefit of doubt only where a firm conclusion cannot be reached
precedent_relied_upon: Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka (2007) 4 SCC 415; State of AP v. M. Madhusudhan Rao (2008) 15 SCC 582; Raveen Kumar v. State of HP 2020 SCC OnLine SC 869; Murugesan v. State (2012) 10 SCC 383; Aruvelu v. State (2009) 10 SCC 206; Hari Chand v. State of Delhi (1996) 9 SCC 112; Sucha Singh v. State of Punjab (2003) 7 SCC 643; Babu v. State of Kerala (2010) 9 SCC 189; Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1953 SC 364; Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab (1976) 4 SCC 369
judicial_aggravating_factors: Axe blow to the head of an elderly victim, with knowledge that it would in all probability cause death
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds cancelled; appellants directed to undergo the remainder of their sentence

case_title: Kala Singh @ Gurnam Singh v. State of Punjab
accused_victim_relationship: Acquaintance (drank together); prior dispute over alleged theft of the appellant's pigeon
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34 and s.201 (charged); final conviction under IPC s.304 Part II r/w s.34 and s.201
evidence_type: Chemical examiner report; other evidence and material on record (testimony not detailed in the judgment)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden fight in heat of passion over sudden quarrel; no pre-meditation; no intention to cause death; counsel submitted appellant had served over three years
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.302/34 and 201 IPC; life rigorous imprisonment (s.302/34) and 3 years RI (s.201), plus fine
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 713 DB of 2003) partly allowed: conviction altered to s.304 Part I r/w s.34; 12 years RI and Rs.10,000 fine; s.201 conviction maintained
offence_finally_established: IPC s.304 Part II r/w s.34 (culpable homicide); IPC s.201
neutral_facts: On the day in question, the accused, a co-accused and the victim obtained a bottle of liquor from a house and went to a bridge over a minor canal, where they drank it. A quarrel broke out between the accused and the victim, the accused alleging that the victim had stolen the accused's pigeon. The scuffle took place on the spur of the moment. During the scuffle the co-accused, who was carrying a rod, struck the victim on the head with it. The victim fell down and did not respond even after about half an hour. The accused and the co-accused then moved the body and placed it in a minor canal. The incident occurred one day before panchayat elections. Evidence on record included a chemical examiner's report showing that the victim had consumed liquor, along with other material on record describing the sudden nature of the fight.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a rod blow to the head; body then placed in minor canal
number_of_offences: 2 charged; 2 finally upheld in modified form (s.304 Part II/34 substituted for s.302/34, and s.201)
financial_property_loss: Alleged theft of the appellant's pigeon; no monetary value stated
premeditation_planning: Court found no premeditation; the quarrel and scuffle arose on the spur of the moment
motive: Quarrel over alleged theft of the appellant's pigeon (sudden quarrel accepted on the evidence)
key_evidence_accepted: Evidence on record showing a sudden scuffle without intention to kill; chemical examiner report showing deceased had consumed liquor (as noted by High Court)
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Body shifted to the minor canal after the blow when there was no response for half an hour
custody_duration: Not stated (counsel submitted the appellant had served more than three years of sentence)
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 08.02.2019 and 01.03.2019; Supreme Court: 21.09.2021
legal_representation: Appellant: Bharat Sood, P. S. Sudheer, Advocates. State of Punjab: Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Ms. Mandakini Singh, Karanvir Gogia, Ms. Shivangi Singhal, Ms. Ashima Mandla, Advocates
investigation_status: Trial completed; accused convicted by Sessions Court
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted ss.302/34 and 201, life RI. High Court: s.302 altered to s.304 Part I r/w s.34, 12 years RI, s.201 maintained. Supreme Court: s.304 Part II r/w s.34, 7 years RI, fine maintained, s.201 maintained
prosecution_argument: No grounds to interfere with conviction or sentence; leniency already shown; Uday Singh distinguishable on facts
defence_argument: No intention to kill; sudden fight in heat of passion; High Court should have convicted under s.304 Part II, not Part I (relying on Uday Singh); request to reduce sentence given over three years served
legal_principle_applied: Absence of intention to cause death or such bodily injury as likely to cause death, with sudden fight in heat of passion, warrants conviction under s.304 Part II rather than Part I
precedent_relied_upon: Uday Singh v. State of U.P. (2002) 7 SCC 79; Shahajan Ali & Ors. etc. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors. etc. (2017) 11 SC 807
sentencing_rationale: Conversion to s.304 Part II reflected the absence of intention to kill and the sudden fight; the judgment gives no separate sentencing reasoning for seven years
judicial_mitigating_factors: Sudden fight in heat of passion upon sudden quarrel; no pre-meditation; no intention to cause death
other_sentence_order: Rs.10,000 fine (s.304 Part II/34) maintained; s.201 conviction, 3 years RI and Rs.500 fine maintained

case_title: Sadakat Kotwar and Anr. v. The State of Jharkhand
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
evidence_type: Eyewitness (two injured eyewitnesses), medical (injury reports), other prosecution witness testimony
aggravating_circumstances: Deadly weapon (dagger) used; grievous stab injuries near chest and stomach, a vital part of the body; accused pushed the victim's husband out of the house before the stabbing
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.307 r/w s.34; sentence not stated in the judgment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction under s.307 r/w s.34 upheld
offence_finally_established: Attempt to murder under IPC s.307 r/w s.34
neutral_facts: The prosecution case is that two accused persons pushed the victim's husband out of a house. Thereafter, the first accused stabbed the victim with a dagger in the ribs, and the second accused stabbed another injured person with a dagger on the right side of the stomach and on the left ribs. The prosecution examined ten witnesses. Two of them were the injured persons, who both supported the prosecution account. Other prosecution witnesses gave consistent statements. The medical evidence recorded an incised wound of about one inch by one inch, muscle deep with haematoma, on the left side of the other injured person's chest in the fourth and fifth intercostal space. It also recorded an incised wound of about one inch by half an inch, pleura deep, in the eighth intercostal space of the left half of the victim's chest. Both injuries were described as caused by a sharp cutting instrument. No sudden quarrel was alleged, and the blows did not appear to have been struck in the heat of the moment.
physical_harm: Two injured persons with grievous incised stab wounds to the chest and stomach/left ribs; no death
premeditation_planning: Not found; court noted no sudden quarrel or heat of the moment, and inferred intention from the weapon, body part and injury
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of injured eyewitnesses PW7 and PW8; consistent testimony of PW1, PW2, PW4 and PW10; injury descriptions on the medical record
witness_credibility: Injured eyewitnesses PW7 and PW8 found credible; no reason to doubt; other witnesses consistent
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 01.07.2019; Supreme Court: 12.11.2021
legal_representation: Accused: Shree Prakash Sinha, Ms. Mohua Sinha, Rakesh Mishra, Nawalendra Kumar, Shekhar Kumar (Advs.). State: Arunabh Chowdhury, AAG, with Ms. Barnali Chowdhury, Ms. Pragya Baghel, Shantanu Sagar, Vishnu Sharma, Abhishek Roy (Advs.)
investigation_status: Trial completed with 10 prosecution witnesses; FIR and charge sheet dates not stated
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.307 r/w s.34 IPC. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld (01.07.2019). Supreme Court: appeal dismissed (12.11.2021)
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: The offence at most falls under s.323 IPC because it was a single blow/injury, not attempt to murder
legal_principle_applied: Intention inferred from weapon, body part chosen and nature of injury; a single blow on a vital part can support s.307 conviction; injured eyewitness evidence has great evidentiary value
precedent_relied_upon: State of M.P. v. Mansingh (2003) 10 SCC 414 (relied on); Mahesh Balmiki v. State of M.P. (2000) 1 SCC 319 (referred to); Jai Narain Mishra v. State of Bihar (1971) 3 SCC 762 (held inapplicable)

other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Parubai v. State of Maharashtra
victim_age: Not stated for a single victim; two child victims: Akash aged 5 years, Nikita aged 2 years
accused_victim_relationship: Relative: co-wife (the deceased Mandabai was the first wife of the accused's husband); the accused was step-mother of the two children
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.436
evidence_type: Circumstantial (primary); chemical analysis of frock; recovery of kerosene can (disbelieved); dying declarations; extra-judicial confession (disbelieved); medical evidence
confession: Extra-judicial confession to father-in-law (PW-1) that kerosene was sprinkled and fire set; disbelieved by the High Court as not trustworthy and not relied on by the Supreme Court
aggravating_circumstances: Death of three persons, two of them small children; incident described as gruesome
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.302 and 436; sentence imposed (amount/term not stated in judgment)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed (judgment dated 12.10.2017)
neutral_facts: On the intervening night of 2 and 3 August 2006, at about 2.30 to 3.00 am, a fire broke out in a small house of three rooms. The house was occupied by the accused, the accused's husband, the husband's first wife, the first wife's two children, the husband's parents and a servant who occupied one room. The husband had gone to another town that day to buy tractor tyres, and the mother-in-law had gone to her daughter's home. The accused came out of the house without any injury. The first wife and her daughter ran out with burn injuries, while the son died inside the house. The father-in-law, who had been sleeping on a cot outside, woke in the confusion and arranged for a jeep to take the injured to hospital. The first wife and daughter died the next day from their burns. Police seized the daughter's burnt frock from the scene under a panchnama and sent it for chemical analysis, which reported kerosene residues. A kerosene can said to smell of kerosene was recovered from nearby bushes at the accused's instance, but it was not sent for chemical analysis. The father-in-law stated that the accused had made an extra-judicial confession to him that kerosene had been sprinkled and the fire set. A sister of the first wife gave evidence of an oral dying declaration, and a police head constable recorded a separate dying declaration. The first wife's declaration said the household slept in the house with a lantern lit at night, and that cooking and tractor diesel were kept there. Medical evidence was presented on the cause of the deaths.
physical_harm: Deaths of the first wife (Mandabai) and daughter (Nikita) from burn injuries the next day in hospital; son (Akash) burnt to death inside the house; accused unhurt
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.302 and s.436); 0 finally upheld
financial_property_loss: Destruction of the house and adjoining cowshed
motive: Not identified. Alleged by the High Court: desire for domestic dominance and removal of the first wife and children; the Supreme Court found this could not be accepted as a strong motive
key_evidence_accepted: Chemical analysis of Nikita's frock reporting kerosene residues, taken at face value but held insufficient alone; deceased's declaration that kerosene was used for lanterns and cooking; admitted layout of the house and non-injury of other occupants; PW-1's account that he was sleeping outside
witness_credibility: High Court disbelieved PW-1's extra-judicial confession account and the oral dying declaration; the Supreme Court relied on PW-1's account of sleeping outside and waking on the accused's shouts, and held the disbelieved evidence could not support conviction
post_offence_conduct: Came out of the house unhurt and raised shouts; High Court inferred she did not alarm or rescue the others, which the Supreme Court held could not by itself establish guilt
bail_history: On interim bail at the time of the Supreme Court judgment
trial_duration: offence: 2/3 August 2006; trial judgment: 16.11.2007; High Court: 12.10.2017; Supreme Court: August 10, 2021
legal_representation: Appellant: Sudhanshu S. Choudhari, Adv. State of Maharashtra (respondent): Sachin Patil, Rahul Chitnis, Aaditya A. Pande, Geo Joseph, Advs.
investigation_status: Complaint lodged by father-in-law implicating the accused; investigation by PSI Phad; trial completed; charge sheet not stated
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.302 and 436 IPC. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction set aside, accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Not stated
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain pointing to guilt that must be true, not may be true; suspicion cannot replace proof; failure to explain under s.106 is only an additional link once other links are proved
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; Devilal v. State of Rajasthan (2019) 19 SCC 447
other_sentence_order: Appellant set at liberty; bail bond discharged

case_title: Jarnail Singh & Anr. v. State of Punjab
accused_occupation: Bus conductors of the Punjab Roadways depot
accused_victim_relationship: Co-worker (conductors allegedly acting in connivance with the General Manager)
evidence_type: Documentary (seized tickets, way-bills, enquiry report), recovery evidence, oral testimony of inspection team and checking officers
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted the three conductors; three years rigorous imprisonment, Rs.1000 fine, six months additional in default. Four accused acquitted; eleven convicted in total
high_court_outcome: Appeal disposed; conviction of the three conductors confirmed; other accused acquitted
neutral_facts: A complaint by a bus driver of a state roadways depot alleged that the depot's general manager, in connivance with conductors and others, had been selling and using tickets printed on his own and sold through persons who collected money for him, causing large loss to the depot. Following the complaint, an inspection committee of three officers checked three buses on two routes on a given day. The inspectors took into possession old tickets, tickets whose value had been increased by affixing stamps, driver diaries and way-bills, and cash found in a conductor's ticket bag. The committee recorded statements of conductors, the general manager, a traffic manager and an assistant mechanical engineer, and prepared an enquiry report. Only a photocopy of that report was available. The seized tickets were later shown to two witnesses at a police station. None had been sealed, and tickets from the three buses were not segregated. Neither witness had been present at the recovery, and neither could say which tickets related to which bus. The inspection witnesses could not identify which conductor had been carrying which tickets. No passenger who had bought such tickets was examined. The prosecution case rested on these tickets and the inspection report.
physical_harm: None mentioned
financial_property_loss: Alleged loss of crores of rupees to the depot; not proved. Excess cash allegedly found at inspection was also not proved
motive: alleged: financial gain from selling self-printed tickets through persons who collected money for the general manager
key_evidence_accepted: None. The Court did not rely on the seized tickets or the enquiry report
witness_credibility: Court found PW-8 and PW-15 could not connect the tickets to the buses or the conductors; PW-20, PW-21 and PW-22 could not identify which accused had which tickets
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Already on bail at the Supreme Court stage; bail-bonds discharged
trial_duration: offence: 11.05.1996 (inspection; complaint dated 04.05.1996); trial judgment: 28.01.2002; High Court: 14.09.2009; Supreme Court: 12.07.2022
legal_representation: Appellants: Neeraj Kumar Jain, Sr. Adv., with D. P. Singh and others. State of Punjab: R. K. Rathore and Ms. Jaspreet Gogia
investigation_status: FIR registered; police report under s.173(2) CrPC filed; charges framed against 15 persons; 23 prosecution witnesses examined
procedural_irregularity: Enquiry report produced only as a photocopy; original's existence and loss not proved; State did not pursue secondary evidence; seized tickets not sealed or segregated

case_title: Sumitha Pradeep v. Arun Kumar C.K & Anr.
accused_occupation: Advocate (as stated in the Sessions Court's order, recording the victim's counsel's submission)
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (maternal uncle of the victim)
evidence_type: Victim's statements (s.164 CrPC and to police and magistrate), medical examination, counselling records, school report
aggravating_circumstances: Accused is the victim's maternal uncle; victim aged 12; allegations of sexual assault; victim's academic performance adversely affected by trauma
trial_court_outcome: No trial held; Sessions Court declined anticipatory bail (order dated 4 July 2022)
high_court_outcome: Conditional anticipatory bail granted to accused (order dated 25 July 2022)
neutral_facts: The victim, a 12-year-old girl, is the niece of the accused, who is her maternal uncle. It is alleged that on 14 December 2021, at the accused's house where the victim and her mother had stayed for some days, the accused asked the victim to sit on his lap. He then hugged her, kissed her on the cheeks and tried to kiss her on the lips. It is alleged that he attempted to remove her top, touched her breasts and made sexual comments, and that the victim cried out, after which he released her. The allegations state that the incident occurred in an upstairs bedroom while no other person was present. The victim, previously an excellent student, afterwards declined markedly in her studies, with her grades falling from mostly A grades in sixth standard to mostly C grades in seventh standard. She was taken for counselling. In the first session she did not open up, and in the second session she disclosed the incident. She had not told her mother earlier, out of fear. The complaint was made about six months after the incident. A first information report was registered on 27 May 2022. A medical examination of the victim was conducted, and her statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was recorded. Her statements to the police and to a magistrate describe the incident. The counsellor's statement and the victim's school report form part of the material.
physical_harm: No physical injury stated; psychological trauma and decline in academic performance
number_of_offences: 7 charged; 0 finally upheld (no conviction; accused not tried)
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Victim's s.164 CrPC statement, read with the FIR allegations, treated as supporting serious allegations (prima facie, for bail purposes)
witness_credibility: Not assessed; the Supreme Court expressly declined to express views on the merits
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Sessions Court refused anticipatory bail (4 July 2022); High Court granted conditional anticipatory bail (25 July 2022); Supreme Court set aside the High Court's grant
trial_duration: offence: 14-12-2021; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 25-07-2022; Supreme Court: 21-10-2022
legal_representation: Accused (respondent no.1): Raghenth Basant, Ms. Zehra Khan, Ajay Krishna, Harshad V. Hameed, Dileep Poolakkot, Mrs. Ashly Harshad. Appellant (victim's mother): Gaurav Agrawal, Ms. Anu K. Joy, Alim Anvar, Arvind Gupta. State: not separately shown
investigation_status: FIR registered (Crime No. 442 of 2022, 27 May 2022); medical examination and s.164 statement done; charge-sheet reportedly filed (per accused's counsel, not verified by Court)
procedural_irregularity: High Court's para 9 observations were unwarranted and overlooked FIR allegations; High Court appears not to have followed the binding coordinate-bench decision in Joy
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions Court): anticipatory bail refused. High Court: anticipatory bail granted with conditions. Supreme Court: appeal by victim's mother allowed, High Court order set aside
prosecution_argument: High Court erred in granting anticipatory bail in a serious POCSO case; victim's trauma and academic decline; s.29 POCSO presumption; risk of interference with investigation
