case_title: State through the Inspector of Police v. Laly @ Manikandan & Another etc.
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute (prosecution case): the accused allegedly suspected the deceased of informing on the whereabouts of a friend of the accused; relationship between accused and victim otherwise not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.302 r/w s.34; charge sheet also cites IPC ss.341, 506(2) and s.3(1) TNPPDL Act
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW1, sole reliable eyewitness); recovery of blood-stained aruvals; postmortem and blood-stained clothing (Ex.P.16)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted A1 under s.302 IPC and A2 and A3 under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000 each (default three months simple imprisonment)
high_court_outcome: Appeals allowed; convictions set aside and all accused acquitted
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 (A1); IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (A2 and A3)
neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that three accused, following a dispute linked to the murder of a friend of theirs on the same day, suspected the victim of having revealed that friend's whereabouts. While the victim was travelling in a car with an eyewitness and another person, the accused, riding a two-wheeler and armed with weapons, obstructed and dashed the car, breaking its windscreen with aruvals. One accused caused an injury to the victim's right shoulder. The victim ran away to a shed, where the accused chased him and caused further injuries inside. The eyewitness stated that he saw all three accused enter the shed and then come out, leaving the victim lying injured; the victim was found dead. A complaint was given at the police station and an FIR registered on it. Investigators recovered blood-stained aruvals and conducted a postmortem. Of six eyewitnesses examined, three did not support the prosecution. The eyewitness was cross-examined at length but maintained his account.
physical_harm: Injury to the victim's right shoulder from an aruval; further injuries inside the shed; death on the spot
number_of_offences: 4 charged (IPC ss.341, 506(2), 302; TNPPDL Act s.3(1)); 2 finally upheld (IPC s.302 and s.302 r/w s.34)
motive: alleged: suspicion that the deceased had informed on the whereabouts of a friend of the accused, who had been murdered
key_evidence_accepted: Deposition of PW1, the sole eyewitness, on both the attack in the car and the attack in the shed; blood-stained aruvals and blood-stained clothing noted in the record
witness_credibility: PW1 described as star and eyewitness; fully cross-examined yet stood by his account and fully supported the prosecution; found trustworthy and reliable
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 31.07.2013; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 12.06.2018; Supreme Court: 14.10.2022
legal_representation: Accused: Rao Ranjit (Adv.); State: Dr. Joseph Aristotle S., Ms. Nupur Sharma, Shobhit Dwivedi, Sanjeev Kumar Mahara (Advs.)
investigation_status: FIR registered on complaint; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; case committed to Sessions and tried
procedural_irregularity: High Court noted complaint not marked, FIR dispatch to Magistrate at 7.00 p.m., and the constable not examined; Supreme Court held FIR timing contradictions not a ground to acquit
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted (s.302; s.302 r/w s.34). High Court: appeals allowed, accused acquitted. Supreme Court: acquittal set aside, convictions restored
prosecution_argument: PW1 is the eyewitness to both parts of the incident and fully supports the prosecution; no reason to disbelieve him; relied on Krishna Mochi
defence_argument: High Court reasons cogent; three eyewitnesses turned hostile; PW4 disbelieved; complainant Mahendran and independent witnesses not examined; contradictions on injuries; PW1 was outside the shed; weapon recovery not proved; doubt on timing and place of incident (relied on Kunju Muhammed)
legal_principle_applied: Conviction may rest on sole eyewitness testimony if trustworthy and reliable; recovery of weapon not a sine qua non; non-examination of complainant or FIR timing contradictions not grounds to discard eyewitness evidence

case_title: Shraddha Gupta v. State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_occupation: Household lady (as claimed by the appellant; not independently stated by the Court)
previous_criminal_record: Not stated (appellant's counsel contended she is not a habitual offender; no record described)
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (sibling; the appellant and the deceased were daughters of the same father, in a property dispute)
statutory_provisions: Gangsters Act, 1986 ss.2 and 3 (charged against appellant); underlying case Case Crime No. 337/2016 under IPC ss.147, 304, 504, 323, 506, 120-B
weapon: None mentioned (a car was used to ram the victim's scooty)

aggravating_circumstances: Alleged: planned murder by an organised gang led by a mastermind for pecuniary gain; alleged order to kill the driver as he might give evidence
trial_court_outcome: Not stated for the appellant (no trial verdict against her in this judgment; Special Court took cognizance against eight co-accused)
high_court_outcome: Writ petition under s.482 CrPC dismissed and refusal to quash Gangsters Act proceedings upheld; review application also dismissed
neutral_facts: The victim was travelling on the rear seat of a scooty driven by her servant, returning from a district court in the evening. Near a temple, the victim and her driver saw a car with several persons parked nearby. The car followed the scooty and, near a village, rammed into it, and both the victim and the driver fell onto the road. The car then stopped near the driver, and a person in it shouted that the driver should also be killed because he might give evidence. The assailants fled when passers-by gathered. Passers-by helped the driver take the victim to a hospital, where she died. An autopsy was conducted that night. The victim's sister lodged a written report the next day, alleging prior enmity between the family and the accused. Investigation later relied on call recordings between co-accused, provided to the investigating officer by the complainant, which led to the identification of additional accused. Investigators found that the daughters of the victim's late father had been in prolonged litigation over the division of his immovable properties. The prosecution's case was that one accused was the leader of an organised gang who planned the killing for pecuniary gain, with other co-accused, including the later-added accused, joining in. A gang chart was prepared and a supplementary charge sheet was filed against the later-added accused.
offence_severity: Minimum 2 years and maximum 10 years imprisonment, plus fine of not less than Rs. 5,000 (Gangsters Act s.3(1), as quoted)
physical_harm: Death of the victim after the car rammed her scooty; the driver fell on the road (injuries not described)
number_of_offences: 2 charged (Gangsters Act ss.2 and 3) against the appellant; 0 finally upheld (no conviction; proceedings not quashed)
premeditation_planning: Not decided by the Court; planning and conspiracy were alleged by the prosecution/State
motive: alleged: pecuniary benefit from a long-running property dispute among the family members
key_evidence_accepted: None assessed; the Court relied on the allegations as presented and on the statutory definitions, not on trial evidence
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 23.05.2016; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 27.09.2019 (writ order), 10.11.2020 (review order); Supreme Court: 26.04.2022
legal_representation: Appellant: Divyesh Pratap Singh and others (Advs.); State of UP: Sanjay Kumar Tyagi and others; respondent no.4: Shuvodeep Roy and others
investigation_status: FIR registered 24.05.2016 (Case Crime 337/2016); charge sheet and supplementary charge sheet filed; Gangsters Act FIR registered 27.05.2019 against the appellant and two co-accused
procedural_irregularity: None noted by the Court (appellant alleged the gang chart was maliciously submitted)
appeal_history: Trial court: not stated for the appellant. High Court: writ petition under s.482 CrPC dismissed (27.09.2019); review dismissed (10.11.2020). Supreme Court: appeals dismissed.
prosecution_argument: The appellant is a member of the gang who took part in anti-social activity (conspiracy to murder for pecuniary gain), so she can be prosecuted under the Gangsters Act even on a single FIR; no bar like MCOCA or GCTOC applies.
defence_argument: A single FIR/charge sheet for one murder cannot make the appellant a gangster or gang member; she was not named in the FIR and was added later under s.173(8) CrPC; the allegations are not anti-social activities; Piyush Kantilal Mehta and the Gujarat High Court decision were relied on.
legal_principle_applied: A single offence/FIR/charge sheet suffices for prosecution under the Gangsters Act if the accused is a gang member who indulged in a s.2(b) anti-social activity by violence, threat, intimidation or coercion for undue advantage; statutory provisions are read as they are.
precedent_relied_upon: Piyush Kantilal Mehta v. Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad City, 1989 Supp (1) SCC 322; Karansinh Chetansinh Vaghela v. State of Gujarat, 2021 SCC OnLine Gujarat 1260 (both cited by the appellant and noted as referred to; the Court's reasoning rests on the statutory text)
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: M. Nageswara Reddy v. The State of Andhra Pradesh and Others
accused_victim_relationship: Political rivals/prior enmity: the High Court described the accused as members of a rival faction; the accused's defence was political rivalry and past enmity
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PW1, PW3, PW5); injured eyewitness testimony (PW6, PW7); medical and documentary evidence
aggravating_circumstances: Per prosecution case: multiple assailants armed with hunting sickles, indiscriminate hacking of the victim, and injuries to the driver and another occupant
trial_court_outcome: Accused 1-3 convicted under ss.148 and 302 IPC; life imprisonment (s.302) and one year RI (s.148). Accused 4-11 acquitted of all charges
high_court_outcome: Appeal of accused 1-3 allowed; their conviction reversed and they were acquitted. Complainant's appeal against acquittal of accused 4-11 dismissed
offence_finally_established: Accused 1-3: IPC s.302 (murder) and s.148 (rioting with deadly weapon)
neutral_facts: On an evening in January 2007, at about 8:30 p.m., a group of eleven accused persons, armed with hunting sickles, allegedly emerged from behind a sumo vehicle and surrounded it near a clinic in Kurnool. The vehicle was carrying the victim, the victim's brother, other occupants and a driver. Three of the accused allegedly forcibly opened the front left door, dragged the victim out, and hacked him repeatedly with hunting sickles, causing his death on the spot. Other accused allegedly struck the vehicle's glass windows with sickles and broke them. Two accused allegedly hacked the driver, causing bleeding injuries to his shoulder, hand and ribs. Further accused allegedly chased the fleeing occupants, and one occupant was injured. The injured driver and another injured occupant were taken to hospital. A first information report was lodged on the statement of the victim's brother, and the investigating officer recorded witness statements, collected medical and documentary evidence, and arrested the accused. The prosecution relied on the testimony of three eyewitnesses, two injured eyewitnesses and the medical evidence. The accused denied the charges.
physical_harm: Victim killed by hacking with hunting sickles; driver (PW6) suffered bleeding injuries to right shoulder, hand and side ribs; PW7 injured while fleeing
number_of_offences: 7 charged; 2 finally upheld (ss.148 and 302 IPC, accused 1-3)
financial_property_loss: Damage to vehicle windows (charged under s.427 IPC); no monetary value stated
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness identification of accused 1-3 by PW1, PW3 and PW6; testimony of injured eyewitnesses PW6 and PW7; the incident as proved by PW7's deposition; FIR lodged within seven hours and sent to Magistrate within 24 hours
witness_credibility: Court found no material contradictions among eyewitnesses and injured eyewitnesses regarding accused 1-3. Relationship to the deceased did not by itself discredit PW1, PW3, PW5. PW6, as injured eyewitness, had greater reliability. High Court's reasons (minor contradictions, planted witnesses) were held unwarranted. PW7 could not identify assailants but the incident was proved through his evidence
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: 18.01.2007; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 21.02.2018; Supreme Court: 07.03.2022
legal_representation: For appellants (original complainant and State): A. Sirajudeen, Sr. Adv., with others. For respondents (original accused): Guntur Prabhakar, D. Ramakrishna Reddy and others
investigation_status: FIR registered as Crime No. 7 of 2007; investigation completed; chargesheet filed against all eleven accused; case committed to Sessions Court
procedural_irregularity: Alleged interpolation of time in FIR and seven-hour delay in lodging FIR. Court held not fatal: point not raised at trial, not put to investigating officers, and FIR sent to Magistrate within 24 hours
appeal_history: Trial court: accused 1-3 convicted under ss.148 and 302 IPC (life imprisonment); accused 4-11 acquitted. High Court: accused 1-3 acquitted; complainant's appeal against accused 4-11 dismissed. Supreme Court: appeals 72/2022 and 74/2022 allowed, trial court conviction of accused 1-3 restored; appeal 73/2022 dismissed
prosecution_argument: High Court wrongly gave weight to alleged FIR time interpolation, which was not raised at trial or put to investigating officers; FIR sent to Magistrate within 24 hours as required; eyewitness and injured eyewitness testimony consistent; minor contradictions not material; relatives not interested witnesses merely by relationship; High Court failed to reappreciate PW5's evidence; injuries supported by medical evidence
defence_argument: FIR time altered from 0.30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m.; seven-hour delay and FIR reaching Magistrate at 4:30 a.m. despite short distance; so FIR and testimony of PW1, PW3, PW6 and PW7 were properly disbelieved and accused falsely implicated
legal_principle_applied: Relatives' evidence not discarded merely because they are relatives; injured eyewitness testimony has greater reliability; delay in lodging FIR not fatal absent material prejudice; first appellate court must reappreciate all evidence; concurrent acquittals not interfered with where plausible; roles of accused compared individually
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated (court refers generally to a line of decisions on injured eyewitnesses without naming any case)
other_sentence_order: Accused 1-3 directed to surrender within four weeks to undergo the remaining sentence

case_title: Jasdeep Singh @ Jassu v. State of Punjab
accused_socioeconomic_status: Not stated by the Court. Complainant's counsel alleged the accused are influential persons; no finding made.

neutral_facts: At about 12:45 a.m. on 21 April 2011, the victim was shot dead on a street in Jalandhar. The prosecution case was that the victim believed a raid on a hotel run by his family had been instigated by the accused, and that a quarrel preceded the incident. A witness who went looking for the victim saw the accused grappling with him under a street light. A friend of the victim was also present; this witness later turned hostile at trial. The prosecution alleged that, shortly before the shooting, two of the accused made the remark 'what are you seeing now', after which another accused, who had already drawn a gun and brandished it at the victim, took out a gun from his pocket and fired a single shot. The victim was taken to a hospital about three kilometres away in a car, and a complaint was lodged. The investigating officer completed the investigation and recovered weapons. Medical evidence was on record. A further witness claimed to have overheard a prior plan to commit the murder, but this account was contested. The defence examined its own witnesses. The evidence on the fight and the sequence of events was disputed in its details, including the supplementary statement attributed to the victim's father.
physical_harm: Death of the deceased from a single gunshot
number_of_offences: 1 charged (s.304 Part I IPC, with s.34 IPC as liability provision); 0 finally upheld against A3 and A4

witness_credibility: PW13 disbelieved (improbabilities; contradicted by cousin DW1). PW6 exaggerated and made concerted efforts to improve the case. PW10 turned hostile; his prior statement was considered by the trial court.

case_title: Anuj Singh @ Ramanuj Singh @ Seth Singh v. The State of Bihar
accused_occupation: Manoj Singh: government service (junior engineer, per defence alibi evidence); Anuj Singh: Not stated
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour; prior enmity over a land dispute
statutory_provisions: Charged: IPC s.307 (with s.34 for co-accused) and Arms Act s.27; finally upheld: IPC s.324 and Arms Act s.27
weapon: Firearms (guns) used by the two appellants; spear and lathi used by co-accused
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; medical evidence (PW-8 doctor); defence alibi evidence (DW-1, DW-2)
aggravating_circumstances: Use of firearms by the two appellants in an altercation over land
mitigating_circumstances: Injuries inflicted on non-vital parts of the body (noted by the Court)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.307 r/w s.34 (5 years RI, fine Rs.5,000) and Arms Act s.27 (3 years RI, fine Rs.2,000)
high_court_outcome: Conviction under s.307/34 IPC modified to s.324 IPC (2 years RI, fine Rs.5,000); Arms Act s.27 conviction and sentence confirmed

neutral_facts: The incident arose from a dispute over a boundary wall on land claimed by the victim. The victim was repairing a mud wall that had fallen in rain, with the help of hired labourers. A neighbour objected to the repair work and said the land was his. A verbal altercation followed. The neighbour went to his house and returned with a second man, both carrying guns. Two other men then arrived carrying a spear and a lathi. The two armed men fired shots at the victim. One shot struck the victim's left leg and another struck the victim's right arm or hand. The other two men then assaulted the victim with a spear and a lathi. On hearing the gunshots, family members and villagers came to the scene, and the four men ran away. The victim was taken to a private clinic. The doctor who examined the victim recorded entry and exit wounds on the right forearm and left leg, with charring of the skin at one site. He stated that all injuries were caused by firearms and were simple in nature. He also stated that tattooing may not appear over a wound if fired from 6-7 feet. Several eyewitnesses, including family members and persons present nearby, testified that the two armed men were present, carried guns and fired at the victim after the altercation. Some witnesses were declared hostile. One of the accused said he was posted elsewhere on duty that day, and a defence witness supported this, but a prosecution witness said he was present at the scene. The investigating officer recorded the victim's statement, visited the scene and noted an ongoing dispute over the land.
offence_severity: Maximum three years, or fine, or both; minimum not stated
physical_harm: Gunshot wounds to the victim's left leg and right forearm (entry and exit wounds, charring of skin at one site); simple in nature
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.307; Arms Act s.27); 2 finally upheld (IPC s.324; Arms Act s.27)
premeditation_planning: Not found; the Court described the firing as arising from an altercation
motive: Prior enmity over a land dispute (accepted by the Court); the altercation concerned preventing the victim from repairing the wall
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent eyewitness testimony placing both appellants at the scene armed with guns and causing the injuries; medical evidence of PW-8 that injuries were firearm injuries
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses found credible despite minor contradictions on timing and injury location; the alibi of one appellant did not inspire confidence
post_offence_conduct: Not stated

legal_representation: Accused: Mrs. Anjana Prakash, Senior Advocate, with Anuj Prakash, Ms. Jaikriti S. Jadeja, Prabhat Ranjan Raj and Shantanu Sagar. State: Abhinav Mukerji, Saket Singh, Ms. Sangeeta Singh and Mrs. Niranjana Singh (for the Respondent)

defence_argument: No recovery of gun or bullets; unexplained delay in forwarding FIR; contradictions in witness statements cast doubt on the prosecution story
legal_principle_applied: Minor contradictions do not discredit a witness; medical evidence has corroborative value; ingredients of s.324 IPC (voluntary hurt by dangerous weapon such as firearm) applied; s.27 Arms Act follows once s.324 is established
precedent_relied_upon: Narayan Chetanram Chaudhary & Anr. v. State of Maharashtra (2000) 8 SCC 457
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Major Singh v. State of Punjab & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (nephew of the deceased); prior quarrel the previous day in which the victim reprimanded the accused
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged; High Court conviction, set aside); IPC s.304 Part II (conviction in Supreme Court)
weapon: Wooden 'Bahi' (wooden side of a cot frame)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (two sons of the victim); medical (post-mortem); recovery of the weapon following the accused's disclosure
confession: Police-recorded disclosure of where the weapon was hidden, leading to its recovery; the Supreme Court noted the recovery followed the confession (para 12) as part of the evidence
aggravating_circumstances: Blow with great force to the head of an elderly man, causing skull fracture (High Court's view); grudge from the previous day's quarrel
mitigating_circumstances: Provocation from the victim's yelling the previous day; weapon not dangerous; single blow; no intention or knowledge that death would result
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of s.302 IPC on 13.07.2001 (delay in FIR, weak motive, unreliable eyewitnesses, medical contradictions, site plan discrepancies)
high_court_outcome: Acquittal set aside; convicted under s.302 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs.5,000 (03.04.2014)
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, IPC s.304 Part II
neutral_facts: On the day before the incident, the accused quarrelled with the victim, who was the accused's uncle, and abused him; the victim sharply reprimanded the accused. The next morning, at about 10:30 to 11:00 a.m., the victim was walking towards the village bus stand when the accused approached from the opposite direction carrying a wooden side of a cot frame. The accused abused the victim for shouting at and insulting him the previous day, said he would teach him a lesson, and struck the victim once on the head. The victim fell down, and the accused ran away with the wooden piece. Two of the victim's sons, who were standing outside a nearby shop, took their bleeding father to Civil Hospital, Giddarbaha, from where he was referred to Dayanand Medical College, Ludhiana. The victim died the following day. The complainant son gave a written statement to a police officer, which was endorsed and sent for registration of an FIR. Police visited the spot, prepared a rough site plan and lifted blood-stained earth. At the hospital, an inquest was prepared, and a post-mortem found eight injuries, the main one on the head; the doctor opined the cause of death was shock and haemorrhage from the head injury. The accused was arrested some weeks later and, in police presence, indicated where the blood-stained wooden piece was concealed in a wheat chaff room at the accused's residence; it was recovered. Chemical examination found the blood on the piece and on the spot earth matched the victim. Two eyewitnesses, the victim's sons, testified that the accused struck the victim's head with the wooden piece.
physical_harm: Single blow to the victim's head causing skull fracture (as found by High Court); eight injuries in total on post-mortem; death the next day from shock and haemorrhage due to head injury
number_of_offences: 1 charged; 1 conviction stands (s.304 Part II, altered from s.302)
premeditation_planning: Not found by the Supreme Court. The High Court had reasoned the occurrence was not sudden and had a grudge behind it, but the Supreme Court found no intention to kill and did not find premeditation.
motive: Anger and provocation from the victim's reprimand and yelling the previous day (accepted by the Supreme Court)
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness accounts of the two sons; post-mortem evidence of head injury as cause of death; recovery of the blood-stained 'Bahi' with chemical match to the victim's blood
witness_credibility: High Court found the eyewitness version truthful and trustworthy; the Supreme Court accepted the occurrence as proved beyond reasonable doubt and did not disturb this
post_offence_conduct: Fled the spot with the weapon; concealed the 'Bahi' at his residence; arrested on 09.08.1998; the disclosure led to recovery of the weapon
custody_duration: Arrested 09.08.1998; released 13.07.2001 after trial court acquittal; surrendered 04.10.2014; more than eight years' incarceration per the Court
trial_duration: offence: 21.07.1998 (incident; quarrel the previous day, 20.07.1998); trial judgment: 13.07.2001; High Court: 03.04.2014; Supreme Court: 16.06.2022
legal_representation: Accused-appellant: Gagan Gupta. Respondents (State of Punjab & Anr.): R. K. Rathore and Ms. Jaspreet Gogia
investigation_status: FIR registered; site visit, rough site plan, blood-stained earth lifted; inquest and post-mortem done; arrest and recovery made; case committed to Sessions; charge framed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Trial court flagged a 4½-hour FIR delay and late arrest; the High Court found no reason to disbelieve the prosecution on these grounds; the Supreme Court raised no separate irregularity
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted of s.302 (13.07.2001). High Court: acquittal set aside, convicted under s.302, life imprisonment and Rs.5,000 fine (03.04.2014). Supreme Court: partly allowed; s.302 conviction set aside; convicted under s.304 Part II; sentence reduced to period already undergone; fine retained
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Alternatively, the offence was culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s.304 IPC rather than murder under s.302
legal_principle_applied: Distinction between culpable homicide amounting to murder (s.302) and culpable homicide not amounting to murder (s.304); intention is pivotal, with knowledge and the degree of the act also relevant; factors from Pulicherla Nagaraju applied
precedent_relied_upon: Mohd. Rafiq v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2021) 10 SCC 706 (relying on State of Andhra Pradesh v. Rayavarapu Punnayya and Pulicherla Nagaraju @ Nagaraja Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh)
sentencing_rationale: Conviction altered to s.304 Part II because the accused lacked intention to kill and knowledge of likely death; sentence reduced in view of more than eight years already served
judicial_mitigating_factors: No intention to kill; provocation by the uncle's reprimand the previous day; non-dangerous weapon; single blow; no knowledge that a single blow would cause death; period already undergone
other_sentence_order: Release forthwith if not wanted in any other criminal case; fine of Rs.5,000 remains as imposed by the High Court

case_title: Sanjay Puran Bagde & Anr. v. The State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (accused are relatives of the deceased); prior enmity arising from an earlier incident, per the High Court's finding
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony of the victim's wife (PW-6), her statements under s.161 and s.164 CrPC, and the victim's statements to her; no dying declaration
aggravating_circumstances: Accused came to the spot around 3 a.m. with two of them carrying axes; the attack was premeditated; the victim was held while being attacked
trial_court_outcome: Convicted the two axe-wielding accused under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; acquitted the two appellants. Sentence not stated.
high_court_outcome: Appeal of convicted accused dismissed; State's appeal allowed and acquittal of the two appellants reversed
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 read with s.34 (common intention)
neutral_facts: On the night of 2–3 November 2015, at about 3 a.m., the victim and his wife woke up. While the wife was preparing to cook, the victim went out to attend to the call of nature. The wife heard the victim shouting that four persons were attacking him. She ran to the spot and saw two of the accused assaulting the victim with an axe, while two other accused were holding him. On her raising a loud alarm, all of them ran away. She found the victim bleeding. He told her that four of them had caught hold of him and attacked him with an axe. She gave him water at his request, and neighbours carried him into the house. He was then taken to a hospital by auto, where he was declared dead. The reason for the assault was alleged to be an evil eye kept by the victim on the wife of one of the accused. The wife's statements were recorded under Section 161 and later Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. A first information report was registered on 3 November 2015 and, after investigation, a charge sheet was filed. Four persons were charged with murder read with common intention. The wife, as the only eyewitness, gave evidence of the incident as described. No dying declaration was recorded, as the victim was declared dead on arrival at the hospital.
physical_harm: Death of the victim after axe assault; found bleeding; declared brought dead at hospital
number_of_offences: 1 charged (s.302 r/w s.34 IPC); 1 finally upheld against each appellant
premeditation_planning: Yes. The Court found the presence of the accused with axes at about 3 a.m. showed a premeditated intention.
motive: alleged: the victim allegedly kept an evil eye on the wife of one of the accused
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of the victim's wife (PW-6), including the victim's statements to her; identification of all accused; the manner of the incident
witness_credibility: PW-6 (wife) found reliable by both courts; no glaring inconsistency between her s.161 and s.164 CrPC statements; no quibble with the manner of the incident or identification of the accused
post_offence_conduct: Accused ran away when the wife raised a loud alarm; no other post-offence conduct noted
trial_duration: offence: night intervening 2nd and 3rd November 2015; trial judgment: 14.09.2017; High Court: 05.02.2019; Supreme Court: 28.07.2022
legal_representation: Appellants: Akash Kakade, Somanatha Padhan, Swetab Kumar, Ashok Anand, Rakesh Kr. Singh, Bipin Bihari Singh. State of Maharashtra (respondent): Rahul Chitnis, Sachin Patil, Aaditya A. Pande, Geo Joseph, Ms. Shwetal Shepal
investigation_status: FIR No. 79/2015 registered on 03.11.2015; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: two axe-wielding accused convicted under s.302 r/w s.34; two appellants acquitted. High Court: convicted accused's appeal dismissed; State's appeal allowed and the appellants' acquittal reversed. Supreme Court: SLP of the axe-wielding accused dismissed on 20.01.2020; appellants' appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: The appellants only held the victim while the other two attacked, so there was no shared common intention; counsel also sought a re-examination of the entire evidence
legal_principle_applied: Section 34 IPC: common intention requires a simultaneous consensus of minds and participation in the criminal act; participation need not be physical presence; s.34 imposes constructive liability
precedent_relied_upon: Jasdeep Singh Alias Jassu v. State of Punjab (2022) 2 SCC 545; Virendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2010) 8 SCC 407
judicial_aggravating_factors: Premeditated attack with axes at about 3 a.m.; appellants held the victim while the others attacked, showing a shared intention
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Dauvaram Nirmalkar v. State of Chhattisgarh
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (brother); the deceased reportedly quarrelled with and abused the accused, and the deceased was addicted to alcohol
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged and convicted at trial); IPC s.304 Part I (final conviction after applying Exception 1 to s.300); Evidence Act s.106 (burden) referred to
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence (joint presence on the night, absence of any intruder); medical evidence (post-mortem); recovery evidence (pick-axe, blood-stained shirt, body discovered at the accused's residence); disclosure admissible under s.27
confession: Extra-judicial confession at police station on 26th September 2011. Held inadmissible under s.25; only the part leading to discovery of pick-axe and body was relied on under s.27
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Prolonged alcohol-fuelled abuse and threats by the victim; on the night, victim allegedly threatened to kill the accused; sudden loss of self-control
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302 for murder; life imprisonment, fine Rs.1,000, default simple imprisonment for six months
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 400 of 2013) decided by judgment dated 25.02.2019; conviction under s.302 upheld (Supreme Court agreed with High Court on involvement of the accused)
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, IPC s.304 Part I
neutral_facts: The victim, the accused's brother, died from coma caused by shock after multiple fractures to the skull, including the left temporal, frontal, parietal and left occipital regions with a deep lesion, and a lacerated wound on the chin, as recorded in the post-mortem report proved by a senior medical officer. The accused and the victim lived in separate rooms in the same house. Several witnesses, including relatives and a neighbour, testified that the victim was addicted to alcohol, was abusive and ill-tempered, and quarrelled with the accused. Two nieces who were present in the house at the time of the incident gave evidence, and neither reported any intruder or third person that night. It was the prosecution's case that the victim had consumed alcohol and told the accused to leave the house, failing which he would kill the accused. The accused had also tried to kill himself by holding live electrical wires and suffered burns to the hands. On 26th September 2011 the accused went to a police station and confessed. Following the accused's disclosure, a pick-axe was recovered from a wooden box in the residence; the pick-axe and the shirt worn during the incident were found stained with blood. The victim's body was discovered in the house where the accused resided.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from coma due to shock; multiple skull fractures (left temporal, frontal, parietal, left occipital) with deep lesion; lacerated wound on chin
number_of_offences: 1 charged (s.302); 1 finally upheld (converted to s.304 Part I)
premeditation_planning: No premeditation or planning found; the Court held the killing followed sudden loss of self-control
motive: Sudden and grave provocation from the victim's prolonged alcohol-fuelled abuse and threats, culminating in the night's threat to kill the accused (accepted by the Court for Exception 1)
key_evidence_accepted: Joint presence of accused and victim on the night; no intruder evidence; post-mortem findings; s.27 disclosure leading to pick-axe, blood-stained shirt and body; evidence of victim's alcohol addiction and abuse from PW-3, PW-4, PW-8, PW-9, PW-10
witness_credibility: Public witnesses declared hostile but Court relied on their unison deposition on separate rooms and the victim's alcohol addiction; PW-10 did not admit making the statement attributed to her by PW-9; no third-party suggestion put to witnesses
post_offence_conduct: Went to police station on 26th September 2011 and confessed; disclosure led to recovery of pick-axe and discovery of the body
custody_duration: Over 10 years; in custody since 27 September 2011 (as stated by the Supreme Court)
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 25.02.2019; Supreme Court: 02.08.2022
legal_representation: Appellant: Harinder Mohan Singh (Adv.). Respondent (State of Chhattisgarh): Sumeer Sodhi and Dhruv Wadhwa (Advs.)
investigation_status: Post-mortem conducted and proved; accused's disclosure led to recovery of pick-axe and body; trial completed with conviction. Charge sheet filing not stated
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, life imprisonment, fine Rs.1,000. High Court (Criminal Appeal No. 400 of 2013, 25.02.2019): conviction upheld. Supreme Court: partly allowed; conviction converted to s.304 Part I; sentence modified to period undergone
prosecution_argument: Not stated in the judgment as separate submissions; the prosecution relied on the victim's alcohol addiction and abusive conduct to show motive
defence_argument: Not stated in the judgment as Supreme Court submissions; at trial the accused's s.313 statement suggested a third person killed the victim, which was rejected
legal_principle_applied: Exception 1 to s.300 IPC: grave and sudden provocation, loss of self-control, reasonable man test, cumulative provocation with a verifiable final act, and absence of premeditation
precedent_relied_upon: Aghnoo Nagesia v. State of Bihar [1966] 1 SCR 134; K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra [1962] 1 Suppl. SCR 567; Budhi Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2012) 13 SCC 663; Rampal Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2012) 8 SCC 289 (referred to); R v. Duffy (1949) 1 All E.R. 932 (quoted)
sentencing_rationale: Appellant had already been incarcerated for over 10 years, so the sentence of imprisonment was modified to the period already undergone
judicial_mitigating_factors: Sudden and grave provocation from victim's alcohol-fuelled abuse and threats; sudden loss of self-control; the accused's own suicide attempt as evidence of temporary loss of control
other_sentence_order: Appellant to pay fine of Rs.1,000 (default six months simple imprisonment); to be released forthwith on payment if not required in any other case

case_title: State through Deputy Superintendent of Police v. R. Soundirarasu etc.
accused_occupation: Motor Vehicle Inspector (Grade 1), a public servant (Respondent No. 1); Respondent No. 2 is described as a commerce graduate claiming independent income
accused_socioeconomic_status: Alleged in the FIR only: accused described as hailing from an ordinary agricultural family. The Court made no finding on wealth or class.
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 s.13(2) r/w s.13(1)(e); Indian Penal Code s.109 (abetment)
evidence_type: Documentary: FIR, asset, income and expenditure statements in the charge sheet, income tax returns, and the accused's written explanation. No trial evidence had been recorded.
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Special Judge rejected both discharge applications under s.239 CrPC (orders dated 29.03.2016); no sentence, as the case was at the charge stage
high_court_outcome: Revision allowed; orders rejecting discharge set aside; both accused discharged from the charges
neutral_facts: A public servant working as a motor vehicle inspector in a regional transport office was alleged to have acquired and possessed assets disproportionate to his known sources of income during a check period from 1 January 2002 to 31 March 2004. The allegation was that assets were held in the names of the accused's spouse, the accused's father-in-law and the accused's minor son, and that these were in substance held by the accused. Information was received and a preliminary verification was made, after which a First Information Report was registered in September 2005. The complaint listed house sites, lands, a house construction, gold and silver ornaments and household articles, and stated that the family's expenditure exceeded the recorded income for the period. During the investigation, the investigating officer called for an explanation from the accused, who replied in November 2007 denying that he held disproportionate assets. He also furnished income tax returns filed by the spouse from 1990 onwards and returns of a partnership firm from 1993. The investigation found that the spouse had no sufficient independent source of income to acquire the assets, and the spouse was identified as an abettor. The investigating agency then filed a charge sheet.
attempt_completion: Completed (as alleged: possession of disproportionate assets)
physical_harm: None
number_of_offences: 3 charged (PC Act s.13(2), s.13(1)(e), IPC s.109); 0 finally upheld
financial_property_loss: Alleged disproportionate assets of Rs. 24,41,980 (prosecution figure; not a finding)
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Charge-sheet material and documents on record, considered prima facie. The Court relied on them to hold the charge was not groundless; it made no finding on the truth of the explanations.
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Accused gave a written explanation to the investigating officer on 1.11.2007 denying disproportionate assets; the Court did not decide its merits.
trial_duration: offence: check period 01.01.2002 to 31.03.2004 (FIR dated 19.09.2005); trial judgment: 29.03.2016; High Court: 27.04.2017; Supreme Court: 05.09.2022
legal_representation: For the State (appellant): V. Krishnamurthy, AAG, with others. For the accused (respondents): K. Radhakrishnan, Sr. Adv., with others.
investigation_status: FIR registered 19.09.2005; investigation concluded; charge sheet filed as Special Criminal Case No. 36/2008; charges not yet framed
procedural_irregularity: Not stated
appeal_history: Trial court (Special Judge): discharge rejected 29.03.2016. High Court: revision allowed 27.04.2017, accused discharged. Supreme Court: State's appeals allowed, discharge orders set aside, charges to be framed.
prosecution_argument: The High Court wrongly applied a beyond-reasonable-doubt standard at the s.239 stage, considered defence documents and conducted a mini trial, and misapplied Suresh Rajan and Debendra Nath Padhi.
defence_argument: Wife was an independent income earner and income tax assessee, so her assets should not be attributed to the accused; the explanation was not considered; the accused needed only to show a preponderance of probability.
legal_principle_applied: At s.239 the court only asks whether the charge is groundless; s.13(1)(e) shifts the onus of explanation to the accused, but it cannot be discharged at discharge stage. Revisional power is limited to correcting manifest error of law or procedure.
precedent_relied_upon: State of Maharashtra v. Wasudeo Ramchandra Kaidalwar (1981) 3 SCC 199; Central Bureau of Investigation v. T.H. Vijayalakshmi (2021 SCC OnLine SC 923); Onkar Nath Mishra v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2008) 2 SCC 561; State of T.N. v. N. Suresh Rajan (2014) 11 SCC 709; K. Veeraswami v. Union of India (1991) 3 SCC 655; Munna Devi v. State of Rajasthan (2001) 9 SCC 631

case_title: Chotkau v. State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_socioeconomic_status: Very poor; could not afford a lawyer in the Sessions Court and an amicus was provided
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (niece, as stated in the prosecution complaint). No prior enmity between accused and victim found by the court.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.376
evidence_type: Circumstantial (last seen theory) based on testimony of PWs 1 to 3; post-mortem; recovery of clothing. No medical examination of accused; forensic report not produced.
aggravating_circumstances: Victim a six-year-old girl; rape and murder (as held by the Sessions Court)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.302 and 376; sentenced to death
high_court_outcome: Conviction and death sentence confirmed on reference and appeal
neutral_facts: The accused was charged with raping and murdering a six-year-old girl, who was a relative of the accused. According to the complaint lodged by the victim's uncle, at about 4:00 p.m. on 8 March 2012, during the Holi festival, the accused took the victim away on the pretext of showing dance and song performances. When the victim did not return home, a search was made. The accused was not found at home, and the victim's body was found in a sugarcane field on the southern side of the village. A member of the search party stated that he saw the accused leaving the sugarcane field about half an hour later. Another villager said he saw the accused carrying the victim towards the sugarcane field. The prosecution case rested on these eyewitness accounts and on the last-seen circumstance. The FIR was registered at the police station on the evening of 8 March 2012. The post-mortem was conducted by a doctor, who prepared a vaginal smear. A salwar bearing stains was sent for forensic examination, but no forensic report was obtained. The accused was not subjected to medical examination. The investigating officer recorded witness statements and prepared a site map. The victim's clothing, including a salwar, was recovered by the police.
physical_harm: Death of the six-year-old victim; rape alleged. Nature of injuries not described in detail.
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: None of the eyewitness evidence of PWs 1 to 3 was accepted as reliable. The Court relied on the absence of medical examination of the accused as fatal to the prosecution.
witness_credibility: PWs 1 to 3 found completely untrustworthy due to serious contradictions on FIR lodging, the place and handling of the body, inquest details and clothing. Lower courts had wrongly treated these as minor.
post_offence_conduct: Alleged: absconding after the body was found (relied on by lower courts). Not established as reliable by the Supreme Court.
trial_duration: offence: 08.03.2012; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 18.04.2016; Supreme Court: 28.09.2022
legal_representation: Appellant: S. Nagamuthu, Sr. Adv., with others. State: Ardhendumauli Kumar Prasad, AAG, with others.
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed and final report submitted; trial held. Forensic report not obtained; accused not medically examined.
procedural_irregularity: FIR received by the CJM five days late with no explanation; no one identified as taking the FIR to court; contradictory FIR and inquest evidence; no medical examination of accused; forensic report not obtained.
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced to death. High Court: confirmed on reference and appeal. Supreme Court: appeals allowed, conviction and sentence set aside.
prosecution_argument: No reason for PWs 1 to 3 to implicate the accused; their evidence was found cogent by two courts; the FIR delay did not prejudice the accused; s.313 defects do not vitiate findings absent prejudice; forensic evidence is not always mandatory.
defence_argument: PWs 1 to 3 untrustworthy; unexplained five-day FIR delay; serious contradictions on the body and inquest; last seen evidence insufficient; key witnesses not examined; forensic/medical evidence not produced; s.313 not complied with.
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain excluding innocence (panchsheel); FIR delay assessed under s.157(1) CrPC for creditworthiness; medical evidence under s.53A CrPC is important where the victim is dead and the case rests on circumstantial evidence.
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda (1984) 4 SCC 116; Meharaj Singh (1994) 5 SCC 188; Bhajan Singh (2011) 7 SCC 421; Brahm Swaroop (2011) 6 SCC 288; Balram Singh (2003) 11 SCC 286; State of Rajasthan v. Daud Khan (2016) 2 SCC 607; Jafarudheen (2022 SCC OnLine SC 495); Krishan Kumar Malik (2011) 7 SCC 130; Rajendra Pralhadrao Wasnik (2019) 12 SCC 460
other_sentence_order: Release forthwith unless wanted in connection with any other case

case_title: Central Bureau of Investigation v. Shyam Bihari & Others
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34
weapon: Fatal injury from a .12 bore gun (not recovered); service rifles (.303) issued to accused; country-made pistol alleged by PW-15
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-3, PW-6, PW-15); circumstantial (GD entries, ballistic report, presence at spot); medical (autopsy); recovery of empty cartridges
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of s.302/34 IPC; benefit of doubt extended
high_court_outcome: Delay condoned; leave to appeal against acquittal rejected; Government Appeal dismissed (26.07.2012)
neutral_facts: On the night of 24 June 1987, the victim was travelling on a scooter with two companions on a separate scooter toward a village to attend a marriage. Near a road turn at about 9.30 pm, the two companions say that in the scooter light they saw three uniformed men on the road, one carrying a stick and two carrying rifles. The man with the stick flashed a torch at them, and the two scooters skidded. One of the uniformed men allegedly urged others to shoot, and shots were fired. The victim was hit, collapsed, and was taken to a hospital in the presence of police, but died on the way. The two companions escaped to the village. The FIR was lodged by one companion, and a separate case was registered on a rival version describing an armed criminal group and police retaliatory fire, in which two empty cartridge shells were recovered from the spot. Villagers and police arrived at the scene. Three uniformed constables were on patrol that night and had left the police station with rifles and 50 rounds each. Ballistic examination found that some empty cartridges at the spot were fired from the service rifles of two of the constables, while two others were not matched to any of the three. The autopsy showed the fatal injury came from a .12 bore gun, which was not recovered from any of the accused. One witness claimed to have seen the accused fire a country-made pistol, and the accused were said to have remained at the spot after the incident.

neutral_facts: The victim, a police constable working as record keeper at a police station, was using the station's official telephone in the reporting room for five to seven minutes. The duty officer, a sub-inspector, told the victim to free the line because urgent calls might come in, but the victim continued the call. Around 5.55 pm the duty officer asked the accused, a guard posted at the station and carrying a semi-automatic fire carbine, to ask the victim to end the call. The accused entered the room, placed a hand on the victim's shoulder and asked the victim to end the call. The prosecution's initial account was that the victim playfully pushed the accused while holding the carbine. During the struggle the carbine became entangled in the chain attached to the accused's belt, and five rounds fired. Five bullets struck the victim in the neck and chest. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead. An offence was first registered on the duty officer's statement. The victim's father complained to senior police officers, and the investigation was transferred to the Crime Branch, which alleged that the victim had seen the accused and the duty officer in a compromising position and that they had threatened to kill him. Ballistic reports recorded close-range firing. A later report stated that the carbine could be cocked by entanglement with a chain if the change lever was not at the safety position, and would then fire if the trigger was pressed. Eyewitness accounts described the entanglement and accidental firing. A witness said he heard the accused tell the duty officer that the accused's children would be ruined, and heard the duty officer's reply. Several other persons present did not support the prosecution.

Two eyewitnesses said they saw the assault. One of them had earlier given a police statement that differed from his court testimony, and the other was not present when the assault began and said he came out after an alarm that the victim was beating the son of one of the accused. Neither eyewitness lodged a report. A named first information report was lodged the next morning at about 10 am by a village chowkidar of a neighbouring village, who said no eyewitness had informed her; she had come to the spot after hearing loud noises and found the body near a temple. Villagers guarded the body overnight. The next day, the police conducted an inquest, collected blood-stained earth from the spot, and seized a lathi lying near the body. The site plan showed that the body was about 300 feet from the place of assault, and drag marks were noticed. Lathis and clothes were said to have been recovered at the instance of each accused from their houses, but the serologist could not confirm the origin of the blood on them. neutral_facts: The victim was married to the accused in 1987 and the couple had two children. The victim's family alleged that the accused harassed the victim because of insufficient dowry. The victim's father approached the village sarpanch, who promised to counsel the in-laws after the festival. On the Diwali day, the victim was found burnt and was taken to a hospital in another city with about 91 per cent burns. The admitting doctor recorded that the victim said her husband had poured water to extinguish the fire. legal_principle_applied: Delay in FIR judged on whether the explanation is plausible on facts; alibi is a rule of evidence under s.11 Evidence Act, 1872, requiring cogent evidence and strict scrutiny; minor contradictions in eyewitness testimony not fatal; unsubstantiated claims of other enemies rejected
precedent_relied_upon: Apren Joseph v. State of Kerala (1973) 3 SCC 114; State of M.P. v. Ratan Singh (2020) 12 SCC 630; Bhagwan Singh v. Dilip Singh alias Depak (2023 SCC OnLine 1059); Binay Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (1997) 1 SCC 283; Ram Jag v. State of U.P. (1974) 4 SCC 201 (referred)

case_title: Markash Jajara v. State of Assam & Anr.
accused_socioeconomic_status: Poor (described as having poor financial conditions)
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (son-in-law; husband of the accused's daughter)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (Exception I of s.300 IPC considered by the Supreme Court)
evidence_type: Extra-judicial confession (oral, to daughter and villagers); testimony of victim's wife (PW-6) on confession and victim's conduct; medical evidence (post-mortem and autopsy surgeon); circumstantial evidence (incident inside accused's house, accused alone with body); non-eyewitness testimony of victim's brother (PW-8)
confession: Extra-judicial oral confession by the accused to his daughter (PW-6) that he murdered the victim with a bamboo stick, also reported by PW-1 (confession before villagers). Courts below relied on it heavily; the Supreme Court read PW-6's evidence in its entirety and accepted that the accused caused the injuries.
aggravating_circumstances: Fatal head injury (three lacerations on head, per post-mortem and autopsy surgeon); no other aggravating facts noted by the Court
mitigating_circumstances: Grave and sustained provocation by the victim's drinking and ill-treatment of the accused's daughter; loss of self-control; no premeditation; motive to protect daughter rather than to kill; accused's poor financial condition
trial_court_outcome: Guilty under s.302 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs.10,000 (six months simple imprisonment in default)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (conviction under s.302 IPC replaced by culpable homicide not amounting to murder)
neutral_facts: The victim, who had been living with his in-laws for about three to four months, was found dead inside the house of the accused by the victim's brother, who had gone there after learning that the victim had been assaulted. The brother lodged a first information report the same day stating that the accused had struck the victim with a bamboo stick. The body was lying on the kitchen floor. The post-mortem report recorded three lacerations on the victim's head, and the autopsy surgeon opined that the head injury was fatal and caused instantaneous death. The brother was not an eyewitness. The victim's wife, the accused's daughter, stated that she was away at work and returned around 4 p.m. to learn of the killing; out of fear she did not enter the house until police arrived. She stated that she questioned the accused, who confessed to having murdered the victim with a piece of bamboo. She testified that the victim was an alcoholic who quarrelled with her and the accused after drinking and ill-treated her. The accused's wife supported the prosecution to the extent that the victim was killed by the accused, but did not witness the occurrence. A witness stated that the accused confessed before villagers. The accused was arrested and a chargesheet was filed. The prosecution case rests on the confession, the fact that the incident occurred inside the accused's house, and the accused being alone with the body.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from three head lacerations (forehead, left mastoid region, below chin); autopsy surgeon opined the head injury was fatal and caused instantaneous death
number_of_offences: 1 charged; 1 finally upheld (s.302 conviction modified to culpable homicide not amounting to murder)
premeditation_planning: Court found no premeditation or planning
motive: Accepted by the Court: to prevent the victim from misbehaving with the accused's daughter after consuming alcohol, and to force him to mend his drinking and ways
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW-6 read in entirety, including cross-examination on victim's alcoholism and ill-treatment; statement that the accused and victim were the only ones present in the house; post-mortem findings and autopsy surgeon's opinion
witness_credibility: Supreme Court found PW-6's version, including her admissions on the victim's conduct, deserved appreciation in its right perspective; PW-8 admittedly not an eyewitness
post_offence_conduct: Accused confessed to daughter when she questioned him about the incident; was taken to the police station after police arrived
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: 03.10.2016; High Court: 12.03.2019; Supreme Court: 03 November 2023
legal_representation: Appellant: Gaurav Agrawal, Advocate. State of Assam (respondent): Nalin Kohli, Senior AAG, with Aastik Dhingra, Anshul Malik and Shuvodeep Roy, Advocates
investigation_status: FIR registered under s.302 IPC on ejahar of PW-8; accused arrested; chargesheet filed; nine prosecution witnesses examined; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: guilty under s.302, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; culpable homicide not amounting to murder; sentence reduced to ten years rigorous imprisonment
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Not stated in Supreme Court proceedings; before the High Court the defence argued there was no eyewitness and that the alleged confession to the daughter could not be relied upon
legal_principle_applied: Exception I to s.300 IPC (grave and sudden provocation; sustained provocation considered; provocation must not be sought or voluntarily provoked)
precedent_relied_upon: None cited by the Supreme Court; High Court relied on Ajay Singh v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 12 SCC 341 on the wording of extra-judicial confession
sentencing_rationale: Ends of justice adequately met by reducing life imprisonment to rigorous imprisonment of ten years, given the provocation and absence of premeditation
judicial_mitigating_factors: Persistent and sustained provocation by the victim's alcoholism and harassment of the accused's daughter; loss of self-control; no pre-meditated intention; motive to protect daughter
other_sentence_order: Release on completion of reduced sentence unless required in any other case; pending interlocutory applications disposed of

case_title: Prakash Nayi @ Sen v. State of Goa
accused_occupation: Worked at a store (per prosecution case); otherwise not stated
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated (the victim was working at the store where the accused attacked him; no personal connection described)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (defence raised under IPC s.84)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW2); medical evidence (hospital treatment records, doctors' depositions and certificates); conduct evidence; family witness evidence on prior treatment
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
mitigating_circumstances: Prior treatment for schizophrenia-type illness before the incident; later fitness to stand trial; subsequent recovery (noted by the court)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; sentence not stated
high_court_outcome: Conviction upheld by Division Bench, Bombay High Court at Goa (CRLA No.63 of 2006, dated 02.06.2008)
neutral_facts: On the morning of 14 May 2004, at about 6:00 a.m., the accused attacked the victim with an iron locking plate inside a store where the victim was working. The store belonged to the brother of the accused's grandfather. The prosecution alleged there was no motive, no provocation and no premeditation. An eyewitness saw the incident. After the assault, the accused took the object out of the store, walked to a nearby bus stand, returned and left the object in the shop, then went back to the bus stand and sat on a chair without attempting to leave. Before the incident, the accused had been an in-patient at a government hospital in Bhiwani, Haryana, from 17 to 26 November 2003. The records noted anxiety neurosis with reactive depression, symptoms of acid peptic disease and mild hypertension. The treatment given was akin to that for schizophrenia, and the medicine Thioril was prescribed. After the incident, a government doctor examined the accused. She later certified that the accused had chronic schizophrenia, probably from around age 14 or 15, and was not fit to stand trial. A later certificate, issued after in-patient treatment, stated the accused could stand trial. Her statement was recorded about sixteen years after the occurrence. An uncle of the accused testified about the earlier treatment. A relative of the accused's grandfather who was examined found no abnormality. The doctor who physically examined the accused after the incident stated the accused was mentally well.
physical_harm: Death of the victim caused by assault with an iron locking plate
premeditation_planning: No finding of premeditation or planning; the prosecution case was that the attack was without provocation or premeditation
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Evidence of the Government doctor (AW1/DW1) on schizophrenia and the certificate of unfitness to stand trial; evidence of AW2 on prior treatment; the fact of prior treatment
witness_credibility: Court found the Government doctor's evidence withstood cross-examination and should have been accepted; the fact of prior treatment was undisputed and corroborated by AW2; the courts below wrongly disregarded this evidence
post_offence_conduct: Per prosecution case: took the object out, returned it to the shop, went back to the bus stand and sat without attempting to leave. The court did not rely on this conduct; it said the conduct was ignored by the courts below
bail_history: Not stated (a bail application was considered at trial; outcome not stated)
trial_duration: offence: 14.05.2004; trial judgment: 25.07.2006; High Court: 02.06.2008; Supreme Court: 12.01.2023
legal_representation: Appellant: Aftab Ali Khan (Supreme Court Legal Services Committee) with associates; State counsel not stated
investigation_status: Not stated (trial was conducted; investigation and charge sheet details not given)
procedural_irregularity: Courts below did not discuss the prior treatment or accept the doctors' evidence; the Supreme Court called for a report from the District and Sessions Judge, Bhiwani, because the prescription and other documents could not be deciphered
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC (25.07.2006). High Court: conviction upheld (02.06.2008). Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction set aside and accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: Not stated (the judgment does not record State submissions)
defence_argument: Plea of insanity under IPC s.84: the accused was of unsound mind at the time of the act, supported by evidence of schizophrenia and prior treatment, so the accused is entitled to the benefit of s.84
legal_principle_applied: Legal (not medical) insanity test under IPC s.84; burden on accused discharged on preponderance of probability (Evidence Act s.105 read with s.8); conduct before, during and after the offence considered; CrPC Chapter XXV reasoning
precedent_relied_upon: Surendra Mishra v. State of Jharkhand (2011) 11 SCC 495; Hari Singh Gond v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2008) 16 SCC 109; Bapu @ Gajraj Singh v. State of Rajasthan (2007) 8 SCC 66; Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v. State of Gujarat AIR 1964 SC 1563; Devidas Loka Rathod v. State of Maharashtra (2018) 7 SCC 718
judicial_mitigating_factors: Not applicable to sentencing; court weighed prior insanity indicated by prior treatment, the doctor's evidence, and the later fitness to stand trial as grounds for acquittal
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds discharged; pending applications disposed of

case_title: Kashibai & Ors. v. The State of Karnataka
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (accused no.3 was the victim's husband); parents-in-law (accused nos.1 and 2)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.498A r/w s.34; IPC s.306 r/w s.34 (acquitted on appeal)
evidence_type: Oral testimony of family and neighbours on dowry harassment; medical (post-mortem) evidence; documentary evidence; hostile witnesses
aggravating_circumstances: Alleged and accepted for s.498A: physical and mental harassment of the victim over dowry demands for cash and gold
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.498A r/w s.34 (2 years SI, Rs 2,000 fine each) and s.306 r/w s.34 (5 years SI, Rs 5,000 fine each); accused no.4 acquitted
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim married one of the accused about three years before the incident. The victim's mother complained to police that, after the marriage, the victim's husband, parents-in-law and brother-in-law ill-treated the victim physically and mentally over demands for dowry in cash and gold. The complaint stated that the victim died by jumping into an open well in a field in a village on a morning in February 2010. Twenty-one witnesses and documentary evidence were presented at trial. The victim's parents, an uncle, a person who arranged the marriage and two neighbours testified about dowry demands and harassment of the victim by the accused. Four witnesses turned hostile. The post-mortem doctor recorded the cause of death as drowning due to asphyxia, but gave no opinion on whether the death was suicidal or accidental. The victim's mother first alleged that the victim had been thrown into the well, later admitting she had not seen the body there. She also said one accused had told her by telephone that the victim had accidentally slipped. Other witnesses did not know whether the victim had jumped or slipped. When the body was taken out of the well, all four accused were present near the well.
offence_severity: Not stated for s.498A. For s.306 (acquitted): imprisonment up to ten years and fine; no minimum stated
physical_harm: Death of the victim by drowning due to asphyxia; the post-mortem report recorded injuries on the body but the court did not find whether the death was suicidal
motive: Dowry demands for cash and gold, with resulting physical and mental harassment; the court accepted the harassment for s.498A but found no proven abetment of suicide
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of parents, uncle, marriage arranger and neighbours on dowry demands and harassment (accepted for s.498A); post-mortem report on drowning due to asphyxia; no evidence accepted showing abetment of suicide
witness_credibility: Harassment evidence from parents, uncle, marriage arranger and neighbours was accepted as establishing s.498A. Four witnesses turned hostile. The mother admitted not seeing the body and not stating suicide in her complaint; the father, marriage arranger and uncle had no knowledge of how the victim fell into the well. The court gave no credit to any evidence of abetment.
post_offence_conduct: As recounted by the mother, accused no.3 telephoned her saying the victim had accidentally slipped into the well; the court did not treat this as a finding
custody_duration: Served two years of imprisonment under s.498A r/w s.34; exact custody period not stated
trial_duration: offence: 07.02.2010; trial judgment: 11.02.2014; High Court: 06.03.2021; Supreme Court: 28.02.2023 (judgment date; hearing date not given)
legal_representation: Appellants (accused): Ms. Afshan Pracha, Prakash Jadhav, Anirudh Sanganeria, Ravichandra Jadhav. State/respondent: Shubhranshu Padhi, Vishal Bansal, Ms. Rajeshwari Shankar, Niroop Sukirthy, Md. Ovais
investigation_status: Complaint registered at Bableshwar Police Station under ss.498A and 306 r/w 304 IPC; trial completed with 21 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court (II Additional Sessions Judge, Bijapur, 11.02.2014): convicted under ss.498A and 306 r/w 34. High Court (06.03.2021): appeal dismissed. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; s.498A conviction upheld, s.306 conviction set aside
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Not stated
legal_principle_applied: To convict under s.306 IPC, the death must be suicidal and abetment under s.107 must be proved, requiring evidence of instigation, conspiracy or intentional aid and a positive act by the accused. The s.113A Evidence Act presumption is discretionary and is not raised merely by a suicide within seven years of marriage.
precedent_relied_upon: M. Mohan v. State Represented by the Deputy Superintendent of Police (2011) 3 SCC 626; Mangat Ram v. State of Haryana (2014) 12 SCC 595
sentencing_rationale: Appellants had already served the two-year sentence for s.498A r/w s.34, so they were set free forthwith
other_sentence_order: Appellants directed to be set free forthwith

case_title: Munna Lal v. The State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: long-standing quarrel of about ten years between the victim and the accused's side, including a property dispute
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302
weapon: Gun (bandook), kanta (sharp-edged weapon), tamancha (locally made gun), lathi (stick); none seized
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-2, PW-3); medical (PW-1 post-mortem); recovery (bullet recovered at inquest by PW-4)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and life sentence upheld
neutral_facts: On a September morning in 1985, at about 10.00 hours, the victim and his son had come to a field after ploughing their land when four men emerged from a neighbouring field. The son stated that the men were armed with a gun, a locally made gun, a sharp-edged weapon and a stick, were hurling abuses and calling for the victim to be killed. He stated that one accused fired gunshots at the victim, another struck him with a sharp-edged weapon, another struck him with a stick, and the others beat him. A passer-by who was said to have witnessed the incident gave a similar account. Other persons said to have been present were not examined. The victim died at the scene. The post-mortem found gunshot entry and exit wounds to the abdomen and thigh, lacerations to the face and an incised wound to the abdomen. A written complaint was lodged at about 12.10 hours. During inquest a bullet was recovered from blood at the victim's hip. The weapons were not seized and no ballistic report was obtained. The investigating officer did not give evidence. A statement from the passer-by was recorded about 24 days after the incident. The families had a dispute over land and property and a long-standing enmity dating back about ten years.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock and haemorrhage; gunshot entry and exit wounds to abdomen and thigh, lacerations to face, incised wound to abdomen
motive: alleged: long-standing enmity and property dispute between the victim's family and the accused; the Court accepted the enmity as a reason PW-2 might have falsely implicated the accused
key_evidence_accepted: Medical evidence of PW-1 on cause of death and injuries; PW-2 and PW-3 testimony was not accepted as unimpeachable and was treated with caution rather than relied on alone
witness_credibility: PW-2 (son of victim) inimical to accused, testimony to be taken with caution; PW-3 a chance witness whose presence was not justified and who was not wholly reliable; PW-4's bullet recovery held doubtful
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: Served sentences in excess of 11 years and 11 months, per the judgment
bail_history: Accused were on bail during High Court appeal; directed to surrender after dismissal of appeal; later taken into custody and applied for bail
trial_duration: offence: 5 September 1985; trial judgment: 29 January 1986; High Court: 9 July 2014; Supreme Court: 24 January 2023
legal_representation: Accused: Mr. Mukesh K. Giri; State: Mr. Sanjay Kumar Tyagi
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial held
procedural_irregularity: Investigating Officer and other named witnesses not examined; weapons not seized; no ballistic report; s.161 statement of PW-3 recorded about 24 days after incident
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside, accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: Courts below scrutinised evidence meticulously; PW-2 and PW-3 reliable eyewitnesses; omission to seize weapons and absence of ballistic report not fatal where credible ocular evidence exists
defence_argument: Long-standing enmity and false implication; PW-3 a chance witness whose presence was unexplained (Jarnail Singh relied on); s.161 statement delayed 24 days; non-examination of Investigating Officer and witnesses fatal; licensed gun not seized and no ballistic report
legal_principle_applied: Evidence weighed not counted; oral testimony classed as wholly reliable, wholly unreliable, or neither (requiring corroboration); defective investigation not always fatal; non-examination of IO fatal only if prejudice; benefit of doubt where prosecution story uncertain
precedent_relied_upon: Jarnail Singh v. State of Punjab (2009) 9 SCC 719 : [2009] 13 SCR 774 (referred to; defence relied on it for chance-witness scrutiny)
other_sentence_order: Appellants to be set free immediately if not wanted in any other case

case_title: Mohd Muslim @ Hussain v. State (NCT of Delhi)
previous_criminal_record: No (prosecution has not shown involvement in any other case)
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: NDPS Act s.20, s.25, s.29; IPC s.120B
evidence_type: Recovery of ganja from co-accused; statement of co-accused who led to arrest; confessional statement of accused; bank statements of a co-accused; call records
confession: Confessional statement of the accused; prosecution relied on it, and the court only noted that reliance at the bail stage
aggravating_circumstances: Alleged recovery of 180 kg of ganja from co-accused; prosecution alleged accused was mastermind (court noted this was not backed by evidence of extensive dealing)
mitigating_circumstances: No contraband recovered from accused; no other case shown against him; age 23 at arrest; two co-accused on bail; over 7 years in custody with slow trial

high_court_outcome: Regular bail refused (order dated 08.09.2022); trial court directed to expedite trial and conclude within six months
neutral_facts: Following secret information, police conducted a raid on 28 September 2015 and allegedly found about 180 kilograms of ganja in the possession of four persons, who were arrested. During the investigation, one of the arrested persons was taken to another state to identify co-accused persons. At his instance, the accused was arrested in the early hours of 3-4 October 2015. The accused was not found in possession of any narcotic drug, and no other contraband was recovered from him. The prosecution alleged that another co-accused purchased ganja and transferred money from his bank account to the bank accounts of the accused and others before supplying the drug to a further person. Bank statements of that co-accused were relied upon to show that money had been transferred to the accused. Call records were said to show regular contact between the accused and the co-accused. The prosecution also relied on a confessional statement given by the accused. The prosecution alleged that the accused was the mastermind behind the supply of narcotic substances from another state, but no evidence of extensive dealing in narcotics was identified, and no involvement in other cases was shown. Two co-accused persons, who were not present at the raid and from whom no contraband was recovered, were the recipients of the transfers and the holders of documents relating to a seized car. One witness reportedly stated during trial that Rs. 50,000 was received from the accused. A chargesheet was filed on 29 February 2016.
physical_harm: None noted
number_of_offences: 4 charged (NDPS Act ss.20, 25, 29; IPC s.120B); 0 finally upheld (bail appeal, no conviction decided)

motive: alleged: payment for ganja supply through money transfers
key_evidence_accepted: No evidence was finally accepted (bail stage). The court noted reliance on the co-accused's statement, the confessional statement and bank statements, and found no further recovery from the accused
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: Over 7 years and 4 months (in custody since 03.10.2015, barring interim bail)
bail_history: Interim bail granted on several occasions (wedding ceremonies; ailing mother); regular bail refused by district court (08.06.2022) and High Court (08.09.2022); granted by Supreme Court
