case_title: Ansar Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Anr.
previous_criminal_record: Yes. Both respondents have a chequered criminal record; earlier both were found guilty under s.302 IPC.
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated as a personal relationship. Alleged motive: the victim's father-in-law was a witness in an earlier criminal case against one respondent (prior enmity).
statutory_provisions: IPC s.147, s.148, s.149, s.307, s.302, s.120-B, s.34; Explosive Substances Act s.3, s.4
evidence_type: Eyewitness; recovery (two country-made pistols, magazines, mobile phone, cash); disclosure statement of an arrested accused; motive material
confession: None. A disclosure by another arrested accused implicated one respondent; the Court did not rely on it as a confession or finding against the respondents.
aggravating_circumstances: Murder in broad daylight; alleged contract killing; material indicating motive; both respondents have criminal records; alleged involvement in the present case while on bail in an earlier case
trial_court_outcome: Not stated. Trial was ongoing with only one witness examined when the Supreme Court decided the appeal.
high_court_outcome: Bail applications allowed on 23.09.2021; both respondents granted regular bail
neutral_facts: The victim, the son of the complainant, was present with the complainant and companions outside a bank branch when one accused allegedly threw a grenade at him. Other accused then allegedly began indiscriminate firing. The victim died on the spot and another person present was injured. Two persons were caught at the scene with the help of the public. One gave his name and the other did not. Two country-made pistols, two magazines and a mobile phone were recovered from them. A sum of cash was also recovered from the persons apprehended, as stated in the complainant's first information report. During interrogation, one arrested person allegedly disclosed that another person and his brother had sent the arrested persons to commit the killing. The case was described as a contract killing. The investigation found that one alleged accused was present at the spot during the occurrence, while the other was alleged to be part of the conspiracy to eliminate the victim. The alleged motive was that the victim's father-in-law had been a witness in an earlier criminal case registered against that alleged conspirator. Eyewitnesses included the complainant and two others.
physical_harm: Death of the victim (Ashfaque Ahmad); injuries to Razi Ahmad @ Manu
premeditation_planning: Court observed prima facie that it was apparently a contract killing with a conspiracy to eliminate the victim; not finally determined
motive: alleged: the victim's father-in-law was a witness in a criminal case against one respondent, who had been convicted under s.302 IPC in that case
key_evidence_accepted: Prima facie only: eyewitness account of the complainant and two others; two accused arrested at the spot; material indicating motive
witness_credibility: Not assessed. The Court expressly declined to express views on the merits; one eyewitness had yet to depose.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated for the offence. During trial, respondents sought exemption from personal appearance and one was absent with non-bailable warrants issued.

legal_representation: For appellant (complainant): Siddharth Dave, Sr. Adv. For respondents (accused): Basant R, Sr. Adv., and others. For State: Sharan Thakur, A.A.G. and Additional Advocate General.
investigation_status: FIR registered (Case Crime No. 17 of 2018); investigation found respondents' alleged involvement; trial pending with only one witness examined

defence_argument: Counsel submitted that cogent circumstances are needed to cancel bail and there were no supervening circumstances warranting cancellation

case_title: Shiva Kumar @ Shiva @ Shivamurthy v. State of Karnataka
previous_criminal_record: No. First offence; the appellant's counsel also submitted he has no antecedents
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
evidence_type: Recovery (body at accused's instance; clothing and footwear near body); complaint by maternal uncle reporting victim missing
aggravating_circumstances: Brutal manner of killing after rape; victim was a woman working late-night shifts; the facts shock the conscience

neutral_facts: The victim, a woman employed by a company with an office in Electronic City, Bengaluru, often had to work late into the night or early morning. The company provided employees with cars on designated routes. At about 2:00 a.m., the victim left the office intending to take the company vehicle on route no. 131. The accused, who was the driver of a company vehicle, told the victim that the route 131 vehicle was not available and that she would have to travel in his vehicle on route no. 405. The victim got into the car driven by the accused. The victim's maternal uncle lodged a complaint stating that the victim was missing. The victim's dead body was later recovered at the instance of the accused. The victim's clothes and footwear were found near the body. The victim was 28 years old when her life was cut short in a brutal manner. The prosecution case was that the accused committed rape and murder of the victim after taking her in his vehicle.
offence_severity: Maximum: death penalty (judgment refers to an offence punishable with death penalty; alternative life imprisonment). Minimum: not stated
physical_harm: Death of victim after rape; injuries not described
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Prosecution proof of rape (s.376) and kidnapping/abduction (s.366); recovery of body at accused's instance; recovery of clothing and footwear near body
witness_credibility: Not stated
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
custody_duration: Approximately 17 years and 2 months (as submitted by appellant's counsel)
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 31.05.2016; Supreme Court: 28.03.2023

investigation_status: Complaint lodged by maternal uncle; body recovered at accused's instance; charge sheet and FIR details not stated

prosecution_argument: Constitutional Courts can impose modified sentences even where death penalty is not imposed; the most stringent punishment was contemplated and the High Court reiterated the Trial Court's view
defence_argument: Modified sentence can be imposed only by Constitutional Courts and only when commuting death penalty; Sessions Court could not impose it; relied on Sriharan and Swamy Shraddananda

neutral_facts: On the night of 21 August 2008, two accused entered a house while the victim's father, who also ran a gold and silver business from the premises, was away. The accused concealed iron rods under their clothing and attacked two inmates, the victim's son and the victim's wife, who were both killed. Gold ornaments of about 3.5 kg and cash of Rs 18,340 were taken. The father returned to the house around 10 pm to 10:30 pm, after receiving word of loud cries from the house, and found the bodies in pools of blood near iron rods, with gold missing from the shop almirah and showcase. Neighbours had gathered outside. Three witnesses, independent of one another and with no known animosity toward the accused, each said they saw one or both accused running away from the house that night carrying bags. Medical officers recorded death from brain injury and haemorrhage following a head injury and found the deaths homicidal; blood-stained iron rods were found near the bodies. Following a written report lodged around 11 pm, police apprehended one accused at about 1.15 am carrying a bag containing gold ornaments and cash, and that accused allegedly confessed. The second accused was arrested at about 4 am and produced a bag with gold ornaments; blood-stained clothing was seized from both. case_title: Balu Sudam Khalde & Anr. v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated; the only connection described is a verbal altercation between appellant No. 2 and the deceased on the night of the incident, with no prior relationship or enmity described.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (convicted); IPC s.323, s.324 and s.504, each r/w s.34, were also charged (accused Nos. 1-4)

aggravating_circumstances: Nine blows with a dangerous weapon (sickle and sword) on an unarmed, helpless victim; injuries on vital parts of the body

neutral_facts: Late on the night of the incident, the victim was talking with a friend near a car consultancy shop in a slum area when one of the accused passing by approached him, and a verbal exchange followed. Shortly afterwards, the accused arrived with others and a fight broke out. The victim's friend was struck on the head with a sickle and a sword and was bleeding. The victim was then severely attacked with a sickle and a sword, receiving multiple wounds to the hands, wrist, arm, shoulder and chest. A neighbour came out of his house during the assault and asked what the fighting was about. The injured friend asked a rickshaw driver known to them to watch the victim and then went with a neighbour to the police station to report the incident. Police took the victim to hospital, where he was declared dead. The post-mortem examination found multiple injuries, including a stab wound to the right chest that cut the ribs and entered the lung. The doctor opined that this injury was sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death, and that the injuries were caused by sharp-edged weapons. Three eyewitnesses gave oral evidence, including the injured friend, the neighbour and the rickshaw driver. The rickshaw driver stated that the injured friend told him what had happened. Following statements made by the accused in police custody, weapons were recovered in the presence of panch witnesses. A chargesheet was filed after investigation.

case_title: Parveen Kumar v. The State of Himachal Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband of the victim)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.498-A; IPC s.306; Evidence Act s.113A (presumption as to abetment of suicide)
weapon: Aluminium phosphide tablets (insecticide) consumed by the victim
evidence_type: Circumstantial (proof of prior complaints and cruelty, presumption under s.113A); documentary (FIR, complaints, maintenance petition, daily diary entry, post-mortem referral); oral evidence of the victim's brother and two defence neighbours
aggravating_circumstances: Victim had filed three cases against the accused during her lifetime; death within seven years of marriage; accused did not inform the victim's parents immediately after the incident
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.498-A IPC; two years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.1,000 with default clause; acquitted under s.306 IPC
high_court_outcome: Accused's appeal against s.498-A conviction dismissed; State's appeal against s.306 acquittal allowed and accused convicted under s.306 IPC
offence_finally_established: IPC s.498-A (cruelty by husband) and IPC s.306 (abetment of suicide)
neutral_facts: The accused married the victim in October 1992, and a male child was born to them in December 1993. Earlier, the victim had lodged a first information report alleging cruelty by the accused and had filed a complaint under Sections 107/151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and a petition seeking maintenance for herself and her child. The victim later returned to the matrimonial home. On 26 September 1994, at about 1:45 a.m., the victim consumed tablets of aluminium phosphide, an insecticide. She was taken to hospital but died at about 5:00 a.m. the same day. The police recorded the death in the daily diary register and sent the body for post-mortem. On 1 October 1994 the victim's brother lodged a first information report alleging that the accused had subjected the victim to cruelty and forced her to commit suicide. After investigation, a chargesheet was filed under Sections 498-A and 306 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution relied on the victim's three earlier proceedings against the accused, the fact of poisoning and death, and the fact that the death occurred within seven years of marriage. The accused was said to have told investigators that the victim took the tablets by mistake, believing them to be insecticide, and had not informed the victim's parents immediately after the incident. The defence relied on a suicide note stating the victim acted because of intolerable pain and illness, and on two neighbours who said the couple's relationship was cordial.
offence_severity: Maximum ten years imprisonment and fine (s.306 IPC); no minimum stated in the judgment
physical_harm: Death of the victim from consuming aluminium phosphide tablets; died at hospital the same day
motive: Cruelty and harassment by the accused that drove the victim to suicide (as concurrently found by the trial court and High Court)
key_evidence_accepted: Marriage on 10.10.1992; birth of a male child on 18.12.1993; three cases filed by the victim against the accused (FIR 59/1993, complaint under s.107/151 Cr.P.C., s.125 Cr.P.C. maintenance case); proved poisoning by aluminium phosphide and death; concurrent finding of cruelty under s.498-A
witness_credibility: Two defence neighbour witnesses did not inspire confidence, given the undisputed prior cases filed by the victim; the court made no separate assessment of the victim's brother (PW-3)
post_offence_conduct: Did not inform the victim's parents immediately after the incident; court treated this as indicating guilt. State alleged he tried to mislead the investigation by claiming the tablets were taken by mistake (alleged only)
trial_duration: offence: 26.09.1994; trial judgment: 24.02.2000; High Court: 16.03.2011; Supreme Court: 23 September 2024
legal_representation: Accused: Ashok Tobria, M.S. Yadav, Rajesh Kumar Pandey, S.Y. Usmani and others (Advs.). State: Vikrant Narayan Vasudeva, Sarthak Chiller, Rohit Lochav (Advs.) for the Respondent-State
investigation_status: FIR lodged on 01.10.1994 by victim's brother; investigation completed; chargesheet filed under s.498-A and s.306 IPC; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Suicide note (Exhibit DF) not duly exhibited for admission in evidence
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.498-A, acquitted under s.306. High Court: s.498-A conviction upheld; State's appeal allowed and convicted under s.306. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed, conviction upheld
prosecution_argument: Accused tried to mislead investigation; death within two years of marriage after three complaints by victim; s.113A presumption rightly raised; defence witnesses unconvincing
defence_argument: Settlement of the earlier cases was not an admission of guilt; no cruelty allegations between June 1993 and the death; suicide note shows suicide due to pain and illness; no presumption under s.113A; conviction cannot rest on conjecture and surmise
legal_principle_applied: Section 113A presumption is discretionary and arises only if basic facts (suicide within seven years of marriage and cruelty by husband) are proved; cruelty under s.498-A and abetment under s.306 must be proved beyond reasonable doubt
precedent_relied_upon: Hans Raj v. State of Haryana [2004] 2 SCR 676 : (2004) 12 SCC 257; Naresh Kumar v. State of Haryana [2024] 2 SCR 830 : (2024) 3 SCC 573 (s.113A gives discretion, no mandatory presumption)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Victim's three prior cases against the accused for harassment and cruelty; death within seven years of marriage; accused did not inform the victim's parents immediately
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Sandeep v. State of Uttarakhand
accused_socioeconomic_status: Poor economic background; was supporting his entire family
previous_criminal_record: No (no bad antecedent apart from the present offence)

statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; Arms Act s.25/27 (Arms Act charge ended in acquittal)
weapon: Country-made pistol (12 bore), described as a katta
evidence_type: Eyewitness (P.W.1, P.W.2); medical (post-mortem by P.W.7); recovery of pistol and empty cartridge on pointing out; scene material objects (torch, lantern, bloodstained soil and cot); FIR
aggravating_circumstances: Firearm killing; wounds showed blackening and tattooing (close-range firing); the appellant was armed with a gun
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden provocation over refusal to give jaggery; no premeditation; no bad antecedent; poor economic background; good jail conduct; possibility of reformation; long incarceration
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; rigorous imprisonment for life with fine of Rs.1,000 (default 3 months RI); co-accused acquitted; Arms Act charge acquitted
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No.65 of 2006) dismissed; conviction and sentence affirmed

neutral_facts: On an evening at about 9.45 pm, the victim was sitting in the courtyard of the home with the victim's wife, talking. Four men from the same village came to the courtyard. The prosecution alleged that they said they would teach the victim a lesson for refusing to give them jaggery (gur), and that one of them fired a firearm at the victim. The shot struck the victim's right chest and arm. The victim's son and grandson, who were nearby, heard the shot, reached the courtyard within moments and reported seeing the four men fleeing. The victim was taken to a government hospital, where a doctor declared the victim dead. A written report was lodged the following day and a case was registered. The investigating officer inspected the scene, prepared an inquest report and a site plan, and seized a torch, a lantern, bloodstained soil, a bloodstained cot and bedding. Acting on information given by one accused, police recovered a 12-bore country-made pistol and one empty cartridge from a field near a transformer. The post-mortem found two firearm wounds of entry, on the right arm and right chest, with blackening and tattooing around them; death was due to shock and haemorrhage from firearm injuries, and both wounds could have been caused by one bullet. Eyewitnesses testified that the accused were armed and that one of them fired on the exhortation of the others. One eyewitness explained the source of light at the scene. The investigating officer's account differed on whether the shooting was instigated by others. Several discrepancies in the prosecution evidence were noted.
offence_severity: Maximum: death or life imprisonment (as stated in Navas quoted by the Court); minimum not stated
physical_harm: Death of 70-year-old victim from two firearm wounds of entry (right upper arm and right chest) with fractured ribs; shock and haemorrhage
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.302 r/w s.34; Arms Act s.25/27); 1 finally upheld (IPC s.302)
premeditation_planning: No premeditation found; the court held the act arose from sudden provocation
motive: Sudden provocation arising from the victim's refusal to give jaggery (gur)

case_title: Karakkattu Muhammed Basheer v. The State of Kerala
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (registered marriage on 17.05.1989, dissolved by deed dated 31.07.1989, as recorded in the judgment)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302; IPC s.201; both read with IPC s.34 (charged)
evidence_type: Circumstantial (no eyewitness); medical (postmortem); witness testimony on presence and sighting; recovery of bag, blood-stained items and weapon
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of murder (s.302) and s.201 IPC; life imprisonment under s.302 and 7 years RI under s.201 for the accused
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed on 18.10.1996; conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: The body of the victim was found in a paddy field in the early morning of 17 August 1989 by a passer-by on his way to work. A postmortem examination found six antemortem injuries on the left side of the head, fractured into multiple fragments, plus abraded contusions on the right wrist and left knee. The head injuries were sufficient to cause death and could have been caused by a coconut scraper. The medical expert estimated death about 30 to 35 hours before the postmortem. The prosecution alleged that the accused and a co-accused were in an illicit relationship, and that the victim often stayed at the co-accused's house. The victim's mother and sister said the victim left for that house around 7:30 PM on 16 August. The co-accused's two children said the victim left their house around 9:00 PM and did not return. A witness said he saw the back of a person he assumed was the accused entering the house around 11:30 PM. The prosecution alleged that during an altercation about the relationship, the accused struck the victim on the head repeatedly with a coconut scraper, dragged the body out, and carried it about one kilometre to the paddy field. A taxi driver said he saw a man he identified as the accused at a bus stand at about 5:30 AM on 17 August, wearing a shirt, lungi and towel. A bag said to contain blood-stained clothes, a blanket and a head towel belonging to the accused was said to have been recovered on 27 August. Blood-stained cotton swabs, cloth and the coconut scraper were said to have been recovered from the co-accused's house, in the presence of three witnesses who said they were only shown the items.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from head injuries (six antemortem injuries fractured into multiple fragments); abraded contusions on right wrist and left knee
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.302 and s.201); 0 finally upheld
motive: alleged: illicit relationship between the accused and the co-accused; the court did not accept this motive as proved
key_evidence_accepted: Victim's presence at the co-accused's house until about 9:00 PM on 16.08.1989, from the unchallenged evidence of the co-accused's children; the court otherwise found the chain of circumstances against the accused incomplete
witness_credibility: Sighting witness (PW14) unreliable: saw only the back and assumed identity. Bag witness (PW18) contradicted the recovery account. Recovery witnesses (PW26-28) did not see seizure. Taxi driver (PW20) saw from a distance and origin not established.
post_offence_conduct: Not stated (prosecution alleged the accused left town on the morning of 17 August; the court found this not established)
trial_duration: offence: 16-17 August 1989; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 18.10.1996; Supreme Court: 05 November 2024
legal_representation: Accused/Appellant: Thomas P. Joseph, Sr. Adv., with Dr. Linto K.B., Tom Joseph, Dinny Thomas, Advs. State: Harshad V. Hameed, Dileep Poolakkot, Mrs. Ashly Harshad, Farhad Tehmu Marolia, Amar Nath Singh, Shivam Sai, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR/case registered as unnatural death; investigated; final report submitted against the accused and co-accused; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Weapon and blood-stained item recoveries not made in the presence of independent witnesses; discrepancy in the date of the bag's handover to police; no handwriting expert evidence on the letters

defence_argument: Case rests only on circumstantial evidence with glaring gaps; the chain is incomplete and leaves room for other explanations; the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence test: the chain must be complete and point only to guilt; any missing link or reasonable alternative hypothesis entitles the accused to benefit of doubt; last-seen theory needs corroboration

No child was born in the first five years of the marriage, and the victim was allegedly subjected to physical and mental harassment on that account, leading to a return to the parental home for a time. After the victim returned to the matrimonial home, a son was born. About twelve months before the death, the victim told the victim's father that the accused had sold gold ornaments the victim had received as streedhan at the marriage. When the victim demanded their return, the victim was allegedly physically and mentally harassed. On 18 April 2021 the victim's father was informed that the victim had died by hanging. It was alleged that the harassment by the accused compelled the victim to take the victim's own life. An FIR was registered on the same day at the victim's father's instance. The investigation produced the FIR, the investigating officer's chargesheet findings, and statements of the victim's father, other witnesses and the victim's cousins. These described repeated complaints by the victim of physical and mental harassment by the accused, including the sale of the ornaments and harassment on demand for their return. The cousins' statements mentioned only incidents that occurred about a year before the death.

case_title: Pradeep Kumar v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated (only alleged: co-accused A-2 borrowed money from the deceased; not relied on by the Court)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34
weapon: Dandas (sticks); no sharp-edged weapon recovered, though the doctor attributed an incise wound to a sharp-edged weapon
evidence_type: Circumstantial (no eyewitnesses); also medical post-mortem evidence, recoveries, forensic (FSL) blood-group report, alleged extra-judicial confession, and last-seen witnesses

neutral_facts: On the evening of 10 April 2004 the victim left a workplace on his motorcycle after receiving two phone calls, saying he had to go to a market. The next morning his family reported him missing. His body was later found lying in a field with his throat tied with cloth, one eye badly injured and injuries to the head. The post-mortem doctor found an incised wound that, in the doctor's view, was caused by a sharp-edged weapon. Investigators recorded statements from several persons. One witness said he saw four young men on a motorcycle carrying sticks near a bypass that evening, one of them with blood-stained clothing, and noted a registration number. Another said he saw three young men on a motorcycle holding sticks at a road junction around 10 pm and recognised one of them. A third said he saw the victim seated on a motorcycle with one of the accused at a junction. After a surrender, the accused were said to have made an extra-judicial confession before a village sarpanch, who also said he had seen the victim earlier that evening. Police recovered sticks, a pair of trousers and a mobile phone. Forensic tests reported blood of the same group as the victim on the sticks and trousers. No sharp-edged weapon was recovered. The recoveries were not made in the presence of any independent witness. The case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence, with no eyewitness to the killing.

witness_credibility: PW-10 (Sarpanch) not trustworthy; PW-11 (chance witness) completely unreliable; PW-12 (chance witness) does not inspire confidence; PW-16 (relative) version highly improbable and unreliable; IO's recoveries lacked independent witnesses
post_offence_conduct: Alleged surrender on 17.04.2004 through the village Sarpanch with an alleged extra-judicial confession; the Court found the confession false and unbelievable

legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence test: circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, exclude every other hypothesis, and form a complete chain; suspicion cannot replace proof beyond reasonable doubt

neutral_facts: On an evening in January 1999, the victim's brother (the informant) and the informant's son were sitting together warming themselves by a fire when the victim was about to walk home. Three men came to the spot to confront the victim over a fight that had broken out between them the previous day. One man carried a pharsa, another a kulhari and the third a lathi. According to the informant's first information report, one attacker struck the victim on the head with a pharsa and another struck him with the same weapon. A third blow was struck with a kulhari. When the victim fell, the lathi-carrying man struck his legs, and a further pharsa blow was delivered to his head. A person who tried to rescue the victim was struck on the shoulder with a lathi. The victim died about two days later from his injuries. A medical examination recorded four incised wounds to the scalp, and the rescuer had two blunt injuries. Police arrested the accused in stages. A lathi was recovered from one accused and a kulhari from another, and a blood-stained pharsa was recovered from a third. The fourth named person had no recovery made against him. The informant and the injured rescuer gave eyewitness accounts of the attack.

neutral_facts: The victim and the first accused married in 2007, and a male child was born in 2008. Around January 2009, a passport application for the minor child was submitted to the Regional Passport Office, Bengaluru, and a passport was issued shortly afterwards. The victim alleges that his signatures on that passport application were forged and that the application was submitted while he was outside the country. The accused side contends that the victim had consented to the passport and later sent a sponsorship letter citing the child's passport number. The victim lodged a complaint on 13 May 2010, registered as an FIR under sections 420, 468 and 471 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The first accused had earlier complained of cruelty by the victim and his family. During the investigation, the charges under sections 468 and 471 were initially dropped. The State Forensic Laboratory expressed no opinion on the questioned photocopied signatures, citing bad line quality of strokes. A private laboratory report obtained by the victim, dated 15 July 2013, opined that the signatures did not closely resemble the victim's specimen signatures. A passport officer was implicated for allegedly withholding the original passport application. A supplementary chargesheet was later filed.

post_offence_conduct: Not stated

legal_representation: Appellants: Ranbir Singh Yadav, Mohammed Sharookh, Prateek Yadav, Anzu K. Varkey, Mahesh Sharma, Chembugari Abheeshna (Advocates). defence_argument: Victim consented to the passport and sent the sponsorship letter citing its number; State FSL report was inconclusive and should prevail over paid private report; no prima facie case; complaint was a counterblast to the cruelty complaint; discharge sought under Krishna Chawla
legal_principle_applied: Cheating (s.420) requires deception, dishonest inducement to deliver property, and dishonest intention from inception, with damage or injury; forgery requires fabrication of a false document with dishonest intent; s.173(8) further investigation requires fresh evidence; continuing proceedings without these ingredients is abuse of process

case_title: Velthepu Srinivas and Others v. State of Andhra Pradesh (Now State of Telangana) and Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Accused and victim from the same village and same family group (as stated in the judgment); alleged political rivalry and animosity after a Gram Panchayat election in which the victim's sister won and the wife of one accused (A-4) lost.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34 (for A-3 altered to IPC s.304 Part II)
weapon: Axe, sword, stone and knife (a stick was also seized as material object)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PWs 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8); medical (post-mortem by PW-11); recovery of weapons and lungi on accused's pointing; Section 164 CrPC statements; forensic report; photographs and sketch of scene
confession: Confessional statement recorded by PW-18 leading to recovery of axe, sword and knife; the judgment does not expressly rely on it for the decision
aggravating_circumstances: Multiple sharp-weapon injuries (12 injuries, 10 by sharp weapons); fatal injury at back of neck by axe; victim dragged from auto-rickshaw and attacked by several accused
mitigating_circumstances: For A-3 only: did not wield the axe, used only a stone, some witnesses said he merely threatened them, no common intention found
trial_court_outcome: All four convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 500 each, default one month simple imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Initial acquittal of all accused (21.06.2007) was set aside by the Supreme Court and remanded; on remand the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence and dismissed the appeals (26.04.2022)
offence_finally_established: A-1, A-2 and A-4: murder under IPC s.302 r/w s.34. A-3: culpable homicide not amounting to murder under IPC s.304 Part II
neutral_facts: The victim was travelling to a nearby town in an auto-rickshaw on a morning in November 2001, with two co-passengers. The accused are four men from the same village and family group as the victim. Earlier, a relative of the victim had won a village council election against the wife of one accused, and the resulting rivalry between the two groups is alleged to be the motive. When the auto-rickshaw reached a house belonging to one accused, one accused stopped the vehicle and pulled the victim out by his legs. Another accused joined in and dragged him toward that house. The accused are alleged to have attacked him with an axe, a sword, a stone and a knife. The victim's son, an eyewitness, reported the matter to the police the same evening. The investigating officer found the body in the front yard of the house, took photographs, prepared a sketch, and conducted an inquest in the presence of panch witnesses. The post-mortem recorded twelve injuries, ten caused by sharp-edged weapons, including a partial amputation of three fingers of the left hand and a deep lacerated wound at the back of the neck. The cause of death was given as cardio-pulmonary arrest due to transection of the spinal cord at the atlanto-occipital joint. On 23 November 2001 the accused were apprehended. One accused gave a confessional statement, after which an axe, a sword and a knife were recovered from bushes in a field. Several eyewitnesses described the sequence of the assault, the weapons used and the role of each accused. Among them, several said one accused struck the victim's head with a stone. Recovered objects were sent for forensic examination.
physical_harm: Death of the victim on the spot; 12 injuries including 10 sharp-weapon wounds, partial amputation of three fingers of left hand and a deep lacerated wound at back of neck with transection of spinal cord
number_of_offences: 1 charged (s.302 r/w s.34 IPC); 1 finally upheld for A-1, A-2 and A-4; A-3's conviction altered to s.304 Part II
motive: alleged: political animosity between the two groups arising from the Gram Panchayat election result
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony (especially PW-6, plus PWs 1, 3, 4, 7, 8) accepted for A-1, A-2 and A-4; post-mortem findings relied on, including the fatal neck injury caused by axe; for A-3, the consistent eyewitness account that he struck the head with a stone
witness_credibility: Trial court and High Court found PW-6 credible and consistent; Supreme Court accepted eyewitness accounts as correctly appreciated for A-1, A-2, A-4; for A-3 the Supreme Court relied on the consistent account of the stone blow, while noting his threats as described by some witnesses
post_offence_conduct: Apprehended on 23.11.2001 and produced before the Circle Inspector; no absconding or flight noted
trial_duration: offence: 15.11.2001; trial judgment: 24.02.2005; High Court: 26.04.2022 (earlier High Court acquittal 21.06.2007, set aside and remanded); Supreme Court: 06.02.2024
legal_representation: Appellants (accused): Gaurav Agrawal, D. Abhinav Rao, Ms. Prerna Robin, Rahul Jajoo, Devadipta Das. State: Krishan Kumar Singh (learned counsel for the State). Respondent No. 2: Sirajudeen, Senior Advocate
investigation_status: FIR registered on complaint of the victim's son; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed 09.01.2002; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Trial and High Court did not separately analyse A-3's role and mechanically inferred common intention from his presence and family relation with the other accused
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302/34, life imprisonment. High Court (first): acquitted all accused (21.06.2007), set aside by Supreme Court and remanded. High Court (after remand, 26.04.2022): confirmed conviction and dismissed appeals. Supreme Court: convictions of A-1, A-2, A-4 upheld; A-3 convicted under s.304 Part II and sentenced to 10 years
prosecution_argument: Not stated
defence_argument: Not stated
legal_principle_applied: Common intention under s.34 must be shown by evidence; presence and family relation are insufficient. Where common intention to murder is absent, liability may rest on knowledge that the act is likely to cause death, under s.304 Part II
precedent_relied_upon: Camilo Vaz v. State of Goa, (2000) 9 SCC 1; Bawa Singh v. State of Punjab, 1993 Supp (2) SCC 754; Sarup Singh v. State of Haryana, (2009) 16 SCC 479; Ghana Pradhan & Ors. v. State of Orissa, 1991 Supp (2) SCC 451
sentencing_rationale: For A-3: no common intention to murder, no axe used, only a stone; knowledge that a stone blow to the head is likely to cause death; sentence of 10 years under s.304 Part II. For A-1, A-2, A-4: life imprisonment upheld under s.302/34
judicial_mitigating_factors: For A-3: did not wield the axe, had only a stone, merely threatened some witnesses, was not shown to have shared common intention to murder
judicial_aggravating_factors: Fatal injury at the neck inflicted with an axe by A-1, followed by assault by A-2 and A-4; multiple weapons used against the victim
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Deepak Kumar Shrivas & Anr. v. State of Chhattisgarh & Ors.
accused_victim_relationship: Prior financial dealing: money paid by respondent no.6 to the appellant for a job for her daughter; no family or personal relationship stated
statutory_provisions: Not stated
evidence_type: Documentary and testimonial material from preliminary police enquiry (recorded statements, enquiry report); FIR allegation of cash payment with no bank transactions
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Not stated
high_court_outcome: Writ petition under Article 226 for quashing FIR and proceedings dismissed
neutral_facts: The victim alleged that the accused and his brother took about Rs 4 lakh in cash in April 2019 on the promise of securing a job for the victim's daughter in a government department or the private sector, to be provided within three months. According to the FIR, no job was provided and the payment was made entirely in cash with no bank transactions. Earlier, in 2021, the other party had complained to the district Collector that the victim had demanded money for securing a job for the accused's brother and had paid about Rs 80,000 cash plus further bank deposits. The complaint was referred to the police for enquiry. The Station House Officer recorded statements from both parties and other persons. In that enquiry the victim stated that Rs 4 lakh had been paid for the daughter's job. Both sides alleged that false complaints were being made against each other. The enquiry noted that the parties did not produce the documents, call records or recorded conversations sought, and it recommended closing that complaint. Later, on 27 July 2022, the victim lodged an FIR against the accused and his brother. Before registration, a further enquiry found that both parties had made allegations against each other of taking money for providing jobs.
physical_harm: Not stated
financial_property_loss: Per appellant's complaint: Rs 80,000 cash plus about Rs 20,000 deposited in bank accounts; per FIR allegation: Rs 4 lakh paid in cash in April 2019
motive: Court accepted: FIR lodged to recover money under coercion and pressure, not for prosecution of an offence
key_evidence_accepted: Recorded statement of respondent no.6 in the earlier enquiry that she paid Rs 4 lakh for her daughter's job; the record of the earlier enquiry
witness_credibility: Court found the parties' conduct and claims prima facie tainted with suspicion; the complainant's unexplained delay raised doubts on the authenticity of the claims
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
trial_duration: offence: April 2019 (alleged payment); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 11.07.2023; Supreme Court: 19.02.2024
legal_representation: Appellants: Sameer Shrivastava, Dr. Sangeeta Verma, Shivendra Dixit. Respondents (including State counsel, not separately identified): Gautam Narayan, Ms. Asmita Singh, Harshit Goel, Sujay Jain, Sachin Patil, Kailas Bajirao Autade, Sunil Kumar Sethi
investigation_status: FIR registered as Crime No. 248 of 2022 on 27.07.2022 after earlier preliminary enquiries; the proceedings arising from it were quashed by the Supreme Court
procedural_irregularity: Court noted an unexplained delay of about three years in lodging the FIR; no other procedural lapse noted
appeal_history: Trial court: Not stated (FIR stage). High Court: writ petition under Article 226 dismissed on 11.07.2023. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, proceedings arising out of FIR 248 of 2022 quashed
prosecution_argument: A cognizable offence was disclosed; investigation should continue and the appellant can challenge the charge sheet and seek discharge later; it was a clear case of cheating
defence_argument: Earlier enquiry on similar mutual allegations was not substantiated; FIR is a mala fide counterblast to recover money; the FIR is barred by delay of more than three years
legal_principle_applied: Criminal proceedings may be quashed where the FIR's object is recovery of money under coercion rather than prosecution, considering unexplained delay, prior inquiry and abuse of process; police must exercise heightened caution in such disputes
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
other_sentence_order: Impugned High Court order set aside and all proceedings arising out of FIR No. 248 of 2022 quashed. Court also made general suggestions to police to exercise heightened caution (para 15)

case_title: Ram Singh v. State of U.P.
accused_victim_relationship: Political rival and prior enmity with the informant (the victim's son) over a village Pradhan election; no direct relationship with the deceased is described.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.301 r/w s.302; IPC s.307 (chargesheet also cites s.34 for s.307)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; medical (post-mortem) evidence; seizure of cartridge tikli and pellets; police and village-head testimony
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.301 r/w s.302 and s.307 IPC; life imprisonment for s.301/302 and 5 years RI for s.307, concurrent. Co-accused acquitted.
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: On an evening, the victim was sitting on a cot in the open space in front of the family house near the entrance. Her two sons were sitting nearby, and two neighbours sat on another cot. They were chatting under a lantern hanging from the roof. At about 8 pm, the accused arrived from the north with a co-accused. The prosecution alleged that the co-accused told the accused that one son was causing trouble and should be killed. The accused then fired a country-made pistol. The bullet struck the victim's left breast, and she died immediately. The targeted son said he bent below the cot. The witnesses gave differing accounts of where people were sitting and whether the son had stood up. The son lodged a written report at a police station at midnight on the same day, stating that the two men ran away towards the north. The police seized a cartridge tikli from the wound, a 12 bore cartridge from the cot, and 12 pellets from the wound. The post-mortem recovered 55 pellets from the body. The pistol was never recovered. The pellets and tikli were not sent for ballistic examination. Blood-stained clothes and soil samples were sent to a chemical examiner, but no report was received. Another son who was present and the scribe of the report were not examined. A village head said he heard the firing and learned of the death later from a passer-by, who was also not examined. The prosecution case mentions a prior rivalry over a village election and related cross cases.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a gunshot wound to the left breast, bone-deep, with broken ribs, lung and heart lacerations; 55 pellets removed at post-mortem
motive: alleged: prior political enmity over the village Pradhan election between the accused and the informant; the court did not decide motive
key_evidence_accepted: None accepted as sufficient to prove guilt. Eyewitness evidence was found unreliable; medical evidence of the gunshot wound was noted but did not cure the gaps.
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses (informant and PW-2) were not found credible: versions of positions and movements were inconsistent; PW-3 said he did not see a pistol; material witnesses were not examined.
post_offence_conduct: As alleged by the prosecution witnesses, the accused and co-accused ran away towards the north after the shooting.
bail_history: Supreme Court issued notice on the prayer for bail; outcome of bail prayer not stated
trial_duration: offence: not given (FIR lodged 19.08.1982 at midnight); trial judgment: 28.05.1983; High Court: 05.02.2018; Supreme Court: 21.02.2024
legal_representation: Accused: Pradeep Kumar Mathur, Chiranjeev Johri, Chandra Nand Jha, M.K. Tiwari, Sitesh Kumar, Arvind Kumar (Advocates). State: Rana Mukherjee, Sr. Adv., Samarth Mohanty, Ankit Goel (Advocates).
investigation_status: FIR registered as No. 252/1982; chargesheet filed; trial held
procedural_irregularity: Material witnesses (the other son and the scribe, and a passer-by) not examined; adverse inference drawn; pellets and tikli not sent for ballistic examination; weapon not recovered; chemical examiner report not received
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted and sentenced. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, accused acquitted (benefit of doubt).
prosecution_argument: Ocular evidence proves the accused fired the fatal shot; given the gruesome nature of the killing and witness testimony, conviction is justified and the High Court rightly dismissed the appeal.
defence_argument: Eyewitnesses were interested and political rivals and not true eyewitnesses; material witnesses not examined; no weapon recovered and no ballistic link; the co-accused was acquitted on the same evidence, so the accused should also be acquitted; no evidence exists.
legal_principle_applied: Non-recovery of weapon and absence of ballistic expert are not fatal alone, but become fatal where eyewitness evidence is not credible and material witnesses are not examined. Benefit of doubt applies where co-accused with identical evidence was acquitted (parity).
precedent_relied_upon: Javed Shaukat Ali Qureshi v. State of Gujarat, (2023) 9 SCC 164; Munna Lal v. State of U.P. (2023); Gurucharan Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1963 SC 340; Sukhwant Singh v. State of Punjab, (1995) 3 SCC 367; State of Punjab v. Jugraj Singh, (2002) 3 SCC 234; Gulab v. State of U.P., (2022) 12 SCC 677; Pritinder Singh v. State of Punjab, (2023) 7 SCC 727
other_sentence_order: Appellant directed to be released from jail forthwith, if not required in any other case

case_title: Chandan v. The State (Delhi Admn.)
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302
evidence_type: Eyewitness; forensic (blood matching); recovery (knife and shirt); medical (post-mortem)
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; sentence not specified in the judgment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: On the evening of the incident, the victim and the accused were walking a few steps ahead of the victim's sister-in-law, who was returning from a local market. She saw them grapple with each other and then saw the accused stab the victim several times with a knife the accused was carrying. The victim collapsed and the accused ran away. The victim was first taken to a nearby private clinic and then advised to go to a hospital, where the victim was declared dead on arrival. A post-mortem the next day recorded multiple incised stab wounds on the body. One wound entered the left chest cavity, injuring the pericardium and the tip of the left ventricle; the examining doctor opined that this injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, which was due to shock and haemorrhage. The doctor stated that the injuries were possible with the recovered knife, which had been produced in a sealed parcel. An FIR was registered the same day based on the eyewitness's statement. Shortly afterwards, police received information and found the accused coming from the side of a drain, carrying a blood-stained knife and wearing a blood-stained shirt. The accused was apprehended and the knife and shirt were recovered. Forensic analysis found that the victim's blood matched blood on the knife. The eyewitness described the sequence of events in detail, having watched from a short distance, and was cross-examined at length without any material discrediting her testimony.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple stab wounds; post-mortem recorded eight incised wounds, with the chest wound entering the left chest cavity and held sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-2; forensic blood match between victim and knife; recovery of blood-stained knife and shirt from the accused by PW-12 shortly after the murder; post-mortem findings consistent with the weapon
witness_credibility: PW-2 (sister-in-law) treated as the star and reliable eyewitness; lengthy cross-examination did not discredit her; court accepted her account of the sequence of events
post_offence_conduct: Fled the scene after the stabbing; caught the same day in the vicinity carrying the blood-stained knife and wearing a blood-stained shirt
bail_history: Interim bail granted by order dated 09.05.2012; vacated by the Supreme Court, and the appellant directed to surrender
trial_duration: offence: 28.05.1993; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 02.07.2010; Supreme Court: 05.04.2024
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: Ms. Richa Kapoor and Deepak Singh, Advocates. State: Mrs. Aishwariya Bhati, A.S.G., with Mukesh Kumar Maroria, Mrs. Shivika Mehra, Mrs. Rajeshwari Shankar, Alankar Gupta and Akshaja Singh, Advocates
investigation_status: FIR registered 28.05.1993 at Police Station Kashmere Gate; chargesheet filed; 18 prosecution witnesses examined at trial
procedural_irregularity: None noted; doubts raised by the defence on the manner of recovery of the knife were held not to move the case
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC. High Court (CRLA No.130 of 1997, order dated 02.07.2010): conviction and sentence upheld. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Daylight murder established by a reliable eyewitness, supported by the blood match between the victim and the knife and the same-day recovery of the knife and shirt from the accused; the judgment does not separately record the State's oral arguments
defence_argument: Prosecution failed to establish any motive; doubts raised on the manner of recovery of the knife
legal_principle_applied: Absence of motive is of little or no consequence where a reliable eyewitness, with nothing to discredit the testimony, establishes the crime
precedent_relied_upon: Shivaji Genu Mohite v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1973 SC 55; Bikau Pandey v. State of Bihar, (2003) 12 SCC 616; Rajagopal v. Muthupandi, (2017) 11 SCC 120; Yogesh Singh v. Mahabeer Singh, (2017) 11 SCC 195
other_sentence_order: Appellant directed to surrender before the Trial Court within four weeks; interim bail dated 09.05.2012 vacated; copy of judgment to be sent to the Trial Court to ensure the appellant undergoes the remaining sentence

case_title: Babu Sahebagouda Rudragoudar and Others v. State of Karnataka
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: alleged grudge by the accused over the murder of a relative of accused A-4 two years earlier, in which the victim's family members were arraigned
statutory_provisions: IPC s.143, s.147, s.148, s.506(2), s.302 r/w s.149 (charged); High Court convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34; Supreme Court also examined Evidence Act s.27 and s.60
weapon: Jambiya (jambai), axes, sickles and a koyta (as alleged; recovered weapons held not proved)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, PW-4, PW-5, PW-6, PW-15; found unreliable or contradictory); medical evidence (PW-17); recovery and disclosure evidence (PW-27; rejected); FIR/complaint (Ex P-10; treated as post-investigation document)
confession: Section 27 disclosure statements of A-1 and A-2 (Ex P-15, P-16) and voluntary statement of A-3 were not proved and were not relied on
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted all six accused (A-1 to A-6) on 23 July 2005; no sentence
high_court_outcome: State's appeal allowed in part; acquittal of A-1, A-2 and A-3 reversed; convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 50,000 each (default two years); appeals against A-5 and A-6 dismissed; appeal against A-4 abated
neutral_facts: The victim's father owned agricultural land and a house in a village. In the morning of a September day in 2001, the victim went with four farm workers to build a check dam on the family land. The father packed their lunch at midday and visited the field. Work stopped at about 3.30 pm, and the group set off for the village. Near a particular landholding at about 4 pm, several accused allegedly appeared and said that the victim's side had killed a member of their family and that they would take revenge in the same manner. The accused were said to be armed with a jambiya, axes and sickles, and the victim was beaten and fell. The father alleged that he was threatened and hid in bushes until after sunset. He then returned home and told family members. A written complaint was lodged at the police station early the next morning, and an FIR was registered. Investigation led to a charge sheet against the accused and others. Twenty-seven witnesses were examined. Four workers and the father were presented as eyewitnesses, along with another witness. The medical jurist described decomposition of the body and an estimated time of death more than 24 hours before autopsy. Witnesses said it had rained heavily for about three days before the incident. The investigating officer described recoveries of axes, a koyta, a jambiya and sickles made on the basis of statements of the accused. The complainant said police showed him the weapons on the day of the incident. No serological opinion on the weapons was obtained.
physical_harm: Death of the victim after being belaboured with weapons (as alleged); the Court noted that only the deceased was injured
motive: alleged: revenge for the murder of the son of accused A-4 two years earlier; the Court found this motive too remote to impute to the accused and noted it could equally be a motive for false implication
key_evidence_accepted: No incriminating evidence accepted. The Court relied on the medical jurist's time-of-death opinion (PW-17), PW-6's account contradicting PW-1, the rain evidence, the absence of the Daily Diary entry, and the post-investigation nature of the FIR to discredit the prosecution case
witness_credibility: PW-1 (complainant, claimed eyewitness) held wholly unreliable; PW-6's evidence contradicted PW-1's claim to have witnessed the incident; PW-27 failed to prove disclosure and seizure memos
post_offence_conduct: Not stated for the accused; the Court noted that family members and villagers left the body unprotected overnight
bail_history: Accused were on bail at the Supreme Court stage; bail bonds discharged. Earlier bail history not stated
trial_duration: offence: 19 September 2001 (as alleged); trial judgment: 23 July 2005; High Court: 14 September 2009; Supreme Court: 19 April 2024
legal_representation: Accused: Basavaprabhu S. Patil, Sr. Adv., with Geet Ahuja, Anirudh Sanganeria, Samarth Kashyap and Aman Banka. State: Aman Panwar, A.A.G., with V. N. Raghupathy, Manendra Pal Gupta, Shivam Singh Baghal and Harsh Gattani
investigation_status: FIR registered (Ex P-10) on the complaint; investigation concluded; charge sheet filed; case committed to Sessions; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Daily Diary entry not produced; contradiction on whether the complaint was written at the police station or recorded at the complainant's home; FIR held to be a post-investigation document; disclosure and seizure memos not proved by PW-27; no serological opinion obtained
appeal_history: Trial court: all accused acquitted (23 July 2005). High Court: State's appeal allowed in part; A-1 to A-3 convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC (14 September 2009). Supreme Court: appeal by A-1 to A-3 allowed; High Court judgment reversed and acquittal restored
prosecution_argument: The State argued that the High Court re-appreciated the evidence and rightly found the eyewitnesses (PW-1, PW-2, PW-4, PW-6, PW-15) convincing; the FIR was promptly lodged; the trial court's contradictions were trivial and its acquittal perverse
defence_argument: The High Court reversed acquittal without finding perversity or misreading, and re-appreciated evidence as a first court; eyewitnesses did not act as eyewitnesses would; the FIR was post-investigation; the complainant was shown the weapons on the day of the incident; the disclosure statements and recovery memos were unsigned by the accused
legal_principle_applied: Appeal against acquittal may be allowed only where the acquittal suffers from patent perversity, misreading or omission to consider material evidence, or where only the view consistent with guilt is possible; the appellate court must record pertinent findings on these factors. Statements under Evidence Act s.27 are admissible only to the extent they lead to discovery, and the investigating officer must narrate the conversation; the Evidence Act s.60 requires direct oral evidence
precedent_relied_upon: Rajesh Prasad v. State of Bihar [2022] 3 SCR 1046 : (2022) 3 SCC 471; H.D. Sundara v. State of Karnataka [2023] 14 SCR 47 : (2023) 9 SCC 581; Mohd. Abdul Hafeez v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1983) 1 SCC 143; Subramanya v. State of Karnataka [2022] 14 SCR 828 : 2022 SCC Online SC 1400 (relied on). Referred to: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Deoman Upadhyaya [1961] 1 SCR 14 : AIR 1960 SC 1125; Ramanand @ Nandlal Bharti v. State of Uttar Pradesh [2022] 5 SCR 162 : 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1396
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds discharged; accused need not surrender

case_title: Achin Gupta v. State of Haryana & Anr.
accused_socioeconomic_status: Alleged only in the FIR: the accused earns about Rs. 1,50,000 a month. The Court made no finding on this.
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband and wife). A divorce petition filed by the accused in July 2019 and a domestic violence case filed by his mother were also pending between them.
evidence_type: Documentary: the FIR and chargesheet papers. No witness testimony or medical evidence is discussed in the judgment.
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Not stated. The case was pending before the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Hisar; no decision is recorded.
high_court_outcome: Quashing petition dismissed; High Court declined to quash the criminal proceedings under s.482 Cr.P.C. (judgment dated 05.04.2022)
neutral_facts: The victim alleged that after her marriage the accused's family repeatedly demanded further dowry. She said her family had already given cash for a car, gold ornaments and furniture, and that her stridhan was handed over at the wedding. She alleged that the accused's family taunted her about inadequate dowry and beat and abused her over food, household work, and demands for gold bangles and a diamond set. She alleged that the accused beat her when he was drunk, controlled her salary and pocket money, did not allow her to make phone calls, and had an extra-marital affair she was threatened not to disclose. She further alleged that during the Covid-19 lockdown in March 2020 the accused disconnected water and television services and took their minor son away, and that she was forced to return to her parents' home. The initial investigation found the report to be false, but the case was later reassigned to another officer. The family gathered cash from various sources and, on instructions from the callers, left the money in a car at a hospital area and then went to another location. neutral_facts: The victim, who had been arraigned as an accused in a criminal case registered at a police station, came to that police station late at night, accompanied by his advocate and two sisters, to surrender. The prosecution case is that two police officers, the accused, assaulted the victim with fists and sticks at separate intervals inside the police station, causing multiple injuries across his body, after which he became unconscious and was placed in a lockup. The next evening the victim was produced before a Magistrate, who remanded him to judicial custody, and he was lodged in a central prison, where his condition deteriorated. He was taken to a civil hospital and declared dead early the following morning. Two sisters testified that they saw the beatings, and a third detainee in the lockup also gave evidence. The sisters described blows landing on the back, arms, chest, thighs and ankles. A telegram sent by one sister to the state police headquarters alleged custodial torture, and a formal complaint followed about three weeks after the incident. The post-mortem examination recorded multiple external abrasions and bruises and internal injuries, including fractures of the sternum and ribs and ruptures of the lung, liver and spleen. The medical jurist opined that the injuries were fresh, occurring within six to eight hours of death, and that a person with such injuries could not climb stairs without support. The group confronted the victim, caught hold of him and assaulted him with kanta and knives. On hearing his cries for help, the victim's son, another witness and the victim's brother ran towards the spot. As they approached, the accused fired a shot into the air from the pistol, after which the group fled from the scene through the south-western side. prosecution_argument: Clear motive from the property dispute; the appellant was part of the unlawful assembly with common object to kill; firing to enable escape was an overt act; non-recovery of the pistol not fatal; ocular evidence supported by medical evidence; the key eyewitness Laxmi Narain was later killed, so could not be examined
defence_argument: No firearm injuries and no recovery of pistol or cartridge; the appellant's role was only firing into the air; the omission to examine Laxmi Narain and the scribe Kuldeep was fatal; conviction based on suspicion, so the benefit of doubt should be given
legal_principle_applied: Section 149 IPC creates vicarious liability; the question is whether the accused was a member of the unlawful assembly, not whether he actually took active part; no overt act need be imputed to the individual member
precedent_relied_upon: Krishnappa v. State of Karnataka [2012] 6 SCR 1068 : (2012) 11 SCC 237; Vinubhai Ranchhodbhai Patel v. Rajivbhai Dudabhai Patel [2018] 6 SCR 1050 : (2018) 7 SCC 743; Yunis alias Kariya v. State of M.P. (2003) 1 SCC 425
other_sentence_order: None

case_title: Santosh @ Rajesh @ Gopal v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Not stated
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.34, s.120B; Arms Act s.25(1-B)(A)
evidence_type: Circumstantial (recovery of pistol, ballistic report, disclosure statement); no eyewitness implicating the accused
confession: None by the accused. A co-accused's disclosure statement (Exhibit P-35) was relied on by the prosecution to show discovery of the pistol under ss.8 and 27, not as a confession of the accused
aggravating_circumstances: None noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of murder and related offences (IPC ss.302, 34, 120B; Arms Act s.25(1-B)(A)); sentence not stated
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction upheld
neutral_facts: On the night of 13 November 2011, at about 9.30 p.m., the victim and his mother were sleeping at their house in a village in Dewas district. Someone called the victim's name from outside and the victim opened the door. The victim's mother testified that she heard a gunshot and ran towards him. A second shot then struck the victim in the chest and he fell. Going outside, the mother saw the victim's wife and son standing on the opposite side of the house. She also saw two individuals with covered faces fleeing on a motorcycle. A country-made pistol was later recovered from the accused. A ballistic report found that the bullet recovered from the victim's body had been fired from that pistol. The prosecution case was that the location of the pistol was disclosed by a co-accused, who has since died, and that this disclosure led to the recovery of the pistol and to the arrest of the accused. No eyewitness identified the accused as a participant in the shooting. The case against the accused rested on the recovery of the pistol and the ballistic report. A First Information Report was registered on 13 November 2011, and a chargesheet was filed against several persons.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from a gunshot wound to the chest
premeditation_planning: Not stated. The prosecution alleged hired killers, but the Court made no finding on premeditation or planning
motive: Not identified
key_evidence_accepted: Recovery of the pistol (Exhibit P-6) from the accused; ballistic report (Exhibit P-57) linking the pistol to the bullet (Exhibit B-1) recovered from the victim's body
witness_credibility: Not stated as a credibility assessment. The Court noted that no eyewitness implicates the accused
post_offence_conduct: Not stated
bail_history: Granted by the Supreme Court on suspension of sentence on 08.04.2024

legal_representation: Accused (appellant): Ms. Shweta Garg, Ashish Gopal Garg, Rakesh Garg, Advocates. State of Madhya Pradesh: Nachiketa Joshi, Senior Advocate / A.A.G., with Pashupathi Nath Razdan, Pushpender Singh, Mirza Kayesh Begg, Ms. Maitreyee Jagat Joshi, Ms. Ruby, Advocates
investigation_status: FIR registered; chargesheet filed; trial completed with verdict
procedural_irregularity: None noted
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction set aside
prosecution_argument: The pistol was recovered from the accused, and its discovery was based on the co-accused's disclosure statement. The ballistic report links the pistol to the fatal bullet. Both are admissible under ss.8 and 27 of the Evidence Act
defence_argument: Not stated
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain excluding every hypothesis of innocence. Discovery under ss.8 and 27 of the Evidence Act is assessed by considering alternative hypotheses. Further evidence linking the accused to the actual murder is required
